academy-resolution-1775:
In 1775 the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris took a firm step. The school said it would no longer read plans for perpetual motion. Such plans claimed a wheel or mill that runs for all time with no fuel. The French text prints the full terms of the ban.

The school gives hard grounds for the step. Such schemes waste the funds of poor homes, it says, and yield no gain at all. Hope of a prize kept men at the vain hunt for years. The ban marks the point where top science shut the door on the dream.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
In 1875 the third volume of Allen's Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica took its place in the set. The design stays fixed: every known proving symptom, arranged by remedy, with nothing left out for neatness. Allen believed a prescriber should judge the record, not an editor's summary.

Long entries let patterns surface on their own, as the same odd sign recurs across provers. Short ones show how thin some drug records still were. Either way, the volume serves the working method of the school: match the patient's signs to the fullest drug picture available, then choose.

Allen's Encyclopaedia reached Volume IV in 1875, and the archive of provings kept growing steadily. Timothy Field Allen served as gatherer rather than judge, printing proving symptoms from journals, books, and private reports alike. Each remedy entry sorts its harvest by part of the body, in the set's fixed order.

The worth of the whole set lies in that restraint. Later writers could build keynotes and guiding symptoms on ground Allen had cleared, knowing the raw record sat behind them. Volume IV, mid-set, shows the scale of his ambition: ten full volumes to hold what the world's provers had seen.
arxiv-2510-00075:
Rishi Bommasani wrote this 2025 position paper arguing that the NeurIPS conference should lead agreement on AI policy. Good policy needs solid evidence, and science has ways to gather and sum up such evidence. What it lacks, Bommasani argues, is a trusted way to state where experts agree. He proposes that the largest AI research meeting fill that gap itself.

The paper draws lessons from the IPCC, the panel that builds shared views on climate science. Bommasani answers two likely objections head-on in the text. One says AI experts disagree too much for any shared view to form. The other says policy work is not the business of a research meeting. He finds both weak, and he sketches pilot steps NeurIPS could take first. The paper matters as a plan for turning research into policy advice.
arxiv-2510-00175:
Luca Morf and Ravit Helled published this 2025 paper asking what Uranus and Neptune are really made of. Textbooks call both planets ice giants, rich in water and similar ices. Earlier interior models either forced rigid assumptions or used rough empirical profiles. The authors built a framework that stays open-minded yet physically strict, then let it explore both planets.

Starting from random density profiles, their algorithm settles on models matching gravity data and basic physics. The surviving models span rock-dominated to water-dominated interiors for both planets. Every model keeps convective zones of ionic water, a plausible source of the odd magnetic fields. Uranus seems to generate its field deeper inside than Neptune does. The authors conclude the ice-giant label may be a historical accident, and better data are needed to settle the recipe.
arxiv-2510-00875:
Molinari and Thoresen control the false discovery rate with a Bayesian form of the mirror statistic, in this 2025 arXiv paper on high-dimensional statistics. Picking predictors from thousands of candidates, as in biomarker studies, demands a bound on how many picks are false. The mirror statistic gives that bound, but its frequentist form needs two sets of coefficient estimates from splitting the data in half. The authors replace the split with a Bayesian fit.

Its posterior supplies both sides of the mirror statistic, so no data are thrown away. Automatic differentiation variational inference keeps the computation scalable, and priors such as the horseshoe shrink null coefficients as required. The method covers continuous and discrete outcomes, interactions, and mixed models with repeated measurements. In simulations it held the false discovery rate at its target, erring conservative at worst. It compared well with idealized knockoff procedures.
arxiv-2510-01075:
Goswami and eleven co-authors investigate lattice distortion in the tetraboride HoB4 in this 2025 arXiv paper on condensed matter physics. In HoB4 the holmium form a Shastry-Sutherland lattice, and the crystal orders antiferromagnetically near 7.1 kelvin, with a second transition near 5.7 kelvin. Competing magnetic and quadrupolar order parameters, coupled to the lattice, were suspected behind the phases. The team probed the structure with x-ray diffraction and ultrasound, backed by crystal field calculations.

Below the lower transition the structure turns monoclinic, which the authors read as the fingerprint of ferroquadrupolar ordering. The softening of one elastic modulus near that temperature fits the same picture. Between room temperature and 3.5 kelvin the distortion amplitude reaches half an angstrom. A lattice instability starts at the first transition, well above the quadrupolar one. Crystal field analysis points to a degenerate ground state for the holmium ions.
arxiv-2510-01375:
Ibrahim, Rozanov, and Rei turn retrieval from a permanent crutch into a teacher whose lessons the student eventually memorizes. Agent models fail predictably in interactive tasks, grabbing items before conditions are met or repeating commands. Retrieval guidance fixes behavior at run time, but the database and overhead follow every deployment forever.

Failed episodes are mined for compact, reusable hints about what went wrong. A teacher, armed with one retrieved hint, produces cleaner solution trajectories. Students train on those trajectories with the hints stripped out, forcing real internalization. Household and shopping benchmarks showed large success gains with fewer tokens spent. Two model sizes confirmed the pipeline is not a one-scale trick. Hint removal is the step that separates learning from copying. Token savings against the retrieval teacher ranged widely by environment. Failures become the curriculum under this scheme.
arxiv-2510-01475:
Mulayim and co-authors ran a rare head-to-head field trial: a reinforcement learning controller and a model predictive controller each ran an occupied Indiana home's heat pump for a month. Predictive control saves energy but demands heavy engineering per house, limiting scale. Learning promises automation, yet real homes had barely tested it.

The learning controller saved slightly more energy than the predictive one against the existing thermostat. Comfort suffered modestly more under the learner before normalization. Normalized for comfort, the two approaches landed close. Less engineering effort was the learner's decisive practical edge. West Lafayette hosted the occupied test house and its heat pump. Safety and comparability constrained both deployments equally by design. Twenty-two versus twenty percent savings headline the energy comparison. Engineering hours are the scalability currency houses pay in. Field evidence beats simulation folklore for practitioners.
arxiv-2510-01775:
Dhiman and five co-authors observe nonlinear motion at the level of single excitations in this 2025 physics paper. Nonlinear behavior usually needs strong driving, which clashes with delicate quantum applications like sensing. Their platform joins a mechanical oscillator to a superconducting microwave circuit. The circuit's strong Kerr nonlinearity reshapes how the whole system responds.

That nonlinearity lowered the threshold for nonlinear dynamics by four orders of magnitude. Self-sustained oscillations then appeared at drive levels of only a few photons. The team also built a theoretical model of the device and tested it carefully. Its parameter-based predictions matched the measured behavior in detail. Such agreement signals a deep grasp of the physics at play. The authors argue this platform suits experiments with non-classical microwave drives. It could serve future quantum sensors that need nonlinearity without brute-force power.
arxiv-2510-02175:
Ablinger and six co-authors compute the three-loop matching relations of the variable flavor number scheme in this 2025 particle physics paper. Colliders probe quarks across huge energy ranges, where heavy quarks gradually behave as light ones. The scheme stitches those regimes together with matching relations for parton distributions. This paper delivers them at three-loop order for the single-mass case.

Both unpolarized and polarized distributions are covered, in a process-independent form. Light partons plus charm and bottom distributions receive numerical results. The polarized sector uses the Larin scheme, with two-loop results also given in a second common scheme. Fast numerical codes for the massive operator matrix elements accompany the paper. Precision phenomenology at the LHC depends on exactly these ingredients. Matching errors otherwise masquerade as new physics in distribution fits. The work completes a long-running symbolic computation program for heavy-flavor transitions.
arxiv-2510-02475:
Li and co-authors bring statistical model checking to processor side channel security. Their 2025 computer architecture paper tackles a measurement problem. Side channels leak secrets through timing and cache behavior. Attacks and defenses both vary by chance in real machines. Noise from other running programs adds more randomness. Simple abstract models miss the details where leaks live. Statistical model checking tests real simulator traces instead. It gives rigorous guarantees about security properties. Architects can use detailed cycle-by-cycle simulators directly. No separate formal model needs building first.

Three case studies demonstrate the approach in practice. The method handles rich properties with clear confidence levels. Variability from system noise becomes part of the test. Defenses can be compared on equal footing. Security claims gain numbers instead of impressions. The authors urge architects to adopt the technique broadly. Better testing should yield better processor defenses.
arxiv-2510-02575:
Anderson and El-Azab clarify when a simpler picture of crystal dislocations stays valid. Their 2025 materials theory paper studies continuum dislocation dynamics. The theory tracks defect lines in metals through density fields. Coarse graining those fields can erase parts of the population. Oppositely aimed line pieces cancel in the averaged description. One leading theory treats dislocations as nearly parallel bundles. A rival spreads them over local directions instead. The difference is really about spatial scale. Fine resolution resolves single lines with nothing erased. Coarse resolution lets whole loops share one point.

The authors build a profile of orientation fluctuations. It measures deviations from the local average direction. A volume averaged version links fluctuations to the graining length. Transport of the lines depends on those fluctuations directly. Modelers can now see which regime their mesh sits in. Metal plasticity predictions rest on this choice. Clear regime boundaries prevent silent modeling errors.
arxiv-2510-02975:
Barjini and Mattila track the bending of a flexible robot arm with cheap sensors. Light arms save energy but flex and vibrate as they move. Knowing the true tip pose is thus a real challenge. Their method treats the arm as a chain of stiff segments. Each unit reports tilt and spin for its segment. A complementary filter blends those readings into joint angles.

Particle swarm tuning set the filter's parameters from ground truth data. A small neural network then mopped up the leftover errors. The network uses radial basis functions to correct position and angle. Bench tests checked the full chain during vertical motion. Root mean square errors landed near two ten-thousandths of a meter. Angle error was of the same tiny order. Only the inertial units are needed while the arm runs. The design avoids costly or fragile external sensors.
arxiv-2510-03075:
Farid and co-authors ask what lets image generators mix known ideas in new ways. A model may know red cars and blue boats separately. Painting a red boat tests compositional generalization. The team varied design choices in controlled experiments. Two factors stood out across the trials. The training target's form was the first factor.

Models trained on continuous distributions composed ideas well. Models trained on discrete category targets composed poorly. The second factor was how fully the prompt described the parts. Complete conditioning helped, while thinned conditioning broke compositions. The team then patched a discrete model called MaskGIT. An added continuous objective, based on JEPA prediction, relaxed its loss. Composition scores for the patched model improved. Circuit analysis hinted at cleaner, factor-wise pathways inside. The findings give builders two clear design rules. Objectives and conditioning should guard meaning structure.
arxiv-2510-03475:
Abhijeet and Chakravorty present a 2025 arXiv paper that reframes robot control methods inside one optimization lens. Optimal control picks action sequences that steer a system at lowest cost. Two workhorse methods, DDP and iLQR, grew up as cousins with murky kinship. The authors view both through constrained sequential quadratic programming, a method for hard optimization. That lens shows exactly where the two methods agree and where they part ways.

Their analysis casts iLQR as a principled member of that family, not a cheap knockoff of DDP. iLQR always yields a cost cutting direction and carries convergence guarantees. DDP and Newton style steps lack those guarantees far from the best path, and tests on pendulum and cart pole tasks back the theory. Skipping second order terms turns out to help, not hurt, in this light. Control engineers gain a clearer map for choosing tools on robots and self driving systems.
arxiv-2510-04175:
Kozioł presents this 2025 arXiv paper reporting a hidden force in sheared crystals that breaks the symmetry of sound waves. Molecular dynamics simulations of face-centered cubic crystals, set up as in dislocation studies, showed behavior that static elasticity cannot explain. Interpreting the simulations through a chain-of-springs-and-masses model revealed the culprit. A force appears inside the crystal perpendicular to the applied shear, along the dislocation line direction.

The force is dynamic in origin and grows with the square of the applied pressure. It breaks the axial symmetry of transverse acoustic wave propagation. Consequences include a nonlinear, inelastic crystal response and chaotic patterns in atomic motion. Kozioł derives an effective interaction potential analytically and builds a matching dynamical model. The findings warn that simulation setups standard in dislocation research generate physics beyond textbook elasticity. Crystal plasticity models may need to account for this symmetry breaking.
arxiv-2510-04475:
Matheus Castro and Gary Froyland wrote this 2025 paper in dynamical systems on counting the best behaved measures. When one system maps onto another, the natural prize is a measure of maximal relative entropy. Such a measure spreads as evenly as the base system allows. Earlier work on symbolic systems found only finitely many such measures in nice cases. Castro and Froyland asked what happens for smooth skew products, where a chaotic base drives a smooth fiber.

They prove that such a system has at most countably many ergodic hyperbolic measures of maximal relative entropy. Countable is weaker than finite, yet it still rules out a continuous swarm of maximizers. For two dimensional fibers with positive relative entropy, the same countable bound holds. Their bound is sharp: they build a smooth example with infinitely many such measures. The result extends a symbolic theory into the smooth world.
arxiv-2510-04575:
Juliane Klamser and Ludovic Berthier wrote this 2025 paper on how a still particle mass can erupt into chaos. They simulated a dense two dimensional assembly of particles that repel each other. Pairs of particles pushed with non reciprocal forces, where the push back is not equal to the push. Below a sharp threshold strength, the system settles into an absorbing state with no motion. Above it, the mass churns in a chaotic steady state.

The chaotic phase shows tangled velocity patterns and strong mixing across the sample. Its look recalls active turbulence in swarms of self propelled agents. The onset of chaos follows the scaling laws of directed percolation, a classic universality class for such transitions. That match holds with striking precision in their data. The authors argue the transition is generic for dense disordered materials driven from within. Glasses, granular piles, and dense active matter all share that setup.
arxiv-2510-04875:
Demi Allen, Thomas Jordan, and Benjamin Ward wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on how often fractal points return near a moving target. The shrinking target problem follows points whose orbit keeps landing inside targets that shrink over time. The size of that returning set is measured by its Hausdorff dimension. Most studies use round targets on self similar spaces. This paper uses rectangle targets on self similar carpets, fractal sheets built by repeated scaling.

The authors compute the dimension of the returning set. A surprise emerges: the answer depends on where the rectangle is centered. In most problems the center played no role at all. The rectangle breaks the symmetry that made position irrelevant. Their result extends a theorem of Wang and Wu from the round case. Exact dimensions tell dynamicists how large the exceptional returning sets truly are. The center dependence warns that geometry details can matter in fractal dynamics.
arxiv-2510-05375:
Andrea C. Burgess and six co-authors color combinatorial designs without ruining any block in this 2025 arXiv paper. A weak coloring assigns colors to points so no block ends up monochromatic. A block-equitable coloring goes further, balancing color counts inside every block. The paper extends both ideas from block designs to group divisible designs and packings.

The authors determine exactly when a uniform group divisible design admits a block-equitable coloring. They give a direct construction of maximum two-colorable packings with block size four. A known size bound for such packings generalizes to more than two colors. They also prove uniform designs exist with arbitrarily many groups and almost any chromatic number. Structural analyses of small Steiner-derived examples round out the picture.
arxiv-2510-05675:
Pandey and Jain ask when a growing, dividing chemical system truly reproduces itself. Models of protocells and bacteria couple internal chemistry to a division rule. Balanced growth means no chemical species dilutes or accumulates across generations. Their 2025 paper shows reproduction survives only when growth and division fit together.

The same chemistry can meet three very different fates. Compatible choices give balanced exponential growth across generations. Other choices give balanced but nonexponential growth instead. Incompatible choices kill the system through explosion or collapse. The linear Hinshelwood cycle anchors the model family they study. Division triggers when a sensed variable crosses its threshold value. The authors classify which division processes produce each outcome. A geometric framework organizes the analysis across linear and nonlinear models. The rules should help design stable self-reproducing synthetic cells.
arxiv-2510-05775:
García-Oliva and colleagues disentangle why the Elbe River runs low on oxygen near Hamburg. Hypoxia episodes threaten the ecosystems and services of urban rivers. Many biochemical processes produce or consume oxygen along the river's course. Their 2025 process-based model separates their contributions in space and season.

Upstream of the city, photosynthesis and respiration dominate the oxygen budget. Downstream, mineralization, nitrification, and re-aeration take over instead. The city itself forms a transition zone of rapidly changing depth. Pathogen-driven algal lysis there may add organic matter and flip the balance. Seasonal change comes mainly from differing temperature sensitivities of the rates. Management of estuarine water quality gains concrete guidance from the split. Phytoplankton abundance also drops sharply downstream of the city in observations. One river is therefore several reactors, not a single homogeneous one. The pattern likely extrapolates to other urban rivers.
arxiv-2510-05975:
Li and colleagues design proximity graphs with provable nearest neighbor guarantees. Proximity graph indexes dominate approximate nearest neighbor search empirically. Worst-case guarantees for their query quality have largely been missing. Their 2025 alpha-convergent graph prunes edges by a shifted-scaled triangle inequality.

If the query sits within a constant distance of its true neighbor, the graph finds it exactly. Retrieval takes poly-logarithmic time under bounded intrinsic dimensionality. Otherwise the same structure still returns an approximate neighbor efficiently. A practical variant applies the pruning locally within each point's neighborhood. The adaptive variant avoids manually tuning the alpha parameter. It cuts distance computations by over fifteen percent versus the best baseline. Search steps fall by over forty-five percent. The pruning rule transfers to other proximity graph methods as well. Accuracy-efficiency trade-offs improve consistently across real-world datasets.
arxiv-2510-06175:
Yao and six co-authors present VecInfer, a method for shrinking language models' key–value cache. The cache stores attention data during generation and eats memory, especially at long contexts. Vector quantization compresses it well at moderate widths, but accuracy collapses at ultra-low widths when key outliers wreck the codebook.

VecInfer applies smooth and Hadamard transforms that suppress key outliers before quantization. The codebook then covers the real distribution, and quantization gets much easier. A custom CUDA kernel fuses dequantization with computation to cut memory traffic. Across long-context and math reasoning tests, VecInfer beat existing quantization baselines. At only two bits per value it matched full-precision performance. It sped large-batch attention nearly threefold and cut latency roughly eightfold on a Llama model at very long context. Cheaper caches mean longer conversations on the same hardware.
arxiv-2510-06275:
Mishra and three co-authors reproduce XRec, a framework for explainable recommendation. XRec, proposed by Ma and colleagues in 2024, uses collaborative instruction tuning so models can explain recommendations. Reproduction matters because the original relied on a proprietary model.

The team rebuilt the experiments on the original code, swapping GPT-3.5-turbo for Llama 3. They extended it by altering input embeddings, or deleting output embeddings, of the Mixture of Experts module. The reproduction confirms XRec generates personalized explanations effectively. Collaborative information improved stability, as originally claimed. Yet XRec did not beat every baseline on every metric. The extension shows Mixture of Experts embeddings strongly shape explanation structure. The mixed verdict is a useful reminder that headline claims in recommender research deserve independent checks with open models. They release an open-source evaluation implementation, making future checks cheaper and more transparent.
arxiv-2510-06675:
Xu Bai, Muhammed Islam, Rajkumar Buyya, and Adel Toosi work on placing software services across cloud and edge computers. Their 2025 paper addresses latency-sensitive apps built from microservices, which are small modular units. Resources at the edge are varied and change over time. Fixed placements quickly become poor choices.

Their algorithm, REACH, uses reinforcement learning to move services in real time. Unlike older methods, it updates only the pods that actually need to move. That selective approach cuts the overhead of rescheduling. Tests ran on a real Kubernetes testbed with three benchmark applications. REACH cut average end-to-end latency by about eight to ten percent across those apps. It also smoothed out latency spikes when cluster conditions changed. Compared with default placement, latency fell much further in some configurations. The work targets apps that must answer fast while running partly at the edge.
arxiv-2510-07075:
Yu Li and four co-authors find a carbon material that conducts heat better when stretched, defying the trend. Their 2025 paper studies screw-dislocated graphites, carbon structures threaded by spiral defects. Most materials lose thermal conductivity under even small strains. That fragility threatens high-performance electronics, which need heat flow.

Simulations driven by a machine-learned atomic potential revealed the anomaly. Cross-plane thermal conductivity rose under both stretching and squeezing. Under tension along the dislocation axis, it more than doubled at strains. The stretched structure tilts its dislocation interfaces, lengthening the heat transfer paths in a helpful way. Compression instead strengthens the interlayer forces, speeding phonons along. Under compression, conductivity climbed by over seven hundred percent in their runs. The material beats multilayer graphene by an order of magnitude. An analytic formula links conductivity to dislocation count and strain. Designers gain a recipe for strain-tunable heat spreaders.
arxiv-2510-07175:
Han, Song, Lee, and Jo measure how much language models have memorized psychology test material. Their 2025 paper studies surveys used to rate values, personality, and moral views. Researchers often give these surveys to models and report the scores as traits. That practice fails if models simply recall the surveys from training. The team built a framework to quantify that contamination. It checks three things: recall of items, recall of scoring, and matching target scores.

The study covered twenty-one models and four widely used surveys. Popular inventories showed strong contamination. Models not only recalled the questions, but also grasped how answers map to scores. They could even steer their answers toward a chosen target score. That finding undercuts many published claims about model personalities. The framework lets researchers run those checks.
arxiv-2510-07275:
Huang tackles the geometry questions that a cutting-edge equation solver needs when its walls are defined only by a formula. The 2025 conference paper concerns Walk on Stars, a Monte Carlo method for partial differential equations. Queries like the closest silhouette point had no reliable method on such surfaces. The author reformulates every needed query as a constrained optimization or satisfaction problem.

A branch-and-bound search using interval arithmetic then solves those hard, non-convex problems rigorously. The work is the first to handle closest silhouette points and Robin boundary radius bounds on closed implicit surfaces. With all queries in place, the solver can work mesh-free inside implicit domains. Limits remain: boundary sampling is still slow, and neural surface fields are not yet supported.
arxiv-2510-07375:
Kokron and Chen sharpen a variance-cutting trick for cosmology simulations by extending it to three-point statistics. Their 2025 paper studies control variates, cheap analytic estimates paired with costly simulations to cancel noise. Perturbation theory supplies candidates that can be computed exactly. The test case is the matter bispectrum, which measures how density waves couple across scales. Eulerian perturbation theory gives tractable variates for any statistic, but their grip on the simulated signal fades as scales combine. The popular Zeldovich approximation behaves oppositely, correlating worse at large scales here.

The authors design a shifted control variate that keeps the correct leading behavior and a computable bispectrum. On a mid-redshift matter bispectrum, it matched the noise reduction of averaging ten thousand simulations at the largest scales. That equivalence means one expensive simulation plus algebra can do the work of a small computing center.
arxiv-2510-07475:
Zhang and co-authors recast the tuning of multi-agent system prompts as a problem in probabilistic inference. Their 2025 paper introduces MAPRO. Teams of language model agents beat single agents on many workflows, but their prompts interact explosively: the search space balloons, and when output fails, nobody knows which agent to blame. MAPRO formulates prompt choice for the whole system as maximum a posteriori inference, the search for the most probable joint configuration. A language-guided variant of belief propagation passes messages between agents to solve it.

Across diverse tasks, MAPRO beat single-agent and multi-agent prompt optimization baselines of every type. The framework works as a plug-and-play layer over existing systems. Its optimization trajectories remain interpretable, showing operators how the prompt set evolved and why.
arxiv-2510-07575:
Cheng, Wohnig, Gupta, and a large group of co-authors argue that AI benchmarking is broken and propose to rebuild it like a proctored exam. Their 2025 position paper catalogs the rot. Static public test sets leak into training data. Developers report scores selectively, fueling hype cycles. Weak quality control lets biased evaluations favor particular approaches, sometimes unintentionally. The authors compare the situation to financial markets before credible rating agencies: without trusted oversight, claims cannot be priced.

Their remedy is a unified framework that is live, secret, and quality-controlled by construction. A prototype called PeerBench combines reputation-weighted validators, rolling renewal of tasks, and fully auditable aggregation of scores. Secrecy blocks contamination, liveness blocks overfitting to a frozen set, and auditability blocks quiet manipulation.
arxiv-2510-07775:
Mahmoud and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a cost of making language models more truthful. Work on hallucination has improved detection and reduced false statements. The authors show that these gains can weaken safety alignment. Models that answer more factually also refuse harmful requests less reliably. The cause lies inside the model, where the features for hallucination and refusal overlap.

Because the features overlap, alignment methods suppress factual knowledge by accident. Fine-tuning on benign, safety-curated data can degrade refusal behavior. The authors propose separating refusal features from hallucination features with sparse autoencoders. They then protect the refusal directions during fine-tuning through orthogonalization. On reasoning tasks and harmful-request benchmarks, the method preserved refusals and task skill at once. The study warns that truthfulness and safety must be tuned together, not traded blindly. Builders should test for this side effect in every alignment run.
arxiv-2510-08075:
Hao, Liao, Jing, and Wei wrote this 2025 statistics paper extending conformal selection to candidates that must satisfy several conditions at once. Drug discovery, precision medicine, and model alignment all shortlist candidates under limited budgets. Conformal selection controls the false discovery rate rigorously, but only for a single threshold. Real shortlists combine conditions, joined by and or by or. The authors' algorithm, MCCS, handles both with finite-sample guarantees.

For conjunctive conditions they design a new nonconformity score with regional monotonicity. For disjunctive conditions they apply a global multiple-testing procedure. Together these keep the false discovery rate controlled under multiple constraints. Experiments across domains showed MCCS beating baselines, generalizing across condition combinations, and scaling to multi-task settings. A same-domain assumption remains a limitation. Still, the work matches the tool to how shortlists are actually built.
arxiv-2510-08375:
Sebastian Schuster, Jessica Santiago, Justin Feng, and Matt Visser revisit limits on primordial black hole dark matter in a 2025 arXiv paper. Primordial black holes formed in the early universe might make up some dark matter. Limits on their share come from Hawking radiation, the slow glow that evaporates small black holes. Most limits assume a plain Schwarzschild black hole that neither spins nor carries charge.

Real astrophysical black holes spin, matching the rotating Kerr solution better. Charge is usually dismissed, since today's black holes neutralize fast in space. But early-universe extensions of particle physics could leave primordial holes charged, even if the charged particles later vanished. The authors show such charges can greatly change evaporation limits. The effect is strongest for near-extremal holes, which sit close to the maximum charge or spin allowed.
arxiv-2510-08475:
Jhen Hsieh, Kuan-Hsun Tu, Kuo-Han Hung, and Tsung-Wei Ke turn videos of human hands into robot skills in a 2025 arXiv paper. Teaching two-handed dexterous manipulation usually needs motion capture, depth sensors, or scanned object models. Their framework, DexMan, works directly on third-person videos of people handling rigid objects. It controls a full humanoid robot in simulation, not just floating hands.

DexMan needs no camera calibration, depth data, or ground-truth motion labels, the authors stress. Contact-based rewards improve learning from noisy hand and object poses estimated in wild videos. On the TACO benchmark, it set state-of-the-art object pose estimation scores. Its reinforcement learning policy beat prior methods by nineteen percent success rate on OakInk-v2. Skills can also come from synthetic videos, enabling large diverse training sets. This avoids manual collection and costly motion capture entirely.
arxiv-2510-08575:
Haofei Xu, Daniel Barath, Andreas Geiger, and Marc Pollefeys make Gaussian splatting recurrent in a 2025 arXiv paper called ReSplat. Feed-forward splatting models are fast and handle sparse inputs, but one single pass limits their accuracy. ReSplat instead refines its 3D Gaussians iteratively, learning update rules rather than computing gradients. The rendering error itself serves as the feedback signal guiding each refinement.

Because feedback comes from the model's own renders, it adapts naturally to unseen data at test time. A compact starter model works in a heavily subsampled space, producing sixteen times fewer Gaussians than per-pixel rivals. That thrift keeps the recurrent updates cheap enough to run repeatedly. Experiments spanned two, eight, and sixteen input views, several resolutions, and the DL3DV and RealEstate10K data sets. ReSplat reached state-of-the-art quality while using far fewer Gaussians and rendering faster.
arxiv-2510-08675:
Cheyanne Shariat, Kareem El-Badry, and Soumyadeep Bhattacharjee test how trustworthy stellar age estimates are using twin stars in a 2025 arXiv paper. Precise ages underpin Galactic archaeology, the reconstruction of the Milky Way's history. Wide binaries are ideal testbeds: both stars formed together, so their inferred ages should agree. Mismatches expose underestimated errors in age catalogs.

Subgiant ages using spectroscopic metallicities proved consistent within their reported uncertainties. Fractional uncertainties of five to ten percent are realistically achievable for those stars, they find. Published photometric subgiant ages, by contrast, underestimate true uncertainties by factors of two to three. Spectroscopic ages for red giants and red clump stars had reliable uncertainties but lower precision, at twenty-five to thirty percent. Precise subgiant ages hinge on accurate metal and alpha-element measurements.
arxiv-2510-08975:
Shi and colleagues link the solar wind that reaches Earth to how magnetically tangled its source regions were, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The wind is a constant stream of charged particles from the Sun. Its source areas, called active regions, range from simple single-polarity patches to complex knots of mixed polarity. The team sorted every active region from two full solar cycles, spanning 1999 to 2020, into simple, intermediate, and complex classes.

Complex regions made up only about an eighth of all regions, yet they supplied well over a third of the active-region wind measured near Earth. As complexity rose, the wind carried stronger magnetic fields, higher charge states, more helium, and a stronger chemical fingerprint of low-atmosphere material. The authors conclude that complex regions are disproportionately effective wind factories. Their fierce fields and frequent activity heat plasma harder and lift helium-rich gas into the upper atmosphere.
arxiv-2510-09075:
Winn reviews how bound pairs of heavy quarks serve as thermometers for the hottest matter made on Earth, in this 2025 arXiv paper. When heavy ions collide, they briefly melt into quark-gluon plasma, where quarks move freely instead of being locked inside particles. Quarkonia, tidy bound states of a heavy quark and its antimatter twin, form early and then must survive the plasma. How many emerge, and in which states, reports on whether the melt truly happened.

The review emphasizes the qualitative picture built up in recent years. For charmonium, pairs built from charm quarks, a share of the signal appears to be born inside the plasma itself rather than surviving from the collision, a hallmark of deconfinement. For the heavier bottomonium family, the excited states melt away in a strict sequence, weakest first. Winn closes with an outlook on what the next round of experiments should settle.
arxiv-2510-09175:
Zhan and co-authors teach a computer to map brain networks in groups rather than pairs, under rules that keep the maps honest, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A functional brain network links regions whose activity rises and falls together. Most models connect only pairs of regions, missing dependencies involving several at once. Hypergraph models capture such group links, but they are slow and built from hand-made rules, not learned from data.

Their framework, GCM, learns group-level structure end to end under four global constraints, including signal synchronization, subject identity, and expected edge counts. It works at four resolutions, from one scan to a whole project. Across five datasets and two task settings it beat nine baselines and ten recent methods. Relative accuracy rose by up to about thirty percent, and computation time fell by about ninety-six percent. The authors also show which parts earn the gains.
arxiv-2510-09675:
Khaoula Sghaier, Badis Hammi, Ghada Gharbi, Pierre Merdrignac, Pierre Parrend, and Didier Verna survey security for software-defined vehicles in a 2025 arXiv paper. Modern cars increasingly run outsourced applications and receive continuous over-the-air updates, extending their working lives. That software-centric design widens the attack surface far beyond that of connected and autonomous vehicles as usually studied.

The authors note that research has not clearly separated software-defined vehicles from other connected cars, and that security work on them lies scattered. Their survey lays out the ecosystem, the enabling technologies, and the main cyberattack entry points created by the architecture and its operations. They introduce a layered taxonomy mapping concrete exploit techniques onto core vehicle properties and attack paths. With that map they analyse representative studies and experimental approaches, aiming to consolidate a young field and show where its defences remain thin.
arxiv-2510-10075:
Salomon Ibarra, Frida Cantu, Kaixiong Zhou, and Li Zhang detect model shortcuts in time series classification in this 2025 arXiv paper. Deep networks now beat classical distance-based methods on classifying time series. But they can rely on spurious correlations, patterns in the training data that do not hold in the real world.

Such shortcuts inflate test scores while hurting generalization. The authors use gradients, the signals that show what a model is sensitive to, to detect when a network leans on a shortcut. Catching the behavior matters because time series classifiers run in medicine, finance, and industry, where a brittle cue can fail silently. Their method offers a diagnostic before deployment, not just an accuracy number.
arxiv-2510-10275:
Majumder and Nabadwip Sarkar study uniqueness of entire functions in this 2025 arXiv paper in complex analysis. Uniqueness theory asks when knowing that two functions share certain values forces them to be identical. Here the shared data involve a function, its derivative, and its shift, the same function moved by a fixed amount.

The authors prove two results in this setting. One of them settles an open problem posed earlier by Majumder and co-authors about a conjecture of Li and Yang. Shift and derivative conditions together are delicate, since the two operations interact. Closing a named open problem gives the subfield a firmer base for the next round of questions.
arxiv-2510-10475:
A H M Rezaul Karim and Ozlem Uzuner describe their entry to a 2025 shared task on pulling medical orders out of doctor and patient conversations, in this arXiv paper. Orders cover medications, lab tests, imaging, and follow up actions. For each order, systems must find its type, description, reason, and source in the transcript. Their MasonNLP system placed fifth among 17 teams, in a field of 105 total submissions.

Their approach is deliberately simple. They used a general instruction tuned model, LLaMA-4 with 17 billion parameters, with no extra training on medical data. A single worked example in the prompt guided the model. This setup earned an average F1 score of 37.76 points across the task's measures, with clear gains on finding reasons and sources. Karim and Uzuner argue that large general models, paired with careful prompt design, make strong and scalable starting points for clinical language tasks.
arxiv-2510-10675:
Deven Panchal introduces a deliberately simple framework for building AI agent workflows, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Agentic systems that chain model calls can automate complex multi step tasks. Existing frameworks, however, often add heavy complexity, steep learning curves, and boilerplate code. Panchal's open source Python framework, simpliflow, targets rapid creation and deployment of linear, deterministic workflows instead, configured declaratively through JSON files.

Its modular design separates agent management, workflow execution, and post-processing, which keeps it easy to use and extend. Through LiteLLM it supports over 100 large language models out of the box. Panchal demonstrates uses from software development simulation to real time system interaction. A comparison with LangChain and AutoGen positions simpliflow as the tool optimized for simplicity, control, and speed where workflows are deterministic. The paper's claim is modest but clear: many agent applications do not need the heaviest machinery available.
arxiv-2510-10775:
Amber Li, Aruzhan Abil, and Juno Marques Oda predict stock movements with a graph neural network built for market wide shocks, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Graph models capture how stocks influence each other, but messages often propagate too slowly when a macroeconomic shock hits all firms at once. Their model, OmniGNN, is an attention based, multi relational dynamic network. It adds macroeconomic context through varied node and edge types.

Its central device is a sector node that acts as a global intermediary. Shocks can spread across the graph through this hub instead of diffusing hop by hop over long paths. Attention layers weigh each neighbor's contribution, and transformers capture how relations evolve over time. In experiments on public datasets, OmniGNN outperformed existing stock prediction models. It proved particularly robust during the COVID-19 period, when sudden market wide moves punished slower designs.
arxiv-2510-10875:
Hong Chen and Siddhartha Sahi answer a question Macdonald left open about his multivariable hypergeometric series, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In a 1980s manuscript, I G Macdonald defined two families of series built from Jack polynomials, symmetric functions depending on a parameter. For one parameter value they reduce to older series of matrix arguments studied by Herz and Constantine. Macdonald asked for equations pinning these series down. Chen and Sahi construct three explicit differential operators.

They show the two variable series is the unique solution of the first operator's equation, and the one variable series the unique solution of the third, under symmetry and boundary conditions. The second operator also pins down the one variable series, but only among series satisfying an extra stability condition as the number of variables varies. Earlier work had covered only small cases. The third operator appears to be new even there.
arxiv-2510-11375:
During the Maunder minimum, when sunspots nearly vanished for decades in the late seventeenth century, a handful of astronomers kept drawing the spots that appeared. Nadezhda Zolotova and Mikhail Vokhmyanin review and reanalyze those records in this 2025 arXiv solar physics paper. Their sources are the observations, drawings, and engravings of John Flamsteed in England and Philippe de La Hire in Paris between 1684 and 1702.

The authors reconstruct the coordinates, areas, and numbers of the sunspots and groups in these records. They compare the resulting time-latitude diagram with the reconstructions by Spoerer and by Ribes and Nesme-Ribes. They also estimate the sidereal differential rotation rate of the Sun and its latitudinal profile from the positions. They also evaluate what fraction of the sunspot groups obey or violate Joy's law, the tilt pattern of bipolar groups, testing whether that pattern held during the minimum.
arxiv-2510-11575:
A dip in starlight that looked like a planet turned out to be two small stars eclipsing each other, and volunteers spotted it first. Sean M. O'Brien and a large team of professional and citizen scientists characterize the system NGTS-EB-8 in this 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. The pair was flagged as a planet candidate in Next Generation Transit Survey data by participants in the Planet Hunters NGTS citizen science project.

High-resolution spectroscopy showed the supposed planet is a double-lined eclipsing binary: both stars are near-equal M-dwarfs. By modeling the photometry together with radial velocity measurements, the team determined an orbital period of 4.2 days and derived the masses and radii of both stars. Such near-twin M-dwarf pairs are valuable benchmarks for testing low-mass star models. The discovery showcases how volunteers surface candidates automated searches miss.
arxiv-2510-11675:
Dipkamal Bhusal and colleagues tackle a trust problem in explaining how deep neural networks make decisions. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents FACE, a method that pulls human-understandable concepts out of a network so people can see what ideas drive its predictions. The authors argue that older automatic methods often extract concepts that do not match how the model actually decides, so the explanations mislead.

FACE builds on a matrix-splitting technique and adds a penalty that keeps the concept-based predictions close to the model's original predictions. It also learns from the classifier's own labels, which older methods ignored. The team proves that their penalty bounds how far the two sets of predictions can drift apart. Tested on the ImageNet, COCO, and CelebA datasets, FACE beat rival methods on measures of faithfulness and sparseness.
arxiv-2510-11875:
Srikanth B. Iyengar surveys a flowering of algebra that grew out of one of mathematics' most famous proofs. In the 1990s Andrew Wiles, with Richard Taylor, proved that semistable elliptic curves are modular, settling a conjecture tied to Fermat's Last Theorem. The proof's machinery, called modularity lifting, compared two rings through the deformation theory of Galois representations. Iyengar's 2025 arXiv article reviews the pure commutative algebra that this machinery spawned.

The overview covers congruence modules, complete intersection rings, Koszul complexes, and a quantity called the Wiles defect. It explains freeness criteria, tests for when a module behaves like a simple stack of copies of a ring. Iyengar focuses on recent joint work with Sylvie Brochard, Chandrashekhar Khare, and Jeffrey Manning. A companion article by Khare, Manning, and Iyengar covers the number theory payoffs. Together the two pieces map a landscape where algebra and number theory keep enriching each other.
arxiv-2510-11975:
Zouaoui Bekri and Nicola Fabiano introduce a new contraction condition in fixed point theory. A contraction is a mapping that pulls points closer together, guaranteeing a unique point that maps to itself. Two classical families, Singh's contractions and Chatterjea's, each capture this idea differently. Their 2025 arXiv paper merges them into one condition, the Singh-Chatterjea contraction, imposed on the p-th iterate of a mapping, meaning the map applied repeatedly.

The authors prove fixed point theorems for these mappings in complete metric spaces, where every Cauchy sequence converges. Their results extend and unify the classical theorems of Singh and Chatterjea, recovering each as a special case. Convergence is part of the package: iterating the map from any starting point homes in on the fixed point. The paper supplies illustrative examples showing the new condition covers mappings the older ones miss. A simple numerical implementation demonstrates the iteration in practice.
arxiv-2510-12475:
Dutta reviews how jets from newborn low mass stars regulate star formation and record its history, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics review. Protostars feed from accretion disks buried in dusty envelopes. Their jets carry off angular momentum, the rotational inertia that would otherwise halt accretion. Without jets, material could not keep falling onto the growing star.

The review traces jets through molecular lines at millimeter wavelengths and atomic and molecular lines in the infrared, each probing a different gas. Recent instruments, the James Webb Space Telescope and the ALMA array, have transformed the field with sharp, sensitive views. Together they reveal warm shocked gas and cold molecular flows in the same systems. Dutta discusses jet structures, speeds, rotation, chemical composition, and magnetic fields, and what they imply for jet launching and disk evolution. Future large surveys with both facilities should bring further breakthroughs.
arxiv-2510-12575:
Khan proves a duality between two families of algebraic structures built from star shaped diagrams, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. The structures are weighted A infinity algebras, generalizations of ordinary algebras with infinitely many higher operations, constructed in her previous work from diagrams used in symplectic geometry and knot theory. Koszul duality is a symmetry that exchanges an algebra with a resolution of its opposite in a precise sense.

This paper is the second part of that project. In proving the duality, Khan constructs a new box tensor product for weighted A infinity bimodules, the two sided versions of these algebras. She also verifies a correspondence between maps of weighted A infinity algebras and one class of A infinity bimodules. These tools are the technical heart of the result. The work completes a duality picture begun in the earlier part.
arxiv-2510-12875:
Hallam and co-authors study the quantum Mpemba effect in this 2025 arXiv paper, where a system starting farther from equilibrium can settle faster than one starting closer. They explain the effect through symmetry: a starting state breaks a symmetry, and settling means restoring it. Their testbed is a one-dimensional chain of spins with interactions that fade slowly with distance.

A strong magnetic field first creates a prethermal regime, a long-lived near-equilibrium state with an effective continuous symmetry that lets the effect appear. A classic theorem limits that symmetry when interactions reach too far, so field strength, interaction range, and starting temperature all compete. The authors map that interplay systematically and show the effect can be tuned, with possible tests in trapped ions, polar molecules, and diamond defect centers.
arxiv-2510-12975:
Yeats and collaborators link score matching to local intrinsic dimension in this 2025 arXiv paper. Local intrinsic dimension measures how many dimensions data truly need near a point, even when stored in a high-dimensional space, and it is a fundamental quantity in learning theory. Diffusion models can estimate it, but existing routes need many model passes or gradient computations, which strains limited hardware.

The authors prove that local intrinsic dimension forms a lower bound on the denoising score matching loss, the training objective of diffusion models. This motivates using that cheap loss value itself as an estimator. A related implicit loss also approximates the dimension through the normal direction count and connects to a recent estimator. On a manifold benchmark and with a large image diffusion model, their estimator stayed highly competitive while using far less memory as problems grew.
arxiv-2510-13075:
Kalabizadeh and colleagues adapt brain MRI segmentation models across hospitals and populations in this 2025 arXiv paper. Segmentation models for the hippocampus, a memory structure whose shrinkage tracks dementia, often degrade on new datasets. Scanners change image style and populations change anatomy, called content shift. Their framework adapts without any labels in the target domain.

Style gaps are handled by simple harmonization through z-normalization. Content gaps are handled by a bidirectional deformable registration network. That network trains jointly with the main model and the discriminator network. It aligns source images to the target anatomy with plausible transformations focused on the region of interest. Beyond a synthetic test set, tests on three hippocampus datasets with varying atrophy showed the method beating existing baselines. Transferring from young healthy volunteers to dementia patients improved Dice scores over the source-only baseline by a wide margin.
arxiv-2510-13475:
Hou and co-authors simulate elastic turbulence in two-dimensional Taylor-Couette flow. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies a chaotic flow state in fluids with almost no inertia. Such fluids, like dilute polymer mixes, build elastic stress that can destabilize the flow. The state draws interest for boosting mixing and heat transfer in tiny devices.

Long simulations trace how the instability starts and how the wild state then behaves. The purely elastic instability proves supercritical, which settles a point of past dispute. The flow is mildly directional yet strongly uneven across the gap. Most action hugs the inner wall, in a band like a boundary layer. In that band, the measured stats and spectra match both theory and past experiments. The flow runs between two cylinders, with the inner one rotating. Elastic turbulence was first seen in swirling flow between two disks.
arxiv-2510-13675:
Zhou and co-authors teach a model to name what it sees by grounding images in the Wikidata knowledge graph. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles open-domain visual entity recognition, where labels are real-world entities, not fixed classes. Most target entities never appear in training, and rare ones dominate the tail. Linking a photo to the right entity demands context beyond pixels.

Their framework, KnowCoL, fuses images and text descriptions in one shared space through contrastive learning. Entity descriptions, type hierarchies, and relational context all guide the matching. On the OVEN benchmark, adding text and structured knowledge lifted accuracy sharply. The gain was largest for rare and unseen entities, the hardest slice of the task. Their smallest model lifted unseen-entity accuracy by 10.5 percent over the prior best system while using far fewer parameters, the team reports. Structured knowledge, not scale alone, drove the improvement.
arxiv-2510-14275:
Anthony Thomas challenges a common belief about effective field theory, the framework used to calculate nuclear reactions and atomic nucleus properties, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Effective field theory works at the energies of interest while encoding short-distance physics in constants, and its successes have convinced the nuclear physics community that its predictions are model independent.

Thomas explains why this is not the case. The constants absorbed into the theory, the choices of which terms to keep, and the regulators used to tame infinities all carry model assumptions. Two equally valid effective theories can give different answers for the same result. Uncertainties can be too small if the model dependence is ignored. The paper is a caution aimed at practitioners. Effective field theory is an organizing tool. Its results should be presented with their model dependence stated rather than marketed as assumption-free predictions.
arxiv-2510-14375:
Xiaofeng Cai and co-authors design a numerical scheme for the Boltzmann equation, the basic equation of gas dynamics, in this 2025 arXiv paper. It stays accurate across the huge range of scales from free molecular flight to ordinary fluid flow. Such multi-scale transport defeats simple methods, which either demand very fine grids in fluid regimes or give wrong answers in kinetic ones.

Their asymptotic-preserving semi-Lagrangian discontinuous Galerkin scheme follows particle trajectories for transport while updating moments, the averages, with a penalty procedure. Borrowing a Shu-Osher form inside an implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta time stepper lets the scheme capture the correct limiting fluid system. The authors establish order conditions for both the time stepping and the new moments update, and prove stability for the linear model using hypocoercivity techniques. Experiments across test problems confirm the scheme's accuracy, its asymptotic-preserving property, and its robustness.
arxiv-2510-14675:
Dutly and co-authors report, in a 2025 arXiv paper, an attack that undermines a recent Intel defense for secure enclaves. Enclaves are protected regions of a processor where secret code and data run. Attackers have used carefully timed interrupts to step through enclave code one instruction at a time. Intel's AEX-Notify extension was meant to stop exactly that kind of deterministic single-stepping.

The authors show that single-stepping is not actually needed. Their AEX-NStep attack counts interrupts probabilistically instead, and it still works against enclaves with the defense enabled. One stated guarantee of the defense, called obfuscated forward progress, turns out not to hold. To prove the point practically, they built an attack that leaks an ECDSA signing key from a protected enclave. The results extend the original security analysis of the defense and point to what future mitigations must handle.
arxiv-2510-14775:
Taziaux and a large team of co-authors hunt, in a 2025 arXiv paper, for the faint radio glow of dwarf galaxies. The glow reveals how star formation pushes back on small systems. Dwarf galaxies have shallow gravity wells, so feedback from their stars can reshape them. Radio continuum emission traces cosmic rays, which mediate much of that feedback. The team observed fifteen nearby irregular dwarfs, eleven gas-rich star-formers and four blue compact dwarfs.

Using the Australia Telescope Compact Array across three radio bands, they detected continuum emission in eleven of the fifteen galaxies. Detectability tracked star formation rate, far-infrared brightness, and stellar mass closely. It showed no significant link to hydrogen content or rotation speed. The radio spectra often curved instead of following a single power law, a sign of more complex physics underneath. Formal model comparison confirms one power law cannot describe these galaxies' radio output.
arxiv-2510-14875:
Ma and co-authors simulate, in a 2025 arXiv paper, the gas that dying red supergiant stars shed into their surroundings, which later supernovae crash into. Many hydrogen-rich supernovae show signs of dense circumstellar gas, but its origin is debated. Using a radiation transport scheme inside AREPO, a moving-mesh code, the team ran three-dimensional radiation hydrodynamic simulations. Their subjects were red supergiant envelopes of ten and twenty solar masses.

Strong pulsations lift surface material far out, to distances matching the circumstellar density inferred for supernova SN 2013fs. Light pushing on dust then drives lopsided outflows, while convection gives the surrounding gas order-of-magnitude density differences from place to place. The authors draw three lessons. This material is mostly bound gas, not a steady wind. Highly aspherical surroundings are common and can arise from convection alone, no companion star required. And one-dimensional models miss the physics here.
arxiv-2510-15575:
Yi Tao and ten colleagues merge radar sensing and radio communication into one system for swarms of drones. Their 2025 arXiv paper argues that sharing hardware and spectrum makes drone teams lighter and more capable, . The design uses millimeter-wave radar signals of a standard radar kind.

A new waveform carries data in both signal delay and amplitude while still measuring distance and speed precisely. Random antenna selection plus compressed sensing keeps the top measurable velocity intact. A chirp-division scheme then lets many drones transmit without interference, allocating time and frequency slots dynamically. A fused processing loop demodulates data and estimates sensing parameters together. Simulations under dynamic flight showed the scheme working, beating a comparison system on communication and sensing, though plain radar still sensed slightly better. Urban clutter degraded performance somewhat but left the system robust.
arxiv-2510-15675:
Quantum networks need entangled states shared between chips, ideally carrying more than one bit per photon. Molly Thomas leads a seventeen-author team demonstrating this in a 2025 arXiv physics paper. They distribute four-dimensional path-encoded entangled states between two photonic chips over optical fiber. The challenge is keeping phase coherence across several light modes during transmission. Their new stabilization algorithm finishes each correction round in just two measurement rounds, for any mode count.

Full tomography across the two chips verifies a state fidelity of eighty-six percent. Without stabilization, the same setup manages only about eight percent fidelity. The entanglement entropy measured is essentially one, as expected for their target state.
arxiv-2511-00275: Jan Wiegerinck contributes a short note in complex analysis, the study of functions of complex numbers. He builds an example of a Laplace transform, an integral that turns one function into another, whose growth is irregular rather than orderly. The example settles a question listed in Hayman's List, a known set of open problems in the field. The note is brief and aimed at specialists.
arxiv-2511-00375:
Xin Wang, Yunhao Xiao, and Rui Qiao introduce PolyRecommender, a system that helps researchers find promising polymers for a target need. It reads each polymer two ways: as chemical language through PolyBERT, a model trained on polymer text forms, and as a molecular graph through a graph encoder. Language similarity first pulls a candidate list from the wider pool.

Fused embeddings from both views then rank the candidates against several target properties at once. Because the two views carry complementary knowledge, the ranking stays robust across related properties. The authors frame the system as a general multimodal pattern for AI-guided materials design. For polymer scientists, it offers faster, more reliable shortlists for next-generation materials.
arxiv-2511-00475:
Travis Barrett, Amit Kumar Mishra, and Joyce Mwangama propose a new use for variational autoencoders: calibrating sensors. An autoencoder compresses data into a compact latent code and rebuilds it; their twist trains that latent space to serve directly as the calibration output. One model then does two jobs at once, reconstructing raw readings and emitting corrected values.

A proof of concept on an existing multi-sensor gas dataset shows the idea works. Outputs from both heads, the calibration output and the reconstruction, stayed statistically similar to their respective ground truths. The authors discuss how future testing should proceed and how the approach could expand. If it holds up, calibration could ride along inside the same network that already processes sensor streams.
arxiv-2511-00575:
Sarbari Mitra and Soumya Bhoumik introduce Perrin cordial labeling, a new vertex labeling scheme for graphs inspired by the Perrin number sequence. In graph labeling, numbers assigned to vertices induce labels on edges, and balance conditions on those labels reveal structure. The Perrin sequence grows by adding the terms two and three steps back, giving this scheme its distinctive arithmetic flavor.

A labeling assigns distinct Perrin numbers to vertices, and each edge takes the parity of the sum of its endpoint labels. The labeling counts as cordial when the numbers of even- and odd-labeled edges differ by at most one. The authors test which graph families admit such labelings, analyzing structural properties family by family. The scheme forges a fresh link between number theory and graph structure.
arxiv-2511-00775:
Mingyang Li, Yu'an Li, Zhang, and Zhao tackle a measurement problem in cell biology: how to spot Levy walks, a motion pattern with occasional long jumps. Catching that pattern needs data across very different scales of time and space, which experiments rarely provide.

They extend a microscope based method called differential dynamic microscopy to self propelled particles whose run times follow a heavy tailed law. Tests on synthetic images show detection works when the scales reached are about ten times the particle's persistence length. Applied to real data, the method finds no Levy signature in E. coli, while E. gracilis fits the active Levy picture better.
arxiv-2511-01675:
Tamás Kriváchy documents a data bug quietly corrupting citation counts across many online-only Springer Nature journals, including Scientific Reports, Nature Communications, the Communications and npj families, and many BMC titles. The errors reach back to articles from 2001.

Most likely caused by an API response error in the publisher's metadata, countless references point wrongly at Article Number 1 of a volume. The fallout is lopsided: a few articles are massively over-cited while many others lose citations they earned. In both Scientific Reports and Nature Communications, five of the ten most-cited articles carry article number 1. Kriváchy cross-checked the distortion in Crossref, OpenCitations, Semantic Scholar, and the journals' own sites, and traces the cause to the messy shift from page numbers to article numbers.
arxiv-2511-02475:
Jürgen Cito and Dominik Bork argue that AI code generation makes an old software engineering discipline newly important: modelling. Generative tools turn prompts into systems that look finished, which erases the line between prototype and engineered product, while robustness, security, and maintainability may silently be missing. Rather than treating models only as blueprints drawn before coding, the authors propose recovering models from AI-generated systems after the fact.

Recovered models can restore human comprehension of what was built and then guide how the system evolves. Two loops use them differently. In an agentic loop, software checks and repairs the system against the models automatically. In a human reflective loop, the models expose hidden assumptions for people to inspect and revise. The paper catalogues candidate model types and shows how a recovered model can surface implicit assumptions as constraints worth reviewing.
arxiv-2511-02575:
S. F. Pate and six co-authors, reporting for a global analysis effort, narrow down how much of the proton's spin is carried by its strange quarks. The answer hides in the strange axial form factor at zero momentum transfer, and extracting it requires fitting two kinds of scattering data together: neutral-current neutrino scattering and parity-violating electron scattering. Earlier fits were weak at low momentum transfer because no neutrino data existed below a certain threshold.

The new fit adds MiniBooNE neutrino and antineutrino data for the first time, which requires modelling how neutrinos interact with the carbon nuclei in that detector's target. Three distinct nuclear models were tried. The constraint on the strange axial form factor at low momentum transfer tightened tremendously over earlier work. The authors still call for more data, especially scattering events with a single visible proton, such as the MicroBooNE experiment can provide.
arxiv-2511-02775:
Eleftheria Solomonidi and Luiz Vale Silva revisit a rare decay of the D0 particle, which splits into two pions plus an electron or muon pair. Such decays test the Standard Model, since the usual suppression of flavor change in charm quarks makes them sensitive probes. Their 2025 paper follows earlier work in modeling the decay through intermediate resonances.

For the first time, they add a cascade path where the D0 first yields a pion and an a1(1260) particle, which then decays through a rho into the lepton pair. That path turns out to supply one of the largest shares of the decay rate. With it, the Standard Model prediction matches LHCb data better than ever before. The same model settings also fit related four-body hadronic decays measured by three experiments.
arxiv-2511-02875:
R. Yamamoto Ravenor studies the gap between university rules on generative AI and what academics actually do with it. As these tools spread through teaching and research, such policy-practice voids become a real governance problem. The 2025 study prototypes a ten-item instrument that asks indirect questions, set inside a structured interpretive framework, to surface the gaps without blunt self-reporting.

Three filtered indicators come out of the signals. One gauges assessment capacity, proxied by the share who would fully allow AI in exams. A second tracks sector-level necessity, drawn from heavy users who still credit AI with large contributions. A third maps ontological stance, splitting those who see AI as different in kind into material and immaterial views. Ravenor offers the tool for auditable policy checks.
arxiv-2511-02975:
Sirui Liu, Thomas Videbaek, and W. Benjamin Rogers fight a shape problem in self-assembling tubes. When DNA-origami pieces close into a cylinder on their own, heat-driven bending lets many wrong diameters form. Their 2025 paper tries templated growth instead: assembly starts from a precisely made seed, so the growing tube inherits the seed's diameter and twist.

They made seeds two ways, by multi-part assembly and by sorting one seed type out of a mixed batch with gel methods. Tuning seed and monomer counts and the temperature let tubes grow from seeds without fresh tubes starting elsewhere. Templated tubes followed their seeds closely, raising the yield of the target shape. Changing the seed's diameter even steered one monomer type into tubes of several sizes.
arxiv-2511-03075:
Markus Buchholz and four colleagues introduce AURA, a team framework for diagnosing faults in underwater robots. Anomalies at sea can be novel, so pure automation is risky, and pure human review is slow. Their 2025 design joins a language model, a high-fidelity digital twin of the robot, and a human operator in one loop.

Two agents split the work. A low-level agent watches telemetry and turns odd signals into a plain-language problem statement. A high-level agent then talks the case through with the operator, grounded in outside knowledge, to find root causes. Confirmed diagnoses become training examples that sharpen the low-level agent. The loop aims to turn a static tool into a partner that improves with every incident.
arxiv-2511-03275:
Taishi Katsuragawa, Shin'ichi Nojiri, and Sergei D Odintsov place wormholes inside a growing universe and ask what changes. Their setup uses four scalar fields whose target geometry mirrors the curvature of space itself. In that frame, wormholes can stay stable even where normal energy rules fail.

Growth changes the balance: the cosmic fluid shifts effective density and pressure enough that the energy rules can hold after all. Stranger still, one linked universe can face a finite future end while its partner does not. Near the throat, paths can cross to the safe side before the end and return after it passes. The authors also build wormholes shaped by dark matter halo profiles seen around galaxies.
arxiv-2511-03375:
Mengyao Guo and co-authors watch fifteen newcomers co-create picture stories with a vision-language model. Making a visual tale with an artificial partner raises a core question: how do words and images build meaning together across a sequence? Sessions ran in three phases with GPT-4o as the image partner.

Users learned to exploit the extra meaning images carried beyond their prompts, refining wording round by round. Four styles of teamwork stood out, and a set-based analysis found three routes to strong word-image interplay: teaching partner, technical expert, and visual thinker. Hurdles included cultural mismatch in generated scenes. The study maps how novices grow into skilled co-authors with generative tools.
arxiv-2511-03575:
P P Biswas and colleagues explain the broad iron glow in active galaxy spectra as reflection from a warm corona above the disk. A lamp of X-rays above the central black hole lights the flow from outside. In their two-slab picture, a warm, energy-shedding corona sits on the disk and both heats and reflects.

Lines from highly stripped iron ions, smeared by relativity near the black hole, merge into the broad profile seen by telescopes. Varying spin, viewing angle, lamp height, and dissipation reshapes that profile in testable ways. Photoionization modeling with a dedicated code grounds the line strengths. High-resolution spectra could thus probe the warm corona, a layer whose nature has stayed murky.
arxiv-2511-03675:
Geoff McDonald and Jonathan Bar Or demonstrate Whisper Leak, an attack that guesses prompt topics from encrypted chat traffic alone. Encryption hides words, but streaming replies leak packet sizes and timing, and those rhythms vary with topic. Sensitive uses in health, law, and private messaging make that leak more than a curiosity.

Across twenty-eight popular models, topic sorting reached near-perfect scores on a standard ranking measure. Even when target chats hid among ten thousand decoys, many models gave up every flagged case correctly while recovering a useful slice of targets. One flagged topic was money laundering, a worst-case privacy failure. The work presses providers to pad or reshape traffic before metadata becomes a transcript.
arxiv-2511-20075:
Verschuur, Oratis, Sanjay, and Snoeijer watch bubbles pinch off inside stretchy polymer liquids. Their 2025 paper asks how elasticity changes bubble breakup. Pinch-off is the moment a fluid neck thins and snaps. Polymer drops famously form threads that delay breakup. Bubbles were expected to behave much the same way.

Experiments showed no thread at all for dilute solutions. The bubble neck simply thinned and broke cleanly. Threads appeared only at high polymer concentrations. There the needle size suddenly mattered a great deal. Simulations and theory used the Oldroyd-B polymer model. Polymer stress still spikes during bubble pinch-off, they found. But the spike grows far weaker than in drops. Stretching happens mostly in the radial direction here. That weaker divergence explains the missing thread. Bubble threads also prove thinner and shorter-lived than drop threads. No universal exponential thinning law fits the bubble data.
arxiv-2511-20575:
Polson and Sokolov solve hard optimization problems by sampling instead of searching. Their 2025 paper designs Monte Carlo methods for mixed integer and linear programming. Such problems mix whole-number choices with continuous quantities. The trick recasts a constrained problem as simulation from a distribution. Good samples cluster near the best feasible answers.

A Boltzmann distribution encodes the goal and constraints together. Solving then means simulating from truncated distributions well. Multivariate exponentials and Gaussians are the needed targets. Kent and Davis algorithms supply fast simulation for them. The approach descends from Pincus and simulated annealing traditions. Portfolio choice shows the method on a finance staple. The classic farmer problem from stochastic programming follows. Both show the machinery handling constraints gracefully. Soft penalties replace hard walls during annealing. Future work includes scaling to larger instances.
arxiv-2511-20775:
Daniel Maschmann and colleagues report in 2025 a dust mystery inside young massive star clusters, caught by the James Webb Space Telescope. Dust grains are forged by supernovae and ageing stars, but how much a cluster produces at each life stage is hard to tally. The team studied 22 clusters heavier than 100,000 solar masses, aged 3 to 100 million years, imaged with Webb's MIRI instrument. Nineteen had already blown clear of their dust.

Yet the clusters glow anomalously at 10 micrometres, a silicate signature ionised gas cannot explain. Only one cluster shows the PAH features of carbon dust. Candidate sources include red supergiants, yellow hypergiants, and supernova ejecta, though the supernova story predicts X-rays seen in only three clusters. The three most massive clusters, above a million solar masses, are the brightest emitters. They shine at least a magnitude beyond any known stellar source, hinting at a rare mechanism of extreme masses.
arxiv-2511-21275:
Henrik Ueberschär proves in 2025 a Liouville-type theorem for Schrödinger equations, settling when a solution that fades at infinity must vanish everywhere. The setting is a solution on all of space, with a nonnegative bounded potential, the case tied to disordered quantum systems. The Landis conjecture, from the 1950s, says fast enough exponential decay forces the solution to be zero.

Ueberschär's condition is far weaker and local at infinity: if the solution's mass over any sequence of unit-width shells shrinks to zero, the solution is zero everywhere. No global decay rate is assumed. As a corollary, Landis holds for solutions with fast algebraic decay, slower than any exponential. The result extends to exterior domains and to nonlinear Schrödinger equations of a certain class, under conditions on where the potential vanishes. Meshkov showed the conjecture fails for complex potentials, framing the result's strength.
arxiv-2511-21675:
