Sadegh Shirani and Mohsen Bayati estimate treatment effects when experiments leak across a network, in 2025. In social and physical systems, treating one unit spills onto others through interaction pathways nobody observes. The natural fix, mapping the network, is usually impossible. Their claim is bolder: for population-level effects, the network itself is not needed.

What matters is how interactions shape outcomes over observation rounds. Shirani and Bayati pin down, from axioms, when the outcome distribution follows a low-dimensional recursive equation, and give minimal conditions for such evolution mappings to exist. The framework is a distribution-level cousin of difference-in-differences, exploiting parallel evolution across treatment scenarios rather than side-by-side paths for each unit. Randomization does double duty: beyond removing confounding, it implicitly samples the hidden spillover channels, enabling consistent learning about varied spillovers. Causal message passing puts the theory to work.
arxiv-2511-21875:
Chiba-Okabe and Plotkin model a conflict of interest in online marketplaces: the platform running the reputation system also profits from sales. In their theoretical model, buyers cannot tell honest sellers from cheats in advance, so they rely on the platform's reputation signals to decide. Sellers adapt over time, and the platform earns commission on completed transactions.

That setup gives platforms an inherent incentive toward rating inflation, because rosier reputations mean more sales and more commission. The distortion is self-limiting, since if signals become meaningless, trustworthy sellers leave and buyers stop buying altogether. Strikingly, profit maximization can involve deliberately investing to make reputations less accurate. But when the platform can freely set its commission fees, maximum profit may instead come from paying for an accurate system. The referee's own incentives thus shape how much trust a market can sustain.
arxiv-2511-21975:
Huwyler proposes a framework for judging whether AI projects pay off once risks are priced in. Standard ROI math treats AI like ordinary software, but AI cuts some risks while creating new ones: malfunctions, attacks, bias lawsuits, and penalties. His Risk-Adjusted Intelligence Dividend framework builds the change in risk directly into the return calculation.

The method adapts annual loss expectancy and Monte Carlo simulation to compare risk before and after implementation, alongside gains and reserves. The context is unforgiving: the EU AI Act allows fines of 35 million euros or 7 percent of global turnover for prohibited practices. Industry surveys find median AI returns near ten percent with payback taking two to four years in the figures he cites. Hidden technical debt alone can erode projected returns by 18 to 29 percent if unserviced, according to research quoted in the study.
arxiv-2511-22075:
Mutlu, a computer scientist, extends Gradual C0, the only practical gradual verifier. A tool that lets programmers prove software correct gradually, mixing static proof with runtime checks wherever the written specification is still imprecise. Its specification language struggles with complex expressions, and this work adds pure functions, side-effect-free functions usable inside specifications. A standard feature of static verifiers that gradual verification had lacked because axiomatizing them under imprecision is technically delicate.

The design contributes a new strategy for axiomatizing pure functions when specifications are imprecise, together with a modified formal function rule in Viper. Pure functions let users encode observer methods naturally and express refinements of existing predicates, making specifications for recursive heap data structures, like linked lists and trees, considerably easier to write. Implementation in Gradual C0 and a full soundness proof are left as future work.
arxiv-2511-22175:
Zhong and Karki, physicists, make an atomically thin semiconductor respond to light it should ignore. Monolayer molybdenum disulfide has a direct bandgap suited to photodetectors, but its single-atom thickness absorbs weakly, and photons below the bandgap energy normally produce no photocurrent at all. Depositing gold nanoparticles on the monolayer changes that. The particles' localized surface plasmons drive a nonlinear interaction that generates a broadband supercontinuum, white light, which the MoS2 then reabsorbs through efficient resonant energy transfer.

Under femtosecond pulses at 1030 nanometers, the nanoparticle-assisted photocurrent exceeds the monolayer's own two-photon photocurrent by more than an order of magnitude. Because the trick works with near-infrared photons below the bandgap, it points toward sub-bandgap photodetectors for optical telecommunications. The authors note that optimizing nanoparticle shape, size, and composition should push the enhancement further, while the hybrid suits fundamental energy-transfer studies.
arxiv-2511-22275:
Li, Shi, and Deng build a benchmark for testing whether chatbots can read users' minds. Their setting is conversational recommenders, systems that suggest items through dialogue. Good recommendations depend on inferring what a user wants, intends, and believes, a skill called theory of mind. Older tests rely on staged Sally-Anne stories about hidden objects, far from real conversation.

Their benchmark, RecToM, is built from human-annotated recommendation dialogues. It grades two skills. Cognitive inference means grasping the mental states behind what was said. Behavioral prediction means choosing the right next move based on those states. Top models do fine on coarse intention labels but drop sharply on fine-grained ones. They also lose track of changing intentions as dialogues unfold, and chain-of-thought prompting helps only a little. Models sometimes flatter perceived preferences instead of answering soundly, a sycophancy the benchmark exposes.
arxiv-2511-22375:
Yu examines a clash between two ways of updating beliefs. Bayesian conditioning revises probabilities when the new fact is an event in the existing outcome space. Maximum Entropy instead picks the least committed distribution that fits the new fact. Trouble starts when the new fact, such as a die being loaded so its average roll is five, is not an event in the original space.

One fix enlarges the space so the new fact becomes an event, and Skyrms argued the two then agree exactly. Critics, citing Friedman and Shimony, replied that the agreement is trivial. Yu argues the critics face a dilemma: either the result is a harmless side effect of Skyrms's approach, or it undermines every way of enlarging a space. The second horn would mean Bayesian conditioning cannot absorb genuinely new kinds of information, while Maximum Entropy handles such cases without difficulty.
arxiv-2511-22475:
Lin, Yang, Lin, Chen, and Fan merge two families of image generators into one. Adversarial models learn from a critic and generate in one step but train unstably, while flow models learn a smooth transport from noise to data and are stable yet need many steps. Their adversarial flow model keeps the flow model's deterministic noise-to-data mapping but trains it adversarially, so it generates natively in one or a few steps.

Unlike consistency methods, the model never learns the flow's intermediate steps, saving capacity and avoiding accumulated errors. On ImageNet at 256 pixels in a single step, their extra-large model set a new best FID score of 2.38 in its class, lower meaning closer to real images. They also trained networks of 56 and 112 layers end to end by repeating blocks, reaching single-pass FID scores of 2.08 and 1.94 beating their multi-step versions.
arxiv-2511-22675:
Cianchi, Giannetti, Passarelli di Napoli, and Scheven prove fine regularity results for a model of non-Newtonian fluid flow. The stationary Orlicz-Stokes system describes an incompressible fluid whose stress responds nonlinearly to deformation, with growth governed by an Orlicz function rather than a fixed power. The authors ask how smooth local solutions must be, measuring smoothness fractionally, through Besov space membership of an expression of the velocity's symmetric gradient.

The fractional differentiability established depends on a balance between the operator's nonlinearity and the external force's integrability in Orlicz spaces. Stronger forcing yields stronger fractional smoothness, up to the nonlinearity's limits. The pressure term receives treatment in Orlicz-Besov spaces. Matching results are proved for the associated plain elliptic system without the divergence constraint. A modular-form Poincaré-Sobolev inequality in Orlicz spaces on finite-measure domains is key to the proofs, and may serve other nonlinear problems.
arxiv-2511-22775:
Khatua and Choi review a family of magnets built on the trillium lattice, a three-dimensional network whose structure is intrinsically chiral, meaning it lacks mirror symmetry. On this lattice, competing interactions frustrate the spins, preventing simple magnetic order, while antisymmetric Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya couplings add handedness to the spin arrangements. The review surveys the topological phenomena and chiral spin states recently identified in such compounds.

Two materials anchor the discussion: the magnetic insulator K2Ni2(SO4)3 and the intermetallic EuPtSi, where noncollinear magnetic ordering and magnetic skyrmions, tiny swirling spin textures, have been observed. The authors map out theoretically proposed chiral quantum phases these systems might realise, including chiral spin liquids and spin fractons. They stress that quantum fluctuations, rare in three-dimensional systems, survive here despite high connectivity. Open questions and promising probes are laid out for a field aiming at both fundamental insight and spintronics applications.
arxiv-2511-22875:
Nasser, Poitevin, and Dalton make a fragile step of X-ray crystallography harder to break. Serial crystallography at free-electron lasers produces thousands of patterns from crystals in random orientations, and each must be indexed, its orientation recovered, before any structure can be built. The hardest patterns have few reliable peaks, heavy background, spurious reflections, or highly skewed unit cells.

Their algorithm formulates indexing as a symmetry-aware lattice decoding problem: the loss incorporates lattice symmetries while trimming outlier peaks inconsistent with any plausible orientation, a basis reparameterisation stabilises skewed lattices. A small-sample objective mode recovers orientations from very few reflections. Differential evolution searches orientations, Babai's nearest-plane algorithm assigning indices. On three protein datasets from the Coherent X-ray Imaging Data Bank, the method matched or beat indexers such as XGANDALF and TORO, with gains on few-peak and skewed-cell patterns. It used extremely little memory.
arxiv-2511-23075:
Zhao and colleagues target a blind spot of vision-language models. They describe images well but reason poorly about 3D space, misjudging distances, sizes, and how views of the same room fit together across viewpoints. Earlier fixes fed models extra 3D data such as depth maps or point clouds. Or they bolted on a geometry encoder whose features were merged only shallowly.

SpaceMind works from ordinary color images alone at test time, pairing a spatial encoder, VGGT, with a standard 2D image encoder. Its key step is a camera-guided fusion module that treats the camera's viewpoint as an active guide, biasing and weighting spatial tokens by geometric importance before the language model sees them. The design set new state-of-the-art results on three spatial benchmarks, VSI-Bench, SQA3D, and SPBench, beating both open and proprietary systems on two of them by large margins.
arxiv-2511-23175:
Chandra and Tawarmalani build an optimization framework for a family of risk measures, the quantile-based summaries decision-makers use to cap losses under uncertainty. This replaces treating Value-at-Risk and Conditional Value-at-Risk as separate problems. Their two-stage construction models integrated quantile functions and turns the task of minimizing such a measure into a bilinear optimization problem, which is NP-hard but structurally tractable.

Within the framework, minimizing Value-at-Risk appears as the limiting case where the quantile interval collapses to a point. The field's standard Conditional Value-at-Risk overestimate falls out as a special case that reduces to a linear program. The authors derive new convex under- and over-estimators that bound the optimum more tightly. They demonstrate the approach on network traffic engineering, minimizing a quantile of the worst unmet demand across probabilistic link-failure scenarios.
arxiv-2511-23275:
Laplante and colleagues speed up Bayesian inference for discrete models whose normalizing constants cannot be computed. The doubly intractable problems where both likelihood and posterior are known only up to an unknown factor. Standard fixes use expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo, so the team instead builds a generalized Bayesian posterior around a new log-ratio matching divergence. Designed to stay conjugate, updatable in closed form, for exponential family models.

They prove the generalized posterior is consistent and satisfies a Bernstein-von Mises theorem, so its large-sample shape matches what honest Bayesian inference would give. Then test it on hard cases including Ising and Potts random fields, an autoregressive count series, and a Conway-Maxwell-Poisson graphical model. In their experiments the method ran between 10 and 6,000 times faster than state-of-the-art Bayesian computation, a gain large enough to make these expressive discrete models practical instead of avoided.
arxiv-2511-23475:
Zhong and colleagues present AnyTalker, a new framework for audio-driven talking videos with several people interacting at once in one scene. A setting earlier systems handled only with hundreds or thousands of hours of curated real multi-person footage. Their design extends a Diffusion Transformer with an identity-aware attention block, called Audio-Face Cross Attention. That iteratively processes identity and audio pairs, so the number of drivable people can freely scale arbitrarily.

Training cleverly avoids the data bottleneck, learning multi-person speaking patterns from single-person videos alone through concatenation-based augmentation and then refining interactivity in tests with only a few genuine multi-person clips. Full experiments show strong lip synchronization, visual quality, and natural turn-taking style interactivity. And the team also contributes the first dedicated interactivity metric and benchmark dataset for judging how naturally generated video groups converse on screen together.
arxiv-2512-00175:
Estimating cause and effect is hard when some important variables were never measured. Helen Guo, Elizabeth Ogburn, and Ilya Shpitser compare two proxy-based methods for that problem in a 2025 study. Proxy variables stand in for the hidden factors and can restore identification under the right conditions.

One approach uses bridge equations, solving integral equations to recover the causal target. The other decomposes arrays, recovering latent factors from counterfactual quantities through eigenspace structure. A direct comparison helps researchers choose between the two families, which matters in health and social science studies where hidden confounding is common. Both families are used in epidemiology and economics, where hidden variables are routine. For a reader new to the field, the side-by-side look at both paths is a clean way to learn. It shows what each path asks of the data at hand.
arxiv-2512-00275:
Sharper satellite images help responders map disasters quickly, but the models behind them must stay light and fast. Yi Liu and co-authors propose HIMOSA in 2025, a lightweight super-resolution framework for remote sensing imagery. Existing methods often trade performance against computational efficiency.

HIMOSA uses a hierarchical mixture of sparse attention to raise image resolution with limited resources. Real-time efficiency and small model size are critical in disaster detection and response, the authors' motivating case. Better lightweight upscaling could put high-quality image enhancement on drones and field hardware, not just in data centers. Sparse attention spends computation only where the image needs it most. That economy is what makes the framework lightweight enough for field use.
arxiv-2512-00975:
Haotian Liang and a large team at Shanghai AI Laboratory present MM-ACT in a 2025 robotics paper. A generalist robot policy needs two gifts at once: semantic understanding for planning tasks, and the ability to act on the world through prediction. Many systems split those jobs across separate models.

MM-ACT unifies text, image, and action in one shared token space. It generates across all three channels in parallel, learning from that multimodal generation to decide its moves. One model that can describe, imagine, and act could plan more coherently. The work tests whether parallel generation makes robot behavior smarter.
arxiv-2512-01175:
Lilian Markenzon and Claudia Justel study a special class of graphs in a 2025 paper. Strictly interval graphs are simultaneously strictly chordal and interval graphs, two well-known families with strong structure. Interval graphs model overlapping intervals, while chordal graphs have no long chordless cycles.

The authors present a new characterization of this class. Their characterization leads to a simple linear recognition algorithm, a fast test that decides whether a given graph belongs to the class. Structural and spectral properties are also covered. Fast recognition matters because interval-like graphs appear in scheduling, biology, and network modeling.
arxiv-2512-01275:
Tiantian Chu, Chen Chen, Jia Ye, Xin Xiong, and Sihua Shao survey a new direction for 6G networks in a 2025 paper. Integrated sensing and communication aims to make one system both communicate and sense its surroundings, saving spectrum and hardware. Radio frequency versions face spectrum crowding, limited sensing resolution, and interference.

The authors review retroreflective optical integrated sensing and communication as an alternative. Retroreflectors bounce light straight back to its source, giving strong, trackable signals without radio spectrum. The paper covers the technologies, applications, and future directions of this optical route. It maps how light-based sensing might complement radio in future networks.
arxiv-2512-01575:
Kevin Vidarte and co-authors give a real-space method to compute orbital magnetization in crystals. That trait tells how a crystal's electrons swirl as a whole. Past methods worked in momentum space, which can strain for large or messy cells.

Their method builds a spectral function from the commutator form of the operator. Chebyshev expansions make the sums exact and fast. Adding up to the Fermi level gives the total value. Real-space tools open the trait to big cells, defects, and disordered solids. Chebyshev sums scale well to large cells, since each term is a sparse matrix product that parallel hardware can run with ease.
arxiv-2512-01675:
Felix Nutzel, Mischa Dombrowski, and Bernhard Kainz lift image generation for rare diseases. Text-to-image diffusion models make fine images for common prompts. In medical use, rare conditions form a small tail of data. The tail output then collapses in quality and variety.

Their GRASP method adds guided residual adapters with sample-wise splits. Adapters steer the model toward tail cases. Better tail images can augment scarce training sets. That helps diagnostic tools learn rare pathologies they would else miss in clinics with few real cases. Adapters are small add-ons, so clinics can tune the base model for their own rare cases without retraining the whole network.
arxiv-2512-01875:
Johnson and co-authors report first detections of methanol maser lines from a rare transition family. Masers amplify radio lines in star-forming clouds. Class II methanol masers mark high-mass star birth. The team found maser action in a rare family of transitions.

Signals appear toward three southern high-mass regions. A line from the heavy isotope form was also caught as a maser for the first time. New maser lines give fresh probes of temperature and density near young massive stars, where other tracers fail. Isotope lines shift by a known offset, so a matched pair of masers confirms the rare family beyond a single-line coincidence.
arxiv-2512-02175:
A metric graph is a network whose edges are real line segments with lengths, glued at vertices, like a transit map drawn to scale. Rajat Vadiraj Dwaraknath and Lexing Ying study in 2025 how to sample from probability distributions living on such graphs, a basic task for computation on networks.

The metric structure supports differential operators and stochastic processes, so waves and random walks can live on the graph, not just at its nodes. Sampling methods must respect that continuous geometry. Efficient sampling on metric graphs feeds applications from traffic and infrastructure modeling to quantum graphs, where the edges' lengths carry the physics.
arxiv-2512-02275:
Personas generated by language models can flatten the people they imitate into stereotypes, a risk with real weight when the people are a minority group. Chantelle Wu and eight co-authors present a 2025 case study of Persona-L, a system that models personas of people with Down syndrome and watches for stereotyping in its own output.

The system combines a large language model with retrieval-augmented generation, grounding personas in retrieved material. Existing persona tools often oversimplify or produce stereotypical profiles of people with Down syndrome, so the team built stereotype detection into the system itself. Their case study shows both the promise of careful persona design and the vigilance it demands.
arxiv-2512-02375:
Drone mapping usually waits until the flight ends to build its 3D model, too late for disaster response. Liyuan Lou and six co-authors present in 2025 an online photogrammetry system that judges reconstruction quality mid-flight and steers the drone to fill the gaps.

Most real-time methods merely process frames quickly, without grading the growing mesh or guiding capture. Their explore-and-exploit scheme pairs an incremental quality indicator with predictive path planning. Time-critical geospatial work, from flood mapping to maintaining live digital twins, needs maps that improve while the drone is still in the air.
arxiv-2512-02575:
Samuele Fracassi and five co-authors study a diode effect for electric current carried without resistance. A superconducting diode lets large supercurrents flow one way but not the other. Such one way dissipationless transport has long been sought for superconducting technology.

Their 2025 theory work places the effect in a quantum spin Hall system joined fully to a superconductor. They show how the imbalance in critical currents arises there, and how it can be tuned. Controllable superconducting diodes could become building blocks for low power quantum and sensing devices of the future. A diode that can be tuned by hand is worth more than one fixed at the plant for all time.
arxiv-2512-03075:
Entropy is a basic measure of spread and disorder in physics. J. A. S. Lima and M. H. Benetti present a new form of it in this 2025 work. They build from the ground up, starting with a power-law spread of particle speeds.

Their new measure uses two settings and does not add up in the usual way. They link it to heat and energy rules in the paper. Such links help test whether a new measure fits known physics. The work may aid study of gases and plasmas where power-law speed patterns appear. Students of statistical physics will find a compact case for testing new entropy ideas.
arxiv-2512-03175:
A big space can be glued from smaller pieces. Arthur Ramos and co-authors use that idea in this 2025 work on the Seifert-van Kampen theorem. The theorem finds the loop group of a whole space from the groups of its parts.

The team builds a modular version of the method using computational paths. In that view, equality is shown by explicit chains of rewrites under set rules. Formal steps like these can be checked by computer proof tools. That makes complex topology results more reliable and easier to reuse. Modular pieces let others swap parts of the proof without redoing the whole argument.
arxiv-2512-03475:
Patients often carry more than one brain disease at once. Hongtao Hao and Joseph Austerweil present Joint Progression Modeling in this 2025 work. Standard event-based models assume a single disease per person, which mixed pathology breaks.

Their probabilistic framework treats single-disease paths as partial rankings. It builds a prior over joint progressions from those parts. The work is tied to Alzheimer's research, where mixed pathology is common. Joint models could give patients and trials a truer picture of decline. Mixed pathology is the rule in older brains, so single-disease models risk false stages.
arxiv-2512-03775:
The Model Context Protocol has become popular middleware connecting language models to tools, but it ships with almost no built-in security. Biwei Yan and a large team argue in a 2025 security preprint that developers must add encryption themselves. Hand-rolled cryptography has a long record of misuse, and here it guards sensitive data and services.

The team built MICRYSCOPE, a detector designed for cryptographic misuse in this ecosystem. It translates crypto code from many languages into one shared representation, maps function dependencies, and tracks sensitive data flows against established rules. Applied to more than nine thousand servers, it found crypto logic in several hundred, and about one in five of those misused it. Misuse clustered in certain registries, in Python code, and in developer tools. Case studies uncovered leaked API keys, weak DES encryption, and MD5-based authentication bypasses.
arxiv-2512-03975:
When a search query is ambiguous, a conversational assistant can ask a clarifying question, and some proposed questions could be sponsored by advertisers. Kshipra Bhawalkar, Alexandros Psomas, and Di Wang analyse that marketplace in a 2025 game theory preprint. Should the suggestion slots and the following ad slot be auctioned together or separately?

The authors build a formal model of such interactive platforms and compare the two designs. A joint design based on the VCG mechanism can allocate suggestions and ads jointly, and it achieves efficient, truthful outcomes, though it is more complex to run. The simpler modular design, with separate mechanisms for each stage, turns out to suffer strategic inefficiency with an unbounded price of anarchy. In plain terms, splitting the auctions can cost arbitrarily much welfare, a concrete warning about an apparently harmless shortcut.
arxiv-2512-04075:
Cosmologists reconstruct how galaxies drift, beyond the smooth expansion of the universe, from their redshifts and estimated distances. Adi Nusser shows in a 2025 cosmology preprint that scatter in those distance estimates poisons the reconstruction in two ways. One bias corrupts individual ones and can be corrected; the other survives correction and distorts the velocity field.

The second, velocity Malmquist bias, appears because noisy distances place them at wrong positions, inventing fake gradients. Using the Tully-Fisher relation as his test case, Nusser shows both its forward and inverse forms give unbiased velocities for objects at one true distance. Yet neither removes the field-level bias. A modified Wiener filter modelling the link between observed and true distance helps but suppresses amplitudes. Learning methods mimic that filter, so he argues they will not rescue it. His prescription: use observed redshifts.
arxiv-2512-04275:
Strong gravitational lenses, where one galaxy bends another's light, are rare: they alone can weigh dark matter substructure at cosmological distances. Juliana S. M. Karp and the DESI collaboration present them in a 2025 astrophysics preprint, more than four thousand candidates found spectroscopically.

The team searched spectra of six million luminous red galaxies from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument for oxygen emission lines that should not be there. Such lines betray a background star-forming galaxy, possibly lensed. From foreground and background redshifts and the line flux, they compute each candidate's probability of being a lens. They expect about half to be real, with Einstein radii spanning a wide range, pending high-resolution imaging. The sample recovers the host of a known multiply imaged supernova. Confirmed lenses will serve time-delay measurements of the Hubble constant and flux-ratio probes of dark matter substructure.
arxiv-2512-04575:
Ting Li, Deren Han, and Tanxing Wang study a tuning knob inside prediction-correction algorithms, a strong family of methods for optimization problems with curved costs. Such algorithms first predict a step, then correct it. Their descent direction can be read as the plain gradient direction plus an adjustment set by the prediction step. Older methods always set the adjustment weight to one. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks what values that weight may safely take.

The authors answer through the lens of differential equations. For pseudo-convex problems, the safe range runs from just above one half up to one. For plain convex problems, the full range from zero to one works. They prove convergence across those ranges. Numerical tests show the best speed comes when the weight makes the method match the classic versions. The result gives users a principled dial instead of a fixed habit.
arxiv-2512-04675:
Siwei Chen, Peipei Xie, Shengyuan Xu, and co-authors deliver the first full third-party security audit of Gleeok-128, a fast cryptographic construction. Gleeok is a family of keyed pseudorandom functions built from three parallel permutation branches whose outputs combine by XOR. Low latency makes it attractive for protecting data in real time. Its three-branch design, though, complicates both safety margins and attacks. Their 2025 arXiv paper takes the challenge head on.

The team built a two-stage search framework, based on mixed-integer programming, to construct differential-linear distinguishers branch by branch and for the full cipher. They add an integral-based key recovery method shaped for multi-branch designs. The analysis produced distinguishers reaching several rounds in each branch and in the full construction. Measured correlations gauge how close the attacks come. Independent audits like this tell designers whether a new cipher's safety margin is honest.
arxiv-2512-04875:
Qing Xu, Yanqian Wang, Xiangjian He, and co-authors present SP-Det, a chest X-ray lesion detector that writes its own prompts instead of waiting for a doctor's notes. Promptable detectors localize disease well when given good textual hints. Hand-written prompts, though, are slow to produce and impractical in busy clinics. Their 2025 arXiv paper removes the expert from the loop with a dual-text prompt generator.

The generator works without expert annotation. Semantic context prompts describe global patterns of disease across the film. Disease beacon prompts zoom in on the marks of each specific condition. Fused together, the two text streams guide multi-label detection, where one film can hold several findings at once. The design aims for precise boxes around each abnormality. Self-prompted detection could speed triage in hospitals that lack specialist time for annotation.
arxiv-2512-04975:
Sitaram Ramakrishnan and a large team of co-authors map how the layered nickel compound La4Ni3O10 changes its crystal structure under pressure and heat. Nickelates of this family can carry electric current with no resistance when squeezed, but the details of that behavior depend on which crystal form the material takes. At ordinary conditions the compound settles into a slanted, doubled structure.

Using X-rays on high-quality crystals grown from molten salts, the team shows the crystal switches straight from its high-temperature square form to the slanted form. There is no in-between stage, as some had expected. Computer calculations back the finding, and the switch can be pushed down toward very low temperatures by squeezing. The team also caught faint extra reflections tied to a wave-like ordering that had before been seen only in crystals grown a different way.
arxiv-2512-05075:
J. E. Pérez-Rodríguez, R. Esquivel-Sirvent, and A. Camacho de la Rosa study how plates drilled with elliptical holes steer heat carried by light at very small gaps. Patterned materials, called metamaterials, let engineers tune how surfaces interact with electromagnetic waves. Round holes keep the response the same in every direction. Stretching the holes into ellipses breaks that sameness and makes the response depend on direction. That knob is what the authors set out to measure.

Combining the theory of fluctuating electrodynamics with simulations, they compute the near-field heat flow between two such plates as orientation, stretch, and the gap between plates vary. The oval holes give sharper control over which wavelengths couple across the gap and how the surface waves excite, modulating the heat flux. The findings offer design rules for devices that must manage heat at the nanoscale or turn it into power.
arxiv-2512-05175:
J. A. Patel and six co-authors chart the weather of WASP-189 b, an ultra-hot Jupiter circling a hot, fast-spinning star. Using phase curves from the TESS space telescope, backed by archival data from CHEOPS, they watch the planet's glow rise and fall around its orbit. Planets this hot can depart strongly from cooler hot Jupiters, and the host star's spin squashes it, which transits can reveal.

Inverting the phase curve gives a temperature map of the planet. The dayside shines by its own heat, the nightside is effectively dark, and heat moves poorly from day to night. The gravity-darkened transits show the planet is on a near-polar orbit around its star. Comparing with earlier results turns up no sign of the orbit precessing. With atmospheric modelling, the picture is a world of fierce dayside heat, negligible reflected light, and extremely inefficient heat transport.
arxiv-2512-05775:
Longkang Zhu, Xinli Shi, Xiangping Xu, Jinde Cao, and Xiangyong Chen study optimization spread across a network, where machines must cooperate while the problem itself keeps changing. Two practical limits bite: talking to neighbors is costly, and true gradient information may be unavailable or noisy. Their 2025 framework, Online Compressed Gradient Tracking, attacks both. Messages between nodes are compressed, with an error compensation trick that keeps the squeezing from wrecking accuracy.

Two variants cover two feedback styles. One works from a single function value per step. The other uses stochastic gradients. Both lean on gradient tracking, so the distributed estimates stay aligned despite compression. The authors prove dynamic regret bounds for each variant: the running cost of their choices stays close to the moving best answer. Experiments confirm low regret with far less communication than standard schemes. The work speaks to systems where bandwidth, not computing, is scarce.
arxiv-2512-05875:
H Radhakrishnan, C Ortix, and J Venderbos define a new response quantity for two dimensional magnetic bilayers. A bilayer antiferromagnet has two atomic sheets with opposing magnetic order. Apply an electric field across the sheets, and the magnetization answers. The strength of that answer is what the authors name the layer dipole magnetoelectric polarizability. It mirrors a known spin quantity.

They derive a microscopic formula for the new quantity. They then evaluate it in two minimal models: a buckled square lattice, and a magnetic topological insulator bilayer. In the buckled lattice, part of the response turns out to be quasi-topological, a robust contribution tied to the layer pseudospin. That degree of freedom records which sheet an electron sits on. The result extends the topological magnetoelectric story into the bilayer world. It hands experimentalists a concrete, topology protected target.
arxiv-2512-05975:
Max Potratzki, Manuel Adams, Timo Bröhl, and Klaus Lehnertz invent a single number that says how irregular a time series is, and prove it knows the difference between order and chaos. They call it circulance. Signals become ordinal patterns, then a network of which pattern follows which. Circulance reads the topology of that network: how the flow of patterns circulates, or fails to.

On canonical model systems with known regimes, circulance sorted signals sensitively and robustly along a smooth spectrum from regularity to randomness. The measure then went to work on real, messy, high dimensional data: long term recordings of the human brain and of the Sun. In both, it separated distinct dynamical regimes. A number that moves when the regime changes earns its place.
arxiv-2512-06075:
Himansh Rathore, Gurtina Besla, Roeland van der Marel, and Nitya Kallivayalil argue the Small Magellanic Cloud is still reeling from a crash. The SMC's gas shows a smooth velocity gradient, long read as a spinning disk. But its stars do not rotate, its depth is oddly large, and its centers are offset. Their simulations find a culprit: a collision with the Large Magellanic Cloud one hundred million years ago.

The simulated SMC then matches the oddities. A tidal tail explains the depth; the gas gradient is radial motion, not rotation. Ram pressure killed the gas spin and shoved its center aside. Collisions like this remake irregular dwarfs into spheroidals. Reading the SMC as mid transformation changes every observation's meaning.
arxiv-2512-06375:
Dietmar Ferger and Niklas Rosar prove a limit result in probability theory about where the lowest points of random processes settle. They work with several families of random processes at once, each taking vector values and allowed to jump, in the class known as cadlag processes. For each family they track the point where the process reaches its minimum.

They show these lowest points, taken together, settle toward a random closed set built from the lowest points of the limit processes. When each limit process has just one lowest point, the result sharpens into the classic form: the lowest points converge to that single vector of minima. Results of this kind, called argmin theorems, underpin estimates in statistics where the answer is defined as the point that makes some random score smallest.
arxiv-2512-06575:
Fariza Dahes tests whether a compact image classification design that shone on brain scans also works on mammograms. The design builds on a small modern convolutional network. It adds a pooling fusion that mixes average and peak responses. It also adds a light channel attention block and a smoothing loss meant to keep features tidy. On Alzheimer brain images it had scored well while running on modest hardware.

Dahes retrained it on a mammography set merged from three public collections, against plainer rivals with the same added modules. The pooling fusion and attention block again lifted the ability to tell classes apart and cut missed cancers, the false negatives that matter most in screening. The smoothing loss, though, gave no measurable gain here, which suggests its value depends on the setting. Extra grading, heat maps of where the model looks, and a dashboard round out the study.
arxiv-2512-06775:
Han-Ze Li and five co authors test the quantum Mpemba effect in circuits where every part can reach every other. The classical Mpemba effect is the oddity that a hotter system can cool faster than a warm one. Its quantum cousin concerns how fast a system restores a broken symmetry, tracked here through entanglement asymmetry in random unitary circuits with a conserved charge and long range interactions.

They start from three kinds of tilted product states: aligned, alternating, and aligned with a central domain wall. The effect appears for the aligned starts at every interaction range. It never appears for the alternating starts. For the domain wall start it survives only when the interactions are effectively short ranged, with timing that scales as a power of subsystem size. The lesson is that interaction range and the charge bias of the start together decide whether the paradox shows up.
arxiv-2512-06975: Daniele Fargion and co-authors, including Maxim Yu Khlopov, predict an unusual glow near the Sun's dark disk in very high-energy sky surveys. Cosmic rays of very high energy skim past the Sun and can shatter into pions. Those fragments yield gamma photons and muons, and then pairs of electrons, bent and smeared as they travel. On Earth they would appear as gamma-like air showers, more plentiful than the rare true local gamma rays at such energies. The LHAASO array may soon observe these secondaries and disentangle them.
arxiv-2512-07075:
Shiwei Guo and co-authors ask whether large language models truly understand how cultures differ, or merely speak many languages. Fluency, they note, is not the same as grasping norms, values, and unspoken rules. Existing tests fall short in three ways: they lack real-life scenarios, map cultural concepts weakly between societies, and rarely demand deep cultural reasoning. The team's answer is SAGE, a scenario-based benchmark built by aligning core cultural concepts across societies.

Grounded in cultural theory, SAGE sorts cross-cultural skill into nine dimensions. From a few hundred core concepts the authors generated thousands of test items spread over fifteen everyday scenarios in four broad situation types. The set can keep growing, and trials show it transfers to other languages. Results expose patterned weaknesses in current models, varying by both dimension and scenario.
arxiv-2512-07175:
Yibo Wang and co-authors stabilize a training trick in which a language model teaches itself using its own output. Self-play fine-tuning mixes the model's synthetic samples with scarce real data, round after round. Existing versions judge progress by the gap between rewards on real and synthetic text. Ignoring the absolute values, and the authors show that focus can degenerate: training wobbles instead of settling. Their method, SPACE, borrows noise contrastive estimation to anchor the process to the real distribution.

Synthetic samples are treated as an auxiliary stream, and the model learns to tell them from real ones in a binary judgment. That keeps each stream's reward meaningful on its own, giving a steady objective. Theory shows the method's optimum matches the true data distribution and that convergence is provably stable.
arxiv-2512-07375:
Yezi Liu and co-authors present LUNE, a lightweight way to make a large language model forget specific facts. Models absorb vast knowledge in training and cannot easily drop a piece on request, yet privacy law, bias repair, and plain error correction all demand exactly that. Older unlearning recipes fine-tune the whole model or edit its weights directly, both expensive and disruptive. LUNE instead trains only small low-rank adapter modules, leaving the backbone frozen.

The training signal is negative only: examples teach the adapters to suppress, or replace, the targeted knowledge where it lives in the model's middle layers. Because so few parameters move, the edits stay local instead of warping the whole model. Across several factual unlearning tasks, LUNE matched the forgetting achieved by full fine-tuning and by memory-editing methods.
arxiv-2512-07675:
Miguel Calvo-Carrera and Peter Catto wrote this 2025 plasma physics paper on fusion stellarators. Stellarators confine plasma in a twisted magnetic cage for fusion energy. New designs are nearly quasisymmetric, which tames ordinary plasma transport.

Fusion-born alpha particles are the worry that remains in these designs. Collisions can trouble alphas that sit under resonant conditions. Near rational surfaces, small helical errors in the field change its direction and strength. Streaming motion and tangential drift nearly cancel for passing alphas there.  A thin collisional boundary layer then forms around the resonance. The authors build an analytical model of the resulting energy transport. Their drift kinetic treatment shows losses can grow significant near rational surfaces. Error fields with matching wave numbers drive the effect. They also test when the simpler quasilinear picture stays valid. It holds only below a limit on error size.
arxiv-2512-07775:
David Thorne, Nathan Chan, Christa Robison, Philip Osteen, and Brett Lopez wrote this 2025 robotics paper. Autonomous robots plan and perceive through geometric maps of their surroundings. LiDAR sensors pour out far more map data than any robot can store.

Different algorithms want different maps at different scales, compounding the problem. Picking a small, informative subset of the data is a hard combinatorial task. Their system, OptMap, distills maps online for the application at hand. Its engine maximizes set functions that show diminishing returns, called submodular functions. Polynomial-time algorithms for that job come with near-optimal guarantees. A novel reward function scores informativeness while shrinking input size and cutting bias. A streaming variant reorders the incoming scans on the fly. That trick improves quality and fights order bias.   Online change detection shows off its practical value for robots.
arxiv-2512-08075:
Christian Massao Konishi and Helio Pedrini, computer scientists in Brazil, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about detecting deforestation in the Amazon rainforest. Brazil official PRODES program monitors cleared areas each year from satellite images, and machine learning can support that work by comparing images over time. Earlier models, though, were hard to compare and often missed modern designs.

The authors evaluate many change detection models on one unified dataset, from fully convolutional networks to transformer based designs with self attention. They test pre and post processing tricks such as filtering small predicted patches and enhancing image texture. They also try combining models, which beat every single model on its own. Their best combined score matched recent published work. The study gives future deforestation detection research a cleaner, shared baseline to build on.
arxiv-2512-08275: Xiaojun Huang, Scott James, and Xiaoshan Li, mathematicians in complex geometry, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. They study a pseudoconvex domain in complex space of dimension above one, possibly unbounded, that has a special boundary point: a non smooth, strongly pseudoconvex polyhedral one. Their result concerns the Bergman metric of such a domain, a natural geometric structure built from its holomorphic functions. They prove this metric is not Einstein, ruling out a highly symmetric possibility for this class of domains.
arxiv-2512-08375:
Fernanda M Baeta, a mathematician in convex geometry, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. She studies valuations, rules that assign a number to each convex Lipschitz function defined on a polytope. Her goal is a complete characterization: a list showing that every valuation with certain symmetries has one fixed form.

Baeta proves that any valuation which is upper semicontinuous, respects affine changes of coordinates, and stays invariant under dual epi translations must be a combination of just three ingredients. Those are the domain volume, a constant term, and a surface area functional of affine type. She also establishes matching dual statements for finite valued convex functions. Characterizations like this matter because they show a whole class of measurements is governed by a few basic ones. For convex geometry, the result ties the young theory of functional valuations back to classical affine surface area.
arxiv-2512-08875:
Joshua Ward and coauthors show that language model based generation of synthetic tabular data can leak private training records through memorized digit strings. Two common approaches are studied: fine tuning smaller models on tables, and prompting larger models with examples in context. Both are widely used to create high quality synthetic data sets.

The authors introduce a simple membership inference attack that uses only the generated synthetic data. It targets the string sequences of numeric digits in synthetic rows. Across many models and data sets, the attack exposes large privacy leakage. In some cases it classifies membership almost perfectly, even for leading models. To counter the risk, the authors propose defenses, including a sampling strategy that perturbs digits during generation in a targeted way. Tests show that defense can defeat the attacks with only a small loss in fidelity and utility of the synthetic data.
arxiv-2512-09075:
Rohan Venkat, Soo May Wee, and Hsiao Wen Chen study whether gas absorption around galaxies depends on viewing angle. Their sample is a uniform set of isolated galaxies at low redshift from a Magellan halo survey. Archival imaging gives disk inclination and orientation for every galaxy,.

A subset also has calcium absorption measures. The authors compare absorption strength with projected and corrected distance from each galaxy. Across the full sample, no significant link between absorption strength and azimuthal angle is found. A seeming excess of strong magnesium absorbers near the major axis, in the well oriented subset, is not statistically significant under a rank test. Calcium absorption shows low covering fraction and no angle dependence. After accounting for projection and imaging biases, the absorber distribution looks random, with no firm evidence for directional structure at small distances.
arxiv-2512-09375:
Sihe Chen, Luv Verma, and Bruce A. Maxwell ask a basic question about neural radiance fields, models that learn a 3D scene from photos and render new views. Nearly all training uses ordinary sRGB images, and little attention has gone to the color space in which the network actually learns. A classic model of reflection suggests a logarithmic view of color might separate lighting from surface color more cleanly.

To test that idea, the authors filmed about thirty scenes with a GoPro camera, carefully recovering linear data. They trained radiance field models in several color spaces, including linear, sRGB, and log RGB, converting outputs to a common space for fair comparison. Log RGB space consistently rendered better quality, was more robust across scenes, and did especially well in low light, all at the same input bit depth. Tests across network sizes and model variants confirmed the advantage is stable.
arxiv-2512-09475:
Romain Dalidet leads a team presenting a precise way to measure how the spacing between resonances varies across an optical microresonator. That spacing, the free spectral range, reveals the device's group velocity dispersion, which governs how Kerr frequency combs behave. Combs are important light sources for photonics and quantum technology, so measuring them well matters.

Their method uses a fine wavemeter to read resonance positions over a broad five-terahertz bandwidth in silicon nitride microresonators. The whole setup is fiber-based and plug-and-play, making it easy to use compared with more elaborate rigs. By carefully studying each resonance's position, they extract both second- and third-order coefficients describing how the spacing expands. The authors offer the approach as a robust tool for dispersion work in integrated photonic circuits, supporting next-generation comb sources and quantum photonic devices.
arxiv-2512-09675:
Leyi Pan leads a team presenting d-TreeRPO, a reinforcement learning framework for diffusion large language models. Those are a newer kind of language model that generates text by refining noise rather than writing left to right. Reinforcement learning improves such models' reasoning, but existing methods are unreliable for two reasons. Rewards are sparse and hard to verify, which corrupts the advantage estimates training depends on. Their probability estimates also ignore the gap to the true expectation over all decoding orders.

Their framework uses tree-structured rollouts and computes advantages bottom-up from verifiable rewards, giving checkable step-by-step signals. They also prove that raising prediction confidence shrinks the probability estimation gap, and they add a time-scheduled self-distillation loss that boosts confidence late in training. Across reasoning benchmarks the method beat baselines and improved over the base model, with large gains on Sudoku and Countdown puzzles.
arxiv-2512-09775:
Vladimir Balditsyn and colleagues propose ways to quantify uncertainty in machine learning systems that run in computing settings, where models are embedded throughout daily infrastructure. Such systems cannot be engineered like ordinary software. Models are trained on high-dimensional examples rather than written to a specification. So the boundaries of where they work reliably are unknown, and error-free performance cannot be guaranteed.

The authors adapt and jointly apply a selected set of techniques for evaluating, at runtime, how relevant a model's outputs are. That attaches a trustworthiness signal to each output. They apply and evaluate the approach in human activity recognition, a domain that is highly varied and constantly changing, where sensor data and behavior patterns shift. Their results show the approach matters in that setting. The paper discusses the help the uncertainty information gives to domain experts who must decide when to rely on the system.
arxiv-2512-09975:
Nicolas Beldiceanu shows how to enforce a strong consistency property in constraint problems arranged as a grid. The setup has a matrix of variables. Each row must be accepted by a given finite automaton, a machine that checks sequences against a pattern. Each column must satisfy one shared constraint. Directly reasoning over the whole grid is expensive. Beldiceanu builds a synchronized product of the row automata, adapted to the column constraint, and uses it to decompose the problem in a Berge-acyclic way.

The decomposition uses one regular constraint and one table constraint per column. With it, generalized arc consistency is achieved: every value left in a variable's domain can still take part in a full solution. Applied to a hydrogen distribution problem, it finds optimal solutions and proves optimality quickly.
arxiv-2512-10075:
Jocelyn Nembé builds a universal scheme for how measure concentrates, the fact that random quantities in high dimensions hug their averages. The starting point is symmetry: if a probability law is reshaped by a smooth change of coordinates, its concentration traits transfer with it, in the pulled back geometry. Viewed this way, classic inequalities, Hoeffding, Bernstein, Talagrand, and Gaussian isoperimetry, become faces of one geometric invariance principle. The coordinate change is a free parameter, and Nembé proves a best one exists for any such class, pinned down through Fisher-Rao geometry.

For heavy tailed or multiplicative data, the best coordinates give far tighter bounds than the naive choice. The full theory covers transport cost inequalities, isoperimetric profiles, and functional inequalities, all set by the group of coordinate changes. Connections run to information geometry, optimal transport, and Riemannian theory.
arxiv-2512-10175:
Seog-Jin Kim and Rong Luo prove a coloring theorem for squares of sparse planar graphs. The square of a graph joins vertices that are at distance one or two, so coloring the square means nearby vertices all differ, a model for assigning frequencies without near interference. List coloring is the harder variant: each vertex may only use colors from its own list. Wegner conjectured tight bounds for squares of planar graphs decades ago, and the maximum degree three case is settled. Attention has turned to when six colors suffice for list coloring the square.

The authors prove six colors always suffice for planar graphs with maximum degree at most three that contain no cycles of lengths four through eight. Forbidding that band of short cycles buys the stronger bound. The result improves a 2008 theorem of Cranston and Kim, which needed more forbidden lengths.
arxiv-2512-10575:
Hang Ding and a large team take on reward modelling for role play, where a language model acts as a character with a set profile. Reward models guide models toward human preferences, but in open-ended, subjective territory like role play they drift far from human judgement, missing persona and style. The authors set out to measure that gap properly for the first time.

Their benchmark, RoleRMBench, grades reward models across seven fine-grained skills, from narrative management to role consistency and engagement. And it exposes large, consistent gaps for general-purpose models, worst in narrative and style. Their proposed model, RoleRM, learns from continuous implicit preferences, turning subjective ratings into consistent pairwise supervision. It beat strong open and closed reward models by a wide average margin, with the largest gains in narrative coherence and stylistic fidelity.
arxiv-2512-10675:
The Gemini Robotics Team report a way to grade robot policies inside a generated world. Video foundation models can simulate scenes realistically and at scale, but robot evaluation with them had mostly stayed close to the training distribution. The team built a generative evaluation system on the Veo video model, tuned for robot action conditioning and consistency across camera views.

Image editing and multi-view completion let the system vary scenes along several axes at once: new objects to handle, new backgrounds, new distractors. That fidelity let it predict the relative performance of policies in both ordinary and out-of-distribution conditions, measure which kind of novelty hurts most. And red-team policies for behaviour that breaks physical or semantic safety rules. The claims rest on more than sixteen hundred real-world evaluations of eight policy checkpoints across five tasks for a two-armed manipulator.
arxiv-2512-10775:
Antonio Ferreiro, Alex Fleuren, and Niels Martens ask a philosophy of physics question with real stakes for cosmology. In scalar-tensor theories of gravity, is the scalar field part of spacetime, or is it a form of matter? Such theories underpin mainstream models of inflation and dark energy. So the answer shapes what physicists think the universe is made of.

The authors focus on the Jordan and Einstein frames, two mathematically equivalent ways of presenting the same theory that swap the field between geometry and matter. Working through the interpretational options, they argue no clean categorisation survives: the spacetime-matter dichotomy becomes untenable here. Yet the category of spacetime can be pried apart from the category of gravity itself. And gravity stays a viable concept even when the dichotomy falls, a distinction they press as the paper's positive claim.
arxiv-2512-10875:
Julio Del Castillo, Mats Granath, and Evert van Nieuwenburg improve a workhorse algorithm for finding quantum ground states. Quantum imaginary-time evolution steers a system toward its lowest energy state, but running it on real hardware eats measurements. And both accuracy and cost hinge on how the Hamiltonian is divided into local domains and pieces. Their multiple-time variant changes the recipe itself.

Using more than one imaginary time in the evolution, they show, raises the fidelity of the prepared ground state and cuts the measurement overhead compared with the original algorithm. While keeping its deterministic character and its freedom from hand-designed ansätze. Unlike its predecessors, the method can be parallelised. Even for Hamiltonians with non-local interactions, where intuition says partitioning should hurt, they show a partition can still bring a computational advantage. The result is a cheaper, sharper ground-state tool for near-term quantum machines.
arxiv-2512-11175:
Jaden Sidhu, Sanaea Rose, and Frederic Rasio simulate how stars collide and age inside the dense clusters that surround giant black holes at galaxy centres. These nuclear star clusters pack stars so tightly that collisions can reshape the population and create exotic stars. Earlier work often treated collisions separately from the stars' own evolution.

The team followed a sample of sun like stars embedded in a relaxed cluster, evolving each star's mass, size, and life stage as collisions occurred. Near the black hole, most stars collided while still in their long stable phase. Farther out, collisions happened later, when stars had swollen into red giants. Which type dominates depends on how steeply star density rises toward the centre. The authors also estimate that several of the closest known stars to our own galaxy's black hole have likely collided during their lives.
arxiv-2512-11475:
Shifeng Xiong proposes a disarmingly simple replacement for the random sampling machinery that dominates Bayesian statistics. Bayesian computation usually runs Markov chain Monte Carlo to approximate a posterior spread that cannot be written down. The new discretization approximation instead evaluates the posterior density at a set of pre chosen support points and treats those values as probabilities of a discrete spread.

Every quantity of interest, from means and standard deviations to quantiles, is then read off the fully known discrete stand in. Xiong proves how fast the approach converges as points are added, and shows that quasi Monte Carlo point sets match the fastest integration rates, generally beating the best possible sampling rate. Procedures for drawing samples and summary points from the approach are included. Benchmarks in low and high dimensions performed well, suggesting a rule based route to everyday Bayesian work.
arxiv-2512-11875:
Ting Luo and Yan Wang study how authoritarian states craft stories about big events on social media. Their frame sorts events by two traits: whether they help or hurt regime legitimacy, and how easily citizens can check the official tale against other sources.

Using posts by government, state media, and celebrity accounts in China, the team extracts subject verb object triples to map the skeleton of each story. Across four major events, legitimacy stakes shaped how hard the state pushed and which beliefs it stressed. Citizen checking power shifted the balance between top down control and bottom up response. Propaganda, they conclude, is adaptive storytelling, tuned event by event to hold public trust.
arxiv-2512-12175:
Haoyang Chen, Richong Zhang, and Junfan Chen rethink how examples guide large language models in a 2025 paper. Models can learn a task from a few examples shown in the prompt. Picking those examples by likeness alone does not ensure their labels agree, and mixed labels can mislead the model.

The authors view the process as label spread across near items, and link label agreement to error bounds. They then build synthetic data that uses both meaning and labels, and pick examples with a method called TopK-SD. That method beat plain TopK picking on many benchmarks. The paper offers a fresh way to explain why in-context learning works.
arxiv-2512-12375:
Hyunkoo Lee and six co-authors present V-Warper for personalizing generated videos in a 2025 paper. The goal is a video that shows a user's subject, like a pet or product, while following a text prompt. Past methods need costly video based fine tuning or huge video data sets, and looks still drift across frames.

V-Warper needs no video training. A light first stage learns the subject's global look from a few reference images, using small adapters. At generation time, a second stage finds matching regions by meaning and warps rich appearance details into them, with masking for safety. Results kept identity better while holding prompt fit and motion.
arxiv-2512-12475:
Grace E Calkins, Jay W McMahon, and David C Woffinden adapt state transition tensors for aerocapture analysis in a 2025 paper. Aerocapture slows a spacecraft by dipping through a planet's atmosphere into orbit. Strong, changing drag forces make fast semi-analytical propagation hard. Transition tensors expand the flight path in a Taylor series, but full tensors need huge numbers of equations as dimensions grow.

Directional tensors project the state onto a smaller basis to cut that cost. The team builds new bases, including augmented Cauchy Green tensors tuned to targets like apoapsis radius, the orbit's far point. Their tensors cut cost while keeping accuracy on apoapsis and final energy, and beat older directional versions on key subsets.
arxiv-2512-12575:
Srimanta Middey and four co-authors review extreme disorder in crystalline perovskite oxides in a 2025 article. Perovskite oxides, with formula ABO3, are central to condensed matter physics for their rich electronic and magnetic behavior. High entropy oxides, where five or more elements share one crystal site, add extreme chemical disorder to that framework.

The review surveys fast progress in making and measuring these complex mixed perovskites. Embedding such disorder opens physical effects that plain oxides cannot reach, the authors argue. They summarize what is known about the properties of these materials. They also highlight key insights and promising paths for future research in this new design paradigm.
arxiv-2512-12775:
Pedro Henrique Luz de Araujo and four co-authors test whether persona assigned language models keep their roles over long conversations in a 2025 paper. Such models serve in education, health care, and social simulation, but they are usually judged in short, single round settings that do not reflect real use. Their protocol pairs long persona dialogues of over 100 rounds with evaluation data sets.

Across seven top open and closed weight models, persona fidelity degraded as dialogues grew, above all in goal oriented chats where role and instructions must hold together. A trade-off appeared: as fidelity faded, persona responses grew more like plain baseline responses, which at first had outperformed them on instructions. The protocol gives a systematic way to measure such failures.
arxiv-2512-12875:
Weihan Xu and a large team introduce a new task for media editing: removing one object from both the picture and the sound of a video at once. Past tools edit audio or video alone, so the two can fall out of sync. Paired training data for joint edits is also scarce.

The team built SAVEBench, a paired data set with text and mask guidance for object based edits. Their model, SAVE, edits sound and image in parallel and keeps them aligned. In tests, it removed target objects while keeping the rest of the scene intact. It kept better timing and meaning links than pairs of single-purpose editors.
arxiv-2512-13675:
Ziqian Tang and co-authors argue that classical gravity cannot easily fake gravity-induced entanglement through matter alone. Entanglement made by gravity is often read as proof that gravity is nonclassical. A rival claim says virtual matter moving between two masses could create the same effect with classical gravity.

The authors show that claim fails once realistic matter dynamics are included. For bound matter, binding turns the long-range link into an exponentially short one, with a decay length of only a few picometers. That is well below atomic size and negligible at test distances. For unbound matter, the channel stays negligible before wave packets overlap, and after overlap the masses are no longer separate systems.
arxiv-2512-13775:
Miguel Correia and Celina Pasiecznik prove two basic traits of resonances in scattering theory. Most particles in nature are unstable and appear as resonances, seen as poles on higher Riemann sheets of scattering amplitudes. The question is whether such objects behave like stable particles in key ways.

Using analyticity and unitarity, they show nonperturbatively that resonances are universal: a resonance generically appears in every S-matrix element. They also show factorization: amplitudes split on resonance poles as they do for stable particles. The frame works in any spacetime dimension and across many two-particle cuts, even with infinitely sheeted surfaces. Resonance data are fully encoded on the physical sheet, a result useful for S-matrix bootstrap work.
arxiv-2512-13875:
Michael C. Stanley and co-authors build confidence intervals for bond strength in composite parts checked without damage. Bonded composites are used more in aerospace, where parts must be certified for strength. Checking without damage can check bond traits, but its estimates carry uncertainty that must be gauged for safety.

Their method gives finite-sample intervals for the bond strengths that could match observed data. A statistical inverse model turns swept-frequency sound-wave phase data into an interval for interfacial stiffness, which a known regression maps to bond strength. A calibration step ensures the final interval meets the desired coverage. On simulated data, their method beat a baseline in high-noise settings, with better coverage and smaller intervals.
arxiv-2512-14375:
Aritra Bandyopadhyay, Moulindu Kundu, Victor Ambrus, and Maxim Chernodub study how local acceleration affects dilepton yields from quark gluon plasma in a 2025 paper. Dileptons are lepton pairs. Their yields encode key data on the hot, dense matter made in heavy ion collisions.

The authors treat acceleration as a small change and use a thermal Dirac propagator in an accelerated frame. From it they compute the photon response and extract its imaginary part. A check against the zero acceleration case isolates what acceleration adds to the yields. Such signs could help show how the plasma moves and expands in real collisions, a point the authors stress for future work.
arxiv-2512-14475:
Johann Glock, Clemens Bauer, and Martin Pinzger present Teralizer, a tool that upgrades ordinary Java unit tests into property-based tests. A normal test checks one input and output pair, leaving most inputs untested, while property-based tests try many inputs but demand hand-written rules. Teralizer instead reads the program's own code with symbolic analysis to extract the rules automatically.

On machine-generated tests, the converted tests caught a few percent more planted bugs. Gains on mature hand-written tests were tiny, and across 632 real projects fewer than two percent finished the conversion, mostly blocked by unsupported types. The authors close with a roadmap for fixing those barriers.
arxiv-2512-14575:
Johannes Schmitt settles which intersection numbers on the moduli space of curves are extreme. These numbers, built purely from psi-classes, count curve configurations and show up across geometry and physics. Given a list of exponents, he asks which lists make the resulting number smallest or largest.

Concentrating all weight on one class gives the minimum, while spreading it evenly gives the maximum, he proves, using positivity of the psi-classes and a log-concavity inequality. Just as notable is the method: AI models found and drafted the proof, with part machine-checked in Lean. Schmitt documents the prompts and logs so readers can judge the collaboration themselves.
arxiv-2512-14775: S. V. Chernov presents a math model of the photon ring, the thin ring of light that circles a black hole. The model gives the ring a real thickness instead of treating it as a sharp line, using a thick and lopsided Gaussian shape. Chernov works out the visibility function, the pattern a telescope array would record, along two directions at right angles. The sums cover baselines as long as six times the width of Earth. Such models help observers read the size and shape of black hole images.
arxiv-2512-15375:
Michael Brandenbursky and three coauthors study which measures of twisting survive when smooth maps give way to merely continuous ones. A quasimorphism is a map from a group to the real numbers that is almost a homomorphism, off by a bounded error. The known examples of Gambaudo-Ghys and Polterovich live on groups of volume keeping smooth maps of a manifold.

The authors pin down which of those measures extend in a continuous way to the group of measure keeping homeomorphisms that can be deformed to the identity. The extensions stay valid there, and act as cochains with semi bounded gaps on the full group. One payoff: some bi invariant metrics on the commutator subgroup are unbounded. They also give tests for when a homeomorphism is undistorted, so its powers grow at the slowest rate.
arxiv-2512-15675:
Georg Siedel and co authors show that stylized synthetic data further improves corruption robustness in a 2025 paper. Image classifiers often fail on corrupted inputs such as noise, blur, or weather effects. Synthetic training images help, and applying neural style transfer to them changes their look in ways standard quality scores dislike.

Those stylized images, despite worse Frechet Inception Distance scores, turn out to help training a lot. A systematic study varies both augmentations and their settings, and finds they complement each other and pair well with TrivialAugment, though not with every rule based method. The combined recipe sets state of the art robust accuracy on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and TinyImageNet-C.
arxiv-2512-15875:
Shuo Sun and co authors use tree tensor networks to compute molecular vibrational spectra in a 2025 paper. Vibrational spectra reveal how molecules move internally, but coupled vibrations in many dimensions defeat direct calculation. Tensor networks compress the needed quantum states into linked pieces whose shape, or topology, can be tuned.

The team tests tree shapes from simple matrix product chains to general trees where every node carries a physical leg, as in multilayer time dependent Hartree methods. Two eigensolvers are implemented. On a 64 dimensional oscillator model and on acetonitrile, all shapes reach high accuracy. Inverse iteration refinement brings all 84 acetonitrile states below 1 wavenumber of error, and a comb like tree balances cost and accuracy best.
arxiv-2512-15975:
Laurence Boxer criticizes fixed point claims in digital topology in a 2025 paper, the eleventh in a series. Digital topology studies images made of discrete points, and fixed point theorems there claim that certain self maps must leave a point unmoved. A stream of papers has asserted such results with flawed proofs.

Boxer discusses publications whose assertions are incorrect, incorrectly proven, trivial, or incoherently stated, with sources given for copied or paraphrased material. The note continues the author's earlier papers on the same problem. Its purpose is corrective: to keep the record straight on which fixed point claims in digital metric spaces actually hold.
arxiv-2512-16075:
Hao Tang and four co-authors improve brain imaging in their 2025 arXiv paper. Diffusion MRI can map the direction of nerve fibers in white matter, a measure called fiber orientation distribution. A quick, low-detail scan gives rough results, while a long, high-detail scan is hard on patients and clinics.

The team built FOD-Diff, a 3D diffusion model that predicts the high-detail result from the quick scan. It works on small patches of the brain, uses known brain anatomy to guide learning, and adds attention steps that capture links among the many numbers describing each fiber bundle. In experiments, FOD-Diff beat other state-of-the-art methods at reconstructing the detailed fiber maps. Better maps from short scans could widen the use of this imaging in care and research.
arxiv-2512-16375:
Yotham Cohen, Ealeal Bear, and Noam Soker simulate hungry stars in an arXiv paper published in 2025, accepted by an astronomical society journal. A stripped-envelope star like a Wolf-Rayet has lost its outer hydrogen layers. When such a star gains mass quickly, it normally puffs up, which should prevent a stable accretion disk from forming.

Using the MESA stellar evolution code, the team built a Wolf-Rayet model of 6.03 solar masses and fed it at a high rate. They mimicked jets from the accretion disk stripping away the inflated outer envelope, in hundreds of pulses that alternate adding and removing mass. Removing tens of percent of the added mass cut the expansion by a factor of about two to five. The star keeps a deep gravity well, the disk survives, and large energy release follows, supporting models of luminous red novae.
arxiv-2512-16575:
Yuka Fujii and three co-authors look for missing oceans in work posted to arXiv in 2025, in press at the Astronomical Journal. Future telescopes like the LIFE interferometer will image rocky planets directly and read their heat glow. A planet with no global ocean should show a strong day-night temperature contrast, so that gradient could betray the ocean's absence.

Using the planet Teegarden's Star b as a benchmark, with an equilibrium temperature near 280 kelvin, the team ran the ROCKE-3D climate model with and without oceans. Ocean-free cases with atmospheres of 1 to 10 bar produced phase-dependent flux changes that one-day LIFE observations at two orbital phases could detect. Snapshot spectra add diagnostics but need longer exposures. The authors warn that ignoring three-dimensional structure can bias readings and even fake a water band past 10 micrometers.
arxiv-2512-16775:
Nicolás Medina Sánchez and Borivoje Dakić rebuild the math of identical particles from scratch. Bosons and fermions are usually brought in through creation and annihilation rules tied to second quantization, the language of emission and absorption.

Their route takes quotients of the state space for distinct particles, grouping states that carry no clue about which particle is which. With three working terms, a labeled basis, invariance under mode mixing, and local counting, they derive a new class of creation-annihilation algebras. Those algebras give the partition functions of transtatistics, the broadest known generalization of bosons and fermions that fits the stated terms, widening the menu of particle types physics allows.
arxiv-2512-16975:
Haotian Ye and a large team present InfoTok, an adaptive video tokenizer guided by information theory. Discrete tokenizers squeeze video for language-style models, but fixed-rate squeezing wastes tokens on dull spans and starves rich ones.

The team proves data-blind training is suboptimal in length terms, then gives an ELBO-based algorithm that nears the best length. A transformer compressor built on it assigns tokens by information richness. In tests, InfoTok saved 20 percent of tokens with no loss in performance, and reached 2.3 times compression while still beating past adaptive tools. The result points to leaner, truer video records for multimodal models.
arxiv-2512-17175:
Pablo Rocha writes a short remark on Calderón-Hardy spaces with variable exponents, spaces where the integrability power varies by point. The note revisits a 2016 theorem of his own in Mathematical Inequalities and Applications.

The single aim is to improve the parameter q that appears in that theorem, volume 19, issue 3, pages 1013 to 1030.
