Sharper parameter ranges widen where the older result applies, since Hardy space bounds often hinge on tight exponent windows. The note is brief, six pages, and offers a cleaner statement for later work on variable exponent function spaces.
arxiv-2512-17375:
Tung-Ling Li, Yuhao Wu, and Hongliang Liu show how easily an AI judge can be fooled into saying yes. Many training pipelines let a language model grade answers with a yes or no verdict, and that verdict steers further training. The team finds the verdict rests on one shallow readout inside the model, easy to tip.

Their attack, AdvJudge-Zero, fishes odd tokens from the judge's own output habits and slips them into a reply. The tokens flipped verdicts in over 90 percent of cases in 22 of 24 test setups across six judge families. The same token pool then trained a defense that held up across model families. In training runs, the hardened judge avoided the reward collapses seen with the plain one.
arxiv-2512-17475:
Aaron D'Cruz and Pierre Ricco, engineers at the University of Sheffield, study what happens when a layer of fluid rests on an elastic solid that is shaken side to side. Their 2025 paper follows the motion from the first push onward, covering both the start up phase and the steady repeating pattern that follows.

Their math solution, written as series sums, tracks elastic waves bouncing inside the solid and motion dying away in the fluid. Short bursts appear each time a wave hits a boundary, while a longer settling phase reflects all the waves forming in the solid. The pair test the setup against three uses: measuring a fluid's viscosity indirectly, cutting turbulent drag, and sensing flows in living tissue.
arxiv-2512-17575:
Thomas Micol and three co-authors model how a tiny gas bubble sings differently when it pulses beside another object. Microbubbles are workhorses in ultrasound imaging and drug delivery, and each has a favorite ringing frequency. A nearby sphere, whether stiff, liquid, or jelly-like, bends that ringing in ways that carry information.

Their equations predict the shift from the bubble's size, the neighbor's material, and the gap between them, covering both round and wobbling modes. The payoff is a new probe: sweep the bubble's frequency beside a cell-like particle and read its stiffness from the response. That trick could sharpen elastography, the mapping of tissue softness, down to single cells.
arxiv-2512-17675:
Yudhistira Arief Wibowo runs a tuning study for diffusion models that upscale a single photo. The models dream up fine detail from a blurry low-resolution input, steered by conditioning methods that nudge each step toward matching the original. Those methods bring knobs, and nobody had ranked which knobs actually matter for picture quality.

One knob towers over the rest. The conditioning step size changed results far more than the number of diffusion steps, a surprise since step count gets most of the attention and compute. Step sizes between 2.0 and 3.0 won across the FFHQ face benchmark tests. For practitioners, the message is practical: spend tuning time on step size first, and save the compute that extra steps would burn.
arxiv-2512-17975:
Matthew VanDyke, Kexuan Wu, and Sukanta Bose built CoBiTS, a neural network that helps gravity wave hunters tell real signals from noise. Detectors like LIGO record many short glitches that can mimic a black hole merger. Staff now vet many candidates by hand, which is slow.

CoBiTS reads a short stretch of data from one detector and scores how likely it holds a real merger, a glitch, or both. It was best at high mass mergers set against blip and scattered light glitches, even when the two overlapped. Its design mixes local pattern layers with attention layers that track long range links, a pairing made for time series.
arxiv-2512-18775:
Amit Kumar Pandey and four co-authors peel a blistered film and watch it do something unexpected: roll. Blisters form when layered materials buckle under compression, from advanced two-dimensional materials to protective coatings. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, studies a blistered thin film stuck on a soft base.

Peeling from one end advances the peel front until, at a critical separation, the film's edge reattaches and the film starts rolling spontaneously across the substrate. The measured adhesion force drops sharply at the transition, then holds constant while rolling lasts. Experiments, scaling analysis, and molecular dynamics pin down the contact length that triggers rolling; it comes from the two contact edges interacting and does not depend on the work of adhesion. The effect offers a way to pattern adhesion strength across a surface that starts out uniform.
arxiv-2512-18875: Danil Gubarevich finishes a computation in Gromov-Witten theory, the branch of geometry that counts curves on a space. His space is an even-dimensional complete intersection of two quadrics, one of only two kinds of complete intersections whose Gromov-Witten theory breaks the expected symmetry. Xiaowen Hu had computed every genus-zero correlator but one, which his methods could not reach. This paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, supplies the missing invariant using Jun Li's degeneration formula, completing the genus-zero theory for these spaces.
arxiv-2512-18975:
Stanislav Jabuka and Ehsan Mirbagheri study when a finite distance structure can be faithfully placed inside Euclidean space with the l1 metric. They introduce the pair-cut cone: metrics built from nonnegative combinations of cut metrics that split off pairs of points. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, fully characterizes membership in this cone using quantities computed directly from the metric. They also prove that a metric obeying a system of inequalities lies in the full cut cone, making it l1-embeddable.

The payoff is geometric. The results are applied to sphere-of-influence graphs, where vertices connect when neighborhoods overlap. They decide which graphs admit such embeddings. The authors also exhibit a simple graph admitting no l1 metric from the pair-cut cone at all. Negative examples like this one mark the true boundary of the theory, guiding network designers who model proximity with overlapping spheres.
arxiv-2512-19175:
Amritansh Mehrotra, S. K. J. Pacif, and A. F. Santos put two rival pictures of cosmic expansion head to head. The standard model mixes dark energy with cold dark matter. The challenger, Rh equals ct, expands at one steady rate set by the cosmic horizon. Both are fit to the same fresh data.

The joint test uses cosmic chronometers, supernovae from Pantheon Plus, and DESI acoustic oscillation data. Standard scores and a Bayes factor compare the fits. The standard model wins on overall fit and naturally gives an early slowdown followed by late speedup, which the linear model cannot. Their age estimates differ by more than two billion years.
arxiv-2512-19475:
Ivan Decostanzi, Yelena Mejova, and Kyriaki Kalimeri automate the writing of humanitarian situation reports. Aid decisions ride on these reports, yet drafting them by hand is slow, costly, and uneven. Their framework turns piles of mixed crisis documents into structured, evidence-backed briefings with no human in the drafting loop.

The pipeline clusters texts by meaning, generates its own questions, extracts cited answers, and summarizes at several levels up to an executive brief. Across thirteen disasters and conflicts and more than eleven hundred ReliefWeb documents, questions scored high on relevance and importance. Extracted answers kept citations with solid precision and recall, and machine judging agreed with humans well.
arxiv-2512-19675:
Niclas Griesshaber and Jochen Streb turned multimodal language models loose on a mountain of German patent records. Their source material is 9,562 archival page scans holding 306,070 patents from 1877 to 1918, each page packed with twenty to fifty entries in double columns and mixed Gothic and Roman type. A pipeline built on Gemini models read the scans and structured the contents into a usable dataset.

Benchmarking against human research assistants brought a surprise: the models produced higher quality data, hundreds of times faster and cheaper. The authors open-source the datasets, benchmark, and pipeline so other historians can adapt them, then discuss the economics of this workflow. They present it as a paradigm shift for dataset construction in economic history.
arxiv-2512-19975:
Vincent Coll builds concrete algebra for bending Jordan algebras. These nonassociative algebras were born from quantum mechanics. A quartic identity, the Jordan identity, governs them. He works over a field of characteristic zero. There, the identity matches its standard four-variable polarization. He codes that polarization as a cubic map in the product itself. He calls it the Jordan defect. It vanishes just when the product is truly Jordan.

Linearizing the defect yields a deformation complex in low degrees. Three spaces are joined by two maps. The second cohomology sorts small deformations up to sameness. A named obstruction space holds the main block to extending them. Coll is plain about scope. The build takes only the low-degree part of the full theory. The revised text adds clear examples.
arxiv-2512-20175:
Izumi Hachisu and Maiko Kato explain why the fastest nova in the Galaxy also shone too brightly. V1674 Herculis faded by two magnitudes in about a day, the quickest classical nova known, yet peaked roughly a magnitude brighter than typical very fast novae, earning the superbright label. Their fully self-consistent outburst model, with optically thick winds on a massive white dwarf accreting at a trickle, reconstructs the event's timeline.

A strong reverse shock forms shortly after the white dwarf's photosphere reaches maximum expansion, and the shocked shell it creates stays optically thick while expanding at thousands of kilometers per second. That shell's own light, peaking as it swells to hundreds of solar radii, overtakes the wind's free-free emission and accounts for the superbrightness, while the gamma-ray peak arrives earlier, exactly as observed. A similar model fits another superbright nova, V1500 Cygni.
arxiv-2512-20575:
Matias von Bell and Cesar Ceballos introduce a lattice that quietly contains many famous ones. Flow polytopes, built from acyclic directed graphs, appear across combinatorics and optimization. For each framed graph, the authors define a framing lattice whose diagram is dual to a framed triangulation of the graph's flow polytope.

The Boolean lattice, the Tamari lattice, and the weak order on permutations all emerge as special cases. So do Cambrian lattices, permutree lattices, and many more named structures. The framing lattice proves semidistributive, congruence uniform, and polygonal, with faces only squares, pentagons, and hexagons. Connections to noncrossing partitions and gentle algebras round out a approach that reorganizes a crowded corner of lattice theory under one roof.
arxiv-2512-20675:
Simon Roy and co-authors strip a fashionable research area down to one variable. Vision-language models can supply dense rewards for embodied agents without human labels, and recent papers keep adding fancier learning objectives. But differing data, backbones, and evaluations make the claimed progress impossible to attribute.

Under a unified approach with identical backbones, fine-tuning data, and Meta-World evaluation environments, the team compares recent reward models head to head. Accuracy is judged by consistency with ground-truth reward and correlation with expert progress. A simple triplet loss beats the state-of-the-art methods outright. Much of the field's recent improvement, the authors suggest, came from data and architecture differences rather than the celebrated objectives. Simplicity wins the controlled race.
arxiv-2512-21475:
Xiaoqian Qi, Haoye Chai, Yue Wang, Zhaocheng Wang, and Yong Li work on predicting signal strength in mobile networks. The target quantity, reference signal received power, largely decides a user's communication quality. Operators who predict it well can tune wireless resources and raise throughput. Earlier methods miss how large-scale and small-scale fading intertwine.

Their framework, Channel-Diff, is a physics-informed conditional diffusion model. It draws prior knowledge from network parameters and detailed urban maps. Large-scale priors come from propagation and shadow-occlusion modeling; small-scale priors come from multipath modeling and street-level features. A two-stage training scheme with noise-prior guidance blends this physics with the diffusion network. Channel-Diff improves prediction accuracy by at least a quarter over baselines, transfers better to new settings, and trains efficiently.
arxiv-2512-22175:
Vatsal Baherwani, Yixuan Ren, and Abhinav Shrivastava ask when, during video generation, a diffusion model decides motion versus surface appearance. Practitioners long assumed early denoising steps shape motion and layout while later steps polish looks, but nobody had measured the split carefully. The authors measure it by injecting new conditions during chosen step ranges and tracking the trade-off between changed appearance and preserved motion.

Across several model designs, they always find an early motion-dominant regime and a later appearance-dominant one, with a usable boundary between them. They then simplify one-shot motion customization by training and running only inside the motion-dominant window. The recipe transfers motion strongly without extra debiasing modules or special objectives, and can plug into current editing methods.
arxiv-2512-22475:
Ajaykrishnan E S and Daniel Lokshtanov study fair division where the cake is a graph and every agent's share must stay connected. Exactly p vertices must be allocated so that nobody envies another's connected share. With additive valuations, they prove the problem stays computationally hard in those parameters. The hardness holds even on star graphs with numbers written in unary. That settles an open problem from a 2023 conference paper.

The contrast is sharp: tolerate even a slight amount of envy, and the problem becomes tractable in the same parameters. Their efficient parameterized approximation scheme works on general graphs and even with numbers in binary. The pair of results draws a precise line between exact fairness and near-fairness for connected allocations.
arxiv-2512-22775:
Drishti Gupta and Arun Thalapillil carry out a resurgence analysis of the Euler-Heisenberg Lagrangian, the quantum correction that describes how strong electric and magnetic fields interact with virtual quanta. Earlier studies covered fields arranged at right angles. Gupta and Thalapillil treat the most general constant background, focusing on parallel electric and magnetic fields, where the pattern of hidden singular points is much richer.

They derive large-order formulas for the weak-field expansion terms in both scalar and spinor versions of the theory, showing how two growth patterns mix. Dispersion tools then reveal that the full instanton pattern behind Schwinger pair production sits inside those divergent coefficients. Using improved Padé-Borel resummation, they rebuild the real and imaginary parts from just a modest number of coefficients, checking against exact formulas.
arxiv-2512-22875:
Shen-Shi Du and colleagues combine data from thirty-two gamma-ray bursts to test whether the speed of light is truly the same at all energies. If Lorentz invariance fails at very high energy, light of different energies from a distant burst arrives with small time lags. Each burst's lag pattern can then bound the quantum gravity energy scale. Single bursts give weak, noisy limits because their built-in lag behavior is uncertain.

A hierarchical Bayesian analysis pools the bursts while treating each one's intrinsic lag with flexible spline curves, which the authors identify as the dominant source of systematic error. The pooled limits still sit far below the Planck scale for the simplest models, and the overall verdict is no convincing sign of Lorentz violation in current burst data. The framework is offered as a rigorous template for future searches, including ones that add other cosmic messengers.
arxiv-2512-22975:
Flavia Bonomo-Braberman, Eric Brandwein, and Ignasi Sau study how hard it is to compute two graph parameters that generalize interval graphs. Interval graphs model overlapping intervals on a line. The thinness and simultaneous interval number measure how far an arbitrary graph sits from that tidy world. Their yardstick is modular cardinality: how few blocks, each drawn from a simple graph class, suffice to partition the graph's vertices.

For that parameter they give a linear kernel for the thinness problem and a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for the simultaneous interval number, the first parameterized algorithms known for either problem. Because modular cardinality generalizes older measures like neighborhood diversity and twin-cover number, the results cascade into new algorithms for those parameters too. They also show that under standard assumptions neither problem admits polynomial kernels for width measures such as treewidth or clique-width, marking where the tractability frontier lies.
arxiv-2512-23375:
Xiao Ma, Mohammad Hasyim Taufik, and Tariq Alkhalifah speed up seismic velocity model building, the step that turns recorded echoes into an image of the Earth's interior. Standard methods are accurate but slow, running costly wave simulations. Their framework pairs a neural operator with a generative diffusion prior to get high-resolution models.

The neural operator learns to produce time-lag migration images from trial models, acting as a fast surrogate for the usual modeling-then-migration chain. Through differentiation, the migration speed fed into one input channel is updated until the predicted images match the observed data's images. A diffusion model trained on high-resolution models regularizes the update, so predictions come out cleaner and sharper. Tests on synthetic and field data show the generative neural operator approach produces velocity models at a fraction of the usual cost.
arxiv-2512-23675:
Arnuv Tandon and thirteen co-authors reframe long-context language modeling as continual learning rather than architecture design. Instead of building ever more elaborate attention mechanisms, their model is a standard transformer with sliding-window attention that keeps learning while it reads. At test time it trains on the very context it is given, compressing that context into its own weights through next-token prediction.

Meta-learning during training teaches the model how to learn well at test time, making the method end-to-end in both phases. In scaling experiments, models trained this way tracked the context-length scaling of full-attention transformers, which rival sequence models failed to match, while inference latency stayed constant like a recurrent network's. For very long contexts it ran nearly three times faster than full attention. Code is public.
arxiv-2512-23775:
Amedeo Favitta reviews how axions, leading dark matter candidates, would have been produced if the Peccei-Quinn symmetry broke after cosmic inflation. In that scenario the early universe fills with cosmic strings and domain walls, topological defects whose decay releases axions. Predicting today's axion abundance means understanding those networks, and most estimates lean on huge classical simulations with large built-in doubts.

Favitta presents early results from a different, math-first framework built on nonequilibrium quantum field theory. Using the two-particle-irreducible effective action, the approach derives Fokker-Planck equations for network-wide quantities such as average energy density and typical velocity. The paper discusses how thermal effects, self-interactions, plasma friction, and quantum effects feed into the counts for QCD axions and heavier axion-like particles. It was submitted to the Proceedings of Science. The numbers are still rough, and the author says so.
arxiv-2512-24075:
Jiazhao Shi and five colleagues predict lane changes before they happen. Driver-assistance systems need such warnings a few seconds early. A driver's intent depends on more than the car's current state. Risk builds and fades over time. Gaps open and close. The target lane may not be usable.

The framework turns these pressures into time-based descriptors. They cover risk evolution and gap persistence. They also cover the value of the other lane. Interaction pressure from nearby vehicles is included. So are maneuver feasibility and intent consistency. These signals fuse with patterns learned from raw trajectories. The combined representation classifies the outcome. Choices are left change, right change, or no change. On two German highway datasets, scores stayed high. Results were especially strong near ramps.
arxiv-2512-24275:
Chenjing Bu builds moduli spaces for a class of complexes with extra symmetry. Moduli spaces organize families of geometric objects. The objects here are semistable complexes in Bridgeland's sense. They carry orthogonal or symplectic structure. They live on a smooth complex variety. Bu proposes the result as a compact way to complete spaces of bundles for the orthogonal and symplectic groups.

The spaces built are proper good moduli spaces of the stacks involved. Properness works like compactness. It ensures limiting objects stay inside the space. Supporting results come along the way. They concern fixed point stacks and their good moduli spaces. Mapping stacks from finite groupoids are covered as well. The paper serves geometers who build compact homes for bundle-like objects.
arxiv-2512-24475:
Akanksha Dagore and five colleagues check whether a space telescope's eye has dimmed with age. The Ultra-Violet Imaging Telescope flies on AstroSat, India's first multiwavelength observatory. It launched in September 2015. The telescope images in far- and near-ultraviolet light at once. Its near-ultraviolet channel failed in 2018. Contamination might slowly dull the far-ultraviolet optics.

Nine years of calibration data test that worry. Two steady targets anchor the check: the open cluster NGC 188 and the white dwarf HZ 4. Their far-ultraviolet brightness was tracked across the mission. No significant sensitivity loss appears over the nine years. No unexplained episodic dips appear either. The far-ultraviolet channel remains as sensitive as at launch. Long-lived ultraviolet astronomy from AstroSat rests on firm ground.
arxiv-2512-24675:
Kallal Pal and Sumit Chandok define a new geometric constant for Banach spaces, built from Heinz means and Birkhoff orthogonality. Heinz means sit between the geometric and arithmetic means, while orthogonality here is a generalized notion for normed spaces. Their work follows earlier studies of constants formed from points on a unit sphere.

Bounds are worked out for general spaces, exact values are found for Hilbert spaces, and uniformly non-square spaces are characterized. Links are drawn to convexity, smoothness, and the rectangular constant. Readers in functional analysis also get a characterization of the Radon plane whose unit sphere is a regular hexagon.
arxiv-2512-24775:
Zeray Hagos Gebrezabher reviews phase reduction, a method that replaces the full motion of a rhythmic system with a single phase variable. Oscillators appear across physics, biology, and engineering, and phase models make their interaction tractable. Isochrons, the sets of states sharing the same long-term phase, receive a firm geometric construction using the graph transform theorem.

Isochrons are shown to form an invariant, continuous structure across the basin of a stable limit cycle, clarifying what asymptotic phase means. Higher-order reductions are surveyed as an outlook. Students get a tutorial that joins practical technique with the geometry underneath it.
arxiv-2601-06675:
Tyler Lizzo and Larry Heck evaluate cross-lingual unlearning in multilingual models in 2026. Unlearning aims to remove specific facts from a trained model. Theirs is the first comprehensive evaluation across languages, they report.

They use translated TOFU benchmarks in seven language and script variants. Major unlearning algorithms are tested on those translated fact sets. Most fail to remove facts outside the training language, they find. Utility often remains high even while forgetting fails across languages. Subspace projection consistently outperforms the other methods they tested. It achieves strong cross-lingual forgetting with minimal degradation, they report. Privacy and compliance teams should note the central warning. Deleting a fact in English may leave it intact elsewhere.
arxiv-2601-06975: H. Salo and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with rings around irregular bodies. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Rings have been found around Chariklo, Haumea and Quaoar, three small objects of the Solar System. All these rings are observed near the second-order spin-orbit resonances (SORs) 1/3 or 5/7 with the central body. Suggesting an active confinement mechanism by these resonances. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07175:
Alejandro Radisic wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on pairings for the six-fold cube. The cube here is the set of all strings of six bits, each bit a zero or a one. A matching pairs up the strings, one partner for each. Radisic seeks pairings with a strict kind of balance, tied to the King Wen sequence.

The balance comes from a group of four moves called the Klein four-group, or K4. Two moves make the group: flip each bit, or read the string in reverse. A pairing is equivariant when it stays the same under those moves. For six bits, Radisic proves one such pairing beats all the rest. It uses pairs made by one move or the other, with no mix. Its total Hamming cost is 120. A pairing that used the flip move alone cost 192. The gap shows the gain from strict balance.
arxiv-2601-07475:
Haoqian Meng and colleagues address a hard trade-off in running large language models cheaply. Their 2026 preprint focuses on NVFP4, a fine-grained number format that can make LLM inference faster and lighter. The catch is adapting post-training quantization, which shrinks a trained model to fewer bits, to this new format. Several standard tricks break down at four bits.

Rotation-based methods, the authors explain, disturb the fine-grained block structure NVFP4 needs. Smoothing methods struggle because four-bit errors are large. Mixed-precision methods often clash with hardware built for one uniform precision. Their answer, named ARCQuant, uses augmented residual channels. The paper speaks to anyone trying to serve large models on limited hardware.
arxiv-2601-07675:
Kishan Padayachy, Ronald Richman, and Mario V. Wüthrich adapt a recursive reasoning model to insurance pricing on tabular data. Their 2026 preprint introduces Tab-TRM, short for Tabular Tiny Recursive Model. It draws on the Hierarchical Reasoning Model and its simpler successor, the Tiny Recursive Model. Those models solve problems by reasoning in repeated passes over a latent state. Insurance pricing, though, runs on tables of customer and policy features, not puzzles.

Tab-TRM makes its predictions by reasoning over the input features in that recursive style. Pricing is a core actuarial task where small accuracy gains matter across millions of policies. Tables are the native data form of insurance, yet most new architectures target text or images. A model family built for tables could close that gap. The paper serves actuaries and machine learning scholars who price risk, and tests if such reasoning works for tables.
arxiv-2601-07775:
Sarvin Bahmani and colleagues analyze games where chance, not a player, decides who moves at each node. Their 2026 preprint studies two-player games of infinite duration on a fixed finite graph. In classic random-turn games, control of each node is assigned randomly at every visit. The authors examine the complexity of solving such games. Complexity here means the computational cost of finding who wins.

Random control changes both strategy and analysis. Players must plan for moves they may or may not get to make. Infinite duration games model ongoing systems like controllers and protocols. Knowing the complexity class tells scholars which algorithms can exist. The paper serves theoretical computer scientists working on games and verification. It extends the random-turn idea beyond its classic setting.
arxiv-2601-07875:
Walter Smilga builds the Standard Model of particle physics from representations of spacetime symmetry, in a 2026 preprint. He starts with the Stern-Gerlach experiment, whose results yield the structure of a spin one-half particle. That structure is an irreducible unitary representation of the Poincaré group. Two-particle states in the corresponding representation take the form of integrals over product states. Smilga develops multi-particle representations on that base.

The Poincaré group encodes the symmetries of special relativity. Building particles as its representations is Wigner's classic program. Extending it to many particles tests whether the Standard Model's particle content follows naturally. The paper is phenomenological, starting from experiment rather than abstract axioms. It serves readers interested in the group-theoretic roots of particle physics. The approach asks how much of the Standard Model is forced by symmetry alone.
arxiv-2601-07975:
Fei Li and colleagues locate individual maize plants in drone imagery with a new transformer design. Accurate point-level identification of maize supports field phenotyping and automated stand assessment. Those tasks drive precision agriculture decisions like replanting and yield estimation. The team presents the Additive Kolmogorov-Arnold Transformer. It aims to represent fine-grained plant structures better and to analyze large aerial images reliably. Their 2026 preprint appears in an engineering AI journal.

Young maize plants are small and easily confused with weeds or soil patterns. Point-level output gives each plant a location, not just a field-level count. Kolmogorov-Arnold layers offer a different way to model the plant features. Efficiency matters because farm imagery is vast. The paper serves agricultural remote sensing scholars. It targets a concrete measurement that breeding and farming workflows need.
arxiv-2601-08075:
Simon Montoya-Bedoya and co-authors review ultrasound methods for lithium-ion batteries. Their 2026 arXiv review follows batteries across their whole life cycle, from production to use and aging. These batteries lead in consumer electronics, electric vehicles, and grid storage, yet their inner behavior stays partly unclear.

Standard monitors track voltage and sometimes temperature at the surface. That gives limited news about complex chemical processes inside the cell. Ultrasound can probe the interior without opening the battery. The review covers how sound-based methods monitor health, spot damage, and aid processing, giving battery researchers one map of a growing toolkit.
arxiv-2601-08575: A. S. Mikhaylov and V. S. Mikhaylov derive a dynamic representation of the Weyl solution for the Schrodinger operator. Their 2026 arXiv paper works on the semi-axis for certain classes of potentials. The approach rests on links to an initial-boundary value problem for the wave equation. That wave problem uses the same potential on the half-line. Connecting a stationary spectral object to a time-dependent problem can unlock new solution methods. The representation serves mathematical physicists who study scattering and inverse problems on half-lines.
arxiv-2601-09075:
Jimmie Adriazola and Katarzyna Roszak learn the past law of a quantum system that is open to the world. An open system leaks to its zone, so its next state rests on its past, not just its now. That past pull is held in a memory kernel, a sum that weighs how far past states still count. To find that sum from data is the hard task.

They cast the past law as a Volterra sum form. Volterra forms add up past acts with weights. From state tracks, they fit the weights. A reader who models open quantum gear gets a data first path. It may skip a full model of the zone, which is oft the part we know least.
arxiv-2601-09175:
Daiki Takesako works on when a set of linked smooth tools packs tight in a class of rough spaces. The tools are commutators, which gauge how far two steps are from a swap in order. They are built from a class of mean swing free functions and a part sum tool. The spaces are Morrey spaces, which gauge a function by its size on balls of each span.

He boosts past tight claims by a split of near closed parts of those spaces. Tight sets are key in proofs that a solve step can settle. A reader in this math field gets a more sharp tight test for a hard tool class.
arxiv-2601-09375:
Sudip Ranjan Bhuia and Puspendu Nag work in operator theory, on a class of operators built from Toeplitz structures. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies dual truncated Toeplitz operators and asks when such an operator attains its norm. The operators act on the orthogonal complement of a model space tied to an inner function.

Norm attainment asks whether some vector actually reaches the operator's largest stretch. The authors give a complete framework for deciding the question for this operator class. Results of this kind clarify the fine structure of function spaces used across analysis. They also guide work on related operators in control and signal problems.
arxiv-2601-09475:
An unnamed author's 2026 arXiv paper studies how to calm a quantum system whose equation turns degenerate at the edge. The work treats a degenerate Schrödinger equation with fractional integral damping. The damping term is singular and cannot be integrated in the usual way.

Two cases are handled: damping acting on the degenerate boundary and damping on the regular one. Using resolvent estimates, the author proves polynomial rates for how fast the energy decays. Decay rates tell engineers and physicists how quickly a disturbed system settles. The result adds a careful case to the theory of damped wave and Schrödinger systems.
arxiv-2601-09775:
Faruk Alpay and Bilge Senturk give a tropical reading of the transformer architecture. Their 2026 arXiv paper proves that self-attention, in the high-confidence limit, computes in the tropical semiring. That algebra, also called max-plus, replaces addition with maximum and multiplication with addition.

Taking the zero-temperature limit of softmax turns attention into a tropical matrix product. In that regime, a transformer acts like a tropical polynomial circuit. The result reframes a neural workhorse in exact algebraic terms. It turns a black-box tool into math that can be checked by hand. Such a view could support proofs about what transformers can and cannot compute in the end.
arxiv-2601-09975:
Samuel Blitz, A. Rod Gover, Jarosław Kopiński, and Andrew Waldron study a field law in curved space. The Yang Mills law rules fields like the weak and strong force fields. On a space with no fixed scale, one can seek a like law that keeps scale free form.

Such laws exist in even dims of six or more. They use higher rate terms than the base law. The team gives a short closed form for them. They also prove a key point. If a field meets the Einstein and Yang Mills laws, it meets this new law too. The new law is thus the weaker of the two.
arxiv-2601-10275:
Kei Beauduin proves a new rule for umbral operators. Umbral math treats a row of counts as if it were powers of one mark. That trick turns hard sums into short ones. Operators in this field shift one row to the next.

Beauduin proves a rule that holds for all such operators. That rule then marks out a sub class. In that class, the rule takes a short form. He sorts that class in full. He shows the results on known cases from the field. The work gives the field a new base rule to build on.
arxiv-2601-10475:
Xiaoyu Peng and co authors give a shape tool to test if a rig can be made passive. A passive rig takes in at least as much power as it gives out. Such rigs are firm and safe to link. A fix step can make a live rig passive by feed loops.

The team find a zone in the complex plane that holds the key. They name it the positive damping region. If a rig's plot lies in that zone, a fix with a set index can work. For one in one out rigs, the plot is a Nyquist curve. For wide rigs, a quotient form is used. The tool makes the test a shape check.
arxiv-2601-10875:
Jean-François Babadjian, Martin Rakovsky, and Rémy Rodiac study critical points of the Ambrosio-Tortorelli functional in two dimensions. That functional approximates sharp cracks and interfaces with a smooth phase field. A small parameter controls how thin the smooth zone is. Engineers and analysts use it to model fracture without tracking a crack's edge directly.

The authors follow families of critical points as the parameter shrinks to zero. Under a uniform energy bound, the pairs converge to a limit in the right space. They also track convergence of the phase-field energy itself. Such results certify that phase-field fracture models settle on the sharp physics they claim to mimic.
arxiv-2601-11575:
Sotirios Panagiotis Chytas and Vikas Singh explain LLM behavior with concept attractors. Their 2026 preprint uses iterated function systems for the frame. LLMs map related prompts to similar inner states. That holds at specific layers even when wording differs widely.

The team explains the pull with contractive mappings. In an iterated function system, maps shrink distances step by step. Layers then act as such maps inside the model. They draw states toward concept-specific attractors in space. An attractor is a point or set that paths fall into. This view predicts where representations settle by concept. Applications flow from knowing those stable landing points.
arxiv-2601-11675:
Ritik Raina and five coauthors generate metamers of human scene understanding. Their 2026 preprint presents a tool named MetamerGen. Human vision builds scenes from two kinds of data. The periphery gives low-resolution gist of the whole view.

Fixated spots add sparse but high-resolution detail. The brain merges both into a coherent scene sense. Metamers are scenes that feel alike despite physical differences. MetamerGen makes scenes aligned with latent human representations. Such scenes can probe what the visual system truly keeps. They can also fool it in controlled, useful ways. The work serves vision science and graphics alike.
arxiv-2601-11775:
Felix Adams, Daiwei Zhu, David W. Steuerman, A. Gilad Kusne, and Ichiro Takeuchi bring quantum kernel methods to self-run materials work. In such work, a smart loop picks the next test to run. The aim is to find good new materials with as few tests as can be done.

Each test costs time and stock, so data stay scarce by design. Kernel methods judge how alike two mixes are, which guides the search. A quantum kernel may map mixes in ways that are hard on plain machines. The study links this tool to the search for new mixes across a wide space of choices.
arxiv-2601-12075:
Mehrdad Farahani, Franziska Penzkofer, and Richard Johansson study when language models copy text in place of using stored facts. In retrieval work, a model must weigh facts in its weights against text in the prompt. False but apt prompt text can pull it to copy.

They pull a steering vector from model acts on a built data set. The set splits stray context, which should spark recall, from apt false context, which sparks copying. They find copying is easier to induce than recall. That gap matters for trust in retrieval systems.
arxiv-2601-12175:
Harrison Katz, Jess Needleman, and Liz Medina fit the spread of booking lead times on Airbnb. They treat each day's split of demand across lead days, from 0 to 365, as a compositional vector. They do this for two metrics: nights booked, a volume count, and gross booking value, a revenue count.

The data span 2,557 days, from January 2019 through December 2025, in a large North American region. They report three findings on how the two spreads differ in shape and tail. Hosts and platforms can use lead shapes to plan price and stock.
arxiv-2601-12275:
Paul Disberg, Arash Bahramian, and Ilya Mandel reconcile the kicks of millisecond pulsars, spider pulsars, and low-mass X-ray binaries. Millisecond pulsars are thought to form from X-ray binaries via a spider phase. In that phase, the pulsar eats its companion star.

Yet the system speeds of millisecond pulsars look much lower than those of binaries and spiders. That gap strains the story. The team seek a view that fits all three sets. Kicks set where such systems end up in the galaxy.  Speed data span all three groups in one frame.
arxiv-2601-12475:
Pedro B. Melo and five co authors work at the meeting point of quantum metrology and stochastic thermodynamics. Standard quantum metrology leans on averages over many runs. Its core tool, quantum Fisher information, is one such average. Averages can hide the swings that show up in a single shot, though. Real sensors live through single shots, not averages.

The team introduce conditional quantum Fisher information to fill that gap. The new quantity tracks information along single trajectories, not just in the mean. With it, they study speed limits at the trajectory level. Speed limits say how fast a quantum state can change at best. A trajectory level view gives a more honest bound for noisy, real world sensing.
arxiv-2601-12675:
Yongsheng Chen, Suddhasattwa Das, Wei Guo, and Xinghui Zhong rebuild dynamical systems from raw point cloud data. The data are unlabeled, but they capture the invariant measure of the system. That measure says where the system spends its time in the long run. Its density obeys the steady state Fokker Planck equation, a known physical law.

The team build a mesh free framework that joins physics informed neural networks with score matching. The physics law guides the network, while score matching fits the density shape. Rebuilding a system from its long run footprint is a hard inverse problem. A method that needs no labels and no mesh could serve many fields. Climate, fluids, and biology all produce such point cloud data.
arxiv-2601-12775:
Global ocean forecasting with graph neural networks is pursued in work with no author named in the record. Data driven ocean models have progressed rapidly in recent years. Applying them to global, eddy resolving forecasts remains limited, though. Eddies are the swirling currents that carry much of the ocean energy and heat.

The accurate representation of ocean dynamics across wide spatial scales is the core challenge. Small eddies and basin scale flows must be captured at once. The team use multi scale graph neural networks for this task. Graphs fit the irregular geometry of coastlines and ocean grids. A skillful global forecast would serve climate science, shipping, and fisheries.
arxiv-2601-13075:
Abhinav Rajeev Kumar, Dhruv Trehan, and Paras Chopra ask if an AI guide can coach young scholars. Many students have no access to an expert guide for research. The team asks if a smart tool can move an undergraduate from a rough idea to a full paper.

They built a tool named METIS for that task. It is aware of the stage of work and can call tools as it helps. Its parts include search of past work, picked guides, checks of method, and a memory of past steps. The team tests METIS head to head with two strong chat models, GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4. The study probes where an AI guide helps most and where a human guide still counts.
arxiv-2601-13575:
Thanh-Lam T. Nguyen and co-authors built a data set for likes stated with no plain compare words. Past work on comparative opinion mining read plain cues such as better than. Such cues are rare in real reviews. Most likes are hid. A user pans one item in one review and praises a next in a next review, with no cue to join them.

Their set, SUDO, holds same user reviews in pairs. From a pair, a tool must infer which item the user likes more. That is the true form of the task in the wild. For review teams, a set that fits the hid form gives a fair test past cue hunts.
arxiv-2601-13675:
Li Tuobang asks how monetary policy may lock in the labor share of income in 2026. The labor share is the slice of national income paid to workers. Modern macro theory treats this share as a core value set by top policymakers. They steer it through open market operations, the buying and selling of assets by a central bank.

Yet how that value is set, and if the way is sound, stays hotly debated. Li probes the anchoring effect, where policy pins the share in place. The paper also asks if the setting mechanism is rational. The answer bears on pay, growth, and fairness at national scale.
arxiv-2601-13875:
Henryk Gzyl draws a clear parallel between classical chance and quantum entanglement in 2026. The aim is to make the analogy explicit, in his own framing. On one side sits a classical system with two dependent random variables. On the other side sits a quantum system with two components.

Non-independent probability distributions are the classical core of the piece. Entangled states are the quantum core. Gzyl brings the analogy forth through conditional probabilities. Readers wary of spooky action at a distance get a calm bridge. Familiar stats ideas may ease the path into quantum thinking.
arxiv-2601-13975:
Marco Piccolo, Qiwei Han, Astrid van Toor, and Joachim Vanneste build a detection base for sea life surveys in 2026. Marine biodiversity monitoring needs scale and reliability across complex underwater sites. It supports conservation and invasive-species management. Existing detection tools show a pronounced deployment gap at new sites.

Performance often degrades sharply when a tool moves to fresh waters. Their unified information pipeline aims for robust assessment across heterogeneous domains. The work is the detection layer of a multi-year invasive species initiative. It targets Arctic and Atlantic marine ecosystems, where change is fast. A shared base lets teams in distinct seas use the same tools. That makes counts from site to site much more fair to compare.
arxiv-2601-14175:
Suvrat Raju and Praneeth Netrapalli model why language models err on tasks with one right answer in 2026. Arithmetic is a prime case: it requires a deterministic output. Repetitive processing of tokens from a small set of alternatives is an other. The team argues errors arise inside the attention mechanism.

Small errors in attention accumulate as processing proceeds. When they cross a threshold, the prediction flips to a wrong one. The team derives a quantitative two-parameter relationship from this insight. It links accuracy to the complexity of the task in a testable way.
arxiv-2601-14375:
Murray Brightman, Joahan Castañeda Jaimes, Daniel Stern, and Brian Grefenstette hunt brief X-ray flashes in this 2026 paper. Fast X-ray transients last from a few hundred seconds to a few hours. One enigmatic group of them has no clear origin. Such events have been known for several decades.

Most were found by chance in soft X-ray imaging observations. The team turns to data from NuSTAR, a space telescope for harder X-rays. Their search looks for fast transients in that archive. Readers get a census-style study of a puzzling class of flashes, plus the clues such a search can give about what makes them.
arxiv-2601-14475:
Yajvan Ravan, Aref Malek, Chester V. Dolph, and Nikhil Behari build a wildfire dataset in this 2026 paper. High-altitude, multi-spectral aerial imagery is scarce and expensive to acquire. Yet such data are necessary for advances in machine learning for high-impact problems like wildfire detection. The team introduces a human-annotated dataset from the NASA Autonomous Modular Sensor.

The sensor takes 12-channel aerial images at medium to high altitude, from 3 to 50 kilometers. The images match those used in current United States wildfire missions. Their system localizes wildfires in that imagery in real time with deep learning. Readers get both new data and a detection method trained for real mission conditions.
arxiv-2601-14575:
Mohammadjavad Habibivostakolaei studies moving shapes and their vibration tones in this 2026 math paper. His setting is an embedded annulus, a ring-shaped region. Its boundary evolves by curve shortening flow, which smooths a curve by shrinking its bends. The ambient surface evolves under the two-dimensional Ricci flow at the same time. The question is spectral stability: how steady the Dirichlet eigenvalues stay.

Eigenvalues here are the natural vibration frequencies of the ring. The author uses variational formulas, Rellich-type identities, and harmonic capacity methods. Those tools relate eigenvalue variations to geometric deficit and modulus. The math is dense. It is meant for experts in shape and flow, not for a first read in the field. Readers get quantitative bounds on how tones drift as both flows reshape the surface.
arxiv-2601-14775:
Claudio Gambino rebuilds gravity from quantum scattering in this 2026 thesis. The work sets up one frame that recovers the full content of General Relativity from the classical limit of quantum scattering amplitudes. Amplitudes describe how particles scatter. Their analytic structure, Gambino argues, is the mark of spacetime geometry left in the math.

The frame sets a direct link between quantum processes and classical gravitational observables. Those observables include metrics, deflection angles, and multipole moments. The title names the span: from quantum amplitudes to spacetime geometry, via a multipolar frame for black hole signatures. That is the claim of the work. It is a bold claim, and the work knows it. Each step is laid out so peers can check the chain.
arxiv-2601-14875:
Zhe Chang, Haodong Jin, Ying Sun, Yan Song, and Hui Yu aim to rebuild a moving face in 3D from just one video stream. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets 4D facial avatars, faces that change over time. Demand for such virtual humans keeps growing.

Neural Radiance Fields, or NeRF, can render a scene from learned data. But fine face detail is hard to catch from one camera view. Wrinkles that shift and faint skin texture can be lost. Their GAT-NeRF adds a geometry-aware transformer to sharpen that fine facial detail over time.
arxiv-2601-15275:
Multi-view transformers need a way to know where each image patch sits in space. A 2026 arXiv paper takes up that need with a geometric answer. The models process tokens from a set of posed input images, where each camera position is known.

The authors seek an encoding with three traits. It should mark each patch uniquely. It should let attention stay unchanged under rigid motions of the scene. It should also adapt to the scene's own geometry. Their RayRoPE uses projective rays for the encoding, with similarity tracked across many frequencies.
arxiv-2601-15675:
Rehinatu Usman and Onyedikachi J. Okeke map climate risk in one American city in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their focus is Greensboro, North Carolina, a midsize city in the Southeast. The region is changing rapidly, they note. Their study builds an integrated, intersectional view of climate vulnerability. It moves beyond generalized mapping, which can hide local hotspots.

The team combines several kinds of data at the census tract level. Demographic and socioeconomic data meet health and environmental data. They look for neighborhoods where flood exposure, chronic health burdens, and social disadvantage converge. That overlap marks intersectional risk. City leaders can use such maps to target aid. Cooling, drainage, and clinic support do the most good where risks stack.
arxiv-2601-16175:
Mert Yuksekgonul and coauthors let a model keep learning at test time to find new best marks. Their 2026 preprint asks how AI can find a new top result for a science task. Past test time search prompts a fixed model to try new paths. Here the model trains at test time on that one task. Its train gains skill tied to the task at hand.

Live train lets the model learn from its own tries on the task. Each try gives feed back the fixed path can not use. The team tests if live train beats fixed search. Gains would open a new way to push science tasks. The work frames test time as a train phase.
arxiv-2601-16275:
Xiangkai Sun and coauthors watch the trait lists of a conformal field theory in a lab. Their 2026 preprint deals with theories that look the same at all scales. Such theories sit at the heart of high energy maths. They also sit in maths of matter and phase change. Their trait lists, called spectra, set all acts of the theory.

To see a list in a lab is a rare, hard feat. The team sets up a system whose acts match the theory. Reads of that system then give the list terms. Lab lists test maths that was once pure proof. The work joins cold lab craft to deep field theory.
arxiv-2601-16375:
Andrey Lazarev and Rong Tang set a dual law for graded Lie rings. Their 2026 preprint deals with rings that carry a grade count. A known old law pairs the top sums of a plain Lie ring. That law is a Lie form of the Poincaré dual in shape maths. It pairs the high sums with low sums up to a shift.

The pair set the same law for rings with grades. Grade terms add shifts that the proof must track with care. A dual law lets teams read low sums from high ones. It cuts work in ring sum studies by half in kind. The work firms up graded ring maths.
arxiv-2601-16575:
Sabri Koraltan and a large team map the road for skyrmion work to 2026. Their 2026 preprint is a road map note for the field. Skyrmions are small twist forms in magnet stuff. They join deep maths worth to use in spin and wave gear. Past years brought big steps in stuff types that host them.

The map sums where the field stands and where it must go. Key needs span stuff, read tools and gear proofs. A shared map helps labs pick aims that count most. It also shows firms where use may come first. The work is a field guide writ by many hands.
arxiv-2601-16675:
David Kelly and Hana Chockler ask why sound tools tag songs in the ways they do. Such tools sort clips by style, mood, or type. Yet they often lean on cues that have no link to music. A stray noise or a side trait can tip the tag. Their 2026 preprint uses cause-based tests to find the true cues.

The team tweaks one trait at a time and watches the tag. This shows which traits truly drive the call. It also shows which traits are mere hitchhikers. Past work could fool these tools with ease. Few knew which cues the tools used. Clear cause maps can help build tools that judge songs by sound alone.
arxiv-2601-16975:
Nils Bruin and Brendan Creutz give a way to prove a curve has no whole points. Flat quartic curves are set by fourth-power rules. Some hold no points with whole or ratio marks. Past proofs for that fact were ad hoc. Their 2026 preprint builds a set path based on Brauer-Manin blocks.

Those blocks bar points when local facts clash in sum. The path can also bar splits of low depth. It spreads to smooth curves of all forms. Whole-point hunts sit at the core of number work. A set proof path saves years of case-by-case work.
arxiv-2601-17075:
Shayne Waldron works out rare group forms in quaternion math. His groups are rank-two reflection groups. Such groups act like mirror sets in four-dim space. Marks called systems of imprimitivity sort their acts. His 2026 preprint gives a plain path to find all those marks. Any rank-two group with a clear rule set can take the path.

Quaternion marks pack four real marks in one sign. Mirror acts in that world bend in rich ways. A full list of the marks aids pure group work. It may also feed codes in physics and graphics. Plain paths to full lists are prized in math.
arxiv-2601-17175:
Michael Klass and Victor de la Peña push past two famed rules on stopped sums. Wald's rule and the Optional Sampling rule are those two. Each tells when a stop time can be split from its sum. That split lets means work out as if free. Their 2026 preprint takes on mean-zero martingales in full breadth. Stops may run to no fin end in their frame.

Two core theorems and one broad yield fall out. Such yields firm up when stopped sums can be trusted. Chance work in trade, queues, and tests leans on them. Loose use of the old rules can mislead badly.
arxiv-2601-17275:
Lianlei Shan and four co-authors aim to make language model reasoning more stable. Big models write well, yet multi-step logic can still be shaky. Their output can look like pattern fit, not true step-by-step thought. Past fixes use reinforcement learning with a think-first style. The team adds contrastive learning in latent space to that mix.

Their method rewards sound inner paths and pushes away weak ones. The goal is steady, lean reasoning that holds up across tasks. Better logic in less space would cut cost and error at once. The work speaks to teams that need models to show their work. It tries to make that work more than surface text.
arxiv-2601-17975:
Bryan Min, Peiling Jiang, Zhicheng Huang, and Haijun Xia propose a gradual way to design AI-made user interfaces. Their 2026 preprint deals with generative UI, where a model builds screens from a user's prompt. Building good tools of this kind is hard. Users need to find the many ways a screen can be tuned, while the model keeps its full expressive range. Prompt boxes alone give few hints about what can be changed.

Classic design tools, on the other hand, show options but fix the form. The authors suggest growing the interface step by step as a design method for malleable software. Gradual growth can reveal choices as users need them. The work speaks to anyone building AI tools that users must shape to fit their tasks.
arxiv-2601-18175:
Daniel Russo asks what problem a popular learning trick actually solves. His 2026 preprint studies success conditioning. The recipe is simple: collect runs, find the ones that hit the goal, and train the policy to imitate those runs. It appears under many names, from rejection sampling with fine-tuning to Decision Transformers. Russo works out the optimization problem that this imitation truly solves. Knowing the real objective explains when the trick helps and when it misleads.

A clear answer can unify a scattered set of methods. It can also warn users away from cases where success filtering biases learning. The paper serves the theory of reinforcement learning and goal-based agents. Simple tricks deserve exact accounts, and this one is used everywhere.
arxiv-2601-18275:
Qiufang Yu, Mengmeng Wu, and Xingyu Lan study public views of social platforms where no one else is human. Their 2026 preprint examines multi-agent AI social apps. Apps such as Social.AI fill a feed with many AI agents that mimic human behavior. The result is a bot-centric social network, a new genre. Past research focused on one-on-one chatbots. Platforms where the crowd itself is artificial remain underexplored, so the authors turn to user opinions and experiences there.

What people seek from a crowd of bots is an open question. Companionship, play, and audience all may play a part. The study gives designers and critics a first map of that terrain.
arxiv-2601-18375:
Jonas Golde and three colleagues tackle a snag in sorting text into a tree of labels. Such trees sort items step by step, from broad groups down to fine ones. Real trees can confuse a model when the same leaf name shows up under two near twin parent groups. The model then has no clear line to learn.

Their fix, called TaxMorph, uses large language models to clean up the whole tree at once. The tool can rename a label or merge two labels. It can split one label in two or move a label to a new spot. A cleaner tree should give a model sharper lines to learn from. That in turn should make the sorting of mail, forms, and files more firm and less prone to mix ups.
arxiv-2601-18475:
Xinhui Liu and six colleagues work on free-viewpoint video, where a viewer can move around a scene as it plays. To make that work, a system must rebuild the scene in three dims from a few cams. Live streams add hard caps: the build must be fast, the files must be small, and the view must still look real.

Their plan builds the scene from soft blobs of light, a trick famed for its speed. They stack those blobs in grades, from coarse to fine, so the stream can send just what each viewer needs. Fine grades can ride on top when the link is strong. The aim is smooth, sharp views on live streams with few cams. Such tech could serve sports, shows, and calls where users roam at will.
arxiv-2601-18675:
Aditya Kumar, Mario Cypko, and Oliver Amft teach tools to read the long health files of people with sick kidneys in a way that keeps the sense of the file. Each file is a long chain of tests, drugs, and stays. A tool can crush that chain into a short code that sums up the path of the disease. Most such codes are built to ace one task and are hard to read.

The team ask if a code can stay clear and of use for many tasks at once. They vary how the tool is built and grade how that shifts the worth of the code. A clear code that keeps its skill could serve many wards at once. It could also help staff see why a tool makes a call. Kidney care, with its long files, is a hard test case.
arxiv-2601-18875:
Alberto Salvio gives a full study of how gauge worlds act when they are hot and when they spin. Gauge worlds are the maths home of the forces we know: light, the weak force, and the strong force. Most past work set the heat and the stores of such a world, then read its acts. Spin was left out, or dealt with in plain cases with no gauge force at play.

Salvio takes in all gauge worlds at once, with any store of stuff at their side. The spin of the whole is a set trait, like heat. His study gives the base rules for how such worlds act in that full case. Worlds that spin show up in stars that crash and in the young cosmos. A firm base could guide work on both. It fills a gap in the books of the field.
arxiv-2601-19175:
Jinkyu Sung, Myunggeum Jee, and Joonseok Lee predict whether a link in a network is friendly or hostile. Signed graphs mark each edge as positive or negative, like trust or distrust. The negative edges break the usual rule that neighbors are alike, so standard graph methods stumble without extra machinery.

Their model, built on CopulaGNN, captures how edges relate to each other, not just how nodes do. Linked signs often move together, and modeling that tie should sharpen each guess. Signed predictions serve fraud hunting, social platform health, and any field where ties can turn sour.
arxiv-2601-19375:
Quy-Anh Dang and Chris Ngo steer language model behavior by picking the right layers to nudge. Aligned models still fall to adversarial prompts that coax out harmful acts. Activation steering pushes the model's inner signals at run time. It is a promising defense, but old methods need careful tuning or give only on off control.

Their method selects layers by how well they discriminate the target behavior, and keeps the signal's size intact. Norm preserving control should be steadier across prompts. Run time steering that is stable and selective is a practical guard for deployed models.
arxiv-2601-19475:
Jia-Lin Pei, Guo-Liang Ma, and Adam Bzdak study a puzzle in the physics of particle collisions. Their subject is how pairs of particles spread in angle around the collision point. A standard pattern, called factorization, says this spread can be split into clean, separate parts. The authors ask what breaks that neat pattern.

Measurements from the CMS detector, in collisions of protons with lead nuclei, break the pattern in a way that fluid models do not predict. The team traces the break to a basic rule: total sideways momentum must be conserved. That rule links the particles to each other and spoils the clean split. The result gives physicists a sharper tool for reading flow in small collision systems.
arxiv-2601-19575:
Luisa Jansen, Tim Ulmann, Robine Jordi, and Malte Elson study how research data gets anonymized. Studies on people produce data that others may reuse, but names and details must be stripped first. Recent checks suggest researchers often struggle with this task. Clear, hands-on guidance is scarce, so weak anonymization slips through.

The authors propose borrowing a trick from security testing: red teaming. One team attacks the data and tries to re-identify the people in it. The other team defends by improving the anonymization. Running the attack as a drill exposes flaws before real release. The method turns privacy from a checklist into a tested skill. It could help research groups share data with more confidence.
arxiv-2601-19675:
Hongyaoxing Gu and four colleagues work on shrinking large AI models so they run cheaper. Quantization stores a model's weights with fewer bits. Weight-only post-training methods are popular, but pushing below three bits per weight hurts accuracy badly. Fixing the damage usually needs costly fine-tuning.

Their method, LoPRo, revisits how weights are quantized at a basic level. It applies permuted block-wise rotation, shuffling and rotating blocks of weights before rounding them. Rotation spreads the hard-to-round values more evenly. The aim is better accuracy in the very low-bit range without retraining. Smaller models mean cheaper servers and wider use on modest hardware. The work targets the regime where most current methods fail.
arxiv-2601-19775:
Beth Bjorkman, Sean English, and Johnathan Koch weigh the costs of watching a power grid. Phasor measurement units are sensors that report the grid's state in real time. Placing them is a graph problem called power domination: a set of sensors observes the whole network. Each unit costs money to install, but unobserved parts of the grid carry their own risks and costs.

The authors propose a cost function that balances the two sides. Their model counts both the price of sensors and the penalty for leaving parts unobserved. Grid operators can then choose placements that minimise total cost rather than sensor count alone. The work brings the mathematics closer to real budgeting. It suits utilities deciding how much visibility they can afford.
arxiv-2601-19875:
Stephen McCormick writes on how mass is defined for weighted geometric spaces. In general relativity, the mass of an isolated system is a subtle geometric invariant. Baldauf and Ozuch defined a weighted version for spaces carrying a density. McCormick shows this weighted mass arises naturally from a geometric construction due to Michel, applied to a certain weighted curvature map.

From the same construction he derives a matching definition of the centre of mass. Natural definitions matter because they tend to satisfy the inequalities physicists expect. The note also proves a Riemannian Penrose inequality in this weighted setting. Such inequalities link mass to the size of black hole horizons. The work tidies the foundations of weighted geometry.
arxiv-2601-20075:
Chuan Qin and colleagues make a leading vision-language model easier to interpret without giving up accuracy. CLIP learns joint representations of images and text and now underpins many multimodal systems. Its internal representations are dense and opaque. That opacity blocks inspection of why the model matches an image to a caption.

Their method, Sparse CLIP, co-optimizes interpretability and performance during contrastive training. Sparse representations use few active features, so each feature can carry a readable meaning. The challenge is staying sparse without losing the accuracy that made CLIP useful. Interpretable backbones matter as these models enter products and audits. The work seeks concepts a human can name inside the model's space.
arxiv-2601-20375:
Wei Huang and four colleagues present LLM-AutoDP, a system that uses language model agents to clean and prepare data for fine-tuning. Models tuned on domain data do better in specialized fields, but such data often hold many low-quality samples. Data processing strategies are usually built by hand, through rounds of manual analysis and trial and error.

LLM-AutoDP automates that loop with agents. Automating data prep matters because data quality, more than the tuning itself, often decides the result. A working system could let small teams fine-tune strong domain models without a long manual cleanup first.
arxiv-2601-20775:
Arshia Soltani Moakhar and four co-authors sharpen the theory of learning decision trees by asking questions wisely. Their 2026 paper advances active learning for decision trees as binary classifiers. Active learning picks which examples to label next. Good picks cut the total labels a learner needs. Decision trees are a classic, readable classifier. The paper provides the first analysis of the disagreement coefficient for them.

The disagreement coefficient is a key parameter in label complexity. It measures how much candidate trees quarrel near the best one. Bounding it for trees unlocks provable guarantees on label savings. The authors claim two main contributions in this direction. Their results tell practitioners when active tree learning provably pays. Theory of this kind turns a heuristic art into a budgeted science.
arxiv-2601-20875:
Md Muhtasim Munif Fahim and seven co-authors map how the world's development goals push on each other. Their 2026 paper studies the network of Sustainable Development Goals, or SDGs. Reaching the 2030 goals depends on strategic resource distribution. Money spent on one goal can lift or drag others. The team proposes a causal discovery framework to chart those links.

The framework combines panel vector autoregression with PCMCI+, a test for conditional independence. It includes country-specific fixed effects to respect local context. The data cover one hundred sixty-eight countries from 2000 to 2025. The authors aim to build the first complete causal architecture of SDG dependencies. Such a map could guide funders toward moves with the widest benefit. It turns a slogan about linked goals into a chart of cause and effect.
arxiv-2601-20975:
Nikita Gupta and a large team of co-authors build a harder test for AI research agents. Their 2026 paper introduces DeepSearchQA. It is a benchmark of nine hundred prompts for deep research agents. The tasks demand difficult, multi-step information seeking. They span seventeen different fields. Unlike older tests, this one does not target single-answer retrieval. Nor does it reward broad but shallow factuality.

Each task is hand-crafted to require a complex search plan. The agent must gather evidence step by step. Success means an exhaustive answer list, not one lucky hit. That design bridges what the authors call the comprehensiveness gap. Many agents answer the first part of a hard question and stop. DeepSearchQA grades the whole job. It gives labs a sterner measure of research skill.
arxiv-2601-21075:
Gustavo de Oliveira, Thiago Moreira, and Lucas Chibebe Céleri compute particles born from shaking emptiness. Their 2026 paper studies the dynamical Casimir effect under gravitational waves. Several striking effects arise when quantum fields face dynamical perturbations. Hawking and Unruh effects are famous cousins. The dynamical Casimir effect creates particles from a changing cavity. Here one mirror of an ideal cavity moves.

The mirror's motion is driven by a passing gravitational wave. The authors compute how many particles that motion produces. Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime from violent cosmic events. Their effect on a lab cavity would be tiny but principled. The calculation joins quantum optics with gravity in a clean model. It shows, in theory, how spacetime ripples can stir the quantum vacuum.
arxiv-2601-21175:
A depth-aware machine learning framework for bubble characterization in two-phase flows is presented in this 2026 paper. Understanding the three-dimensional motion of bubbles is essential for interpreting transport and mixing in multiphase flows. Bubbles deform under shear and move rapidly through the flow field. In many laboratory setups, only a single high-speed camera is available. That limits measurements to two dimensions. The framework aims to recover depth from that single view.

Two-phase flows mix gas and liquid in reactors, pipes, and cooling systems. Bubble size and motion govern how heat and mass move. A depth-aware method upgrades cheap single-camera rigs. It infers the missing dimension with machine learning. Better bubble data sharpen models of mixing and transport. The paper serves engineers who study flows they cannot fully see.
arxiv-2601-21375:
Zheng Li and co-authors build a test of teaching skill for language models. Models are often used as study helpers, yet most tests grade them on solving problems, not on teaching. A model can know an answer and still fail to help a student learn it.

Their framework, TeachBench, is grounded in real course syllabi. It grades a model by how much a student's results improve after several rounds of instruction. That shifts the target from right answers to real learning gains. The benchmark gives schools and builders a clearer way to judge AI tutors.
arxiv-2601-21575:
Kirti Sahu and Ranjit Mehatari compute the smallest graphs whose symmetry group is a Hamiltonian group. A Hamiltonian group is a non-commutative group where every subgroup is normal, a rare and tidy structure. Graphs with exactly that group of symmetries are of special interest in algebra.

The authors find the minimal orders of such graphs. They also study the fixing number, the fewest vertices to pin down so no symmetry survives. Both numbers measure how cheaply a tidy group can be realized as pure symmetry. The results add concrete data to the link between group theory and graph design.
arxiv-2601-21775:
Germain Vivier-Ardisson, Michaël Sander, Axel Parmentier, and Mathieu Blondel make two classic selection tools usable inside neural networks. The knapsack operator and the top-k operator pick discrete subsets of variables, which is useful for sparse decisions. But both are piecewise constant, so their gradients are zero almost everywhere.

Without gradients, standard training cannot learn through them. The team's 2026 preprint casts both operators as dynamic programs and derives smooth, differentiable versions by softening the underlying recursions. That gives networks a principled way to learn selections end to end. Applications range from selecting features and items to ranking, wherever a model must choose a few winners and still be trainable.
arxiv-2601-21975:
Pranav Mahajan and co-authors study a gap between what language models say they value and what they actually choose. A model may endorse one value in words, then pick differently when acting in context. Earlier tests of this stated and revealed preference gap leaned on forced binary choices.

Binary prompts mix genuine preferences with artifacts of how the question is asked. The team's 2026 preprint systematically varies the elicitation protocol, the exact way preferences are drawn out, to see how much of the gap is real. How big that gap truly is matters for alignment work. A model whose stated values do not predict its choices cannot be trusted on its word alone.
arxiv-2601-22075:
Kirill Antonov and co-authors search for better camera and instrument lenses with an evolutionary method. Designing a high-performance lens means exploring a high-dimensional space: surface curvatures, glass choices, element thicknesses, and spacings, all tightly constrained. Standard optimizers tend to converge to one local optimum.

That single answer hides many comparably good alternatives a designer might prefer for cost or manufacturability. The team's 2026 preprint guides an evolutionary algorithm with lens descriptors, summaries that keep the search diverse across design families. Better automated lens design feeds cameras, microscopes, and medical optics, where each design is a compromise among sharpness, size, weight, and price.
arxiv-2601-22275:
Cheng Liang and six co-authors speed up video-making models that now pay a steep cost for long clips. Their 2026 preprint, VMonarch, notes that the heed step in these models grows fast as clips grow. They found that real heed patterns in video are sparse and have clear shape.

A class of neat, sparse grids, called Monarch matrices, can match that shape well. The team build the heed step on those grids, with a swap-based method to fit them. The aim is rich video at far less cost. Long, sharp clips may get much cheaper to make.
arxiv-2601-22675:
Shuhan Ye and a large team tune spiking networks for video by matching their pass-band to motion. Spiking networks fire in pulses, saving energy and tracking time well. Their 2026 preprint notes that they shine on still images yet lag on video tasks. The cause, they find, is a pass-band mismatch.

Spiking dynamics act as low-pass filters, which blur the fast cues action needs. Their Fire on Motion method reshapes the band to fit moving scenes. Better video skill at low energy serves cameras and robots. The work names the flaw, then fixes it.
arxiv-2601-22975:
Ximing Lu and a large team offer a simple trick to create endless practice tasks for AI reasoning. Training with verifiable rewards has unlocked strong reasoning in language models. But it is bottlenecked by a shortage of tasks with checkable answers, so gains fade over long training.

Their trick synthesizes new tasks from ordinary internet text that has no built-in answers. Turning raw text into checkable practice could keep training gains going much longer. Cheap, endless tasks matter as models grow hungrier for good training data. Unverifiable internet text is abundant, so a working trick could unlock far more training material than curated sets offer.
arxiv-2603-01775:
Harry Stuart, Masahiro Kaneko, and Timothy Baldwin interview job candidates with an AI expert in this 2026 work. Resumes filter applicants on thin facts, while true expert interviews cost too much to run at scale. Their system aims to draw out rich, role-specific facts from each candidate at low cost.

A language model plays the expert interviewer and updates beliefs about each candidate as answers arrive. Beliefs track rubric traits, the scored qualities that define a good hire for the role. Updates stay calibrated, so stated confidence matches how close beliefs sit to true levels. In simulated interviews, beliefs converge toward the built-in ability levels of fake applicants. The team releases code, anonymized resumes, and calibration tests, which lets others probe both the promise and the risks of AI-led hiring screens.
arxiv-2603-01975:
Raquel Bosch-Romeu, Antonio Falco, and Jose-Antonio Rodriguez-Gallego compress categorical data with a tool borrowed from quantum theory. Their 2026 work builds a density matrix from class-conditional frequencies in labeled data. One-hot encoding places each record in a survey space, and columns tally feature counts per class.

A normalized Gram-type operator from that matrix meets the axioms of a density matrix. Its rank is bounded by the class count, which forces a naturally low-dimensional embedding. Dominant eigenmodes supply the spectral embedding where classification then takes place. Class-conditional density estimates plus a maximum-likelihood rule make the final calls in that space.
