Structural invariances and stability analysis back the method, with synthetic tests probing cardinality, sparsity, noise, and imbalance.
arxiv-2603-02475:
Vitor Pereira Matias, Márcus Vinícius Lobo Costa, and João Batista Neto lead this 2026 study, with Tiago Novello de Brito. AI models inherit bias from their training data, yet fine-grained skin tone lacks good public data. The classic six-tone medical scale represents real skin poorly. Small private sets also block repeatable fairness research.

Their open data set holds over forty thousand images of thousands of people. Labels use a ten-tone scale designed for visual accuracy. Classic vision methods score near chance on the task, they show. Deep learning, by contrast, approaches the accuracy of human annotators. A fine-tuned transformer generalizes best to unseen data sources. That model can audit fairness in large public face data sets.
arxiv-2603-02675:
Shuyi Zhou, Zeen Song, Wenwen Qiang, and colleagues diagnose why safety training for large language models can fail late in a reply. Their 2026 paper blames shallow alignment: a trick opening like Sure, here is can start a harmful answer. As the model writes such an opening, its inner signal of bad intent fades away.

Their fix, TSC-GRPO, first trains a probe that separates true intent from surface style using causal reasoning. Training then bakes that awareness into the model, with penalties that grow as harmful text piles up. In tests the method blocked jailbreak attacks far better than baselines while keeping normal skills intact. The goal is refusal that holds up at any point in a reply.
arxiv-2603-02975:
Bhathiya Rathnayake and Sijia Geng design inverter controls that hold voltage steady on weak grids, with proof. Grid-forming inverters must act like power plants, setting voltage and frequency themselves. Their 2026 controller follows a layered droop design, with an outer voltage loop feeding an inner current loop built by backstepping.

The grid's own voltage is treated as an unknown disturbance whose size need not be known in advance. A deadzone-based suppression scheme drives voltage errors into a small, pre-chosen residual band, with transients decaying at a rate the designer assigns. A separate safety filter, built on barrier functions, enforces hard current limits through a tiny optimization at each step. Simulations show faster recovery from current-limiting events than conventional designs.
arxiv-2603-03275:
Jessie Zixin Li and three others generate realistic human movement patterns that respect group differences. Mobility traces matter for public health and social science, and groups really do move in unlike ways. Yet most trajectory data sets carry no demographic labels, so generators ignore the differences. Their 2026 method, ATLAS, learns from aggregate clues only, never from labeled individuals.

ATLAS starts with unlabeled solo trajectories, region-level movement summaries, and census figures on each region's group mix. It then fine-tunes its generator so simulated movement matches the local aggregates while conditioned on group mix. On real data that does carry labels, ATLAS came far closer to true group patterns than rival methods and neared fully supervised training. The authors add theory on when the approach works, stressing local diversity and informative aggregates, and release their code.
arxiv-2603-03375:
David Wegmann's thesis rebuilds the mathematical foundations of UMAP, the beloved data visualization algorithm, and finds the original scaffolding cracked. UMAP, introduced in 2018, leans on a functor called metric realization from an unpublished draft by Spivak. That draft contains many errors, most copied into the UMAP paper and its successors. The thesis sets out to repair them all in one self-contained document.

Full derivations cover Spivak's functors and the finite variant used by UMAP's creators, with an explicit description of the metric realization and its relatives. The closing discussion turns to the algorithm itself. It examines claims about UMAP's properties and how closely the finite variant really corresponds to the shipped algorithm. For mathematically minded data scientists, the thesis separates what is proven from what is folklore.
arxiv-2603-03475:
Subramanyam Sahoo and three others show that a top mathematics model often reaches right answers by unreliable roads. Latent reasoning models, which think internally rather than writing steps, now serve in tutoring and decision support. Their 2026 audit of a leading seven-billion-parameter math model finds most of its correct predictions, about four in five, emerge through computationally inconsistent pathways. Only a minority rest on stable, faithful reasoning.

Nearly one prediction in eleven is a silent failure: confident and wrong. Measured reasoning quality correlates slightly negatively with correctness, an artifact of a binary scoring threshold. Growing the model nearly fivefold in size brought zero accuracy gain on the evaluated slice, though the authors flag that slice as small. About a fifth of latent plans resemble ordinary chain-of-thought. Their conclusion: headline accuracy can mask deep unreliability, and evaluation must measure stability directly.
arxiv-2603-03675:
Phenyo Phemelo Moletsane and four colleagues test whether offering lessons in a local language changes who learns. Most of the world's learners are multilingual, yet schooling rarely is. Their 2026 quasi-experiment follows nearly three thousand Ugandan learners in a non-formal engineering course delivered by radio and mobile phone. Each learner chose instruction in Leb Lango, English, or a hybrid of both.

The Leb Lango option drew disproportionately rural learners, those with less formal education, and those starting with least prior knowledge, widening participation among the disadvantaged. Merely offering it raised active participation even among learners registered for English. Leb Lango learners began behind but gained faster, finishing with examination results comparable to the English and hybrid groups. Local language choice, the authors conclude, is effective educational technology policy.

cairnes-character-logical-method-1875:
John Elliott Cairnes published The Character and Logical Method of Political Economy in 1875. Cairnes, an Irish economist, was the friend and heir of John Stuart Mill. His book asks a basic question: what kind of science is economics, and how should it reason?

Cairnes defends the deductive method, which starts from known facts about human motives and argues toward conclusions. He answers the German historical school, which wanted economics rebuilt from case studies alone. The book also fixes the limits of the science, separating what economics can settle from what belongs to politics or morals. Clear and firm, it became the classic statement of classical method, read wherever economists argued about how their subject should work.
chanson-croisade-albigeoise-vol-1-1875:
The Chanson de la Croisade Albigeoise is a long poem in Old Provençal that tells the Albigensian Crusade as it happened, from 1209 onward. Two poets made it: a cleric who cheered the crusaders, and a second, nameless hand who took the side of Toulouse. Paul Meyer edited the text in 1875, and this is his first tome. The language is the tongue of the troubadours.

Sieges, burnings of heretics, the fall of Béziers and Carcassonne, and the death of kings crowd the verse. No other work lets readers hear the south of France speak of its own ruin. Meyer adds the apparatus of a modern edition to the old song. It is the crusade's great vernacular narrative.
childers-pali-dictionary-1875:
Robert Caesar Childers gave Pali studies their first dictionary in 1875, A Dictionary of the Pali Language, his life's work. Pali, the language of the oldest Buddhist canon, had few tools for English readers before his book appeared. Childers built entries from the texts themselves, with roots, forms, and citations drawn from scripture and commentary.

Every translator of the Pali canon since has stood on this groundwork, directly or through those it taught. The dictionary also spread knowledge of Buddhist terms and ideas far beyond the academy walls. Childers died young, in the year of publication, yet his single great book founded a field's daily practice in the West.
cia-0000008775:
One week in South Vietnam, April 8 to 14, 1965, fills a CIA situation report on military and political affairs. American Marines had landed at Da Nang the month before, and bombing of the north was under way. Saigon's government, meanwhile, kept changing hands.

Weekly reports stitched battlefield news to the capital's unstable politics in a single judgment. Policymakers used them to track whether the war effort was gaining or slipping. This week's entry catches the conflict at its great turning point, when American ground war began. Reading it now shows escalation judged day by day, not in hindsight.
cia-0000009975:
An American prisoner of war was sighted in Tay Ninh province, South Vietnam, a report dated January 1973 states. Tay Ninh, northwest of Saigon against the Cambodian border, had been a Viet Cong stronghold all war long. The date places the sighting in the ceasefire month itself.

A prisoner seen in the border province as peace began posed the usual hard alternatives. He might be awaiting release, hidden, or misreported altogether. The report entered the postwar files where such questions lived for years. This entry preserves the Tay Ninh claim at the moment the war's fighting formally stopped.
cia-0000010475:
Key problems facing American efforts to strengthen the Near East are listed in a March 1951 CIA paper. The Near East of the title runs from Egypt toward Pakistan in the usage of the time. Washington wanted a friendly barrier along the Soviet Union's southern edge.

The paper names the obstacles plainly: nationalism, weak states, Arab-Israeli conflict, and oil politics. Such candor helps readers see why the grand design kept failing. Alliance schemes drawn in Washington met a region pushing the other way. This early file states the mismatch at the start of a decade of trying.
cia-0000012275:
What a spy sends must be listed. An undated CIA document, its year estimated as 1961, inventories materials and documents to be sent in the Penkovsky case. The manifest belongs to the working file of the operation that ran Oleg Penkovsky, the Soviet colonel whose product filled whole shelves. Lists like this one kept track of a haul too valuable to handle loosely.

The inventory names the pieces of the colonel's product and the papers that moved with them. It shows clerks accounting for secrets with the care of bankers counting cash. For readers, the list is the case file's own catalog of its treasures.
cia-0000012375:
Joseph J. Bulik wrote to the chief of the Soviet Russia division in April 1963 about Oleg Penkovsky, and the memo opens the case's internal reckoning. The colonel had fallen silent the previous October, arrested in Moscow. Now the division that ran him began its post-mortem, asking the hard questions while the wounds were still fresh and the trial still ahead.

Such memos began the lessons-learned work every lost case demands. They weighed tradecraft, warning signs, and choices made under pressure. For readers, Bulik's page is the after-action's first draft: the lost asset assessed by the men who knew him best.
cia-0000013675:
Foreign Relations of the United States, 1961–1963, Volume XXII, covers Northeast Asia. It belongs to the State Department's official documentary series, FRUS. The volume prints the Kennedy years' diplomatic record for the region. It gathers cables, memos, and meeting notes on Japan, Korea, and the China questions. Department historians chose and declassified the pieces. The book sits in this file as the published face of the era's secret diplomacy.

The FRUS volumes are the diplomatic historian's bedrock sources. This one documents the New Frontier's handling of its Pacific allies and rivals. For readers, it offers the government's own record beside the secret estimates.
cia-0000013875: A captured American pilot was seen in Thanh Hoa Province back in January 1966, and a CIA note dated August 5, 1967, records the sighting. cia-0000028175: Soviet preparations for the early launching of an earth satellite are reported in a CIA paper dated in 1957. In October that year Sputnik went up and stunned the American public. The northern region held the capital, Hanoi, and many wartime prison camps. Group sightings carried weight because they suggested organized detention, not strays.

The record preserves the sighting as another thread in the postwar search. Analysts compared its details with earlier reports from the same region. Standing alone it proved nothing. Joined with others, it helped draw the map of claims that investigators would spend the decade testing.
cia-0000042875:
El Salvador: Update 3 on Jesuit Killings is a CIA record dated January 2, 1990. The third numbered update followed the second within the same week. Fast numbering showed how closely the case was being tracked.

Inside, the probe's next steps are recorded in brief form. Brief updates favor facts over judgment, and this one is no exception to that useful rule. The series trusted the reader to draw the larger meaning from the dated facts. Names, hearings, and official statements make up its matter. The file's value is cumulative: set between updates two and four, it keeps the chronicle unbroken for anyone tracing the case today.

Inside, the roster of soldiers is handed over and preserved. Names near a crime scene are where investigations properly begin. The general's act could be read as candor or as control. Either way, the file marks the point at which the army's own paper began to name its men in the case that would define it.

The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000135975: The cable dated 6 January 1954 in the CIA files, now open, deals with detected surveillance of a residence, watchers spotted around a house the operation used. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136275: Dated 1 May 1954, a declassified CIA cable deals with broadcast tape production, the factory floor of the radio station and its daily output. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136375: Money for the new government is the subject of this July 1954 LINCOLN cable on immediate funding requirements. It is impossible to estimate funds remaining in CALLIGERIS's hands, the station admits, because the organization is broke and his receipts were never fully accounted. A PBSUCCESS budget estimate of 750,000 dollars for the period after 7 July was approved, plus 200,000 sent as a special fund. The cable recommends releasing 405,000 dollars at once to liquidate liberation army debts and pay families of the war dead.
cia-0000136875: Headquarters backs the LCFLUTTER team flight plan in this March 1954 cable. The travel rules are pure clandestine craft. Team members stay in different hotels. They meet only at the team point. Each man knows the other only by alias. One man will depart in April. The job can be done in both target areas by May, he estimates. Headquarters asks for more detail. It wants the black travel plan spelled out. It also asks whether the aircraft type is adequate.
cia-0000136975: Use the wire-service text, not the true text. Headquarters gives that advice to LINCOLN in May 1954. The subject is Molotov's reply to an appeal for assistance. Hours were spent on a London-datelined dispatch. It quotes Radio Moscow on Molotov's promise. The quoted language is garbled in this copy. The point survives anyway. For propaganda use, the press version served better than the verified original. Headquarters wanted the field to run with it.
cia-0000139475: A third 1986 report from the DCI's hostage location task force is preserved as document 0000139475. The task force existed because Americans were being seized and held in Beirut and elsewhere, and finding them fell in part to intelligence work. Its reports weighed sightings, sources, and guesses about hidden holding sites. The record for this item names no captive and no place. The file is best taken as one installment in a series that tracked a crisis Washington could not solve by force.
cia-0000141175:
Celina Romero de Gonzalez filed a death claim with the U.S. Department of Labor in March 1969 for her son, Juan Gonzalez Romero. The form says he died on 17 April 1961. That was the first day of the Bay of Pigs landing in Cuba, the CIA-run operation in which Cuban exile air crew flew and died. The claim names her as his mother and lists his brother Modesto among kin.

Forms like this one were the slow paper tail of the failed landing. Years after the event, a mother in Cuba had to state dates, kin, and facts of birth so the U.S. government could judge her claim for death benefits tied to secret work.
cia-06795975: Chernobyl's meltdown cost the Soviet economy dearly. This CIA study tallied the nuclear accident's economic fallout. The price of disaster, calculated. Its contents inform the historical record. This file preserves that declassified assessment. Kept for readers.
cia-06935075: SKUBISZEWSKI, KRZYSZTOF (POLAND), a CIA document. The Polish figure's file. This file preserves that declassified paper. Coming generations can find it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
creative-and-sexual-science-or-manhood-w: Creative and Sexual Science, 1875. The manhood and womanhood. This book preserves that work. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
daneau-dialogue-of-witches-english-1575:
Daneau's Latin dialogue on witches crossed into English in 1575, one year after the original. The translator signed only as T. T. Elizabethan readers could now meet Continental Reformed demonology in their own tongue, in plain English dress.

The dialogue teaches what witches are, how the devil works through them, and how judges should proceed. Ideas formed in Geneva thus entered English debate about its own witch trials. The hunt's theory crossed the Channel in this slim volume. Its arrival shows how fast print moved demonology between countries. English courts and pulpits would argue with Daneau's framework for decades.
darwin-insectivorous-plants-1875:
Charles Darwin published Insectivorous Plants in 1875, after years of experiments on plants that catch and digest insects. Sundews in his greenhouse at Down had caught his eye in 1860. He tested leaves with meat, insects, and chemicals to see how they moved and fed.

Darwin found that leaves of the sundew bend, secrete acid, and dissolve animal matter much like a stomach does. He tested many kinds, from Venus flytraps to butterworts, and mapped how each trap worked. The results stretched the line between plant and animal behavior. The book remains a landmark of plant study, built almost wholly on careful trials anyone could repeat at home.
declaration-causes-necessity-1775:
Congress issued its Declaration of Taking Up Arms in 1775. The full title speaks of the Causes and Necessity of that step. A year before independence, the colonies explain why they fight.

We have counted the cost, the text declares in famed words. Nothing, it says, is so dreadful as voluntary slavery to power. The delegates deny any wish to break from Britain just yet. They blame Parliament's taxes and troops for forcing arms into hands. The Revolution's manifesto sets terms that independence soon outgrew within a year. Its slavery line still echoes through the founding era's debates.
eddy-science-and-health-1875:
Mary Baker Eddy published Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures in 1875, after years of illness and Bible study. The book sets out her system of spiritual healing, in which disease is an error of mortal mind. It became the founding textbook of Christian Science.

Eddy argues that God is all, that matter and sickness have no true reality, and that right understanding heals the body. The closing section, the Key to the Scriptures, reads Genesis and Revelation as spiritual allegory rather than plain history. Her system built a worldwide church, with reading rooms and practitioners in many lands.
emerson-letters-and-social-aims-1875:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Letters and Social Aims in 1875, his final collection in his lifetime. The volume holds Poetry and Imagination, The Comic, Quotation and Originality, and Immortality among its essays in print. Emerson, aging and forgetful, had help from his children and friends in shaping this last book.

Poetry and Imagination restates his faith that metaphor is the mind's first and deepest native tongue in man. Quotation and Originality defends borrowing, since all minds are built from the thoughts of other minds before them. The Comic finds laughter a moral sense, and Immortality closes with serene trust beyond creed and proof in death. Persian Poetry and Social Aims show his range from Hafiz to the manners of American drawing rooms. The book is a gentle envoi to a forty-year career of American letters.
europmc-pmc10017475:
Pei and co-workers review research progress on the glutathione peroxidase family of proteins in a 2023 paper. These proteins, called GPX for short, guard cells against damage from oxygen-based waste. Keeping that chemical balance, known as redox balance, helps decide whether a cell lives or dies.

The review describes the family members and the jobs each one does. It links them to cell growth, death, and disease, and to possible new drugs. The paper gives readers an up-to-date guide to a protein family at the center of cell defense. It is written for both specialists and general readers.
europmc-pmc10268375:
Wu and colleagues review the molecular mechanisms by which tumors resist radiotherapy in a 2023 paper. Radiation is a standard treatment for most solid tumors, from lung and breast to brain cancers. When tumors resist it, local control fails and the cancer returns, so understanding resistance is a clinical priority.

The review explains how tumor cells repair radiation damage to their DNA. It covers low oxygen, stem-like cells, and other shields tumors use. It then surveys drugs and methods that aim to break that resistance and restore the power of radiation treatment.
europmc-pmc10504075:
Lesokhin led the MagnetisMM-3 trial in 2023 on a new antibody drug for a blood cancer that had come back. The cancer is multiple myeloma, which grows in the bone marrow. The drug, elranatamab, links two targets: BCMA on cancer cells and CD3 on immune T cells. That link drags T cells onto the cancer to kill it.

Cohort A held 123 patients with no prior BCMA-targeted care. Lesokhin reports a response rate of 61.0%, with 35.0% in full response. Half of the responders later switched to doses every two weeks. Most of them kept or deepened their response for six months or more. Infections were the most common side effect, at 69.9%.
europmc-pmc10584675:
Barrio-Hernandez and co-authors grouped the known protein universe by shape in 2023. Shape decides what a protein does, yet lab reads of shape lag far behind sequence reads. The AlphaFold data bank holds over 214 million predicted shapes. No past tool could sort that mass at speed.

Their method, Foldseek cluster, compares shapes far faster than older tools. It sorted all bank shapes into 2.30 million groups with more than one member. Of those, 31% had no known label, marking likely new structures. Barrio-Hernandez found that most groups are ancient in origin. About 4% seem tied to one species, hinting at new genes or weak predictions. Shape kinship also surfaced between human and microbe proteins.
europmc-pmc10764275:
Yisimayi and co-authors showed in 2024 that repeat Omicron exposure can break the grip of first-strain immune memory. Vaccines built on the first SARS-CoV-2 strain leave an imprint: the body recalls old antibodies first. That bias blunts replies to new variant boosters. The team tested mice and human groups to gauge the effect.

In mice, one Omicron boost failed when the variant sat far from the first strain. A second Omicron boost fixed much of that gap. In humans, repeat Omicron infections eased the imprint and bred wide defence in blood and nose. Yisimayi profiled 781 antibodies from repeat cases. Many were new, mature types aimed at fresh spots. The team urges dropping the old strain from updated vaccines.
europmc-pmc10767975:
Gargano and a vast team updated the Human Phenotype Ontology in 2024. The resource, called HPO, gives one shared set of terms for the traits of human disease. Computers can then compare cases and hunt gene causes by meaning, not just by words. Clinics and labs use it for diagnosis and gene finds.

Since the last report, 2,239 new terms joined the set. Gargano counts 49,235 new trait notes on diseases as well. Teams in psychiatry, cardiology, and immunity helped build them. The browser now shows terms in ten tongues besides English. A sister set, MAxO, now logs treatments and care steps. Work ties the terms into health records for rare disease care.
europmc-pmc11405275:
Hager and colleagues stress-test large language models on realistic clinical decisions in this 2024 study. AI language models ace medical licensing exams, but exams miss skills real practice needs. Those skills include gathering information, following guidelines, and fitting clinical workflows. The team built a testbed from a major intensive care database.

The dataset holds 2,400 real patient cases across four common abdominal diseases. State-of-the-art models diagnosed significantly worse than physicians across all pathologies, they found. The models followed neither diagnostic nor treatment guidelines reliably. They also failed to interpret laboratory results correctly. The authors warn this poses a serious risk to patients if deployed naively. They then test mitigations, including forcing the models to gather data step by step. Easy integration into workflows also proved difficult.
europmc-pmc1143775:
Arnsten and Dudley probe how a stimulant drug sharpens front-brain function, with relevance to ADHD, in this 2005 study. The drug is methylphenidate, the standard drug for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD. How it helps was unclear. The team used rats, at oral doses giving blood levels like those in humans, on a task that needs the prefrontal cortex, the brain area behind the forehead.

Moderate doses, 1.0 to 2.0 milligrams per kilogram, improved task performance clearly, they found. Higher doses made many rats repeat wrong choices. Blocking either of two receptors erased the gain: the alpha2 adrenoceptor, which answers an alertness chemical, or the dopamine D1 receptor. The authors conclude the drug works through both receptors in this brain area. That area works poorly in ADHD and is highly sensitive to alertness chemicals.
europmc-pmc12311175:
Tufail, Jiang, and Li reviewed how cancers hide from the immune system in 2025. Tumors that evade immune watch can grow unchecked. That evasion weakens many treatments and worsens outcomes. Understanding the tricks is key to beating them.

Tumors suppress nearby immune cells and exploit checkpoint brakes. Gene and chemical changes help them stay hidden. The tumor surroundings and altered fuel use add more cover. Uneven tumor makeup also blunts immune therapy. Tufail surveys fresh treatment ideas that target these escapes. The review maps limits of current immune drugs as well.
europmc-pmc1240575:
Donaldson, Stone, Seaton, and MacNee explored how air particles harm the heart in 2001. Past pollution episodes killed people with heart and lung disease. The harmful part of the pollution mix was unknown. Tiny ultrafine particles were a prime suspect.

Ultrafine particles are under 100 nanometers wide. They are few by weight but vast by number. Contact with immune cells can trigger calcium shifts and stress chemistry. Swelling cells add more oxidants to the mix. Donaldson links these steps to the fatty plaques behind heart attacks. It appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2001.
europmc-pmc1391975:
Viboud, Alonso, and Simonsen examined influenza patterns in tropical regions in 2006. Flu kills an estimated one million people yearly worldwide. Temperate zones see sharp winter peaks. Tropical zones show high activity all year round.

Epidemics there fall between the northern and southern temperate seasons. A new Hong Kong burden study anchors their discussion. Seasonality fades near the equator for reasons still unknown. No environmental link has been convincingly shown yet. Activity does coincide with rainy seasons in some tropical countries. Viboud maps how patterns shift with latitude across the Americas.
europmc-pmc1609175:
Gene studies need a steady yardstick gene, yet common picks wobble. Silver and co-authors ranked seven candidate housekeeping genes in 2006 in human reticulocytes, young red blood cells. They compared each gene pair's gap across 31 samples.

One gene was too faint and dropped out. GAPDH, a sugar-burning enzyme gene, proved most stable. Next came SDHA, HPRT1, and HBS1L. The widely used B2M came last and should be avoided here, Silver warns. Picking the wrong control gene can distort every result in an expression study.  The ranking gives red-cell studies a tested starting point instead of habit.
europmc-pmc1769375:
Colon tumors rewrite genes by splicing as well as by expression level. Gardina and co-authors hunted both changes in 2006 with a whole-genome exon array, covering over a million exons in 20 paired tumor and normal samples.

High-confidence analysis found 160 genes with altered expression. Forty-two of them formed a network affecting cell proliferation, and 29 had unknown functions. A looser analysis added 160 more genes, three quarters unannotated. Algorithms comparing exon shares within each gene predicted new splice variants, several confirmed by lab tests. Gardina shows exon arrays catch a layer of cancer change that gene-level arrays miss.
europmc-pmc1865375:
Wamani and co-authors pooled child health surveys in 2007 to ask whether boys really grow worse than girls in sub-Saharan Africa. Scattered studies had reported more stunting, meaning short height for age from poor nutrition, in boys. The team tested if that gap was systematic and how it varied with household wealth.

They analyzed the 16 most recent demographic and health surveys from ten countries. In every survey, girls had better average growth scores than boys, with the gap significant in most. Pooled scores were minus 1.59 for boys and minus 1.46 for girls, and stunting prevalence was 40 percent in boys against 36 percent in girls. Wealth measures were built from household assets and mother's schooling. The sex gap in stunting persisted across those wealth levels.
europmc-pmc1877875:
Robu, Ekker and co-authors warned in 2007 that common gene-silencing tools in zebrafish trigger a hidden side effect. Morpholinos and small interfering RNAs are injected into embryos to switch off one gene at a time. Both can also hit unintended targets, and side effects are hard to separate from the true result.

Comparing injected embryos with known mutants, the team found the same off-target pattern for both tool types and several targeting styles. The main effect was unwanted cell death driven by activation of p53, the cell's damage guardian. Blocking p53 at the same time erased that off-target death. It did not mask genuine effects, such as the death caused by losing the gene chordin. The authors urge routine p53 co-blocking as a control in knockdown studies.
europmc-pmc1892575:
Vaughn, Martienssen and co-authors charted in 2007 how DNA methylation, a chemical silencing tag, varies naturally between plant strains. In plants the tag lands on repeated DNA in several sequence contexts. The team profiled one chromosome of Arabidopsis thaliana in two strains, Columbia and Landsberg erecta.

Repeated sequences and jumping genes were densely tagged, as expected. Surprisingly, a third of ordinary genes carried low but real tagging inside their transcribed parts. That gene tagging was highly variable: half of tagged genes were tagged in only one of the two strains. A wider survey of 96 plant lines showed the same patchiness. Gene-body tags were inherited, yet were lost often when offspring were crossed. Tags near gene starts were rare, and expression rarely tracked the tagging differences.
europmc-pmc1904475:
Sourisseau, Schwartz and co-authors profiled in 2007 the chikungunya virus behind a sweeping Indian Ocean epidemic. The virus causes high fever, exhaustion, rash, and joint pain in many joints, with lethal brain cases reported. Which cells it infects, and how it causes disease, were unknown.

Recent patient strains grew well in human epithelial and endothelial cells and in primary fibroblasts, and weakly in macrophages grown from blood monocytes. They did not grow in lymphoid cell lines, primary lymphocytes or monocytes, or dendritic cells. Infection killed the host cells and triggered apoptosis, programmed cell death. Drugs that block acid-dependent entry, plus silencing of the entry protein dynamin-2, cut virus production, showing entry runs through pH-dependent endocytosis. The virus also proved highly sensitive to the antiviral action of interferon.
europmc-pmc1974775:
Dröge and Schipper argued in 2007 that oxidative stress distorts signaling, not just structures, in the aging brain. Brain aging brings a growing gap between the body's defenses and reactive oxygen species, visible as oxidized lipids, proteins, and DNA. Those reactive forms also reset the set points of redox-sensitive signaling paths.

One such path is insulin receptor signaling, which oxidative conditions strongly amplify when insulin itself is absent. That pathway in turn suppresses autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and sirtuin activity, both tied to neuron survival. Genetic studies show that weakening insulin signaling extends lifespan hugely in worms, flies, and mice. The authors note that predicted effects of age-related oxidation on sirtuins and autophagy still await direct tests. They also list candidate drivers, from mitochondrial DNA damage to disturbed brain iron and calcium balance.
europmc-pmc2126675: A medical paper on blood viscosity and conditions affecting it after withdrawal. The thick blood. This article preserves that hematology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2128375: A medical paper on the determination of lung volume without forced breathing. The easy breath. This article preserves that pulmonology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131275: A medical paper on the histological expression of the natural resistance of rabbits to infection. The rabbit's defense. This article preserves that immunology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140575: Protein particles in suspension tend to clump and fall, but protective agents keep them afloat, as this paper showed. The researchers tested the stabilizing effect. The guarded suspensions, studied. The article preserves that biochemistry research.
europmc-pmc2215775:
Ungrin, Joshi, Nica, Bauwens and Zandstra developed a high-throughput way in 2008 to grow human embryonic stem cell aggregates. Such aggregates, called embryoid bodies, reveal developmental potential and could supply cells for regenerative medicine. Standard aggregates are uneven and disorganised, slowing progress. The team used centrifugal force to pack single cells into aggregates, then a matching extraction method to collect them.

By controlling the starting cell mix and growth environment, they formed large numbers of well-defined aggregates. The aggregates showed multi-lineage differentiation and much better self-organisation. They formed two joined tissue regions resembling early embryonic layers. A silicon wafer technology allowed hundreds to thousands of aggregates per square centimetre. The synchronised system should support screening for conditions that direct stem cells into specific tissues.
europmc-pmc2265475:
Hill, Goddard and Visscher tackled a genetics paradox in 2008: why most variation in complex traits looks additive. Gene networks suggest interactions between genes, called epistasis, should matter greatly. Yet data across traits and species show most genetic variance is additive, meaning gene effects simply sum. The authors reviewed empirical variance studies and developed new theory based on allele frequency distributions under neutral and other population models.

They find additive variance accounts for over half of total genetic variance, and often nearly all of it. Their theory shows why: even when genes interact in their action, those interactions generate little interaction variance at population level. Allele frequencies shape how gene action converts into variance. The conclusion matters for evolutionary biology, medicine and agriculture, where additive models underpin breeding and risk prediction.
europmc-pmc2289875:
Clement and co-workers recorded brain activity in 2008 in rats under urethane anaesthesia and found sleep-like state cycles. Sleep alternates between activated REM and quiet slow-wave stages. Most anaesthetics instead impose one uniform slow-wave state, suggesting anaesthesia differs fundamentally. The team made long, multi-site forebrain recordings in urethane-anaesthetised rats and tracked muscle tone, breathing and heart rate alongside the electrical patterns.

The rats' brains spontaneously alternated between activated and deactivated patterns in a cycle of about eleven minutes. Individual states and transitions closely resembled the natural REM and non-REM cycle in their electrical components and timing. Muscle tone, respiration and heart rate covaried exactly as in sleep. The alternations also shared sleep's sensitivity to cholinergic drugs and its dependence on basal forebrain activity. Urethane thus mimics the full spectrum of natural sleep.
europmc-pmc2362675:
Leek, Landers, Harris, and Lewis studied dead tissue inside breast tumors in 1999. Such dead zones, called necrosis, form when parts of a tumor starve of blood, and they had been linked to poor outcomes. The textbook view blamed a weak blood supply overall, but this team suspected something more complex.

They measured necrosis, blood vessel density, and macrophage counts in 109 invasive breast cancers. Macrophages are immune cells that gather in oxygen-starved tumor zones. Necrosis tracked both heavy macrophage presence and dense vessel growth nearby, with strong statistical links for each. It also marked aggressive tumors: higher grade, larger size, and low estrogen receptor levels. The authors proposed that fast tumors outgrow their supply in patches, die there, and draw in macrophages that then spur more vessel growth.
europmc-pmc2364775:
Clayton and colleagues counted brain spread in women treated with trastuzumab in 2004. Trastuzumab is an antibody drug for breast cancers carrying excess HER-2, a growth receptor. Clinicians at one Manchester hospital had noticed many such patients developing brain metastases, meaning cancer deposits in the brain.

They reviewed 100 patients who started the drug between 1999 and 2002, and 93 could be fully assessed. Of those, 23, or 25%, developed brain metastases, and among 46 patients who had died, 39% had brain disease found before death. Most of the 23 also lacked hormone receptors and had cancer in internal organs. The authors offered two readings: HER-2 cancers may favour the brain, or longer survival on the drug gives brain deposits time to appear. Either way, they called for new strategies aimed at the brain.
europmc-pmc2424175:
Ancuta and co-authors linked gut leakage to brain disease in AIDS patients in 2008. In HIV infection, microbes leak products from the gut into blood, a process called microbial translocation. One such product, LPS, is a piece of bacterial wall that strongly activates monocytes, a type of white blood cell tied to HIV dementia.

They measured blood LPS in AIDS patients and checked monocyte activation markers. Patients with HIV-associated dementia had higher LPS than comparison groups, and the link held after accounting for virus levels and CD4 cell counts. High LPS came with raised sCD14 and LPS-binding protein, two activation signals, and low levels of antibodies that mop LPS up. Monocytes carried activation markers CD69 and HLA-DR at high levels. LPS was also higher in patients injecting heroin, drinking heavily, or co-infected with hepatitis C.
europmc-pmc2438475:
Wang and co-authors catalogued microRNA changes in cervical cancer in 2008. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA pieces that tune gene output, and their levels go wrong in many cancers. The team cloned small RNAs from a cervical cancer cell line carrying HPV16, the virus type behind most cervical cancers.

They isolated 174 microRNAs falling into 46 species. The most plentiful were miR-21, miR-24, miR-27a, together with miR-205. Two, miR-143 and miR-145, were missing from every cancer cell line tested. Comparing cancer tissue with matched normal cervix confirmed a pattern: miR-126, miR-143, and miR-145 were down, while miR-15b, miR-16, miR-146a, and also miR-155 were up. Adding miR-143 or miR-145 back slowed cancer cell growth. Adding miR-146a sped it up. The authors concluded the shifts are not bystanders but part of what drives the cancer.
europmc-pmc2443375:
Jian and colleagues hunted for reliable reference genes for soybean research in 2008. Gene activity studies compare samples against housekeeping genes, genes assumed to run at a steady level. Work in other species had shown no single housekeeping gene stays steady in all conditions, and soybean, a major world crop, had never been checked.

They tested ten candidate genes across 21 sample pools covering tissues, growth stages, day lengths, times of day, and cultivars. Every candidate varied more than expected. Ranking stability with a tool called geNorm put two genes on top overall: ELF1B and CYP2. Two others, UBQ10 and G6PD, were the least stable and should be avoided, they said. Rankings shifted by condition, so some experiments need two reference genes at once. A second statistical method agreed on the top pair.
europmc-pmc2611975:
Vickers, Cronin, Elkin, and Gonen extended decision curve analysis in 2008, a method they had introduced for judging diagnostic tests and prediction models. Unlike classic decision analysis, it needs no outside data on costs or preferences. It applies directly to a study data set. This paper adds the tools routine use demands.

The extensions cover four things. They correct curves for overfitting. They add confidence intervals. They handle censored data, where follow-up ends early. And they compute curves straight from predicted probabilities. Simulations showed repeated ten-fold cross-validation corrected overfit best. For censored data the method showed little bias and excellent coverage. Competing risks shifted curves as they should. Calculating from probabilities smoothed the curve. The authors provide software to implement the extended method.
europmc-pmc261875:
Ellison and Stillman characterised in 2003 the protein complexes that load a molecular clamp onto DNA at damage checkpoints. When DNA is damaged, checkpoint pathways halt the cell cycle, and two complexes mirror the machinery that loads the replication clamp PCNA: a loader called RSR and its clamp, RHR. The team purified the human loader and tested how it works in a test tube.

RSR loaded RHR onto DNA in a reaction needing energy and specific DNA shapes. The key finding was selectivity: the checkpoint loader preferred DNA with a recessed 5 prime end, while the replication loader preferred recessed 3 prime ends, exactly the opposite. That preference fits roles at stalled replication forks and repair sites. The authors say the work reveals how damage structures are recognised and signalled.
europmc-pmc2666075:
Bianco and Wilson reviewed in 2009 the habenular nuclei, a pair of small hubs near the top of the brain found in every backboned animal. These hubs relay signals from the front of the brain to older centers below, along a pathway so old and kept that it barely changes across species. Oddly, the left and right hubs are not mirror images.

The review covers the wiring of this relay, what it does in behavior, and how its two sides differ. Much of the detail comes from zebrafish, a small striped fish whose see-through young let scientists watch the circuit form. Those studies show how single cells take left or right character, and how the difference is set during early growth. The nearby pineal gland shares the same left-right quirk. The authors argue this tiny asymmetry is a window on how brains build uneven circuits.
europmc-pmc2683575:
Li and co-authors tested in 2009 whether smarter people have more efficient wiring networks in the brain. Common sense suggests intelligence rides on how fast and cleanly brain areas exchange signals, but proof from wiring maps was missing. The team scanned 79 healthy young adults with a method that traces fiber bundles, then built each person's brain network.

Judged by graph measures, the high-IQ group's networks moved information more efficiently. Their networks showed shorter average path lengths between areas, the wiring equivalent of fewer transfers on a trip. Across everyone, higher IQ scores tracked higher global efficiency even after age and sex were accounted for. The pattern held in both simple and strength-weighted networks. Brain wiring economy, the authors propose, is part of the biological basis of intelligence.
europmc-pmc2689275:
Meyer and colleagues sequenced in 2009 the active genes of coral larvae, showing how to do genomics on a creature with no sequenced genome. Reef corals face a warming ocean, yet the molecular tools to study their stress and adaptation barely existed. The team chose the larvae of a reef-building coral, the stage that must settle and found new colonies.

One run of a 454 sequencing machine produced over 600,000 reads, assembled into about 40,000 stitched sequences. Matching against known proteins named roughly 11,000 genes, including most core metabolism and signaling pathways, plus fresh candidates for heat stress and settling. Comparison with a sea anemone genome found about 8,500 clear gene counterparts and around 100 possibly coral-only genes. Over 30,000 single-letter variants turned up in the data, raw material for studying how populations differ and adapt.
europmc-pmc2730575:
Hoffmann and co-authors introduced segemehl in 2009, a program for mapping short sequencing reads to a genome while allowing mismatches plus insertions and deletions. Most mappers at the time used simple seed shortcuts and handled only letter mismatches well. New machines differ in their errors: one type mainly makes mismatches, while another mainly inserts or deletes letters, especially in small RNA reads.

Their method uses enhanced suffix arrays, an index structure for fast searching, under a matching model that handles all three error types. It can also absorb primer or tail contamination at read ends, which reduces manual trimming. In comparisons it ran significantly faster and more accurately than current mappers on both machine types.
europmc-pmc2735675:
Johnston, Shahidi, Sadatsafavi, and Fitzgerald pooled in 2009 treatment outcomes for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, strains that resist the two best tuberculosis drugs. Outcomes are known to be worse than for drug-sensitive disease, but summary rates and risk factors were scattered. They searched studies to December 2008 and pooled thirty-one programs from twenty-one countries.

About six in ten patients had a successful outcome, while roughly one in nine died and about one in eight defaulted, dropping out of care. Male sex, alcohol abuse, low body weight, and added drug resistance predicted worse results. Surgery, no prior treatment, and use of a fluoroquinolone drug predicted success. High default rates likely help resistant disease spread further.
europmc-pmc2736175:
de Haan and co-authors used EEG and graph theory in 2009 to compare large-scale brain networks in Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia. Graph measures describe local clustering, how tightly neighbors connect, and path length, how many steps link distant areas. Whether these two dementias disturb network layout in the same way was unknown.

In twenty Alzheimer's patients, clustering and path length fell in several frequency bands versus controls, which shifts the network from an efficient small-world layout toward a random one. That fits the idea of Alzheimer's as a disconnection syndrome. Fifteen frontotemporal patients showed no such falls, and one measure rose instead, which points toward a more ordered network and a different disease process.
europmc-pmc2744675:
Ford and co-authors built the SAIL Databank in 2009, a Welsh system that links anonymized health and public-sector records for research and policy evaluation. Routine electronic records hold huge research value, but privacy law demands strong safeguards before person-level data can be shared. Their unit set seven objectives covering secure transport, record matching, anonymization, disclosure control, and approved access.

The databank runs on a supercomputer platform and passed an independent audit for information governance compliance. By launch it already held over five hundred million anonymized, encrypted records covering the whole of Wales, about three million people, plus local provider data sets. Rising use by high-quality studies was presented as proof of its utility.
europmc-pmc2819875:
Hayes surveyed the spread of Zika virus beyond Africa in 2009, after an outbreak on Yap Island in the Pacific put the little-known virus on the map. Zika is a flavivirus, kin to dengue and yellow fever, carried by mosquitoes. It was first isolated in 1947 from a feverish rhesus monkey in Uganda's Zika Forest, then found in mosquitoes there a year later.

Human infections were logged across Africa and parts of Asia over the following decades, mostly as scattered mild cases with rash, joint pain, and red eyes. The 2007 Yap outbreak was the first seen outside Africa and Asia. Hayes argues the virus should be treated as an emerging pathogen worth watching.
europmc-pmc2854775:
Wick and colleagues asked in 2010 whether nanoparticles can cross the human placenta and reach an unborn baby. Using donated placentas kept alive in a perfusion rig, they pumped in fluorescent plastic beads of four sizes, from fifty to five hundred nanometers across. The rig circulates fluid through the organ outside the body.

Beads up to two hundred forty nanometers were taken up by the placenta and crossed to the fetal side, while the largest beads did not get through. The tissue stayed viable throughout, so the crossing was not damage. The authors conclude that engineered nanomaterials can potentially reach the fetus, and they urge dedicated safety studies of this overlooked route of exposure.
europmc-pmc2944075:
Zhang and colleagues measured mercury exposure in inland China in a 2010 study centred on Guizhou Province, a region heavily tainted by mining and industry. Eating fish is usually blamed as the main route for the toxic form called methylmercury.

Sampling water, air, farm goods, and other media at four sites, they calculated daily intake for local adults. Intake ran highest near the Wanshan mercury mining area, where about a third of residents passed a United States safety reference level. Surprisingly, rice rather than fish proved the main exposure path, reshaping how inland risk should be judged.
europmc-pmc2981575:
Kirin and co-authors read population history from runs of homozygosity, long genome stretches where both parental copies match, in a 2010 study. Long runs signal recent shared ancestry, such as cousin marriage, while short ones record much older common roots.

Scanning a global dataset, they sorted mostly indigenous populations into four broad patterns: recent relatedness, ancient isolation with little recent inbreeding, a mix of both, and only faint background sharing. Individuals could be placed along the same axes. The runs thus act as a written record of isolation, customs, and ancestry depth, with urban groups showing the least and African farming groups the least of all.
europmc-pmc3048375:
Neale and coauthors proposed in 2011 a new statistical test for finding disease genes among rare DNA variants. Cheap sequencing now uncovers many rare variants, but each is too scarce to judge alone, so they must be weighed as a group. Older burden tests add up effects in one direction, which fails when a set mixes harmful and protective variants.

Their test instead checks the spread of effects across the set, so opposing effects no longer cancel out. Simulations and a real case control dataset showed the test kept good power where burden tests faded. It also behaved well under the null case, avoiding false alarms. The authors offer the method as a standard tool for sequencing studies of common disease. It widens the net for genes whose variants pull in both directions.
europmc-pmc3063175:
Wolkowitz and colleagues reported in 2011 early evidence that years lived with major depression may age the body's cells faster. Depression brings unusually high rates of age related illness and early death. The team measured the protective caps on chromosomes in white blood cells of unmedicated depressed adults and healthy controls. They compared cap length with lifetime depression history and with blood markers of damage and inflammation.

As a whole, the depressed group did not differ from controls. But within the depressed group, longer total time spent depressed meant shorter caps, even after accounting for age. Those with the longest histories looked several years older at the cell level than controls. Shorter caps also tracked with higher oxidative stress in both groups, and with inflammation in the depressed group. The authors call the findings preliminary and suggest cell aging grows with cumulative illness burden.
europmc-pmc3068975:
Robin and coauthors released in 2011 a software package for drawing and rigorously comparing ROC curves, the standard graphs for judging diagnostic tests and classifiers. A curve plots how a test trades catching true cases against false alarms as its cutoff moves. Papers often compare curves loosely, without proper statistics, and small gaps get overread.

Their package, pROC, builds the curves and adds confidence ranges, smoothing options, and formal tests for whole or partial curve areas. It runs in two popular statistics environments, one free and one commercial, with a friendly interface in the latter. A worked case on published clinical data shows a typical analysis end to end. The authors stress that comparing tests at the cutoff ranges doctors actually use matters most. The tool is free under an open license.
europmc-pmc3071375:
Shu and coauthors unveiled in 2011 a tiny genetic tag that lets scientists watch a chosen protein under both light and electron microscopes in the same sample. Electron microscopes give the finest detail but lacked a general purpose tag for specific proteins, unlike the glowing tags of light microscopy. Their tag, miniSOG, is a small light sensitive plant protein, less than half the size of the standard green glowing tag.

When lit, the tag releases a reactive form of oxygen that hardens a stain exactly where the tag sits, making the spot visible in electron images. Tagged proteins landed in the right places in mammal cells, worms, and mice, even after strong preservation. In one test, two partner proteins were shown to sit on opposite sides of the same synapse. The authors compare its potential impact to that of the green glowing tag itself.
europmc-pmc3081075:
Yu-Wai-Man, Griffiths, and Chinnery reviewed in 2011 the two most common inherited optic nerve diseases, both rooted in faulty mitochondria, the cell's power stations. One strikes mainly young men in sudden episodes, while the other creeps forward across life. Both selectively kill the retinal cells that carry vision to the brain, starting with the fibers serving sharp central sight.

Most cases of the sudden form trace to one of three changes in mitochondrial DNA, while the creeping form usually traces to a gene for a membrane shaping protein. Energy failure is part of the story, but the review stresses more: tangled power station networks, transport jams along the nerve fiber, and outside triggers such as smoking and light. Both diseases can also spill beyond the eye into wider nerve problems. New animal models finally allow direct experiments, and protective treatments are entering trials.
europmc-pmc3084475:
Barker, Gout, and Crowe reviewed in 2011 the scale and cost of malnutrition inside hospitals, drawing on Australian and international studies. Roughly two in five hospital patients are malnourished by their reading, yet the condition is often missed, poorly recorded, and rarely referred to dietitians in time. Malnutrition weakens immunity, slows wound healing, wastes muscle, and stretches hospital stays, while raising costs and death rates.

A quick screening with a validated tool at admission can flag at risk patients for prompt dietitian referral, the authors argue. In Australia such screening is not mandatory, which they call a concern, since missed malnutrition also means hospitals lose funding owed under case based payment rules. Their recommendation is direct: make admission screening compulsory and follow best practice guidelines. The review makes the clinical and the financial case in the same breath.
europmc-pmc3184975:
Nadège Minois, Didac Carmona-Gutierrez, and Frank Madeo reviewed a family of small charged molecules in aging and disease in a 2011 paper in Aging. These polyamines cling to DNA, RNA, and proteins and support cell growth and survival. Their levels fall steadily with age, yet cancer cells hoard them, making the same molecules both a longevity lead and a cancer target.

Feeding one family member, or a diet rich in it, extended lifespan in model organisms and raised stress resistance. Blocking production, by contrast, is a standing strategy against tumours that depend on high levels. The review gathers metabolism, transport, and mechanism findings across fields, arguing only the combined picture can explain how one molecule family can slow aging yet feed cancer.
europmc-pmc3197175:
Christopher Brown and colleagues read gut microbe DNA from children developing type one diabetes autoimmunity in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Bacteria had been suspected in triggering the immune attack on the pancreas. Stool from four matched pairs of children was sequenced deeply at the moment disease-linked antibodies appeared, yielding about a million predicted genes.

Hundreds of functions differed between the groups. Children developing autoimmunity carried more genes for sticking to surfaces, moving, and stress survival, and fewer for routine building work. Their gut held fewer of the bacteria making a protective short-chain fat that feeds the gut lining, and more that consume its precursor without finishing it. The authors model a healthy consortium that keeps the gut wall sealed, whose absence may invite autoimmunity.
europmc-pmc3247075:
Jonathan Davey and colleagues took a census of the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in this 2011 paper in BMC Medical Research Methodology. Cochrane reviews sum up trials of health interventions, and their contents reveal much about the state of health research. The team classified every meta-analysis in one issue of the database by specialty, intervention, and outcome type.

They counted more than twenty-three hundred reviews holding over twenty-two thousand meta-analyses, built from more than a hundred thousand individual studies. Pregnancy and childbirth, mental health, and respiratory disease were the best-covered areas, and most analyses compared drugs against placebo or another drug. The striking finding is how small the building blocks are: a typical meta-analysis rests on just three studies, and a typical study on under a hundred patients. The authors stress the need for methods that behave well with tiny datasets.
europmc-pmc3296675:
Neyeloff, Fuchs, and Moreira wrote a step by step guide in 2012 for combining study results inside a common spreadsheet program. Combining many studies into one summary, called meta analysis, is essential for making sense of medical research. Specialist software can be costly, hard to adapt, or weak at drawing the summary charts for simple rates such as how common a condition is.

Their guide shows how to run the combined analysis in Microsoft Excel using either of the two standard statistical models. A companion spreadsheet builds tailored forest plots, the charts that display each study result beside the overall summary. The authors claim this is the first published recipe for drawing such plots for descriptive data with widely available tools.
europmc-pmc3367275:
Värnik reviewed global suicide using World Health Organization mortality data, charting how the burden differs by region, sex, and age and how it has shifted since 1950. The analysis drew on improving national reporting, with worldwide injury mortality estimates anchored on 2008.

An estimated 782,000 people died by suicide in 2008, a global rate of roughly twelve per hundred thousand inhabitants. The male-to-female ratio was highest in Europe, at about four to one, and lowest in the Eastern Mediterranean. Lithuania recorded the highest national rate. Värnik notes the centre of the problem has moved from Western Europe toward Eastern Europe and increasingly Asia.
europmc-pmc3394175:
Receveur-Brechot and Durand asked in 2012 how random the shape of an intrinsically disordered protein really is. Such proteins lack a fixed fold, yet run key jobs in the cell, which makes them hard to picture. The review presents small angle X-ray scattering, a method that reads their average shape in solution.

Borrowing from polymer physics, scattering data can measure how flexible these proteins are. New computing methods build three-dimensional models, or whole families of shapes, that fit the scattering pattern. Pairing scattering with crystallography or NMR sharpens the picture across scales. The authors show the method has become essential for proteins that refuse to sit still.
europmc-pmc3440575:
Cardinale and Arkin examined in 2012 why synthetic biology's engineered systems so often fail once placed inside living cells. Designs that obey their rules on paper behave unpredictably in real organisms, because every device sits inside a shifting cellular and environmental context. The review sets out to name and classify those context effects.

Sources range from temperature and crowding swings to competition for the cell's shared machinery and resources. Imported pathways suffer most, since they never co-evolved with their host. The authors sort the failure modes and review methods to control them, from insulating devices to redesigning the host. Their aim is practical: make biological engineering as predictable as its designers keep promising.
europmc-pmc3472075:
Austin set out clear ways to check whether matched groups in a medical study are truly alike, in Statistics in Medicine in 2009. Researchers often match treated and untreated patients by a propensity score, an estimate of each person's chance of getting the treatment. Any claim about the treatment holds only if the matched groups share similar starting traits.

The paper walks through checks based on standardized differences, variance ratios, fuller summaries, and plots that compare whole distributions. Austin also derives how large a difference can arise by chance when matching has worked. He warns that comparing the scores themselves between groups tells nothing useful. The guidance helps readers judge whether a matched study was built soundly.

frus-1861-d75:

September brought the war's focus back to the coasts and the blockade. Seward's letters to London took up the law of blockade and search at sea. frus-1862-d175:
