Twin reports in one mail let an envoy keep a formal account apart from enclosures or side matters. Adams used the practice often in busy weeks. For the modern reader, this letter is best read beside its same-day mate. Together the two give the legation's full account of its work that week. London's answer, when it came, would turn on battlefield news ten days old or more.
frus-1862-d275:
Filed as Document 275 but dated 1 May 1862, this dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward went to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. The Foreign Relations printers placed it after the general instruction of 2 May.

Out-of-sequence filing is a small quirk with real effects: a reader must watch dates, not numbers, to follow the Paris story. The letter itself belongs to the start of May, when Seward was sending his spring guidance to Europe. It pairs with the general instruction beside it in the file. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d375:
Dated 27 August 1862, Document 375 is a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Viscount Treilhard, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume among the French papers.

Seward wrote two days before the second battle of Bull Run, at the peak of the summer's military anxiety in Washington. Foreign representatives in the capital could hear the guns' echo in official moods within days. Letters of this week, this one included, were written inside that pressure, though their manner stayed formal and measured. The French legation's notes were written in French and printed here in the Department's English. Cases in this channel often mixed the war at home with French designs in Mexico.
frus-1862-d475:
On 4 August 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James E. Harvey, the American minister at Lisbon. The instruction is Document 475 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

August orders to Lisbon came in a month when Confederate cruisers were the Union's growing worry at sea. Ships like the Alabama were slipping out to raid American commerce, and every neutral port's rules mattered. Portugal's Atlantic islands could serve as coaling points or be shut to raiders, depending on how Lisbon ruled. Seward's instruction kept Harvey pressing the stricter reading. The letter is part of the wide, quiet effort to make the whole Atlantic coast unfriendly to Confederate sea power.
frus-1862-d575:
On 20 May 1862 James Watson Webb reported from Rio de Janeiro to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 575 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Webb's May report was written in a South America largely spared the war's direct pressure. Yet Brazil's ports gave the correspondence its themes. So did Brazil's example as a slaveholding empire. He reported the imperial government's temper and the standing of the Union's cause in Rio. Distance made his file sparse beside the European ones, but each letter carried weight for that reason: Washington had no other regular eyes in Brazil. The dispatch is a reminder that the war's diplomacy was hemispheric, not only European.
frus-1862-d675:
On 22 April 1862, William H. Seward wrote from the State Department to Anson Burlingame, the American minister to China. The letter is document 675 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It is one of a matched set of orders Seward sent that spring.

Each outward letter answered reports, gave fresh orders, and passed on news the envoy would need. For the China post, the brief covered trade, treaty rights, and the court's war with the Taiping rebels. This letter's worth lies in the run it belongs to. Read in line, the Seward-Burlingame mail shows two men running a distant brief with care, while a civil war consumed their country.
frus-1862-d75:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 2 June 1862. It stands as Document 75 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d175:
Writing from London on 30 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 175 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

In 1863 the great question in London was whether Britain would treat the Confederacy as a real nation. Adams's reports helped Washington judge that risk week by week. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d275:
Washington's orders to London on 31 August 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 275 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Seward wrote in a firm tone but had to avoid pushing Britain into the war on the Southern side. His instructions walked that line again and again. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d375:
In Washington on 29 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 375 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d475:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington sent an official note to Secretary William H. Seward on 23 April 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d575:
Under the date 20 June 1863, the record holds a letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d675:
On 23 November 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote from Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the United States minister in London. The letter survives as document 675 in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States. That series prints the State Department's own letters from the Civil War years.

Late 1863 was a tense time for ties with Britain. The Union wanted Britain to stay out of the war and to stop help from reaching the South. A reader gets the real working words of that effort, sent at the top level. Single letters like this one, read in order, show how the North made its case week by week.
frus-1863p1-d75:
On 10 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is document 75 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It follows Adams's dispatch that had sent home the Queen's speech.

Seward wrote with fair news in hand: at the opening of Parliament, Britain had shown no wish to meddle in the war. His letters still had claims to press, above all on warships built for the South in British yards. This one keeps the brief moving in a calmer week. It shows the exchange at its working best, each side feeding the other by steamer.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d175: A further letter from Roosevelt to Hull is dated October 30, 1943, and it stands as Document 175 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The cluster of same-day letters between the president and his secretary, at the Moscow Conference's close, is one of the volume's densest knots of paper. The record does not untangle their separate errands. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series for readers to sort in sequence.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d275:
A secret memorandum of conversation at Cairo on 26 November 1943 records a meeting about air supply to China over the Hump, the air route across the Himalayas. It is signed by Generals Arnold, Stilwell, and Somervell, and it answers a demand from Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek.

Chiang wanted a fixed 10,000 tons a month flown in, whatever Southeast Asia operations might need. The generals explain that all C-46 aircraft are assigned to the route. They add that 25 more planes are sought for Mountbatten. Mountbatten's lower figure of 8,900 tons differs from the target by only 1,100 tons, which better efficiency may erase. Chiang closes by accepting the figures, with the understanding that the Air Transport Command will strain to raise the tonnage beyond the target.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d375:
Minutes kept by Major John Boettiger record the dinner at Tehran on 30 November 1943, at half past eight in the evening, given for Churchill's sixty-ninth birthday. Thirty-three members of the three delegations sat down together, with Roosevelt on the host's right and Stalin on his left, and a seating plan is attached.

All the speeches took the form of toasts, in the Russian custom set the night before. Roosevelt opened by proposing the toast to the King, a privilege he had asked as an old friend of George VI. Churchill praised Roosevelt as a defender of the weak and toasted Stalin as worthy of the name Stalin the Great. Stalin answered that the honors belonged to the Russian people, and that in Russia even cowards became heroes, while those who did not were killed. Boettiger notes a shared sense that a historic understanding, and lasting friendships, had been reached.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d475:
President Roosevelt sent a second message to Marshal Stalin on December 3, 1943, as the follow-up to the Tehran Conference continued. Roosevelt was by then at Cairo, preparing for the second conference there with Churchill. The State Department preserved the message in the Cairo-Tehran volume, alongside the day's other traffic.

Paired cables to the same leader on one day usually mean fast-moving business, and early December 1943 gave the alliance plenty of it. Roosevelt's exchanges with Stalin in this period set the tone for cooperation in the war's decisive year. Readers get the alliance's most sensitive channel, running at full speed just after its first summit.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d575:
Dean Acheson, Acting Secretary of State, recorded this memorandum on September 7, 1945. Acheson was minding the department while Secretary Byrnes attended the foreign ministers' meeting in London. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Acheson would become one of the chief builders of the postwar order, and his acting-secretary papers show that order being improvised in its first week of peace. The London meeting was already exposing cracks among the wartime allies. For readers, the memorandum offers a front-row record from the moment the wartime coalition began turning into the Cold War's opposing camps.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d75: Roosevelt wrote to Secretary Hull on October 30, 1943, as the secretary prepared to leave Moscow. The letter is Document 75 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Moscow agreements had to be turned into summit plans at once, and the president's letters that day pushed the work along. The catalog record names the two men and the date. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series' Moscow closing papers.
frus-1944-quebec-d175:
At their afternoon meeting on September 12, 1944, the Combined Chiefs took up coordination with the Soviet Union. Sir Alan Brooke said he felt Stalin's offer should be dropped: missions already existed in Moscow, and the Russians need only appoint a suitable senior officer. Portal warned that exchange missions with field commanders would leak plans and gain nothing. The British recommendations were approved.

Zones of occupation in Germany proved harder. The chiefs agreed the question carried such serious political weight that they could recommend nothing without guidance from their governments. Britain wanted the northwest zone on military grounds. King suggested America could take the southwest if its troops could be supplied through north German ports. The chiefs decided to ask Roosevelt and Churchill for an early decision.
frus-1944-quebec-d275:
General Ismay sent Leahy a draft passage on September 15, 1944, built on an idea General Marshall had raised at that morning's meeting. The Combined Chiefs, the draft says, desired to record the Quebec Conference's main difficulty. It had been finding room and opportunity to deploy against Japan the massive forces every nation concerned was ardent to engage.

In colloquial language, the draft continues, it was a case of "standing room only," even before the curtain rang up. The chiefs made no recommendation on the subject in their final report. But including the thought in the communiqué, and at the closing press conference, would hearten world opinion and depress Japan. A draft communiqué filed with the letter matches the one actually issued.
frus-1944-quebec-d75:
Officials on the Working Security Committee prepared a memorandum dated August 30, 1944. The committee dealt with security questions in wartime planning. Its paper appears among the pre-conference records in the Quebec 1944 volume. The State Department published the volume after the war.

Committee papers like this one turned broad concerns into staff work. Planners weighed security needs as the war moved toward Germany. Their conclusions fed the briefings prepared for Quebec. For readers, the memorandum shows the middle layer of government at work. Specialists framed questions that cabinet officers and leaders would later decide.
frus-1945-50-intel-d175:
A letter dated 4 November 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Eddy). The reader was the Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg). It is document 175 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

The text is one side of an exchange, set out in full under the writer's own name and title. Read in sequence, the letters show two offices testing how far each could push the other. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d275:
The Intelligence Survey Group addressed a memorandum to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) on 13 May 1948. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 275, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d375:
A memorandum dated 18 March 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency (Wisner). The reader was the Under Secretary of State (Webb). The State Department prints it as document 375 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d75:
McCarthy wrote to McCormack on 4 October 1945, the administration chief addressing the intelligence chief inside the State Department. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Two officers of one department, dividing a new duty between them, write a special kind of paper. It is frank and practical, full of the small print of staff and space. This memorandum belongs to the office-building thread of the volume. Readers who follow it learn how the interim research and intelligence service was actually assembled in the autumn of 1945, desk by desk. Such papers rarely make the histories, yet without them the famous plans would have had no house to live in.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d175:
Washington told King Peter, through Ambassador Patterson, what it thought of the Tito–Subasic plan. The State Department's memorandum to the British Embassy of 23 December 1944 is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Eden had suggested the step in a telegram to Halifax five days earlier.

Patterson is cleared to tell the King that the Department has studied the papers with attention. Their principles, taken as a whole, match those the United States holds in its own dealings. But so much turns on the goodwill and cooperation of the men named to run the new government that Washington will not judge the plan's chances. Whether it works in loyal practice, the memorandum implies, only the men themselves can show.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d275:
No linkage: that is the order Stettinius sent Harriman on 3 January 1945 about prisoners. His secret cable, number 18, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers the news that Soviet negotiators had been named for General Deane.

In any talks on repatriation, the Department is extremely anxious that two streams be kept apart. Americans found in German camps are one matter. Soviet nationals found among the German prisoners taken by American forces are another. Trouble has already arisen over who counts as a Soviet national. A few men taken fighting with the Germans bear Slavic names but disclaim Soviet nationality. Over eleven hundred Soviet nationals found in German ranks were handed to the Soviet authorities at a west coast port the week before.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d375:
Hiss took notes as Molotov answered the American report on Dumbarton Oaks at the plenary of February 7, 1945. The Soviet side, Molotov said, was satisfied with Stettinius's report. Certain questions had become much clearer after the explanations. Churchill's remarks had also drawn close Soviet attention.

The outcome, Molotov judged, would secure the unity of the three powers in guarding peace after the war. The Soviet aim all along, he said, was the greatest unity among the three on peace and security. The proposals, with the President's changes, would win cooperation from nations great and small. Hiss's shorthand catches Moscow warming to the world body.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d475:
London news fills these excerpts from Grew's cable of February 4, 1945. Winant had told the Soviet member of the European Advisory Commission of American acceptance, in principle, of five French proposals. They concerned French participation in the surrender, occupation, and control of Germany. The Soviet member thanked him for the advance notice and sought early instructions from Moscow.

Winant had also informed the Soviet and British members of American approval of the protocol on German zones. Further down, the cable turns to the Associated Nations. Medina in Venezuela, it notes, was somewhat taken aback by the President's letter, but appreciated the situation. The digest mixes summit questions with embassy detail.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d75:
Who would be invited to found the United Nations? Acting Secretary Stettinius put that question to the President on 15 November 1944. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, is titled “Invitations to the Conference and Initial Membership.” It records a sharp split with Moscow.

Two issues are set out. First, should only the thirty-five United Nations signatories be invited, or also nine associated nations from earlier conferences? Second, should the sixteen Soviet republics enter as original members, as Moscow demanded? The American position was to invite forty-four nations and refuse the sixteen republics. The British and Chinese stood with Washington on the invitations question.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d175:
The British Chiefs of Staff answered the last American points on the staff agenda in a memorandum dated June 29, 1945. The paper, C.C.S. 880/5, is document 175 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It replies to the U.S. memorandum of June 27 on the coming Anglo-American staff talks.

The British say their paper on command against Japan will include plans to reorganize command in the Southwest Pacific. They agree to put off discussion of Russian participation until after the talks with the Russians end. Papers will be swapped in advance where possible. But the British doubt they can ready their papers more than a few days before Terminal. Those papers cover their own role against Japan and command questions. One directive must wait on the talks themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d275:
The Joint Civil Affairs Committee set out financial policy for Austria in an undated memorandum printed as document 275 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The paper asks for decisions at government level so the military authorities in Austria can do their work.

No decision has been reached, the paper says, on whether Austria must pay reparations, or in what form. American policy favors a sound, united Austrian economy not dependent on Germany, and the form and amount of any reparations should serve that aim. Labor or money reparations would not; capital goods should be limited to items a stable economy can spare. The paper also urges encouraging Austria's private export trade, to divorce her economy from Germany's, and seeks agreement on economic disarmament and on coordination with the Control Council for Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d375:
A late Soviet refusal is reported in Pauley's cable from Moscow of July 14, 1945. All members of the Reparations Commission had agreed on a statement of principles. Each was to submit it to his government for approval. Washington and London had accepted it. That day, though, Maisky said Moscow would not take the last sentence of paragraph eight.

The disputed sentence dealt with paying for imports. In working out Germany's economic balance, it said, means must be provided to pay for approved imports. That payment comes before reparations are taken from current output or stocks. Pauley answered that his government stands firm on the rule. Approved imports are a prior charge on approved exports.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d475: Bonomi called on Kirk in Rome on June 25, 1945. He had just given up the office of President of the Council. His subject was Allied troops in Italy. Their retention, he argued, was essential. It built the people's confidence that order inside the country would be kept. It also deterred foreign elements. Such elements might seek to break that order, by intrigue from within or by threats from without.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d575:
State Department staff wrote a top secret briefing paper on special Manchurian problems, dated July 3, 1945. It is document 575 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It briefs the President on two linked issues: the port of Dairen and the Manchurian railways.

The paper traces Dairen's lease from Russia in 1898 to Japan in 1905. Japan stretched the lease to 99 years in 1915, a move China contests and the U.S. never accepted. If Russia joins the war on Japan, it will likely want Dairen kept a free port. The paper sees no bar to that if trade stays open to all, but backs China's claim to the land. A second part traces the Chinese Eastern Railway and the line south to Dairen and Port Arthur.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d675:
Acting Secretary Grew set out the U.S. terms for a Tangier settlement to Ambassador Caffery on July 13, 1945. The secret wire is document 675 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It answers the French proposals sent by Villard on July 6.

Washington can accept the aims France states for the talks, Grew says. But the term international administration must not be read as the 1923 statute's own machine. The United States never adhered to that statute and cannot do so. A temporary administration much like it would suit Washington, though. U.S. nationals must hold a proper share in it, and Soviet nationals too if Moscow wishes. France may treat the 1923 statute as the legal basis on its side. Grew also proposes that any pact pledge a full conference within twelve months.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d75:
President Truman accepted Stalin's proposed start date for the Allied move into their German zones on June 18, 1945. His top secret telegram, number 297, is document 75 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Stalin had said mine clearing in Berlin would run to late June, and asked that the pullback begin July 1 instead of June 21.

Truman says he has ordered the American commanders to begin the movement on July 1, as Stalin asked. He assumes American troops will reach Berlin earlier, in enough strength to do their work preparing for the conference. A long editorial note explains the swap of messages behind the decision. The exchange fixed the ground on which the Potsdam meeting itself would stand.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1075:
Joseph Jacobs, the American mission chief in Albania, cabled Washington from Tirana on July 21, 1945. Albanian commanders had met in secret the night before over the Greek situation. They fear Greek forces, with quiet British backing, will stage border incidents. British troops might then be invited to occupy southern Albania to keep order.

Jacobs reports two recent clashes. On July 9, armed Greeks crossed near Konispol and tried to plant boundary markers on Albanian soil; shots drove them back. On July 12 and 13, Greek soldiers tried the same near Bilisht and were repelled. Yugoslavia is sending Albania ammunition and artillery. Jacobs cannot say which side starts the incidents, but he is sure they are happening.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1175:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Ambassador Armour in Spain on 16 July 1945, the day before Potsdam opened. Spain under Franco had stayed out of the war, but its regime was a leftover of the fascist age the Allies had just beaten. That made Spain an awkward open question.

At Potsdam the three powers would soon declare that Franco's Spain could not join the new United Nations. Washington's Madrid post had to be ready for that stand and its fallout. This cable shows the home office tasking its envoy on the summit's eve. It links a quiet post to the great talks about to begin.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1275:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent this message to the President on 16 July 1945, the day before the summit opened. The chiefs' word on the eve of the talks fixed the armed forces' stand for the trip. It reached Truman beside the war secretary's letters of the same day.

That date carries a hidden weight. In New Mexico, the first atomic device had just been tested in secret. The men writing and reading this message stood at the edge of a new kind of war. The paper itself is staff business at the highest level: the top brass addressing their commander as the peace talks began.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1375:
The British delegation put a proposal before the Potsdam Conference on 27 July 1945. Britain tabled fewer papers in this part of the volume than the Soviet or American sides. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

A British proposal two days after the change of prime minister carries extra interest. Attlee's new government had just taken over the delegation, and its papers show whether London's line shifted with its leaders. Readers can test that question here in the delegation's own words. The proposal also rounds out the record. With it, all three powers at Potsdam can be read stating their terms in this section of the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-75:
Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes record a session on captured passenger shipping, held July 21, 1945. The top secret record is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The seven captured German liners were again the bone of contention.

The chiefs first approved the conclusions of their 198th meeting. Sir Alan Brooke then stated the British position on the shipping papers. The U.S. amendments, he said with regret, were not acceptable to the British chiefs. The American view, as he summarized it, ran as follows. If the seven captured ships moved to the Pacific, they could make no more than one trip before December 31, 1945. If a review then reassigned them away from the United States, the Pacific assignment would prove uneconomical. Brooke said he appreciated the point, and the argument continued from there.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d775:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Byrnes at Potsdam on July 19, 1945, in document 775. Grew's letters formed a near-daily bridge to Washington. This one dates from the conference's first week. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Home-office letters mixed the urgent with the routine. Both kinds mattered to a secretary abroad. Readers see Grew sorting the Department's world for a busy chief. The document also shows the two men's rhythm settling in. By July 19 the channel carried trust as much as news.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d875: British delegates at Potsdam offered this short draft of Article 19 of the Economic Principles, filed with the July 23, 1945 papers. It says that after reparations, Germans must be left enough to live without outside help. Means must also be provided to pay for imports approved by the governments concerned. Proceeds from exports of current production and stocks would be used first for those imports.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d975:
Edwin Pauley and William Clayton sent this memorandum to General Clay on August 1, 1945. They ask him to press the Control Council to adopt an attached principle on Allied and neutral property in Germany. It would supplement the economic principles and the reparations agreement just approved.

The principle says foreign ownership must not block removals under the agreement. Allied governments would file statements of their nationals' property, and their agents would get access to inspect it. Where owners wish, goods could move without change of title. Otherwise, Reichsmark deposits would be paid and settled in foreign exchange. Neutral owners would receive Reichsmark deposits as compensation.
frus-1958-60v09-d175: A 1958-1960 FRUS document from the Berlin Crisis volume. The divided city tensed again. This entry preserves that record. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
gao-gaoreports-b-295375: FR Countermeasures challenged a February 2005 award at GAO, and the ruling hands down the decision. The firm's grievance got the referee's full review. The protest met the gavel head-on. The gavel came down. The review was complete. The decision held.
gao-gaoreports-b-296875: J.A. Farrington Janitorial Services took its October 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298975: Stewart Distributors took its January 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Distribution deals get the same full hearing as the rest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299175: Geo-Seis Helicopters doubled its March 2007 protest — two case numbers, one aviation fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both claims at once. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-306475: Help America Vote Act audits got a GAO ruling in this January 2006 call, which examines audits and recovery of funds. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides how the vote dollars were policed. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-306975: The National Archives' revolving fund advances got a fiscal ruling in this February 2006 GAO call, which tests the advance payments. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the advances were legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-311275: This 2008 GAO ruling is about designated Employee Agent at B.R. Hardison. The decision answers a legal question about spending public funds. The library keeps it in the public record of federal fiscal decisions. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-175: The anti-drug ad blitz got a GAO audit in 2005, and the report says services were provided, though most funds bought media time. The review follows the ad dollars. The campaign's reach was measured. The spending was tracked. The campaign's reach was measured.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-275: War zone spare parts were running short in 2005, and GAO's report says actions were needed to improve availability of critical items. The review calls for the supplies. The troops' gear deserved the stock. The actions had to come. The troops' gear deserved the stock.

The review counts the missing detectors. The borders deserved the working alarms. The progress was limited. The borders deserved the working alarms.

The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the new forces deserved solid plans. The plans had to be better defined.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-775: Defense supply distribution was improving in 2005, and GAO's report says the Pentagon began upgrades, though further actions were needed to sustain. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the supply lines deserved keeping. The actions had to continue.

The report warns that the housing fund deserved honest accounting. The reestimate had to be understood. The housing fund deserved honest accounting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-275: Energy price indices needed improving in 2006, and GAO's report examines federal actions to improve private price data. The findings target the numbers. The report warns that the gas and power prices deserved honest benchmarks. The indices had to be improved.

The findings demand the blueprint. The report warns that the paper mountain should become digital carefully. The planning had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-475: Armed pilots programs needed more study in 2006, and GAO's report says further study of safety and better controls were required if air carriers participated. The findings demand the research. The report warns that the cockpit guns needed careful rules. The study had to be done.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-575: The UN's internal auditors lacked independence in 2006, and GAO's report says funding arrangements impeded their freedom. The findings expose the leash. The report warns that the world body's watchdogs needed room to bark. The independence had to be protected. The watchdogs needed room to bark.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-675: The federal internet upgrade was just beginning in 2006, and GAO's report says the government was in early stages of the IPv6 transition with key challenges remaining. The findings map the road ahead. The report warns that the net's next chapter needed planning. The transition had to proceed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-75: Island health care funding faced multiple factors in 2005, and GAO's report says federal funding for insular areas was affected by many issues. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the islanders deserved fair care. The factors had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-775: Counting the undocumented got a new method in 2006, and GAO's report describes a grouped-answers approach to surveying the foreign-born. The findings explain the technique. The report shows the invisible population could be estimated honestly. The method had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-275: Filmmakers at the Smithsonian needed clearer rules in 2007, and GAO's report says more information should be given on the impact of filming. The findings demand the disclosure. The report warns that the cameras should not harm the collections. The art had to be protected.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-375: The 9/11 wounds were still open in 2007, and GAO's report says progress had been made on the vulnerabilities, though federal action had to continue. The findings balance credit and warning. The report argues that the lessons of the towers could not be filed away. The vigilance had to outlast the memory.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-75: Child welfare's help systems needed better information in 2007, and GAO's report says improved program, training, and technical assistance data would help. The findings demand the knowledge. The report warns that the vulnerable kids needed smarter support. The data had to serve the children.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-875: Detainees could not get a dial tone in 2007 — GAO's report finds phone-access failures rampant in immigration lockups, plus other shortfalls. The findings document a detention system failing its own standards. The report argues that locked up should not mean cut off.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-375: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at defense Infrastructure: Army and Marine Corps Grow the Force Construction Projects Generally Support the Initiative. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-75: The Government Accountability Office dug into veterans' Benefits: Improved Operational Controls and Management Data Would Enhance VBA's Disability Reevaluation Process in this 2007 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gitagovinda-arnold-1875:
Edwin Arnold sang Jayadeva's Gitagovinda in English in 1875 as The Indian Song of Songs, a rendering of love and faith. Jayadeva's twelfth-century Sanskrit lyric drama tells of Radha and Krishna: their longing, their parting, and their reunion in the spring woods. Songs meant for singing carry the lovers' moods, while Krishna's godhood shines through the human play of desire.

Hindu devotion cherishes the poem as scripture set to music, sung in temples and festivals to this day. Arnold, famed across the world for The Light of Asia, gave its erotic mysticism a lush Victorian voice. His rendering remains the best known English path into Jayadeva's masterpiece for new readers.
guyon-short-method-1775: A Short and Easy Method of Prayer by Madame Guyon, the 1775 guide to contemplative prayer. Her quietist method shaped French spirituality. This edition preserves that devotional classic. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
heckethorn-secret-societies-1875:
Charles William Heckethorn cast a wide net in The Secret Societies of All Ages and Countries in 1875. No guild or cult of note slips past his sweep. The book starts with the rites of Egypt, Greece, and Rome. It runs on to the groups of his own Victorian day.

Knights Templar, Rosicrucians, and Freemasons take long runs of text. So do the Carbonari, the Mafia's kin, and odd cults of the East. Heckethorn tells of signs, oaths, and the ends each group sought. The book is a vast store house of tales on hid groups.
helsinki-final-act-1975:
Thirty-five nations signed the Helsinki Final Act in Finland in 1975, closing a long conference on security in Europe. The United States, Canada, the Soviet Union, and nearly all European states took part. The act was not a treaty, but a set of political promises meant to ease Cold War tensions.

The West accepted Europe's postwar borders as settled, which Moscow had long wanted. In return, the Soviet bloc promised to respect human rights, free movement, and the flow of information. Dissidents across Eastern Europe seized on those promises, forming Helsinki watch groups that pressed their governments to keep them. Historians credit that pressure with helping to loosen the Soviet grip and end the Cold War.
how-to-read-character-a-new-illustrated-: How to Read Character, 1875. The illustrated handbook. This book preserves that manual. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. It retains its place in time. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
hutchinson-spirit-of-masonry-1775:
William Hutchinson, a Durham solicitor and Mason, published The Spirit of Masonry in London in 1775. The book gathers his moral and elucidatory lectures on the Craft. Hutchinson recasts Masonry as a system of morality taught through symbols, a presentation meant for a skeptical age that mocked secret societies.

His lectures explain the lodge's furniture, jewels, and ceremonies as lessons in virtue. The approach founded Masonic philosophical apologetics, the Craft's reasoned defense of itself. Hutchinson writes for brethren and for curious outsiders alike. His Masonry asks to be judged as moral teaching in allegorical dress. The Spirit of Masonry gave English lodges a philosophy, and later lecturers built on his readings for a century.
indian-poetry-arnold-1875:
Edwin Arnold published Indian Poetry in 1875, gathering his verse renderings from Sanskrit sources. Its centerpiece, The Indian Song of Songs, was the first English verse translation of Jayadeva's Gita Govinda. That twelfth-century poem sings the love of Krishna and Radha in songs of great sweetness and daring.

Arnold adds two books from the Mahabharata, wise sayings from the Hitopadesa, and other Oriental poems. His light, musical English aimed to make India's classics sing for Victorian readers. Arnold later won wide fame with The Light of Asia, his life of the Buddha in verse. This earlier volume shows the same gift at work. The Gutenberg text is ebook 25965.
jevons-money-mechanism-exchange-1875:
Jevons published Money and the Mechanism of Exchange in 1875, a short classic on what money is and how it works. He wrote it for general readers as much as for students, in the clear style that marked his best work. At the time, banking crises and currency debates made the subject urgent on both sides of the Atlantic.

The book explains why barter fails, what makes a good currency material, and how coins, notes, and cheques each do money's work. Jevons treats the standard of value, minting, and paper money with calm precision. Generations of students learned the subject from these chapters. The primer is still quoted for its clarity, and historians count it the clearest short book on money in English. It shows a founder of modern economics writing at the height of his powers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lucena-10175:
Lucena, a walled city near Cordova, Spain, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling. In early times it was inhabited almost wholly by Jews and was called the “Jews’ City.” Its Jews traded widely and, by one Arabic account, were richer than those of any other city.

The article recalls the scholars who taught there, above all Isaac Alfasi, who founded a large Talmudic academy in Lucena. It then turns harsh: pressure to convert in 1107, bought off with a large payment, and destruction under the Almohades in 1146, when Jews were robbed and forced to accept Islam. Ferdinand III later gave the city to the bishop of Cordova. The entry preserves the rise and ruin of one of medieval Spain’s most famous Jewish towns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magnus-ludwig-i:
Ludwig Immanuel Magnus, a German mathematician, is the subject of a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born in Berlin on March 15, 1790, he lost his father young. His mother placed him in his uncle's bank. After business hours he studied Euclid on his own. He died at Berlin in 1861.

The article follows a double life of banking and geometry. Magnus volunteered in the artillery during the Napoleonic wars, serving from 1813 to 1815. Back in Berlin he banked by day and taught mathematics at the Cauer academy. By 1834 his reputation earned him an honorary doctorate from Bonn. His papers appeared in the leading French and German journals of the field. Ill health and failing eyes ended his work early. The entry preserves a self-taught geometer who won a university's honor without ever holding its chair.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manoah-b-shemar:
Manoah ben Shemariah Handel, a Polish author, is the subject of a short 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born at Brzeszticzka in Volhynia, he died in 1612. His son preserved and published his father's works. The article names three of them, with their printings at Cracow, Prague, and Lublin.

The first work, Hokmat Manoah, holds his glosses on the Talmud. Those glosses were printed inside the Cracow Talmud edition of 1602 to 1605, and separately at Prague. The second comments on Bahya's Duties of the Heart, printed at Lublin in 1596 and often reprinted. A third work's title page mentions the emperor Rudolph and King Matthias. The son spoke of publishing still more of his father's writing on Talmud, Cabala, and astronomy. The entry preserves a scholar known mostly through his son's care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-matalon-mordeca:
Mordecai Matalon was a sixteenth-century rabbi of Salonica. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He was the uncle of Jacob ben Solomon Matalon, the scholar of the neighboring entry. He stood out as a prominent Talmudist. His companion Samuel di Modena also reports that he was well versed in the secular sciences of his day.

Little of his writing stands under his own name. What survives is quoted work. Samuel di Modena quotes him in his responsa, and Isaac Adarbi cites him in “Dibre Ribot.” Legal answers of his own were printed inside Samuel Kala'i's “Mishpete Shemuel,” published at Venice in 1599. The entry shows how the encyclopedia preserves scholars whose learning is visible only through the books of their friends.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ibn-jair-1:
Meir ibn Jair was an Italian Talmudist and grammarian of the sixteenth century. Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn entered him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Even his name needs explaining. His family name seems to have been Me'iri, since he is always called “Meir of the house of Meir.” “Ibn Jair” likely comes from a blessing written after his name in manuscripts, perhaps meaning “may his light continue.”

Two books carry his name, both printed at Sabbioneta. “Yair Natib,” issued in 1553, treats the law of slaughtering animals. Hayyim Benveniste quoted it often in his great legal digest. A year later came his grammar of the eight conjugations of the Hebrew verb. He revised that grammar late in life and published it again in 1597 under the plain title “Dikduk,” Grammar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendl-sigismund:
Sigismund Ferdinand Mendl was an English politician. Joseph Jacobs and Martha Washington Levy give him a brief notice in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1866. He was educated at Harrow School and at University College, Oxford. In 1888 he was called to the bar at the Inner Temple.

His road to Parliament took three tries. He contested the Isle of Wight unsuccessfully in 1892. He contested Plymouth in 1895. He won Plymouth in the Liberal interest in 1898. He served only until 1900. The entry rests on Who's Who for 1902 and the Jewish Year Book. It records nothing of his speeches or causes. So he stands as a compact specimen of a type. He is the Anglo-Jewish professional entering public life at the century's turn. His path runs school, university, bar, and a brief seat in the Commons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mhushilkar-reub:
Reuben Ezekiel Mhushilkar, a soldier of the Beni-Israel community of India, is the subject of one of the shortest entries in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, written by Joseph Jacobs and J. Hyams. The whole article is a single sentence of service record. He enlisted in the 19th Regiment Native Infantry on January 15, 1849.

The entry tracks his rise through the ranks: jemidar in October 1861 and subahdar in January 1870. It lists the battles where he won medals, at Multan and Gujarat in the Punjab and at four places in central India, then service in Afghanistan from 1878 to 1880. He retired on March 6, 1881, closing a career of thirty-two years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mirkes-solomon-:
Solomon Zalman ben Judah Löb Mirkes was a Lithuanian Talmudist of the eighteenth century, a native of Mir in the government of Minsk. Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn give him a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He first appears in print at Königsberg in 1769, with a funeral oration for Abraham, the late chief rabbi of Frankfurt-on-the-Main.

Two years later Mirkes was himself rabbi of Frankfurt-on-the-Oder, and there he published his two substantial works in a single year. Sharsheret ha-Abotot gathers his novellae, decisions, and discussions on Talmudic questions. Shulḥan Shelomoh is a compendium of the Shulḥan Aruk's Oraḥ Ḥayyim division, arranged according to the later authorities, a working handbook for daily Jewish law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moon-10975:
The moon in Hebrew is yeraḥ, probably the wanderer. In poetry it is lebanah, the white one. That is the starting point of a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn, published in 1906. Genesis makes it the lesser light to rule the night. It was set for signs and seasons. The Psalmist likewise says it was appointed for the seasons.

The article gathers the biblical moon whole. It tells of its course halted at Joshua's word and its New Moon festivals under the word ḥodesh. It tells of its supposed power over sleepers. Psalm 121 promises that the moon shall not smite thee by night. That promise is read against the eastern belief that moonlight blinds the uncovered face. Philology, calendar, and folklore share one short entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosse-rudolf-11:
Rudolf Mosse was a German publisher and philanthropist born at Grätz in Posen on May 8, 1843. Isidore Singer and Isidor Warsaw wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He learned printing as an apprentice and mastered the trade in several cities. At twenty-four he saw his chance in advertising, then little developed in Germany.

His Berlin advertising agency spread to most large cities of Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. He published the Berliner Tageblatt, the Berliner Morgenzeitung, and the Allgemeine Zeitung des Judenthums, and his printing house was among the largest. He also gave on a large scale: pension funds for his many employees and a school for a hundred children. He built a hospital in his native Grätz as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumanovitz-nap:
Naphtali Herz Neumanovitz was a Russian Jewish author. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Jozefow on Feb. 12, 1843. He died at Warsaw on March 11, 1898. His family was known for secular and Talmudic learning.

At eighteen Neumanovitz went to study at Lublin. He later removed to Warsaw and joined Ha-Zefirah. His weekly feuilletons ran under the name Berosh Homiyoth. Friends gathered them into a book after his death. He wrote for Polish magazines at Lublin and for Izraelita. He edited a Hebrew magazine for Jewish youth. His textbooks taught Hebrew, Polish, and German together. They appeared at Warsaw in 1898, his death year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nob-11575:
Nob was a town of priests near Jerusalem. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and J. Frederic McCurdy for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. David fleeing Saul received holy bread there. Nearly the whole community paid with their lives. Isaiah names it in an Assyrian march on Jerusalem.

Nehemiah lists Nob among the towns of Benjamin. It stood close beside Anathoth, north of the capital. Some doubt a priestly town so near Jebusite Jerusalem. The entry answers that treaties were common then. Israel and Canaanite towns often lived by such truces. Cheyne held the name itself a false reading. He thought Gibeon was the place really meant.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oholah-and-ohol:
Oholah and Oholibah are two sisters in a Bible tale. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote on them for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The tale stands in chapter twenty-three of Ezekiel. The names are signs, not real women of flesh. Oholah, the elder, stands for Samaria and Israel. Oholibah stands for Jerusalem and the land of Judah.

Both sisters are shown as wives of God in the tale. Both are false to him and take other loves. Those loves are Egypt, Assyria, and Chaldea, the great powers. Each power uses the sisters and then ruins them. The names hold the sense of the whole tale. Oholah means tent, for God's tent was at Samaria. Oholibah means my tent is in her, for the Temple stood at Jerusalem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ornstein-mordec:
Mordecai Zeeb Ornstein was an Austrian scholar of rabbinic books. The board and M. W. Rapoport wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Lemberg on October 28, 1837. His father was Jacob Meshullam Ornstein, rabbi of that city. His father taught him the Talmud and rabbinic works.

Mordecai showed great skill at a young age in study. Some of his replies stand in his father's book. That book is called Yeshuot Yaakob, in Hebrew words. His quick fame at so young an age fed his pride. He showed that pride in his ways with all men. For long he would take no post as a rabbi. At last Przemysl, a great town, gave him its call. He took the call but died before he could serve.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palmyra-hebrew-:
Palmyra was a city in an oasis of the Syrian waste. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Hebrew name was Tadmor, and its Latin name Palmyra. It lay five days from the Euphrates by road. It lay three days from Aleppo, a town of trade.

Palmyra stood on the high road to the Euphrates river. It grew to a great hub of trade in the East. Men said Solomon founded it when he took Hamath-zobah. That gave him a share of rule on that road. The Jewish realm lost the town under King Jehu. It won the town back under Jeroboam the Second. Jews met Palmyra once more in the third century. Queen Zenobia seems to have been kind to Jews then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedagogics-1197:
Pedagogics, the science of education, gets a long article here. Joseph Jacobs and Louis Grossman wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its base law comes from Deuteronomy. Children must learn the faith so well that they live by it.

In Bible times every home was a school. Every parent served as a teacher of the children. Reading and writing were common skills among the Hebrews. A second rule shaped the teaching itself. The teacher must fit the lesson to the child's own nature. Proverbs adds firm discipline as part of good training.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-petronius-arbit:
Petronius Arbiter was a Latin satirist of Nero's age. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He earns his place here through one mocking fragment. In it he sneers at the Jews of Rome.

Petronius claimed that Jews worship a pig and heaven. He said such worship counts only with circumcision. He also said Jews fast on the Sabbath each week. All three claims are false and absurd. Still, they spread through the whole Roman world. His Widow of Ephesus tale later entered Jewish letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinsker-lev-lev:
Lev Pinsker was a Russian Jewish physician of Odessa. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Poland in 1821. He died at Odessa in 1891, famous across Europe.

Pinsker trained at Moscow and nursed cholera patients there. Within ten years he led Odessa's medical world. He wrote for the press on Jewish freedom and schooling. Then he concluded that Jews must free themselves. His pamphlet Autoemancipation, printed in 1881, urged land of their very own. It stirred debate across the whole continent.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-popper-david-12:
David Popper was an Austrian cellist born at Prague in 1845. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied under Goltermann at the Prague Conservatorium. At eighteen he toured Germany and won instant fame. Critics ranked him among the top cellists of his time.

On his return, Popper joined a prince's orchestra at Löwenburg. Hans von Bülow had urged the post for him. He toured Germany, Holland, Switzerland, and England. In Vienna he became solo cellist in the court orchestra. He played in the famed Hellmesberger Quartet as well. In 1872 he wed the pianist Sophie Menter. By 1905 he taught at the music academy in Budapest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-gaon-mar:
Rabbah Gaon, called Mar Raba, led the school at Pumbedita. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Halevy dates his rule from 640 to 650. Grätz sets it twenty years later instead. He held the post at the same time as Huna of Sura. The two school heads acted as a pair.

The two geonim made a weighty rule on divorce together. By Talmud law a wife may seek divorce in rare cases. A foul disease in the husband is one such case. The new rule dealt with her right to press that claim. The entry sets out the rule and its sources. It shows the geonim at work as lawmakers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raphall-morris-:
Morris Jacob Raphall was a rabbi and author born on October 3, 1798. Joseph Jacobs and Israel Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Stockholm, Sweden. He died at New York on June 23, 1868.

The article follows his schooling in Copenhagen and England. He published a Hebrew review that ill health ended in 1836. He translated Maimonides, Albo, and parts of the Mishnah. In 1840 he fought the Damascus blood charge in four languages. He served eight years as minister at Birmingham. In 1849 he moved to New York's B'nei Jeshurun. The entry traces a preacher who worked on two continents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rembrandt-rembr:
Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Ryn was a Dutch painter born at Leyden. Gotthard Deutsch and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born on July 15, in 1606 or 1607. He died at Amsterdam on October 8, 1669.

The article stresses his close friendship with Manasseh ben Israel. Rembrandt painted Manasseh's portrait in 1645 and etched it later. In 1655 he etched four plates for Manasseh's book. They show Nebuchadnezzar's dream and Jacob's dream, among others. Rembrandt lived long near Amsterdam's Jewish quarter. There he found models for Bible scenes and Jewish life. His portraits are the earliest such portraits of Jews. The entry then lists his works of Jewish interest. It gives dates and where each work is held.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ritter-julius-1:
Julius Ritter was a German physician and author born on October 4, 1862. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Berlin, son of Immanuel H. Ritter. He took his medical degree there in 1887.

The article says he now leads care for invalid children in Berlin. He also heads a bacteriological laboratory there. In 1892 he announced a whooping cough bacillus discovery. Papers in 1893 and 1896 confirmed that finding. A second group of articles treats diphtheria and its serum. His large 1893 work covers diphtheria's cause and treatment. Later papers treat scrofula and sickly children. He addressed a Berlin congress on internal medicine in 1897. The entry records a doctor known for two disease studies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-morit:
Moritz Rosenthal was an Austrian physician born at Grosswardein, Hungary, in 1833. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree at Vienna in 1858 and taught neurology there.

Rosenthal wrote about seventy essays plus several full medical works. They cover stuttering, brain tumors, apparent death, and the use of electricity as treatment. His Klinik der Nervenkrankheiten, on diseases of the nerves, appeared in 1875. It was translated into French, English, Italian, and Russian. Such reach shows how widely his clinical writing was read abroad.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sachs-bernhard-:
Bernhard Sachs was an American physician born at Baltimore on January 2, 1858. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied at Harvard and at four European universities, taking his degree in 1882.

Sachs settled in New York in 1884 and specialized in nervous diseases. From 1889 he taught neurology at the New York Polyclinic as professor. He also served on the staffs of Montefiore Home and Mount Sinai Hospital. His books treat paralysis in children and a familial form of idiocy with blindness. A textbook of nervous diseases followed in 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samson-ben-isaa:
Samson ben Isaac of Chinon was a French Talmudist who lived from about 1260 to 1330. Wilhelm Bacher and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. A peer called him the greatest rabbinical authority of his time.

Samson's Sefer Keritut, printed at Constantinople in 1515, teaches Talmud method. Its five parts cover Ishmael's thirteen rules and Eliezer's thirty-two rules alike. One part names the Tannaim and Amoraim and shows how to decide between clashing views. Easy style and the author's weight made the book a classic at once. He also commented on two Talmud tractates and on divorce law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sanders-daniel-:
Isidore Singer and J. C. Baer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Daniel Sanders. He was a German lexicographer, a maker of dictionaries. Sanders was born at Altstrelitz, in Mecklenburg, on April 12, 1819. He died on March 12, 1897. He was trained in the Jewish school of his home town. He then studied languages, mathematics, and natural history at Berlin and Halle.

Sanders took his doctorate in 1843. For ten years he led the school where he had been trained. His chief work is the Handwörterbuch der Deutschen Sprache, a handbook of German. It appeared from 1859 to 1865. He wrote it in sharp debate with the Grimm brothers' dictionary. He also published a dictionary of foreign words and one of synonyms. Textbooks, letter guides, and a history of German language followed. In 1876 Berlin called him to help purge foreign terms from German.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schlemihl-13275:
Cyrus Adler and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the schlemihl. The word is a popular Yiddish term for an unlucky person. Heine traced it to the Bible name Shelumiel. Phinehas speared a man with that name in the Book of Numbers. Others derive it from schlimm mazzal, meaning unlucky star.

Ghetto tales love the schlemihl's misfortunes. Luck pursues him through no fault of his own. He bears it all without a murmur. Such figures match the Gothamites of English lore and Germany's Schildbürgers. Chamisso made the name famous in his tale Peter Schlemihl. He used it with little regard for its Jewish sense. He may have picked the word up from the Berlin banker Itzig. The article weighs the word's roots and its road into German literature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbethai-ben-:
Shabbethai ben Moses was a legal scholar and prayer poet at Rome in the early eleventh century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Only fragments of his legal decisions survive today. He led the Jewish congregation of Rome as its president.

After Solomon ha-Babli, Shabbethai was Rome's first Hebrew poet. His poems for Passover sit in the Roman prayer book, still in manuscript. One poem carries his name hidden in an acrostic. His penitential prayers also survive, and one was translated by Zunz. His sons Moses and Kalonymus became prayer poets too. The entry recalls a leader who shaped Rome's Jewish worship in verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simchowitz-samu:
Samuel Simchowitz was a Russian rabbinical writer born early in the nineteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He knew rabbinic learning thoroughly from his training. At the same time he read modern literature well.

Essays by Simchowitz appeared in the Petersburger Herold newspaper. Vienna's Orthodox community invited him as rabbi in 1866. He refused that call, and a Warsaw call two years later. Many of his Talmudic novellae remain in manuscript form. His responsa on the ritual codes survive the same way. In 1894 he sat in a great rabbinical synod at St. Petersburg. He died at Slutzk in March 1896. The entry honors a traditional scholar open to modern letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-singer-maximili:
Maximilian Singer was an Austrian botanist, zoologist, and author born in 1857. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Leipnik on February 6 of that year. He took his doctor's degree at Vienna in 1883. He made botany and zoology his main fields of work.

Singer wrote many articles on plants and animals. They appeared in farming journals in Vienna. He also wrote plays, including Junius Brutus in 1879. Two more dramas followed in 1891 and 1896. He wrote libretti for operas as well. One of them, Der Weise von Cordova, had music by Oskar Strauss.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-maz:
Solomon ben Mazzal Tob was a Turkish Hebrew poet and press corrector. Joseph Jacobs and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He flourished at Constantinople in the early sixteenth century. He was active in Hebrew printing from 1513 to 1549. Many printed books of that age bear his signature.

Among them were Kimhi's Sefer ha-Shorashim in 1513. He also worked on the four Turim in 1540. He issued a set of hymns by various authors in 1545. Some hymns in that set were his own work. He also published an introductory poem to a Torah commentary. He left a poem on chess-playing, printed much later in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitzer-benjami:
Benjamin Solomon Spitzer was an Austrian rabbi and champion of Orthodoxy. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was son-in-law of Rabbi Moses Sofer of Pressburg. For more than forty years he led Vienna's ultra-Orthodox congregation. Its synagogue stood in the Shiffgasse of that city.

He was a strong opponent of Reform in Jewish life. In 1872 he attacked Vienna's Culturgemeinde for its Reform measures. A set of his sermons and funeral orations was published in 1892. It also held his novellae, titled Shimlat Binyamin in part. His son-in-law Joseph Baer Kohen issued that collection. He died in Vienna on December 5, 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strauss-charles:
Charles Strauss was a French jurist and politician born in Alsace in 1834. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Gundershoffen on October 14. He set up as an attorney in Paris. He later held posts in the Interior Ministry.

Strauss spent some years in Algeria in important posts. During the Franco-Prussian war he organized army food supply there. He drafted the proclamation of the French republic in Algiers. It was published there on September 4, 1870. In 1888 he became prefect of the Drôme department. On the last day of 1895 he became an officer of the Legion of Honor. His books treat Algeria and French administration. The entry sketches a long official career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szegedin-14175:
Szegedin is a town of central Hungary on the Tisza. Isidore Singer and Adolf Löwinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Jews appear there as tax-farmers under Turkish rule. Records name them in that role in 1552. When the Turks left, the Jews left too.

In 1714 three Jews who settled without leave were expelled. A royal privilege let the city admit or refuse Jews. Szegedin used that right with utmost rigor. One settler slipped in during 1781 without permission. Six families gained leave three years later. Tolerated families grew to fifty-eight by 1799. A 1790 decree froze their standing in place. Jews then began buying houses inside the city. The entry tracks slow admission, family by counted family.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-taxo-14275:
Taxo is a mysterious martyr in the Assumption of Moses. Kaufmann Kohler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. The book calls him a man of Levi's tribe. Under Herod's persecution he died with his seven sons. Zealots were the targets of that cruel campaign.

Taxo urged his sons to die rather than transgress. Their blood, he said, would be avenged before the Lord. There the ancient story breaks off abruptly. Josephus tells of an old man caught in caves. That man killed his family and himself before surrender. He reproached Herod even as a king for baseness. Scholars think the two tales tell one event. Charles read Taxo as a corruption meaning the Zealot. The entry chases one name through text and history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-thomashefski-bo:
Boris Thomashefski was a leading actor of the Yiddish stage in America. Cyrus Adler and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Kiev in 1866. He reached New York in 1881 seeking work.

Soon he organized a Jewish troupe that played at Turn Hall. Three years later he managed theater in Chicago. He settled in New York in 1893 and rose to the top of his field. By 1905 he ran the People's Theater as lessee and manager. He played the chief role in nearly every production there. Most plays came from Latteiner's pen. Thomashefski also wrote plays and published witty sayings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ulmann-salomon-:
Salomon Ulmann was chief rabbi of France and author of a classic catechism. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Zabern in 1806, he died at Paris in 1865. He was the first pupil enrolled at the Ecole Centrale Rabbinique in 1830. He also took its first chief rabbi diploma.

He served Lauterbourg from 1834 and Nancy from 1844. In 1853 he became chief rabbi of the Central Consistory. His catechism of religious instruction appeared in 1845. A third edition was still printing in 1871. In 1856 he organized France's Central Conference of chief rabbis. Its reforms shortened liturgical poems and introduced organs. Confirmation for Jewish youth came from that meeting too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wandsworth-lord:
Sidney Stern, Lord Wandsworth, was an English banker and peer. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in London in 1845. His father, Viscount de Stern, headed Stern Brothers bank. Sidney studied at Magdalene College, Cambridge. He worked in the family firm before retiring.

Stern served as a justice of the peace for Surrey and London. He ran for Parliament four times and lost. In May 1891 he finally won the Stowmarket seat. He held it until raised to the peerage in 1895. He also held a Portuguese viscount title by descent.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wessely-wolfgan:
Wolfgang Wessely was an Austrian jurist and theologian. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Trebitsch, Moravia, on October 22, 1801. He died at Vienna on April 21, 1870. He went to Prague at fourteen to train for the rabbinate. He took law and philosophy degrees there.

Wessely taught religion at Prague's gymnasium from 1831. In 1846 he lectured at the university on Hebrew literature. Austria sent him abroad to study jury trials in 1848. He rose through Prague's law faculty step by step. In 1861 he became a full professor. He was the first Austrian Jew to hold that rank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-george-gar:
George Garcia Wolf (1838-1899) was a merchant who sat in the Cape Parliament. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Great Yarmouth, he trained in trade at Manchester. He then crossed the sea to work in Montreal.

In 1860 he moved on to Kimberley in South Africa. There he opened a general store in the diamond fields. He worked with the top men of that rough camp town. In 1882 the town sent him to the Cape Parliament. His voters gave him a gold box with five hundred guineas. They added a fine framed address of thanks. He held more town posts in Kimberley for some years. Then he went back to England, where he died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-znaim-15275:
Znaim is a city in Moravia whose Jewish community had a long, broken history. Gotthard Deutsch and Isidor Kahan wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews likely settled there in the twelfth century, and a Jews' street appears in a document of 1225. Money lending was their chief early trade.

Persecution struck during the Armleder attacks and the Black Death, and in 1454 the Jews were expelled. For nearly four centuries none could live in Znaim, and visitors paid a special toll. After 1848 they returned, built a synagogue in 1888, and formed a congregation of about 160 families. By 1905 most worked as merchants, with some doctors, lawyers, and engineers among them.
kardec-spirits-book-1875:
Allan Kardec built a faith from talks with the dead in The Spirits' Book, here in English from 1875. Kardec was a school man in Paris who put the same asks to seers in town past town. Their replies, he held, agreed. The book sets those asks and replies in ranks: God, souls, birth past death, and the laws of right and wrong.

His faith, called Spiritism, claims to join science and creed as one. It won hosts of fans, most of all in Brazil. The book is its first and chief text. All its lore starts here.
lartet-christy-reliquiae-aquitanicae-187:
Edouard Lartet, a French digger, and Henry Christy, an English backer, dug the caves of the Dordogne from 1865 to 1875. Thomas Rupert Jones put their great memoir in print in 1875. Its Latin title means relics of Aquitaine, the old name of that part of France.

The book sets out carved bone, stone tools, and the frames of Cro-Magnon man from the caves. It tells of hunts, beasts of the ice age, and art cut in bone and horn. The work is the first learned report on cave life in the stone age, and a base text.
lee-octopus-devil-fish-1875:
The octopus got its first fair trial in Henry Lee's monograph of 1875. The Octopus; or, The Devil-Fish of Fiction and of Fact splits the real beast from the kraken of tale. Lee wrote from his work at the Brighton Aquarium, where he kept the creatures live.

He tells what the octopus is, how it feeds and moves, and how big it truly grows. Then he shows how its arms and bulk swelled, in sailor talk, into a ship-sinking fiend. The book shrinks the legend down to the animal, and the animal stays strange enough. It is the first scientific word on its theme.
liquor-alchahest-or-a-discourse-of-that-: Liquor alchahest, 1675. The immortal dissolvent. This book preserves that discourse. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes.
maine-lectures-early-history-institution:
Maine's Lectures on the Early History of Institutions appeared in 1875, a sequel in spirit to his famous Ancient Law. Maine taught that modern institutions could only be understood by tracing them to their primitive forms. The lectures range widely, drawing on his years in India and on the old laws of Ireland.

He treats kingship, property, and the family in their earliest shapes, comparing the Brehon laws of Ireland with the customs of India and Rome. The comparative method is the star: distant societies are set side by side to reveal a common pattern of growth. Maine writes with the confidence of a man opening a new science. The book was the comparative method's masterpiece in legal history, and later scholars have argued with it ever since, which is its own kind of tribute.
mark-twain-a-biography-volume-i-part-2-1:
Volume one, part two of Paine's biography runs from 1866 to 1875. Its contents open with 'The Lecturer' and 'Highway Robbery.' Chapters then promise a new book and Twain's first book. 'The Innocents at Sea' launches his famous Holy Land excursion.

The Innocents Abroad made him a household name on his return. In Washington a publishing proposition changes his course for good. Olivia Langdon enters the story, and with her, marriage and Hartford. A contract with Elisha Bliss, Jr., sets his book trade in order. Paine shows fame arriving and the humorist settling into authorship. These are the years when Mark Twain became an institution.
mark-twain-s-letters-volume-2-1867-1875:
