Volume two of Mark Twain's Letters runs from 1867 to 1875. It opens with a letter to Bret Harte in San Francisco. Twain reports his first book is out and handsome. He growls at its errors, then begs Harte to say nothing.

He lectures at Cooper Institute the next Monday, he writes. On June 8 he sails for the Holy Land with the pilgrims. That voyage became The Innocents Abroad and made his name. Letters to his family in St. Louis share every turn. Fame, courtship, and marriage fill the years that follow. Paine's comments bind the letters into a living story.
mellon-ms-15-alchemical-and-medical-misc:
Mellon MS 15 is a German paper manuscript of about 1475. Yale's Beinecke Library holds the book, with 99 leaves. Its spine reads Antidotarium Nicolai in gilt letters at the top.

Most works inside are by Nicolaus and treat the art of medicine. Lists of goods in Latin and German stand among them. A tract on the making of brandy adds a trade craft. The hand is neat gothic cursive, with large red capitals at each break. Tall letters on the top lines are stroked red as well. The mix of drug lists and drink craft marks its trade use.
mellon-ms-16-de-consideratione-quinte-es:
Mellon MS 16 holds John of Rupescissa on the fifth essence. The German paper copy is dated about 1475. An unknown hand turned his Latin work into German for this book.

The book keeps its first binding of red brown leather on wood boards. Brass bosses guard the covers, set at the corners and the middle. Two clasps are lost, but the hinges still hold sound. The text runs to 80 leaves in a bold gothic cursive hand. Red heads and capitals run through the whole text. The fifth essence was held to be a strong cure in its day.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol1-1875:
Henri van Laun translated the complete plays of Molière into English, and the first volume appeared in 1875. Molière, who died in 1673, was France's great writer of stage comedy. Volume one gathers his early plays, written before his fame was secure.

The volume holds The Blunderer, The Love-Tiff, and The Pretentious Young Ladies. It also holds Sganarelle and the serious verse play Don Garcia of Navarre. Readers can watch Molière learn his craft: quick plots, mistaken lovers, and servants who outwit their masters. Van Laun added notes on the French stage, and his set stayed the standard English Molière for decades.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol2-1875:
Volume two of Henri van Laun's English Molière came out in 1875, the same year as the first. By the plays in this volume, Molière ran his own company in Paris under royal favor. The centerpiece is The School for Wives, the hit that made him a major figure.

Alongside it stand The School for Husbands and the slight, witty piece called The Bores. Van Laun also prints Molière's own defense, The School for Wives Criticised, plus The Impromptu of Versailles. The Forced Marriage rounds out the volume. Together the plays show comedy turning sharper, as Molière began to mock manners, marriage, and pride in earnest.
moliere-dramatic-works-vanlaun-vol3-1875:
Two of Molière's greatest plays anchor volume three of the van Laun translation, issued in 1875. Don Juan retells the tale of the bold seducer who defies heaven itself. The Misanthrope gives Alceste, a man so wedded to truth that he ruins his own love and standing.

The volume also holds The Princess of Elis, a courtly entertainment with music. Love Is the Best Doctor offers a brisk farce on quack physicians. The Physician in Spite of Himself turns a woodcutter into a fake doctor by force. The mix shows Molière's full range, from deep character study to broad, fast farce.
new-illustrated-self-instructor-in-phren:
An 1875 New York printing of the illustrated self instructor in phrenology and physiology came from S. R. Wells and Company on Broadway. No author is named on the sampled title pages. The book promises over one hundred engravings, like the earlier Fowler printing of the same work.

Its chief extra is a phrenological chart of character for the buyer. The mottoes match the older edition: self knowledge is the essence of all knowledge. Your character, they say, corresponds with your organization. Buyers could mark their own chart and read off traits. Such manuals sold the idea that the head's shape reveals the mind within.
olcott-people-from-the-other-world-1875:
Henry Steel Olcott went to a farm in Vermont to test claims of ghosts in 1875. The farm was the home of the Eddy kin, whose dark room drew crowds. Olcott, then a news man, watched, weighed, and took notes with a cool head and an open mind.

People from the Other World tells what he found there. That trek changed his life. Soon past it he helped found a new creed with Blavatsky. The book is the start point of that creed's tale, writ by a man on the spot. Olcott had served as a law hand and a war sleuth in his past. Those trades taught him to weigh proof with care and calm.
olive-branch-petition-1775:
The Continental Congress sent the Olive Branch Petition to the king in 1775. Shots had been fired, yet Congress still pleads for peace. The text stands as the colonies' last bid for reconciliation.

The delegates swear loyalty, list their wrongs, and beg for redress. They blame grasping ministers, not the king, for the growing crisis. George III refuses to read the plea and brands them rebels. With that door shut, the road to independence lies open. The petition's failure taught moderates that no middle path remained at all. John Dickinson drafted it hoping reason could still stop a war.
openalex-w2107259975:
Louisa Degenhardt, Wai-Tat Chiu, Nancy Sampson and colleagues compared substance use across seventeen countries. Their paper appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2008. Alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs cause much illness worldwide. Sound cross-country data were limited before this work. The data came from World Mental Health Surveys.

Household surveys asked adults about lifetime use. Alcohol and tobacco use varied hugely between countries. Cannabis and cocaine patterns differed just as sharply. The United States showed high rates for several substances. Some poorer countries reported very low illegal drug use. Age and gender patterns also varied by place. The study gives a baseline for global drug policy.
openalex-w2147796775:
Massimo Sartelli, Pierluigi Viale, Fausto Catena, and colleagues published these guidelines in the World Journal of Emergency Surgery in 2013. The World Society of Emergency Surgery panel updated its advice on managing intra-abdominal infections. These infections range from simple appendicitis to severe fecal peritonitis, and death rates stay high despite better surgery and drugs.

The update replaces the panel's 2010 guidelines with evidence-based recommendations. Each recommendation is graded by the strength of its supporting research. A core principle runs through them: control every proven source of infection as soon as possible. Urgency and procedure choice depend on the organ involved, the spread of infection, and the patient's stability. Local resources also shape what is realistic.
openalex-w2154021875:
Simon Hay, Marianne Sinka, Robi Okara, and colleagues published this article in PLoS Medicine in 2010. They describe a project to build global maps of the dominant Anopheles mosquitoes that pass malaria to humans. Control programs lacked good range maps, even though the best control choices depend on which vector lives where.

Big spending on treated bed nets and indoor spraying was not always guided by local mosquito biology. Earlier range maps used mixed methods, from expert opinion to statistics, and could not be merged worldwide. The Malaria Atlas Project set out to fix that with consistent mapping. Shared maps would let programs match tools to the vectors actually present in each region.
openalex-w2175613575:
Maria Prado, Lina Blandón, Luciana Vandenberghe, and colleagues published this review in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2015. They survey milk kefir, an acidic, lightly fizzy fermented milk from the Balkans, Eastern Europe, and the Caucasus. The review covers its makeup, its microbial cultures, its reported health effects, and related products.

Kefir starts from grains, soft lumps of microbes held in a sugar-protein matrix. Inside live lactic acid bacteria, yeasts, and acetic acid bacteria in a shared community. Makers can use living grains, freeze-dried starters, or pure cultures, including a serial Russian method for large batches. Whey can also serve as a growth base. The grains regrow after each batch, passing the culture on.
openalex-w2730180975:
The LHCb Collaboration announced a new particle in this 2017 Physical Review Letters paper, with R. Aaij as first author. The particle is a baryon containing two charm quarks, named with the symbol Ξcc++. Theory had long predicted such doubly charmed baryons. An earlier experiment, SELEX, claimed a related particle with odd properties that other searches never confirmed.

LHCb found a highly significant bump in the combined mass of a lambda-c baryon plus three lighter particles. That bump marks the new baryon decaying in that channel. The doubly charmed particle's longer expected lifetime made it the easier of the pair to catch. Its discovery settles the long-standing puzzle in favor of a real particle, though not with SELEX's reported properties. The find opens a fresh testing ground for the theory of the strong force.
openalex-w2750914475:
Brunno Freire Oliveira, Vinícius de Avelar São Pedro, and Georgina Santos-Barrera introduced the AmphiBIO database in Scientific Data in 2017. It collects traits of amphibians from around the world. Trait-based research links an animal's features to its function and fitness. Such data were scarce for amphibians, even as their numbers crash worldwide.

AmphiBIO holds data on seventeen traits covering ecology, body form, and reproduction. The team compiled them from over fifteen hundred published sources. Coverage spans more than six thousand five hundred species, across all three amphibian orders and sixty-one families. With it, researchers can run large-scale analyses that were impossible before. Trait shifts in shrinking communities can be tracked against ecosystem effects. The database turns scattered natural history notes into a shared research tool.
openalex-w3091894475:
Zannatul Ferdous, Saiful Islam, Tajuddin Sikder, and colleagues published this survey in PLoS ONE in 2020. It measures knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding COVID-19 among people in Bangladesh. The study ran online as a one-time, cross-sectional poll during the outbreak.

Bangladesh had adopted a range of measures to slow the virus, from closures to hygiene campaigns. Whether such population-wide controls work depends on what people know, believe, and actually do. The authors therefore polled residents on their grasp of symptoms and prevention, their stance toward the measures, and their daily habits. Studies of this kind reveal where public messaging lands and where it misses, guiding officials who must win cooperation.
openalex-w3155800275:
F. Sapin, J.-C. Ringenbach, and C. Clerc wrote this geology article on rifted margins. These margins form where a continent stretches, thins, and finally breaks apart, creating new ocean floor. New seismic surveys and drilling now give far clearer pictures of these deep structures than before.

The authors propose a simple way to sort margins by how the crust deforms and how much magma forms. At one end, deformation stays narrow and magma is plentiful. At the other, deformation spreads out and magma is scarce. They list forces that can steer rifting, and stress that margins form a continuum that can change over time.
openalex-w3174482775:
Robin Schmid, Daniel Petras, Louis-Félix Nothias-Scaglia, and colleagues present a new data tool for chemistry in Nature Communications in 2021. Their field, metabolomics, identifies the small molecules in a sample from mass spectrometry data. One molecule can appear as several different ions, which often stay unconnected in the results and waste effort.

Their method, called Ion Identity Molecular Networking, links those ions back to one molecule. It joins the standard network built from fragmentation spectra with a new layer based on matching signal shapes. The tool runs inside the GNPS platform used by many labs. It should cut false leads and make molecule identification faster and more reliable.
openalex-w4406658975:
Felix Busch, Lena Hoffmann, Christopher Rueger, and colleagues review how large language models are used in patient care. Their systematic review appeared in Communications Medicine in 2025. Chatbot-style models spread fast in medicine. Organised evidence on their uses and limits was missing.

The team searched five databases and kept eighty-nine studies from twenty-nine medical specialties. Most studies tested GPT models answering medical questions. Others used the models to write patient information or clinical documents. The review sorts the limits into design problems, such as poor medical tuning, and output problems, such as unreliable text. The map helps clinicians judge where these tools help and where they risk harm.
openalex-w7117325475:
Yusuke Sakai, Fumiya Hori, Hiroki Matsumura, and colleagues pin down the magnetic structure of the compound LaMnSi. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. The material belongs to a family where magnetism and unusual electronic orders compete.

Bulk measurements cannot see which way the atomic moments point. The team uses nuclear magnetic resonance on manganese and lanthanum nuclei. Those nuclei report the local magnetic fields inside the crystal. From the spectra, the authors determine the antiferromagnetic structure directly. The moments order along the crystal's c-axis. A microscopic structure anchors models of this material family. It also clarifies how LaMnSi differs from its better-known cerium cousins.
openalex-w7204225575:
Joaquim Afonso Mucuambi wrote a Portuguese-language paper, from 2026, on the clash between computer forensics and criminal law in cybersecurity. Its case is a massive service outage at UNITEL, Angola's telecom operator. Forensic engineers work amid early doubt and fading digital traces, while economic criminal law demands proof of cause and intent before it can punish. The study reviews records and analyzes Angola's cybercrime laws alongside IT governance.

Writing cybercrime law without tech coupling to IT governance, the author finds, creates mismatched offense types, weak punishment, and risks to basic due-process rights. He urges a cross-field approach that joins global cybersecurity standards and digital evidence rules to due process in Angola.
openalex-w7212003675: Felipe dos Anjos Rodrigues Campos leads a team of seven authors in an epidemiological analysis of leprosy in Uberlandia, Brazil, published in 2026 in the journal Research, Society and Development. The sample available for this entry gives the title, authors, and journal only, without an abstract. The work's stated scope is the pattern of leprosy in the city, and the prevention and control measures that fit its local conditions.
openalex-w7212257175:
Suelem Galucio Costa Gomes, Roberta Yatricy Hipolito Azevedo, and Francesca Aimee Oda da Silva review the path to motherhood, in body and in mind. A pregnancy shifts the body in deep ways, term by term. It also stirs strong and mixed moods. The team read work from 2020 to 2025 in two databases. They asked how the shifts shape a woman's mood, and how they shape her bond with the child she bears.

Worry, fear, and doubt shift with each term, they find. So does the tie a mother feels to the unborn child. Warm back-up from kin and mates acts as a strong shield. It guards mood and eases the path to birth and care. The authors press for care that treats the mind as part of the pregnancy, not an add-on. A calm mother, in their frame, is a health aim in its own right.
openalex-w7213342775:
Raquel Romes Linhares and Regis Nunes Vargas work on a classic rule about how vocabulary grows in a text. Heaps' Law links text length to the number of different words used. Their 2026 paper argues that the classic form leaves out sound structure and word repetition.

The authors add two factors: the share of one-syllable words and a marker for high repetition. They test the new form with computer simulations run many times. They also test it on a large set of English movie reviews. The extended model fits the data better on several standard measures, offering a fuller account of how vocabulary grows.
openalex-w7213414475:
Denis de Gois Marques leads a study of open innovation projects linking industry, academia, and government. Their 2026 work replicates earlier case studies in software engineering. Forty-one undergraduate and graduate students worked in six mixed teams building minimum viable products for real settings.

Twenty participants answered a questionnaire on action research, teamwork, conflict, and knowledge gaps. Views were mostly positive, with gains in knowledge, experience, and innovation. People management, inexperience, and weak engagement were the main difficulties. Staff turnover had limited effect on output and deadlines, though teams had to reorganize. The authors see strong promise in joining academic learning with professional practice.
openalex-w7213424575:
Tiago Escame Gimiliani and Alva Valéria Moro Labs describe a 2025 redesign of youth and adult education in Tarumã, Brazil. Their 2026 case study links curriculum, technology, and health in one plan. It uses document analysis and participant observation in a qualitative design.

Projects included a maths experience scheme, ecological soap making, mobile gardens, and local mapping. A study trip and story sessions with a writer added cultural breadth. Psychology trainees ran activities on social and emotional skills, and guided physical activity promoted health. The authors report gains in self-image and self-esteem. Joined academic, cultural, and digital work, they argue, helps adults return to learning.
openalex-w7213425575:
Ana Paula Reis and Márcia Bitar Portella build a tool to judge how far interprofessional schooling has entered health residency programmes. Their 2026 methodological study concerns multiprofessional residencies in Brazil. The tool, called IMIEIP-Res, examines formal programme documents known as political-pedagogical projects.

The framework has eight dimensions, twenty-four criteria, and four levels of incorporation. Thirteen experts judged clarity and relevance in a modified online Delphi process. A first round kept most criteria and revised seven. A second round lifted overall agreement above the set threshold, with cultural safety gaining unanimous support. The authors present the framework as ready for use, with favourable content validity evidence.
openalex-w7213548075:
Taís Bentemüller Pinto and Fábio Pinheiro Pacheco study young women's feelings about pornography use. Their 2026 qualitative study is set in Fortaleza, Ceará. Ten women aged eighteen to twenty-six took part, through semi-structured interviews and a social questionnaire, analysed by content analysis.

Curiosity, strangeness, and pleasure stood out as positive feelings in the accounts. Guilt, shame, shock, and worry appeared as negative impacts. Social psychology, with its focus on affectivity, frames the discussion. The study does not judge the women or the material in simple terms. Instead, it records how the women themselves perceive and explain the emotions tied to use, adding local evidence to a topic often discussed without women's own voices.
openalex-w7214489175:
Érica Cindra de Lima led a 2026 review on inclusive education in universities, focused on students who are the target group of special education. The team mapped school policies, teaching practices, and steps for ease of access in higher education, using studies published from 2021 to early 2026. They asked how those measures affect access, staying on, and taking part for students with disabilities.

Progress appeared in mentoring, helpful technology, adapted course plans, and school support. Barriers remained as well, in buildings, in teaching methods, and in attitudes. The authors conclude that stronger inclusion depends on joining three things together: real ease of access, teacher training, and steady school support. Without that mix, they suggest, formal policies alone do not remove the hurdles students meet daily.
openalex-w7218364075: Lucas Vinicios Mekelburg led a seven-author 2026 study of morphine dispensing in a private hospital in northwestern Paraná, Brazil, covering January 2024 to December 2025. Morphine is a tightly controlled pain medicine, so its records reveal how a hospital actually uses it. The observational, retrospective study drew on hospital records, considering the pharmaceutical form, the hospital sector, and the amounts dispensed. The evidence sample for this entry ends during the methods description, before the results, so the pattern itself is not described here.
openalex-w7218526575:
Lilian Nascimento Rosa led a 2026 study of nursing leadership seen through humanistic and educational lenses. From articles from 2000 to 2025 and classic works, the team traced its historical evolution and its challenges today in Brazilian health services. Nurse leadership, they note, sits always between caring and managing, the tension in their title.

Nursing leadership was forged in wars, pandemics, and epidemics and spread from hospitals into the community. The COVID-19 pandemic strengthened the need for sensitive, humanized leading while laying bare weak points such as burnout, which harms the professional and the quality of care alike. Leadership in nursing is a field still being built, the authors conclude, marked by the care-manage dilemma. It needs strategies that strengthen humanization and continuing formation, in school and at work alike.
openalex-w7218979275:
Endy Millana Paiva de Souza and Thiago Rodrigues Moreira wrote a 2026 study on making the vehicle property tax progressive in the Brazilian state of Goiás. The tax, known as IPVA, falls on vehicle owners. The current flat model, they argue, violates the principle that tax should follow ability to pay, burdening lower-income classes disproportionately relative to their means.

Progressive rates could turn the tax into a tool of fiscal justice while the state keeps the revenue that funds essential services, they contend. Such a design aligns with the constitution's founding objectives, including building a free, just, and solidary society and reducing social inequality. Reading tax and constitutional principles, the recent constitutional tax reform amendment, and supreme court jurisprudence, the exploratory study concludes that progressivity is the fairest form for this tax under a constitutionalist reading.
openalex-w7220981575:
Roberta Bitencourt dos Santos and five co-authors reviewed research on human pressure on the Tocantins River basin around Marabá, in the Brazilian state of Pará. The city sits where the Tocantins and Itacaiúnas rivers meet, and mining, farming, and commerce all bear on its water, as their 2026 review explains.

Studies from 2017 to 2025 paint a sanitation picture in crisis: only a tiny share of sewage is collected, and about half the population relies on rudimentary pits. Tests found coliform bacteria in most samples along the riverfront, mining adds heavy metals, and disorderly growth worsens floods. The authors name failed basic sanitation as the main driver of the river's decline and call for joined urban and public policy.
plos-pbio-0020075:
Julie L. Christensen, Douglas E. Wright, Amy J. Wagers, and their team followed blood stem cells in unborn mice for PLOS Biology in 2004. Before birth, blood is made mainly in the fetal liver. Late in development the work shifts to the spleen and bone marrow.

The team tracked how stem cells travel through the blood and home to new sites during that shift. Their movement is guided by chemical cues, a process called chemotaxis. Knowing the routes and cues matters for medicine. Bone marrow transplants depend on stem cells finding their way to the marrow, and fetal data shows how that homing is first set up.
plos-pbio-0020175:
David R. Halpin, Juanghae A. Lee, S. Jarrett Wrenn, and Pehr B. Harbury closed their DNA display trilogy in PLOS Biology in 2004. Part three tackles chemistry: how to build small molecules directly on unprotected DNA strands. DNA is fragile, so harsh chemical steps can ruin the tag.

The team shows solid-phase synthesis methods gentle enough to keep the DNA readable. With that piece in place, the full scheme works: build compounds on DNA, route them by sequence, and select the best. DNA-encoded libraries built on this logic are now used to screen millions of compounds for drug leads. The paper is the practical keystone of the three.
plos-pbio-0020275:
Sara L. Sawyer, Michael Emerman, and Harmit S. Malik traced an antiviral enzyme's past in PLOS Biology in 2004. APOBEC3G edits viral DNA and can wreck viruses like HIV as they copy themselves. The team compared the gene across primates and found strong signs of ancient, rapid change.

Fast change driven by selection usually means an arms race. Primates and their viruses have likely fought over this enzyme for millions of years. Each side changed to beat the other. That deep history helps explain why the enzyme varies so much between species. It also guides AIDS research, since HIV carries a protein whose sole job is to defeat APOBEC3G.
plos-pone-0000075:
Claire C. Milton, Christina M. Ulane, and Suzannah Rutherford studied the protein Hsp90 in PLOS ONE in 2006. Hsp90 is a chaperone that helps other proteins fold and stay stable. By buffering small flaws, it lets genetic variation hide, stored but unseen, a trait called canalization.

When Hsp90 is weakened, the hidden variation shows up as new traits. That gives evolution fresh material to select in hard times. The authors probe how tight that control is and what it means for how fast species can change, their evolvability. Hsp90 thus sits at a crossroads of stability and change, one of the most studied balances in modern biology.
plos-pone-0000175:
Takumi Yamagishi, Michiru Ozawa, Chiho Ohtsuka, and colleagues published this developmental genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Evx2 and Hoxd13 are neighboring genes in a cluster that patterns the limbs and body axis. The authors study the DNA between them, showing it restricts which enhancers, booster switches, can reach the Hoxd13 promoter.

Genes in a cluster must be switched on in the right order and place, without cross-talk. A stretch of DNA acting as a fence between boosters and a promoter is part of that control. The work helps explain how the Hox cluster, one of the most famous in biology, keeps its precise choreography.
plos-pone-0000275:
Jean-René Martin, Kelly L. Rogers, Carine Chagneau, and colleagues published this imaging paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Calcium signals, brief rises of Ca2+ inside cells, drive much of brain activity. The authors use bioluminescence imaging, light given off by a reporter protein, to watch calcium signalling in the living brain of the fruit fly Drosophila.

Watching signals inside a living, intact brain avoids the distortions of dissected tissue. The authors demonstrate the method in the fly, a favorite model for brain genetics. The technique lets researchers connect genes to brain activity patterns in real time.
plos-pone-0000375:
Sarah Knox and colleagues studied how a gene system known as TSC guides growing nerve cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. TSC takes its name from tuberous sclerosis, a disorder where faulty TSC genes disrupt development, including in the brain. The team examined how TSC control affects two steps in wiring a nervous system.

Those steps are synapse assembly, where nerve cells build their connection points, and axon guidance, where a growing fiber finds its target. Faults in either step can miswire the brain. By pinning down what TSC does during these steps, the study links a disease gene to the errors behind the disorder's effects on the brain. Those errors happen while the brain is being built.
plos-pone-0000475:
Francesca Ciucci and colleagues linked a growth factor to the benefits of a stimulating environment for the young visual brain, in PLOS ONE in 2007. An enriched environment, with more to see, touch, and explore, is known to speed visual cortical development. The team showed that insulin-like growth factor 1, IGF-1, mediates those effects.

Mediates means the environment's benefit runs through this molecule: raise or block IGF-1 and the benefit follows. Naming the middleman explains how experience changes the brain in chemical terms. It also suggests that the critical-period plasticity of youth might one day be reopened or extended by targeting such factors.
plos-pone-0000575:
Charles R. Holst and colleagues studied two enzymes mice cannot do without at birth, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The secreted sulfatases Sulf1 and Sulf2 edit sulfate patterns on cell surfaces, tuning growth signals. Their roles overlap yet are essential: the team found both are needed for mouse neonatal survival.

Overlapping yet essential is a subtle combination: each enzyme covers partly for the other, but losing both is fatal at birth. That pattern reveals backup systems in development and where they run out. Sulfatases also modify signals that cancers exploit, so their basic biology reaches beyond newborn mice.
plos-pone-0000675:
Avinash D. S. Bala, Matthew W. Spitzer and Terry T. Takahashi matched a barn owl's hearing precision to its neurons, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The barn owl is a night hunter famous for locating sounds with extreme accuracy. Its midbrain holds an orderly map of auditory space, built by neurons tuned to specific directions. The team measured discrimination, the smallest difference in sound position the owl can tell apart.

Their title states that behavioral acuity approximates the resolving power of those space-specific neurons. In other words, the bird hears about as sharply as its best neurons allow. That match shows how single-cell tuning can set the limit of a whole animal's skill.
plos-pone-0000775:
Morgan Kullberg, Björn Hallström, Ulfur Arnason and colleagues tested a shortcut for building the mammal family tree, in PLOS ONE in 2007. They investigated whether expressed sequence tags, short reads from active genes called ESTs, can establish divergences within the placental mammal tree. Their test used established relationships among primates, represented by humans; lagomorphs, by rabbits; rodents, by rats and mice; and artiodactyls, by cows.

If cheap EST data recover known relationships, the method can be extended to species with little genomic data. Placental mammal evolution has contested branch points, and more data sources help settle them. A validated shortcut multiplies the species that can join the tree.
plos-pone-0000875:
Ume Abbas, Roy Anderson and John Mellors modeled whether preventive HIV drugs could slow spread in poorer settings, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The idea, called pre-exposure prophylaxis, is to give antiretroviral drugs to people before exposure. Whether it would help across a whole epidemic in sub-Saharan Africa was unclear.

The authors used a math model of heterosexual HIV spread to test the approach. Models like this let planners weigh benefit, cost and risk before a policy is tried at scale. Their work speaks to a hard choice: a tool that protects one person must also help, or at least not harm, the wider fight against the virus.
plos-pone-0000975:
Qingzhong Xiao, Stefan Kiechl, Seema Patel and colleagues measured vessel repair cells and heart risk in a large population study, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Endothelial progenitor cells help patch the lining of blood vessels. Their number was thought to reflect the body's repair capacity, falling with age and with unhealthy habits and risk factors.

That appealing idea had not been tested at scale. The team measured these cells alongside risk factors, cytokine levels and atherosclerosis, the hardening of arteries, in a large group. Population data can confirm or deflate a neat theory. Either way, the result guides whether these cells belong in risk testing.
plos-pone-0001075:
Filip Swirski, Cedric Berger, Jose-Luiz Figueiredo and colleagues built a near infrared cell tracker for living animals, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Tumor surroundings are complex, so immune cell behavior must be studied at several scales at once. Near infrared fluorescence imaging offers high resolution, sensitivity and depth in living tissue.

Their reagent labels leukocytes, white blood cells, so their immune responses can be watched and counted in vivo. Tracking cells without removing them preserves the very context that shapes their behavior. A tracker that quantifies, not just pictures, lets researchers compare treatments fairly. Cancer immunology depends on tools of exactly this kind.
plos-pone-0001175:
Babies learning language must pull words out of a stream of speech and also notice rules in how words are built. Ruth de Diego Balaguer and colleagues studied both skills in the brain, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Little was known about the mechanisms that let people extract these two kinds of information from speech.

The authors report different neurophysiological mechanisms underlying word extraction and rule extraction. In other words, the brain does not handle the two jobs the same way. That separation helps explain how language acquisition can partly fail, as in some developmental disorders, while other parts stay intact.
plos-pone-0001275:
Pests and pathogens keep evolving resistance to the drugs and pesticides used against them. An unsigned 2007 PLOS ONE article maps the research community that works on this problem. Researchers have built models to identify the main drivers of resistance evolution. The models also predict how well control strategies will work.

The article examines the structure of that research group itself: who works on resistance modeling and how the field is organized. The evolutionary forces behind resistance are its deeper subject. Understanding the group's shape is offered as a way to see the field's blind spots.
plos-pone-0001375:
Yi-Heng Hao and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a protein made by Yersinia, a genus of harmful germs. The protein, called YopJ, blocks signal chains that cells use to react to threats. Those chains are shared by many life forms. The team asked which parts of YopJ let it shut these chains down.

The authors mapped the shape needs for YopJ to work. They show it adds a small chemical tag to block a key step in the chain. It can block the same kind of chain in yeast too. Learning how this block works may help explain how Yersinia disarms host cells during illness.
plos-pone-0001475:
Daniëlle de Jong and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a pain drug tested in Alzheimer's disease. Some had hoped that curbing brain swelling could slow memory loss. The drug tested is a broad anti swelling drug. The trial was blinded, with patients split at random to drug or dummy pills for one year.

The team report that one year of the drug did not slow the decline of the disease. That clear null result matters as much as a win would. It steers funds away from a weak lead. It also sharpens the case that swelling alone is not the driver of this disease.
plos-pone-0001575:
Cordula Koerner-Rettberg and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a chronic asthma model in mice. Long allergen tests in mice can copy the marks of chronic asthma in people. How swelling, scar change, and lung work link in that model was poorly known. The team tracked all three over a long course of tests.

They found poor lung work went with long swelling, but not with scar growth beside the airways. That split breaks a common guess that scars drive the loss. Care aimed at scars alone may thus miss the mark. The work refocuses asthma care on lasting swelling.
plos-pone-0001675:
Ingo Fründ, Niko A. Busch, Jeanette Schadow, and their co-authors measured brain signals of early vision under time pressure in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. People must sometimes react to what they see as fast as possible, and sometimes favor accuracy, which takes longer. The open question was whether the visual system itself processes sights differently under these two demands, or only the later decisions change.

The team recorded electrical brain responses while subjects worked under different speed demands. The full text gives the task, the signal traces, and which early components shifted with time pressure. Finding that even early visual processing bends under pressure reshapes how scientists model the trade-off between speed and accuracy in the brain.
plos-pone-0001775:
Jérémy Bluteau, Sabine Coquillart, Yohan Payan, and their co-authors tested whether touch guidance helps people learn movements in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. New movements are usually learned by watching visual demonstrations. Haptic guidance, from a force feedback device that physically steers the hand, adds cues from the body's own position sense during learning.

The team compared two types of haptic guidance on visuo-manual tracking of trajectories. They report that guidance improves tracking, per the paper's title. The full text gives the task setup, the guidance modes, and the error scores. Results like this feed the design of training systems for surgery, sport, and rehabilitation. In those fields a guiding hand, even a robotic one, may teach faster than eyes alone.
plos-pone-0001875:
Gordon Smith and co-authors compared muscle building in older men and women in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Women tend to have less muscle than men, yet they lose it more slowly with age. The team wanted to find a cause for that gap, so they studied twenty-nine adults aged sixty-five to eighty.

The group measured how fast new muscle protein was made, both after a fast and after a meal, in thirteen men and sixteen women. They also tracked the signals that switch muscle building on. Work of this kind helps explain why muscle loss with age hits the sexes at unlike rates. It may also guide diet and care for older adults.
plos-pone-0001975:
Daniel Scott-Algara and co-authors studied a subset of killer immune cells that rein in HIV, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Natural killer cells and dendritic cells are thought to act in the first hours of HIV infection, before tailored defenses form. Dendritic cells present the virus to the rest of the immune system.

The team watched how the killer cell mix changes when it meets dendritic cells infected with HIV from the same donor. They report that the subset marked by CD85j potently controls viral replication in those cells. Early control points like this could be boosted by vaccines or therapy.
plos-pone-0002075:
Yair Granot, Antoni Ivorra, and Boris Rubinsky proposed medical imaging built on the cell phone, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. World Health Organization reports say that some three quarters of the world population has no access to medical imaging. In poorer countries, over half of the imaging gear on hand sits unused, too complex or broken with no one to fix it.

Their concept shifts the hard parts of imaging onto the phone network. A simple probe sits in the clinic, with processing and display done by phone systems. A design that rides gear people already own could bring scans to places that will never buy a full imaging suite.
plos-pone-0002175:
Scott Raymond, Lisa Treat, Jonathan Dewey, and co-authors used sound waves to help agents cross into the brain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Alzheimer's disease is marked by clumps of a small protein, beta-amyloid, that build up into plaques. Many new drugs and imaging agents meant to attack or reveal those plaques work poorly in living animals because they cannot get into the brain.

The team applied focused ultrasound, which can briefly open the barrier that guards the brain from the blood. In mouse models of the disease, this improved delivery of imaging and therapy agents. Better delivery could make both diagnosis and treatment of Alzheimer's more effective.
plos-pone-0002275:
Kwang Woon Kim, Luigi Moretti, and Bo Lu tested a drug that helps radiation kill lung cancer cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide, and tumors that resist radiation lead to many local failures. Radiation kills partly through apoptosis, orderly cell death, but the group's earlier work showed that removing pro-death proteins makes cancer cells harder to kill.

The team studied M867, a selective inhibitor of caspase-3, a core executioner of apoptosis. Counterintuitively, it enhanced cell death and extended tumor growth delay in irradiated lung cancer models. Understanding such effects could make each dose of radiation count for more.
plos-pone-0002375:
Zheng and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Huajun Zheng, Liangdong Lu, Bofei Wang, among others. Its subject is genetic Basis of Virulence Attenuation Revealed by Comparative Genomic Analysis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis Strain H37Ra versus H37Rv. Tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, remains a leading infectious disease despite the availability of chemotherapy and BCG vaccine.

The commonly used avirulent M. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002475:
Archange joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Cendrine Archange, Jonathan Nowak, Stéphane Garcia, among others. Its subject is the WSB1 Gene Is Involved in Pancreatic Cancer Progression. Pancreatic cancer cells generate metastases because they can survive the stress imposed by the new environment of the host tissue.

To mimic this process, pancreatic cancer cells which are not stressed in standard culture conditions are injected into nude mice. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002575:
Arqué led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Glòria Arqué, Vassiliki Fotaki, David Fernández, among others. Its subject is impaired Spatial Learning Strategies and Novel Object Recognition in Mice Haploinsufficient for the Dual Specificity Tyrosine-Regulated Kinase-1A (Dyrk1A). Pathogenic aneuploidies involve the concept of dosage-sensitive genes leading to over- and underexpression phenotypes.

Monosomy 21 in human leads to mental retardation and skeletal, immune and respiratory function disturbances. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002675:
Esther J. Kuiper and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on the Angio-Fibrotic switch of VEGF and CTGF in proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Authorship is credited in the record to Esther J. Kuiper and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. In proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and connective tissue growth factor (CTGF) cause blindness by neovascularization and subsequent fibrosis. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002775:
Marian C. Bruce and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was effect of transmission setting and mixed species infections on clinical measures of malaria in malawi. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Marian C. Bruce, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. In malaria endemic regions people are commonly infected with multiple species of malaria parasites but the clinical impact of these Plasmodium co-infections is unclear. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002875:
Vivianne Vleeshouwers, Hendrik Rietman, Pavel Krenek and colleagues tackled potato late blight in PLOS ONE in 2008. Potato is the world's fourth largest food crop, yet blight from Phytophthora infestans, the Irish famine pathogen, still destroys harvests. Breeding in broad resistance genes was seen as the best defense.

The team used effector genomics, which studies the proteins the pathogen uses to attack the plant. That approach sped up the search for potato resistance genes and for matching avirulence genes in the pathogen. Growers and breeders can use the method to find strong resistance faster than older crossing work allowed.
plos-pone-0002975:
Sanae Sasaki, Xiao-Song He, Tyson Holmes and co-authors compared flu vaccine responses by past vaccination in 2008. Two vaccines were licensed in the United States: a killed trivalent vaccine and a live weakened one. How prior flu vaccination shapes antibody and B-cell responses to each had not been directly compared.

Published in PLOS ONE, the study examines that influence across both vaccine types. Yearly flu shots are routine advice, so knowing whether past shots help, hinder, or reshape later responses has practical weight. The work speaks to doctors and to people weighing the annual vaccine.
plos-pone-0003075:
Keren Landman, Jan Ostermann, John Crump and co-authors examined partner numbers and HIV risk in northern Tanzania in 2008. Monogamy, with abstinence, partner reduction, and condom use, is widely advocated as a key strategy to prevent HIV in sub-Saharan Africa. The team tested the link between reported partner counts and HIV status.

Men and women reporting abstinence, monogamy, and multiple partners were compared for HIV seropositivity. Their title stresses gender differences in risk. Published in PLOS ONE, such data check whether standard prevention messages match how risk actually falls on each sex. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003175:
Anbarasu Kumarasamy and Edathara C. Abraham study shortened forms of a lens protein in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A significant portion of alphaA-crystallin in human lenses has its tail end cut off at residues 172, 168 and 162. The authors measured chaperone activity, using alcohol dehydrogenase and betaL-crystallin as target proteins, for each cut form.

They report that activity rose in the 1-172 form and fell in the 1-168 form, with the shorter forms also tested. Readers see how small cuts can change a protective protein's help to other proteins. That detail matters for understanding lens clarity and cataract with age.
plos-pone-0003275:
Zhi Xu, Fan Zhang, Bosong Xu and colleagues analyse ancient DNA from a famous tomb workforce in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Variant studies on ancient DNA have attempted to reveal individual origin. Based on cloning sequencing and PCR-restriction fragment methods, the team analysed polymorphisms in the first hypervariable region and coding regions of mitochondrial DNA.

Their title reports mitochondrial DNA evidence for a diversified origin of workers building the mausoleum for the First Emperor of China. Readers see genetics test a historical question about a huge labour force. Mixed origins would fit an empire drawing workers from many regions.
plos-pone-0003375:
Weizhong Li, John C. Wooley, and Adam Godzik faced a data problem in this 2008 paper. Ocean sampling trips had produced millions of protein sequences from sea water. Grouping near-matching sequences is a first step, but the sets were too large for old tools. The authors present a fast way to cluster very large sequence sets.

Their method sorts the huge ocean data into groups of like proteins. Grouping cuts the data down to a size that gene catalogs can handle. The paper shows the approach working on the full ocean sampling set. Faster grouping helps turn raw sea DNA into maps of what microbes do.
plos-pone-0003475:
Wonkuk Kim, Derek Gordon, and Jonathan Sebat tackled study design for DNA copy variants in this 2008 paper. Some DNA stretches appear in unlike copy counts between people. Those variants may shape disease risk and onset. At the time, finding them relied mainly on microarray tools.

Case-control studies need enough people to spot real links reliably. The authors computed power and sample size for such studies. Their method uses a likelihood ratio test built on mixture models. The worked examples show planners how large a study must be. Most gene hunts fail on power long before they fail on ideas.
plos-pone-0003575:
Hong-Hee Won, Hee-Jin Kim, and Kyung-A Lee catalogued human coding variants in this 2008 paper. Data on sequence variation in the human genome were growing fast. Predicting what each variant does to health was growing more urgent. The team focused on variations inside coding sequences.

Their catalog covered protein-coding changes stored in genome databases. It weighed predicted functional effects for each entry. Order in the data helps separate harmless variants from risky ones. Clinicians and gene hunters both rely on such inventories. Clinics already use such lists when they read a patient's genome report.
plos-pone-0003675:
Charlotte A. Oomen, Carlos E. N. Girardi, Rudy Cahyadi, and colleagues published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Depression strikes women more often than men, and early life stress may be one reason why. The team studied what removing rat pups from their mothers does to the developing brain.

They measured neurogenesis, the birth of new brain cells, in the hippocampus. Early maternal deprivation changed that growth in opposite directions in males and females. The split result offers a clue to why depression linked to early stress does not fall evenly on the two sexes.
plos-pone-0003775:
Chrisantha Fernando, K. K. Karishma, and Eörs Szathmáry published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. No model existed for how a neuronal network might copy its own wiring pattern. Such copying could matter for how brains draw conclusions and reuse learned functions. The authors propose a mechanism.

Their proposal copies the topology, the connection layout, of neuronal networks within the brain. They argue it could support causal inference, function copying, and even natural selection among ideas inside one head. The paper gives neuroscience a concrete model of learning by internal copying.
plos-pone-0003875:
Meredith E. Young, Geoffrey R. Norman, and Karin R. Humphreys studied how medical words shape public views in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article asks what happens when plain conditions gain formal medical names. One case they cite is impotence, now more often called erectile dysfunction. New names can change how serious, common, or treatable a condition seems.

The authors set out to test the effect of medical terms on how people judge illness. Their work treats language itself as part of health care, not just a label on it. The findings matter for doctors who choose words with patients. They also matter for public debate about newly named disorders.
plos-pone-0003975:
Maarten A. N. Rits, Karel A. van Dort, and Neeltje A. Kootstra studied gene variants and HIV risk in 2008. Cyclophilin A is a protein HIV uses during infection. Earlier studies tied variants near its gene to HIV susceptibility. They also tied them to how fast disease progresses.

Their PLOS ONE article tested those variants in a defined study group. The authors asked whether the variants affect catching HIV-1 itself. Control regions of genes can tune how much protein cells make. Confirming such effects helps explain why risk differs between people. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004075:
W. Jason Cummings, David W. Bednarski, and Nancy Maizels studied how chemical tags on DNA affect variation in 2008. Homologous recombination repairs damaged genes using a matching donor. That repair is essential for keeping the genome intact. It must pick proper donors and avoid faulty ones.

Their PLOS ONE article reports epigenetic modification stimulates genetic variation. Tags that do not change DNA sequence altered recombination outcomes. Repair can copy small differences from the donor into the target. Such gene conversion quietly spreads variation through populations. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004175:
Achia Urbach and Nissim Benvenisty published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Turner syndrome, caused by having only one X chromosome, is one of the most common chromosome abnormalities in females. About three percent of pregnancies start as XO embryos, yet nearly all of them end during the first trimester.

The usual genetic explanation for this early loss was incomplete. Using human embryonic stem cells as a model, the authors studied why XO embryos so rarely survive. Their work aims at the hidden first weeks of pregnancy, where most of these embryos are lost before anyone knows they existed.
plos-pone-0004275:
Yujung Kang and colleagues published this imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Measuring blood flow in peripheral tissue accurately is hard, yet it is necessary to diagnose poor circulation in limbs. Near-infrared light penetrates tissue relatively deeply, so fluorescence imaging with it has drawn much attention.

The team present a quantitative analysis of peripheral tissue perfusion using spatiotemporal molecular dynamics, tracking how tracer molecules move through tissue over space and time. The method was built for limbs, where poor flow does real harm. Their method aims to turn glowing pictures into numbers doctors can trust. Better flow numbers mean earlier detection of limbs at risk.
plos-pone-0004375:
Macquarie Island is a small subantarctic island south of New Zealand. Its rockhopper, royal, and king penguins often carry a seabird tick called Ixodes uriae. Lee Major, May La Linn, Robert Slade, and co-authors examined those ticks for viruses. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper reports what they found living inside the ticks.

The team isolated viruses from four separate genera in the ticks. The set held a flavivirus, an orbivirus, a phlebovirus, and a nairovirus. All four groups include viruses spread by biting insects or ticks. The finding shows remote penguin colonies host a wide mix of viruses. It also gives disease trackers a baseline for this far southern outpost.
plos-pone-0004475:
Two related gene switches, Pax3 and Pax7, run muscle stem cells, and Charlotte Collins, Viola Gnocchi, Robert White, and co-authors untangled their joint work in PLOS ONE in 2009. Both switches act in development and in adult muscle repair. They are found in satellite cells, the stem cells that sit on muscle fibers, and they switch off as those cells mature into muscle.

The team showed what happens when the switches are kept on: cell growth, cell size, and muscle differentiation all change. Their integrated account explains how the pair balances keeping stem cells in reserve against sending them to repair damage. That balance is central to muscle wasting diseases and to hopes of growing muscle for therapy.
plos-pone-0004575:
A control point that forces immune receptor genes to assemble in the right order is examined by Don-Marc Franchini, Touati Benoukraf, Sebastien Jaeger, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. T cell receptor beta genes are built by V(D)J recombination, a cut-and-paste process. Assembly proceeds in two steps: first one segment joins, then the next.

A constraint nicknamed B12/23 forbids skipping a step. Earlier thinking left open how the first step is initiated. The authors identify recombination signal sequences next to the D beta segment as the trigger point. Getting the order right matters: misassembled receptors can fail immunity or turn against the body. The paper pins down where the sequence of assembly begins.
plos-pone-0004675:
Dong-Joo Cheon and colleagues asked if mice need a known cancer marker to grow and breed, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The marker, called CA125, is used in blood tests to track ovarian cancer in women. The gene that makes it belongs to a family of large, sugar coated proteins.

Even so, the true job of CA125 in the body was still poorly known. The team made mice that lack the gene and watched their growth and breeding. The mice grew and bred without it. That result tells doctors and researchers that loss of this marker alone does not block normal life in mice.
plos-pone-0004775:
Barbara Ingold and colleagues linked uniform MGMT staining to an unmethylated gene switch in brain metastases, in PLOS ONE in 2009. MGMT switch methylation predicts response of brain tumors to certain chemo drugs. Early reports on using those drugs for cancer that spread to the brain showed mixed effects across patients.

The team compared protein staining patterns with switch status in metastases from various cancers. Uniform staining matched an unmethylated, active switch. A simple stain test could thus hint at drug response. That would help select patients for therapy without complex DNA tests. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail.
plos-pone-0004875:
Gary Bren and colleagues studied how the HIV coat protein gp120 boosts HIV growth in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein can switch cells on, push some cells to die, and raise output of immune signals. Through an unknown route, it also made the virus copy itself at a higher rate in the tests.

The team found that the same signals that push cells to die also drive the extra virus growth. That drive needs a cell factor called NF-kB and a protein named procaspase 8. The result links cell death paths to virus spread in a direct way. Blocking that link could one day help lower virus levels in the body.
plos-pone-0004975:
Immune cells blast captured bacteria with superoxide. This oxidative burst is a primary weapon of innate immunity. Yet how it kills was not known. Many assumed DNA was the main target. Maureen Craig and James Slauch tested that assumption in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used the bacterium Salmonella as their subject.

The damage landed outside the bacterium's inner compartment. DNA was not the primary target after all. An extracytoplasmic target takes the hit instead. Pinpointing that target rewrites the textbook account of the oxidative burst. It gives a clearer map of how immune cells kill germs. Future work can now aim at the right structure.
plos-pone-0005075:
Malaria parasites first multiply in the liver. Weakened sporozoites can train the immune system against that stage. Ousman Jobe and colleagues traced how in PLOS ONE in 2009. They immunized mice with radiation-attenuated Plasmodium berghei sporozoites. This treatment confers sterile, long-lasting protection. Protection is linked to liver CD8 T cells.

The study found a special liver dendritic cell population at work. These cells activate the protective CD8 T cells. The chain reveals the immune relay behind the vaccine's power. It is a blueprint for malaria vaccines. Knowing which cells present the parasite helps designers. They can aim new vaccines at the same relay.
plos-pone-0005175:
Mousepox is a lethal disease of mice caused by the ectromelia virus. Its course looks much like human smallpox, so it serves as a model for poxvirus disease. Alejo and colleagues described in PLOS ONE in 2009 a way to build changed forms of the virus.

Using their method, the team made viruses missing a gene called vCD30 and tested them in living mice. Watching how the changed viruses act shows what that gene does during infection. The approach gives poxvirus researchers a toolkit for probing single genes, which can guide work on related viruses that infect people.
plos-pone-0005275:
Signaling by TGF-beta helps set bone size, shape, and strength during growth. Mohammad and colleagues blocked one part of that signal, the type I receptor kinase, and reported the bone effects in PLOS ONE in 2009. The result ran against simple expectations.

Drug treatment had anabolic effects, meaning it built bone up, and anti-catabolic effects, meaning it slowed bone breakdown. Both actions together raise bone mass. A single target that builds and preserves bone at once is a promising lead for osteoporosis drugs. Bone drugs now tend to slow loss or build bone, but not both. A single drug that does both jobs at once would be a rare and prized find.
plos-pone-0005375:
Judging whether a skin growth is dangerous is a pathologist's daily task, done from stained tissue slides. Clinical background about the patient is also available in a database. Ferrara and colleagues tested how that information sways diagnosis in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Slides from ninety-nine clinically atypical melanocytic growths circulated among ten histopathologists. Each case's clinical information could be consulted during review. The study measures whether context sharpens diagnosis or biases it, a practical question for every pathology lab. Ten experts can read the same slide in quite different ways. So a study that counts the sway of background facts helps labs set firm rules for when those facts should be in the room and when they should stay out.
plos-pone-0005475:
Alejo Efeyan and co-authors tested a cancer protection model in mice for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Studies of human cells had suggested a chain of defence: faulty growth signals damage DNA, and the damage triggers a cell alarm that stops tumours. Two proteins, ATM and p53, sit at the heart of that alarm.

The team tested the chain in several mouse setups. They found that ATM played only a small part in the alarm and in stopping tumours in these animals. The result warns that a model built from human cells in dishes may not fit whole animals.
plos-pone-0005575:
Andrew Zolopa and co-authors ran a trial on the timing of HIV treatment in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. People who arrive for care with AIDS often have another serious infection at the same time. Whether to start HIV drugs at once or wait until that infection is treated was not settled.

In the trial, one group started HIV treatment within two weeks, while the other waited until the acute infection was dealt with. Starting early reduced deaths and AIDS progression. That clear result changed practice for some of the sickest HIV patients.
plos-pone-0005675:
Juliana Yordanova and colleagues asked in 2009 whether deep sleep quietly reshapes what the brain has learned without our knowing. Slow wave sleep is known to firm up clear, conscious memories tied to the hippocampus. Hidden, skill-like memories work in a different way and are less well mapped.

The study tests whether a night of deep sleep can reorganize these unspoken task memories. Such a shift would mean sleep does more than store the day as it was lived. It would mean the sleeping brain can rebuild a task in a new form. That idea bears on how practice, rest, and learning should be paced.
plos-pone-0005775:
Valerie Hu and co-authors compared gene activity in blood-derived cells from autistic children and their unaffected siblings in 2009. Many autism risk genes are known, yet how the condition develops stays unclear. Siblings share much DNA and home life, making them strong controls.

The profiles differed in pathways for nerve development and for steroid building. Those shifts hint at biology that could be measured outside the brain. A blood-based signature would ease study and, in time, diagnosis. The team presents its findings as leads to test, in a field that needs firm molecular footholds.
plos-pone-0005875:
Kai Gao and co-authors read saliva in 2009 for fingerprints of cancers growing elsewhere in the body. Saliva is easy to collect, and its use for mouth diseases is obvious. Whether distant diseases, like melanoma or lung cancer, also mark saliva was far less clear.

In mouse models of melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer, the team found disease-linked biomarker profiles in saliva. Systemic illness does reach the mouth's fluids in readable ways. That supports developing spit tests for cancers far from the mouth. Mouse proof comes first; the paper frames what human studies should look for.
plos-pone-0005975:
Compounds from plants have long been a source of new drugs. Rubén Martín, Elvira Ibeas, Juliana Carvalho-Tavares and colleagues tested a group of plant compounds called triterpenic diols in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies astrocytoma cells, a form of brain tumor cell, grown in the lab.

The title reports the outcome: the natural diols push these tumor cells into programmed death. The path runs through harmful oxygen byproducts, a collapse of the cells' power plants, and a stress signal called JNK. A clean chain of steps like this gives drug chemists both a lead compound and a known way it kills cancer cells.
plos-pone-0006075:
Cystic fibrosis lungs live under constant oxidative stress, and their defenses run low. Stéphanie Trudel, Mairead Kelly, Janine Fritsch and colleagues tested one defender in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies peroxiredoxin 6, an antioxidant protein, in lungs of mice lacking the Cftr gene, the gene broken in cystic fibrosis, under an oxidative challenge.

The defender failed to limit damage to the fats in cell membranes, the title reports. A failed defense is useful knowledge: it clears a false lead and points the search elsewhere. The result sharpens the picture of why CF lungs injure so easily, and why antioxidant treatments for them have been hard to make work.
plos-pone-0006175:
Prion diseases, such as mad cow disease and scrapie in sheep, slowly destroy the brain and are always fatal. Evgenia Salta and colleagues asked whether these diseases could pass to gilthead sea bream, a farmed fish, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. In these illnesses, a normal cell protein folds into a harmful shape and builds up in tissue.

The team tested whether the fish could take up the sheep and cattle forms of the disease. Work of this kind maps how far prions can jump between species. That map matters for fish farming, feed rules, and food safety. It also helps scientists judge which animal links need watching and which pose little risk.
plos-pone-0006275:
Alien plants do not just take space; they join the local web of plant and pollinator partnerships. Benigno Padron and colleagues mapped pollination networks on two archipelagos in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Invaders that integrate into native communities can alter the patterns of those mutual partnerships.

The team mapped in detail how invaders changed network measures on the islands. Shifts in who visits whom can raise or lower native plants' reproduction. Island ecosystems show such effects clearly because their webs are small. The findings help managers judge which invaders most threaten pollination.
plos-pone-0006375:
Before two cell membranes fuse, they first stick together over wide areas. Jason Warner, Erdem Karatekin, and Ben O'Shaughnessy modelled that adhesion step in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. SNARE proteins form the conserved core machinery driving membrane adhesion and fusion throughout the cell.

Their kinetic model follows SNARE-mediated sticking from first contact to fusion readiness. Lab assays with reconstituted membranes helped isolate the mechanisms to model. A quantitative model predicts how fusion speed changes with protein numbers. Such predictions guide experiments on secretion and neurotransmission. The model gives labs clear numbers to test when they build the real thing.
plos-pone-0006475:
Anna Vaudano, Helmut Laufs, Stefan Kiebel, and colleagues mapped seizure signals in the brain for PLOS ONE in 2009. Generalised spike and wave discharges are the EEG hallmark of absence seizures. During these seizures, ongoing activity stops briefly and awareness fades. The discharges involve a network linking the thalamus and the cortex.

The team asked about causal hierarchy inside that network during the discharges. Which structure drives, and which follows, matters for treatment. Stimulation or surgery works better when aimed at the true driver. Their analysis of brain recordings offers evidence on the order of events in absence seizures.
plos-pone-0006575:
Jane Palsgaard and co-authors read gene activity in muscle from people with diabetes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gene expression alterations have previously been associated with type 2 diabetes. However, whether these changes are primary causes or secondary effects of the disease is unclear. The team took skeletal muscle biopsies from people with type 2 diabetes and their relatives.

Studying relatives helps, since they share genes but not yet disease. Their title highlights differential regulation of specific metabolic pathways. Changes present in healthy relatives may be causes; changes only in patients may be effects. That logic is key to finding where diabetes begins.
plos-pone-0006675:
Jonathan Levy and colleagues used brain imaging to test a theory of reading in PLOS ONE in 2009. The dual-route cascade model describes how readers turn print into sound and meaning. Evidence for the model came largely from people with acquired reading problems. Brain lesions in those patients are often large and varied, which limits firm conclusions.

The team turned to functional magnetic resonance imaging in healthy readers. They measured effective connectivity, meaning how brain regions influence each other during reading. Their account centers on an efficient reading style. The results let them check the model's predictions in an intact brain. That gives reading science a cleaner test than patient studies alone can offer.
plos-pone-0006775:
Masja Leendertse and her team asked if gut germs change lung defense in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. The germ was Enterococcus faecium, found more and more in hospital patients. Drug-proof strains of it are a growing worry. It is tied to more illness from gut germs of its own kind. It might also make lung illness worse.

The team let the germ settle in mouse guts. They then put a second germ, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, in the lungs. Gut carriage did not change lung defense, as the title states. That clear no narrows where gut carriage does its harm. Lung defense held firm even when the gut held drug-proof germs.
plos-pone-0006875:
Xiangning Chen and colleagues followed a cell-death cleanup pathway into schizophrenia genetics in PLOS ONE in 2009. Apoptosis, programmed cell death, has been speculated to play a role. Their earlier study linked the gene MEGF10 to the disease. MEGF10 helps cells engulf dead neighbors. Partners in that pathway include GULP1, ABCA1, and ABCA7.

The team tested those pathway genes for association with schizophrenia. Testing a whole pathway is stronger than testing one gene. Shared involvement would tie brain development to cleanup failures. Leftover dead cells could disturb developing circuits. The study extends a single-gene hint into a pathway-level claim.
plos-pone-0006975:
Tobias Karlberg, Susanne van den Berg, Martin Hammarström, and colleagues solved a protein structure in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein was paraplegin, part of a protease in the inner membrane of mitochondria. Faults in paraplegin cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, a disease that stiffens the legs. The protein is thought to form a six-part ring that burns ATP for power.

The team crystallized the ATPase domain, the part that uses that fuel. They then determined its three-dimensional shape. A clear structure shows where disease mutations fall. It also gives drug and protein engineers a map of this molecular machine.
plos-pone-0007075:
Adaikkalam Vellaichamy, Arun Sreekumar, John Strahler, and colleagues mapped androgen action in prostate cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in American men. Advanced hormone-refractory cases still had no cure at the time. Part of the problem was poor knowledge of the proteins androgens control.

Using proteomics, the team catalogued proteins that shift with androgen action. Aminoacyl tRNA synthetases, the enzymes that load transfer RNAs, stood out. Their appearance links hormone signaling to the cell's protein-making machinery. That link offers new places to probe how these cancers keep growing.
plos-pone-0007175:
Jerome Mauris and Thomas C. Evans published a 2009 PLOS ONE study of a DNA repair enzyme from a heat-loving bacterium. The bacterium is Aquifex aeolicus, and the enzyme is its MutL protein. MutL helps cut DNA near errors during mismatch repair, the process that fixes wrongly paired bases.

The authors test how adenosine triphosphate, the cell energy molecule called ATP, changes MutL activity. Earlier work had shown ATP was needed for related proteins in humans and yeast. Their results clarify how a simple energy molecule switches on an early step in DNA repair.
plos-pone-0007275:
Joanna Doumanis, Koji Wada, Yoshihiro Kino, and colleagues screened fruit fly cells for modifiers of a disease protein in 2009. The fruit fly is a well established model for human neurodegenerative diseases. Mutant huntingtin protein forms aggregates, clumps that mark Huntington disease in patients.

The authors use RNA interference to turn genes down one by one. They run a high-throughput screen in fly larval brain-derived cells expressing mutant huntingtin. They identify new modifiers of aggregate formation. Each new modifier is a candidate target for easing protein clumping in human neurons.
plos-pone-0007375:
Fabienne Paumet, Jordan Wesolowski, Alejandro Garcia-Diaz, and colleagues found virus-like fusion tools inside bacteria in 2009. Pathogens use diverse molecular machines to enter host cells and manipulate vesicle traffic. Viruses use glycoproteins similar to SNARE proteins, the cell's own fusion machinery, to merge membranes during entry into host cells.

Intracellular bacteria take another route into cells. The authors report that intracellular bacteria encode inhibitory SNARE-like proteins. These proteins can block normal membrane fusion inside the host. Blocking fusion helps bacteria avoid being delivered to destructive compartments. Their finding reveals a subtle weapon in intracellular infection.
plos-pone-0007475:
Darrell Pilling and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on fibrocytes, blood-born cells that help form scar tissue. In scar diseases, white blood cells called monocytes enter tissue and turn into fiber-making cells. The trouble is telling those cells apart from close kin. Monocytes also become macrophages, and fibrocytes look much like plain fibroblasts. Without good markers, the scar-making cells are hard to track.

The team found markers that set fibrocytes apart from monocytes, macrophages, and fibroblasts. Those tags let researchers count and sort the right cells in samples. Clear naming makes every study of scarring stronger. It also helps test drugs meant to stop scars from forming. The work is a sorting tool, but a needed one for the whole field.
plos-pone-0007575:
Anna Gustafsson and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the most common form of kidney cancer. The disease's molecular biology is complex and not fully understood. The team had earlier found that a receptor called Axl, found on tumors, correlates with patient survival on its own. Here they investigated Axl together with Gas6, the molecule that activates it.

A receptor and its activator acting as a pair can drive tumor behavior. Measuring both in tumors sharpens what Axl alone suggests. The signaling pair may help explain why some kidney cancers turn more dangerous than others. Such pairs are attractive drug targets, since blocking either partner can break the signal. The study deepens the case for Axl in kidney cancer prognosis and treatment thinking.
plos-pone-0007775:
John Ludes-Meyers and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It delivers a new mouse tool for studying a tumor suppressor gene called Wwox. The gene spans a fragile stretch of chromosome that breaks often in human cells. Wwox is switched off in many cancers and can slow tumor growth.

The team built mice carrying a conditional copy of the gene. Conditional means the gene can be turned off in chosen tissues or at chosen times. They describe how the mice were made and tested. The model lets researchers ask what Wwox does in healthy tissue and in tumors.
plos-pone-0007875:
Melanie Volke and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests a claim about hepcidin, the hormone that controls iron in the body. Hepcidin limits iron uptake from food and locks iron away in stores. It plays a key role in the anemia that comes with chronic disease.

Low oxygen is known to lower hepcidin levels. Factors that sense low oxygen, called HIFs, were suspected of switching the gene off directly. The authors present evidence against that direct suppression. Their result redirects the search for how oxygen controls iron, an everyday balance with real effects on health.
plos-pone-0007975:
Ismayil Ahmet and colleagues fed blueberries to rats with weak hearts in a PLOS ONE study from 2009. The rats had dilated hearts after a heart attack, a state like human heart failure. Past work had hinted that berry-rich food guards heart tissue.

Rats on the berry diet lived longer and kept stronger hearts than rats on plain food. The gain held over the long term, not just the first weeks. Food alone will not cure heart failure, but the work backs the idea that plant compounds in the diet can help a struggling heart hold on.
plos-pone-0008075:
Jeffrey Mito and colleagues matched a mouse tumor to its human twin by gene pattern in PLOS ONE in 2009. The human cancer is a soft tissue sarcoma. It has no clear cell of origin. Its old name frankly admitted that doctors cannot tell what it is. Mouse models existed, but which human disease they truly mirror was in doubt.

Gene profiles from the mouse tumors lined up with the human sarcoma called undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma. With the match firm, lab results from the mouse can be read with more trust. A good stand-in is half the battle in testing new drugs for a rare cancer.
plos-pone-0008175:
Louise V. Wain and co-authors published a genome-wide study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. ALS destroys the nerve cells that control muscle movement. Most cases arise with no clear family history. The team asked whether extra or missing copies of DNA stretches help explain who develops the disease.

The authors scanned genomes for these copy changes, called copy number variants. They then compared their results with gene sites reported in earlier work. Two past studies had hinted that copy changes may raise risk for cases without a family link. Testing that hint at genome scale helps show where gene dose may matter. It also gives later teams a checked set of sites worth testing again.
plos-pone-0008275:
Marie Ballif and colleagues studied HIV treatment outcomes in Switzerland in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Combination antiretroviral therapy has been very successful in clinical trials.
