After each round they rated noise, closeness, frustration, and whether they would make the same choice in real life. The data support studies of choice under delay.
pmc-13330175:
Chaoyu Lei and a large team present an artificial intelligence tool for measuring eye bulge from face photos in a 2026 study. Eye bulge matters in thyroid eye disease, yet the hand gauge is imprecise and scans cost more with radiation. The tool, ProptoView, learned from thousands of images tied to scan and gauge readings.

Training used images from 763 patients with thyroid eye disease across many visits. Three models used one view, many views, or flexible input. The flexible model matched scans best in the reported agreement values, beating the hand gauge. Outside checks across three countries and five hospitals held up well. Wrong calls at a key size cut point fell versus the gauge. Remote care use is proposed.
pmc-13330475:
Cheng Liu and colleagues mine United States device harm reports for sinus problems tied to dental implants in a 2026 study. Reports came from the FDA MAUDE system for 2015 to 2025 under a set implant code. Text rules hunted sinus stories among millions of narratives, then sorted them into event types.

From 3,386,630 unique reports, the workflow kept 6,386 strong sinus candidates in the reported counts. Blind double checks on 449 sampled records agreed well, and confirmed calls were right in 96.88 percent of that sample in the given validation. Sinus lining tears dominated the rule-based groups. The authors stress that report patterns are not true clinical rates or proof of cause.
pmc-13331175:
Nury Tatiana Rincón Cuenca and colleagues count missed-at-first stroke cases at a Bogotá centre in a 2026 study. Stroke chameleons show odd symptoms that mimic other illness, delaying care. Records covered ischemic stroke admissions from January 2021 to December 2023 at a high-level hospital in Colombia.

Among 635 patients, 78 people, or 12.2 percent in the reported share, counted as chameleons. They scored lower on stroke severity scales and more often showed confusion, dizziness, or behaviour change than other patients in the group comparisons. Middle artery territory was hit less, while multi-area patterns were hit more. Normal early scans were also more common. Spotting odd presentations can speed care, the authors argue.
pmc-13331375:
Fawaz Al-Mufti presents an artwork and artist statement on brain aneurysm language in a 2026 piece. Al-Mufti is a triple board-certified doctor and artist who turns bedside and conflict-zone experience into visual stories. The work uses India ink on Bristol board, breaking the head into a mosaic lattice of light and colour.

The title quotes a phrase Al-Mufti tries to avoid: calling an aneurysm a ticking time bomb for patients. Such words can turn uncertainty into felt doom and spark denial, anger, bargaining, and low mood, the statement argues. Treating and not treating both carry unknowns. Measured, open counselling based on personal risk and trust is the plea.
pmc-13331975:
S. Maria Jilani and a joint team measured how common human papillomavirus infection is among women in Karachi, Pakistan, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Data for Pakistan are thin, especially for women who have never been screened or vaccinated.

Between May 2022 and November 2023, 497 women gave cervical samples that were typed with a sensitive line probe test. Overall, 16.7 percent carried HPV, with high-risk types in 11.8 percent and the peak rate of 21.4 percent in women aged 25 to 34. HPV31 and HPV53 were the most frequent high-risk types at 1.2 percent each, ahead of HPV16 at 0.8 percent, and the low-risk type HPV6 also reached 1.2 percent. The authors argue the diverse high-risk burden supports organized HPV-based screening and a faster vaccine rollout in Pakistan.
pmc-13333375:
Ruilong Li and co-authors computed which sugar and amino acid pair reacts fastest in the first committed step of the Maillard reaction, in a 2026 theory study. That reaction is the chemistry behind browning and flavor in cooked food. The Amadori rearrangement is the fork where later flavor, color, and safety outcomes are set.

Using density functional theory, they mapped the rearrangement for glucose against all 20 amino acids and for leucine against 10 sugars. Leucine cleared the key joining step with glucose at an energy barrier of 93.55 kJ/mol. That is far below the 133.73 to 221.22 kJ/mol range of the other amino acids, and it kept the lowest barriers in later steps at every acidity. Among sugars with leucine, glucose again won, ahead of lactose, xylose, and the rest down to mannose. The authors offer the pairing as a theoretical guide for steering flavor and color in heated foods.
pmc-13336675:
Pengcheng Wu, Zenggang Lin, Lu Yang, and Weisheng Liu turn a usual weakness into a strength in a 2026 glow-materials study. Water normally kills the long afterglow of organic phosphorescent materials. Here water instead strengthens it, by bridging hydrogen bonds inside a rigid framework that holds glowing guest molecules.

Glow strength peaked at a water content of 55 wt.% in the reported tests, since the tighter network steadied the molecules and aided the glow pathway. Swapping guests tuned the afterglow across colors from blue to deep red. The tiny hybrids stayed stable in body-like settings and lit up cells clearly for imaging. Demos also covered layered encryption and humidity sensing.
pmc-13337475:
Liang-Qian Tong and colleagues describe what iodine-hungry neck lymph nodes look like on MRI in a 2026 imaging study. After thyroid cancer surgery, whole-body iodine scans can reveal leftover metastatic nodes, but spotting them before therapy is harder. The team reviewed 32 patients treated at Haikou People's Hospital from June 2019 to May 2024, all with papillary cancer and iodine-avid nodes on post-therapy scans.

Ultrasound had caught nodal spread in only 15.6% of these patients before therapy, while scans found 58 avid nodes in total across the group. On MRI most nodes glowed bright on both main sequences; 65.5% looked round to oval, 69.0% had ill-defined edges, and 91.4% lacked a hilum in the image review. These shared traits could help radiologists flag hidden spread earlier.
pmc-13337775:
Lindan Zhai and colleagues map Chinese research on rehab after knee ligament surgery in a 2026 bibliometric study. Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction is followed by long rehab, and China has a large literature on it. CNKI and Wanfang databases supplied the records.

A total of 1,052 papers from 2005 to mid-2025 were screened and charted with CiteSpace software. Yearly output rose unevenly and peaked at 119 papers in 2024 as reported. Author and institution networks were loose, with Sichuan Orthopedic Hospital among the main centers. Keyword clusters covered nine areas, and hot topics moved from basic rehab toward precise, technology-linked care.
pmc-13337875:
Zugang Yi leads a 2026 randomized trial of pain relief given before tonsil surgery in young children. Eighty children aged 3 to 6 having adenotonsillectomy took part. Half received intravenous acetaminophen at 15 mg per kilogram before anesthesia, and half received saline.

Pain one hour after tube removal, the main measure, was lower with acetaminophen in the reported results. Need for opioid rescue in recovery also fell, from 45.0 percent to 20.0 percent as reported. Delirium scores, home pain medicine use, and harms within a day did not differ. Benefit faded by four hours, so the drug helps early recovery most.
pmc-13338675:
David Rhys Axon and colleagues estimate long COVID in United States adults from a national survey in a 2026 study. Long COVID affects daily life and work, yet social and behavior links are less studied than medical ones. Data came from the 2022 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey.

A total of 11,266 adults stood for a weighted population of about 256 million people in the reported weighting. Of them, 790 people, or 7 percent, met the survey definition of long COVID as reported. Group comparisons and regression organized by the Andersen model tested which background, enabling, and need factors tracked with long COVID. Results guide support toward groups carrying the heaviest burden.
pmc-13341475:
Ultrasound stiffness readings may show steroid effects in fetal lungs, in a 2026 study by Gusztáv Labossa and colleagues. Twenty-six pregnancies between 24 and 34 weeks were scanned with shear-wave elastography before mothers received betamethasone, then 1 minute and 24 hours afterward.

Lung stiffness naturally fell with gestational age. Nothing changed at 1 minute, but by 24 hours lung elasticity had dropped from 1.87 to 1.72 kPa, a significant shift, while liver readings stayed flat. Since antenatal steroids mature the lungs before early birth, a noninvasive way to confirm response in the womb would help obstetric teams judge treatment.
pmc-13342975:
Masoume Akhbari and co-authors test a probiotic yeast in rats in 2026, asking whether it can calm brain inflammation tied to Alzheimer's disease pathways. The yeast, Saccharomyces boulardii, acts through the gut-brain axis, and the team targeted the TLR4 and NF-κB signaling route in the hippocampus after injections of bacterial toxin.

Four groups of rats received the yeast, the toxin, both, or neither over four weeks. Yeast pretreatment partly protected spatial memory, lowered raised NF-κB and IL-1β levels, and saved neurons in the CA1 region from loss. The effect ran through downstream steps of the pathway rather than the receptor itself, hinting at gut-based routes to ease brain inflammation.
pmc-13343975:
Soufyan Fakroun and co-authors reveal a direct handshake between two ancient cell assembly lines in Escherichia coli in 2026. Iron-sulfur clusters power proteins across the cell, while fatty acid making runs through a carrier protein called ACP, and the team showed these paths physically touch.

Binding tests, purification, and modeling placed ACP on IscS, the enzyme that donates sulfur for cluster building, at the very patch IscS uses for other partners. Draining ACP broke cluster assembly and dimmed key iron-sulfur regulators and enzymes, and a drug that disturbs ACP did the same. Similar links appear in yeast and human cells, suggesting evolution keeps tying fat making to cluster building everywhere.
pmc-13346075:
XinKai Li and co-authors map human experience of medical artificial intelligence across the literature in a 2026 bibliometric study. Treating satisfaction as just one strand beside trust, acceptance, and engagement, the team screened work from 2010 to 2025 in two big databases and kept 1,794 publications for mapping.

Output exploded after 2020, reaching 696 papers in 2025, with the United States and China leading and one internet medicine journal publishing most. Topics drifted from robot surgery toward patient trust, ChatGPT, explainable systems, ethics, and nursing workforce strain. Three frontiers stand out: language-model communication, explainability inside the care triangle, and training needs of frontline staff.
pmc-13347075:
Peng Hong and colleagues follow diet and mood in Chinese university students. Their cohort study was published in 2026. It ran for three years. The group held 5,314 students at a Shanghai university. A smart ordering system logged their cafeteria orders. Logs ran from 2020 to 2023. The team scored how inflammatory each diet was. No recall forms were needed.

Mood was checked each year with a standard scale. Mixed models linked diet scores to new depressive symptoms. Results were split by family ties and income level. Till records are the core strength of the design. They give a long view of campus eating. They also show how daily food tracks later mental health.
pmc-13347375:
Tam Minh Le, Chuyen Van Hoang, and Collin G. Joseph make a zeolite from rice husk ash. Their study was issued in 2026. The zeolite breaks down dye with peroxide and light. A microwave route took just five minutes. It gave small analcime grains. Each grain measured near 5.6 micrometres across. A slow hot-water route gave coarser grains. The new material holds no metal. It was tested on indigo carmine dye in alkaline water.

A visible LED lit the test at pH 9. The system cleared about 96 percent of the dye. It needed only 30 minutes. Hydroxyl radicals did most of the work. Superoxide forms helped too. Carbon checks showed partial breakdown of the dye frame. The grains kept working over repeated cycles. Farm waste thus becomes a reusable cleaner.
pmc-13347675:
Hervin N. Heeroo, Tashneem Harris, Matthew White, and Sameera Dalvie review outcomes for cancers of the ear canal and temporal bone in Cape Town, in a study issued in 2026. Charts covered 20 patients newly diagnosed from 2008 to 2023 at a tertiary hospital. The mean age was 60.7 years. Spread to the bone from elsewhere was left out of the set.

Squamous cell cancer led the diagnoses at 70 percent, and 70 percent of patients were treated aiming for cure, mostly by surgery. While the rest had easing radiation or supportive care alone. Return of disease hit 25 percent after a mean of 5.6 months, and mean overall survival was 1.52 years, which stresses early spotting and bold removal where fit.
pmc-13348075:
Chengfeng Li and colleagues test self-heal plant extracts against fatty liver disease through the gut-liver link, in a study issued in 2026. Polyphenols from Prunella vulgaris were profiled by mass tools, checked for blocking a cholesterol-handling enzyme, run in liver and gut cell models. Fed to fatty liver mice with gene-based gut profiling.

Extract and its rosmarinic acid part both blocked the enzyme and eased fat buildup in liver cells while curbing gut cholesterol uptake in the reported assays. In mice the extract lowered liver harm and fat markers, eased tissue damage, and reshaped gut microbes, tying cholesterol handling to microbe balance in this common liver condition.
pmc-13348275:
Supeecha Waiya and colleagues survey fungi and toxins in shop rice across Bangkok, Thailand, in a study from 2026. Fifty retail packs, half polished and half unpolished, were blotted for fungal growth, named by shape and multi-gene reads. Screened for toxins by sensitive mass methods, since daily rice eating makes even low contamination matter.

Fungi touched 12.6 percent of grain, slightly more in unpolished rice, with Aspergillus and allied genera leading the list in the reported finds. Only two toxins appeared, each in two unpolished samples, at levels under the national cap. No banned cancer-linked toxins were found, though handling care for unpolished grain is still urged.
pmc-13349775:
Annalisa Magnani and colleagues ask whether life-built mental reserve softens early memory complaints, in an exploratory study from 2026. Fifty-one older adults with subjective decline, meaning felt worsening despite normal test scores, took full thinking batteries plus mood and anxiety scales, split by reserve built from schooling, work. Leisure life in global and part scores.

Thinking stayed broadly normal while low mood was clinically real in a large share, and reserve links were selective in the reported splits. Higher total reserve tied to better drawing and building skills, lower leisure reserve tied to faster attention tasks. Work reserve linked to mood in a bent, non-straight pattern, backing part-wise reserve checks.
pmc-13350275:
Sophie Haas and co-authors mapped why AI telemonitoring projects for chronic disease stall in a 2026 case study of a German heart failure project. Remote monitoring promises early warning of decline, yet few systems reach daily care, hampered by data quality, unclear rules, and poor fit with clinic routines.

Adapting a standard data project framework to telemonitoring, they rebuilt the project's decisions, constraints, and fixes across its whole life cycle. Publishing obstacles, not just wins, fights the bias toward success stories. Their symptom-and-cause map aims to help future teams design monitoring systems that survive contact with real hospitals.
pmc-13351575:
Chengju Wang and colleagues examine growth and brain development at age 1 year in full-term infants born small for gestational age, in a 2026 study. Babies born small face higher risk of poor development, yet how growth after birth shapes scores is unclear. The clinic sample held 448 small infants and 2,376 infants of expected size.

Development was scored with the Gesell scale alongside weight, length, and head size at 1 year. In the small group, weight at 1 year linked to higher scores in several domains. After matched comparison, the two groups did not differ clearly. Spline models gave weight-ratio reference points near 0.86 to 0.91 for most domains, framed as comparison values rather than treatment targets.
pmc-13351875:
Vivek Sanker leads a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of outcomes for cancer spread to the spine, split by the cancer it came from. Spine spread is common and can cause severe pain and nerve damage, while treatment choices hinge on expected survival. Four databases were searched to April 16, 2025 for outcome studies in any primary cancer.

In total, 123 studies with 38,780 patients covered nine primary cancers, and 61 studies fed the pooled analysis. One-year survival ranged from 46 percent for lung origin to 74 percent for prostate origin. Median survival was shortest for liver origin at 8.2 months and longest for thyroid origin at 59.9 months. Return of disease stayed below 5 percent in most groups.
pmc-13352875:
Hannah Elisabeth Köhler leads a 2026 nationwide survey of youth mental health in Germany after the COVID-19 pandemic. A representative online survey in April and May 2024 covered 1,530 children and adolescents aged 8 to 17 years plus their parents. Emotional and behavioural problems were scored with the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, and quality of life with the KIDSCREEN-10 index.

Problems appeared in 21.1 percent by self-report and 22.4 percent by parent report, while low quality of life hit 27.3 percent, all above pre-pandemic levels. Children in low-income homes were hit hardest. Among all parents, 23.7 percent had needed help for a child's mental health in the past year. Help-seeking inside and outside school was also mapped.
pmc-13355175:
Billie Beckwith-Cohen and co-authors report 2026 gene therapy results in adult dogs with an inherited eye disease that causes blindness. A gene fault in the dogs harms the first synapse of the retina, the link where light signals first pass onward, leaving its ribbons stunted. The team used a virus to add a healthy copy of the gene.

After therapy, the dogs regained vision and their retinal synapses matured and grew longer. A thinned retinal layer thickened and reshaped, showing that adult eye tissue can rebuild links once thought fixed. The work offers hope for a like human disease and for repair in the adult brain more broadly.
pmc-13355275:
Nourah Alazemi and co-authors report a 2026 case of Sweet's syndrome, a rare skin illness, in a 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes. Three days after she started the diabetes drug dapagliflozin, painful red plaques and lumps appeared on both upper limbs, followed by fever. Tests ruled out infection, immune disease, and cancer as causes.

A skin biopsy showed a dense crowd of white blood cells in the upper skin with no vessel damage, which fits the diagnosis. Steroid treatment led to clear improvement. The authors stress that drug-triggered cases should be spotted early, since quick skin checks and steady blood sugar control help patients recover well.
pmc-13357075:
Gang Wang and co-authors studied in 2026 a milk protein gene, CSN3, and its unexpected role in stomach cancer. The gene's pattern in this cancer was unclear, so the team measured it in tumor tissue and cell lines, then tested what changing its level does in dishes and in mice. They also traced its partner proteins and linked pathways.

CSN3 ran high in stomach tumors and tracked with deeper growth, node spread, later stage, and worse survival. Lowering it slowed cell growth and movement and raised cell death, while raising it grew tumors in mice. It linked to inflammatory pathways and more immune cell entry, marking it as a possible marker and target.
pmc-13359575:
James Chmiel and co-authors propose a new player in Alzheimer's disease in a 2026 review. Microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, take many states around the plaques of Alzheimer's, not simply good or bad. Genetic evidence points to a switch protein called PU.1: lower amounts seem protective. The authors describe a possible cell state in which microglia act more like suppressor immune cells.

This state, marked by low PU.1 and a surface protein called CD28, may restrain inflammation near plaques rather than fuel it. The idea joins gene studies with single-cell and tissue maps. The authors stress that human proof is still needed before anyone targets this pathway in patients.
pmc-13359675:
Raluca Mihețiu and co-authors weigh two suspected risks for eye disease in tiny babies in a 2026 study. Retinopathy of prematurity is a leading cause of blindness in early-born infants, as blood vessels in the eye grow wrongly. Anemia and donor blood transfusions have both been suspected of adding risk. The team reviewed babies born at Cluj-Napoca hospital in 2023 and 2024.

They included 124 infants born by 32 weeks and weighing 1,500 grams or less. Babies with and without the eye disease were compared on birth traits, illness, hemoglobin levels, and transfusion history. Pinning down which factors truly matter helps nurseries target eye checks and care.
pmc-13359775:
Enjie Chua and co-authors publish the genome of a freshwater snail in a 2026 paper. Sinotaia angularis lives in rivers and lakes and plays a part in nutrient cycling, yet its genetic blueprint was unknown. Using long-read sequencing plus a chromosome-folding method, the team assembled its DNA at chromosome level for the first time.

The genome spans about 1.13 billion letters, most of it sorted into eight chromosome scaffolds. The team predicted 22,232 protein-coding genes and charted repeats and small RNA genes as well. A solid reference genome opens the way to studies of how this snail adapts, evolves, and can be told apart from its relatives.
pmc-13359875:
Francesca Rothell and co-authors study a hard-to-catch cancer in a 2026 paper. Neurolymphomatosis is lymphoma that invades peripheral nerves. It responds to treatment, yet it is often found only at autopsy. The team analyzed 559 reported cases from 231 publications to ask which tests, combined, can catch it in time.

Patients whose nerve disease came first, without known lymphoma elsewhere, lived longer and were more often biopsied. Others, with lymphoma already known, often skipped biopsy. Combining three tests, a PET scan, MRI, and electrical nerve studies, can quickly point to a biopsy site. Earlier diagnosis means earlier treatment for a disease where delay is the main enemy.
pmc-13360975:
Fatemeh Najafi and co-authors compare wound healing in plants and animals in a 2026 review. Healing keeps living things intact and alive, and the two kingdoms share deep parallels despite vast differences. Two gaps block a fair comparison: plant healing lacks a shared phase system, and no common frame spans both kingdoms. The authors set out to build that frame.

They sort healing into three working phases that apply to a cut leaf and a cut skin alike. Within each phase, they weigh what is shared and what is unique to each kingdom. The point is practical: tricks plants use to seal and regrow tissue may inspire new medicine for human wounds. The frame also gives plant science a clearer language for its own healing steps.
pmc-13361275:
Vania Tanda Widyaya and co-authors screened tens of thousands of coatings at once in a 2026 study. Useful coatings serve health care, energy, and clean water, but finding new ones is slow. The team used droplet microarrays, grids of tiny drops, to mix and test pairs and triples of plant polyphenols and polyamines. About 30,000 coatings were made, each in a drop smaller than a grain of rice.

The sweep found hundreds of new functional materials. Over 225 coatings glowed under light, and more than 100 could drive chemical reduction or grab metals. Seven coatings reliably fought a stubborn germ, Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Each test used tiny amounts of material, so the whole search cost little. The method shows how mini testing can speed the hunt for coatings with real jobs.
pmc-13362075:
Michael Richards and co-authors trace the evolution of nerve-sparing prostate removal in a 2026 review. Cutting out the prostate risks harming the pelvic nerves that control bladder and erections. Even with robots and nerve-sparing skill, incontinence and erectile problems stay common and carry heavy costs for patients and health systems. The team searched major databases through February 2026 for studies on injury mechanisms, outcomes, and cost.

Robotic surgery now accounts for over 80 percent of these operations in the data reviewed. The authors explain how nerves get injured despite care, and what the damage costs over a lifetime. New fluorescence imaging that makes nerves glow during surgery is assessed as a possible safeguard. The review weighs whether seeing nerves clearly could pay for itself in better lives after surgery.
pmc-13362275:
Veronica Suaste and co-authors tracked gene activity changes during a vitamin-based therapy trial in a 2026 study. Ataxia-telangiectasia is a multi-system disorder caused by loss of the ATM protein, which guards DNA. Its loss overworks a partner enzyme and drains cells of NAD+, a molecule many pathways need. Patients were given nicotinamide riboside, an NAD+ booster, for 24 months and showed better coordination and eye movements.

The team profiled gene activity in blood cells over the trial to define the disease's molecular signature. They also checked how pathways answered the supplement. A headline result, reflected in the study's title, is that NAD+ boosting dampened overactive interferon gene signatures. Such immune calming may explain part of the clinical gain and guide dosing of this rare-disease therapy.
pmc-13362675:
Georgios Koktsidis and colleagues present a 2026 review of an odd corner of Lynch syndrome, an inherited condition that raises cancer risk because DNA repair genes fail. Most Lynch tumors show unstable DNA, but some gynecological cancers keep stable DNA despite the repair defect. The team gathered every report they could find on this uncommon pattern across three databases and major meetings.

Only 11 reports turned up, covering 36 such tumors, mostly in the womb lining and ovaries, often in carriers of MSH6 or PMS2 gene faults. No cases appeared for other female cancers, and no data show how these tumors respond to immune drugs. The authors call the group strongly under-studied and urge better tracking.
pmc-13363775:
Mohammad Hassan Mazaherifar and colleagues present a 2026 study on sandwich panels built from recycled paper and cardboard for building insulation. Cores of pure paper, pure cardboard, or a half-and-half mix, puffed with green foaming agents, were faced with fiberboard, oak veneer, or palm fiber sheets. The team measured heat flow and sound absorption and inspected the inner structure with microscopes and element scans.

Cardboard-rich cores were more porous and insulated heat better. Holes in the faces and thicker panels lifted sound absorption. Face choice shifted both traits as well. The authors conclude that trash-stream paper and board can serve as light, non-structural interior panels that warm and quiet rooms, a step toward circular building materials.
pmc-13364975:
Bhaskar Sarma and co-workers open a 2026 work set on a fresh view of weed plants that invade new lands: not just pests to burn, but stock to use. Such weeds spread fast, push out home plants, and cost farms dear. Yet they grow huge mass rich in plant goods.

The set backs a shift from clear and toss to clear, use, and heal. Weed mass could feed soil fix, farm aid, drug hunts, and clean fuel work. That turn fits a loop economy that makes goods with less waste. The editors call for proof that use stays safe for the land.
pmc-13367575:
Edward Chu and co-workers build in 2026 a code tool that marks the thigh bone in bone scan shots on its own. Hand marks take long and vary by hand, yet they feed risk calls for bone break. Their tool pairs a learn net that cuts the bone edge with a shape rule that sets marks.

Trained on 555 scans, the net hits high truth marks. Marks from the tool feed a shape model that calls break risk as well as hand marks, with no clear gap. The pipe gives fast, set marks for wide bone study and care.
pmc-13367775:
Daichi Hosokawa and co-workers look back in 2026 at a heart fix for a birth flaw where a heart artery starts at the wrong spot and runs in the artery wall. The fix, unroofing, is the set care, but leak of the main heart valve after can dog some cases. The team reads 16 past cases.

No deaths or new heart ops show in a mid six month watch. Valve leak grows in near two in five, all mild. A short span from valve joint to the wall run on prior scans ties to leak growth. The small set makes the link a lead to test.
pmc-13373675:
Young-Ju Lim and co-authors grew human arm muscle seed cells in the lab in a 2026 study. Seed cells fix and build muscle, and fresh cells from real tissue beat fixed lab lines for true-to-life tests. Work on arm muscle seed cells has been thin so far.

The team took small bits of arm muscle from surgery waste, broke them down, and grew the cells in dishes. Growth shape and speed were watched day by day. Tests for muscle marks and a step to push cells to mature form checked their type. A sound arm cell bank would help tests of muscle ills and new drugs.
pmc-13374075:
Jianwei Geng and co-authors traced womb harm from a plant toxin in a 2026 mouse study. The toxin comes from a plant family and can cross to the unborn. It is known to stress the ovary of the young. The team gave it to mice in late pregnancy and checked the pups' ovaries.

Pups had grave faults in how their egg sacs formed. Droplets that sort cell notes grew large and stuffed with the wrong parts, much like germ cell grains. A germ grain part drove the growth. Wide gene and protein reads backed the tale. The work warns of a fresh route by which womb toxins harm the next kin.
pmc-13374775:
Alan Haruo Bryce and co-authors weigh a drug for late prostate cancer in a 2026 review. The drug blocks a DNA fix path and is the first of its kind passed for men whose cancer holds a breast gene fault and no longer heeds hormone cuts.

Two trials back its use. One showed clear tumor shrinks in men with the fault, from birth or gained. The next showed a longer span with no growth than a doctor's pick of care, and it beat a strong chemo drug head on. Tiredness, aches, and low blood counts lead the harms. The review sets the drug's place in care.
pmc-13379875:
Vineet Goel and colleagues present a 2026 case of a benign heart tumour that caused a long, unexplained fever. Their patient was a 42-year-old man with fever and general symptoms such as tiredness and weight loss. A heart scan found a large growth in the right upper chamber, reaching across a valve into the chamber below.

Surgeons removed the growth, and tissue tests confirmed it was a cardiac myxoma, the most common benign heart tumour in adults. Such tumours are a rare cause of fever with no clear source. The authors stress that a heart scan is the first test of choice, and that surgery is the only complete treatment, with an excellent outlook afterwards.
pmc-13380975:
Ahmed Reda Ismaieel and co-authors published a 2026 study showing that hawkmoth wings can smell. Insects mainly smell with their antennae, but other body parts can also detect chemicals. The team examined the wings of the tobacco hawkmoth under a microscope and tested their responses.

Each wing edge carried a few dozen sensory bristles. Some had pores typical of chemical sensors, not just touch sensors. Wing tissue also switched on genes for chemical receptors, though one key shared receptor was missing. Electrical recordings showed the wings responded to two amine chemicals. The findings suggest wings help the moth sample smells during flight, adding a new sense organ to the list.
pmc-13386175:
Essack Mitha and a large team report COVID vaccine safety and immune response in people with HIV in 2026 work. Participants on antiretroviral therapy joined the large BNT162b2 vaccine trial between September and November 2020. They were randomly assigned to two vaccine doses or placebo, with reactions tracked for a week after each dose.

Vaccine recipients reported more sore arms, tiredness, headache, and chills than placebo recipients, mostly mild to moderate. No serious adverse events appeared in the month after the second dose among the 201 participants with HIV. Antibody responses against the virus spike were elicited, which supports priority vaccination for this higher-risk group.
pmc-13386475:
Wael A. Hassan, Omar A. El Meligy, and Iman M. Talaat review AI tools against standard risk grouping in localized prostate cancer in a 2026 article. The review covered studies from 2020 to 2025 that compared AI models head-to-head with National Comprehensive Cancer Network groups. Searches of three databases yielded 43 full-text studies that met the entry rules.

Models joining MRI features, PET imaging, and slide analysis beat standard grouping at telling risk levels apart in most reports. Gains stood out for predicting advanced features that drive treatment choices. Quality checks used standard bias and reporting tools, which grounds the authors' call for careful validation.
pmc-13386875:
You Li and colleagues find a host lipid protein that parechoviruses cannot copy their RNA without in a 2026 study. Parechovirus A3 can cause sepsis and brain inflammation in newborns, yet its life cycle was poorly mapped. A genome-wide CRISPR screen hunted the host factors the virus depends on.

The screen surfaced Golgi proteins, led by ATG9A, a lipid scramblase better known from autophagy. Its help proved independent of that cleanup role: the virus needed it for RNA replication, not entry or protein making. A partner lipid mover, ATG2, was also required, which suggests the pair feeds lipids into viral replication sites.
pmc-13386975:
Zhao and colleagues uncover how African swine fever virus dismantles the mucosal alarm, in 2026 immunology research. The virus invades through the airway and gut lining, where type III interferons defend. Infection dampens their production, and the team traced it to a viral protein, pM448R. It targets IRF1, a transcription factor hub that switches on interferon-lambda and restriction genes. It marks IRF1 for destruction by the proteasome, the cell's shredder, via an enzyme, STUB1.

STUB1 attaches K48-linked ubiquitin tags to IRF1, sending it for degradation and silencing it. A virus lacking the M448R gene could no longer do this: IRF1 stayed stable and its genes, including OAS1, OAS2, and ZBP1, rose in infected cells. Zhao frames this as the virus hijacking the host's waste system to breach the mucosal barrier. He identifies the protein as a target for attenuated vaccine design against a disease with no vaccine.
pmc-13387075:
Xueru Wang and co-authors test whether the amino acid serine can protect mouse testes from cadmium, a widespread metal contaminant that impairs male fertility. Their 2026 study gives forty male mice plain water, serine, cadmium, or both in drinking water for eighteen weeks, then examines tissue, hormones, and metabolism.

Cadmium caused marked injury: lower testis weight, disturbed hormones, tissue damage, ion imbalance, oxidative stress, and inflammation, together with weakened barrier proteins between blood and testis. It also suppressed sugar breakdown and the testis's own serine production, switching off several enzymes in that pathway, and increased scarring and germ cell death. Adding serine substantially reversed these changes, restoring metabolic balance, antioxidant capacity, and tissue structure. The authors link the protection to two enzymes, PGAM1 and PHGDH, in serine metabolism, and propose serine as a candidate protective additive.
pmc-13387175:
Ahmad Najem Alshammari and co-authors test whether rosmarinic acid, an antioxidant from rosemary, protects rat testes from the pesticide chlorfenapyr, especially when packed into nanoparticles. The plain compound's poor physical properties limit its use. Their 2026 study gives sixty male Wistar rats one of six treatments for thirty days, including pesticide alone and pesticide with plain or nano-formulated acid.

The pesticide cut testis weight, sperm count and motility, and reproductive hormone levels, while raising oxidative stress, inflammation, and cell death signals. The nano-formulation, carried in chitosan particles, reduced these harms more strongly than the plain acid. Treated animals showed lower inflammatory signalling proteins in the tissue, healthier testis structure, restored sperm production, and normalised hormones, alongside activation of a protective antioxidant pathway. The authors conclude nano-encapsulation substantially improves the compound's protective efficacy.
pmc-13387875:
Md. Israt Hasan and colleagues test custom 3D-printed wrist-thumb splints for De Quervain's tenosynovitis in a 2026 study. Forty patients with the painful tendon condition entered the prospective study, and 37 completed six weeks. Participants received either a standard thumb spica splint or a printed brace shaped to their own hand.

Both groups saw large drops in pain scores and disability ratings across the follow-up visits. Printed-brace users also rated their satisfaction on a standard assistive technology scale. The authors frame patient-specific printing as a feasible comfort upgrade, especially where rehabilitation resources are limited.
pmc-13388875:
Builes-Montaño and colleagues model the dose-response curves of the leading incretin weight-loss drugs, semaglutide and tirzepatide, to find which doses are clinically interchangeable in type 2 diabetes, in 2026 pharmacology research. Arm-level data came from the phase III trial programs of both drugs: 48 treatment arms covering 16,524 participants. Statistical models traced weight change across doses, and Bayesian analysis estimated the probability that dose pairs differ by less than a pre-set equivalence margin of 2 percentage points.

Both drugs showed nonlinear dose-response, with each dose step buying less loss than the last at higher doses. Equivalence probabilities were high for two pairings. Semaglutide 2.4 milligrams matched tirzepatide 10 milligrams with 99.4 percent probability, and semaglutide 7.2 milligrams matched tirzepatide 15 milligrams with 94.8 percent probability in the model. Lower semaglutide doses were not equivalent to higher tirzepatide doses. Builes-Montaño offers the map for clinicians switching patients between the drugs without losing ground.
pmc-13395575:
Xiao-Yang Pan and co-authors name, in 2026, three new grass species from Changdu in Tibet, China. The grasses belong to Kengyilia, a wheat kin group of high Asian lands. Shape study, cell checks, and gene reads all fed the naming. Each species shows its own mix of hair, husk, and bristle traits that set it apart.

Cell staining showed each carries six sets of chromosomes from three parent lines. Family trees built from gene and leaf genome data placed them near three cousin genera. Two species drew their mother line from one cousin, and the third from another. The authors say the finds enrich plateau grassland science. Such grasses matter for grazing lands.
pmc-13395975:
Eliza B. Geer and co-authors measured day-to-day symptoms in people with acromegaly, a hormone disorder driven by excess growth hormone, in a 2026 study. All patients were on long-acting injected somatostatin drugs, the standard treatment meant to hold the disease in check.

Thirty-one patients filled in daily surveys for three months, rating seven core symptoms and two extra ones on scales from zero to ten. A flare was counted when a score jumped by at least two points against the prior two-day average. A final survey asked about daily life, treatment satisfaction, and health care use. The design captures how symptoms rise and fall between clinic visits rather than at one visit alone.
pmc-13396075:
Nina Sharp and co-authors tested whether tweaking the color mix of ordinary white light can ease the pain of light sensitivity during a migraine attack. In their 2026 study, 21 adults with migraine were studied while an untreated attack was under way.

Each person sat under four kinds of enriched white light, boosted toward blue, cyan, green, or red, for ten minutes each in random order, with dark breaks between. Brightness was held at 400 lux throughout. Headache strength and visual discomfort were scored before and after each spell. The setup keeps the practical feel of normal room light while testing claims that certain wavelengths soothe and others provoke.
pmc-13396475:
Sajib Kumar Sarkar and co-authors sequenced the active genes of gallbladder cancer, a rare but fast-moving cancer of the biliary tract, to map what goes wrong inside its cells. Their 2026 study compares 13 tumors with six matched healthy samples.

The scan found 1,319 genes working at abnormal levels, 528 turned up and 791 turned down. Programs driving cell division, including E2F targets and a checkpoint before division, were switched on, while bile acid handling and estrogen response programs faded. Network analysis grouped genes into modules and named hub genes, and the Aurora kinase pathway stood out. Key candidates were checked again in patient tissue and cell lines.
pmc-13397475:
Jianyu Liu and colleagues sort teenagers with major depression into symptom groups, paying close attention to poor sleep. Their 2026 study covers 711 young patients who had never taken antidepressant drugs. Depression in teens varies a lot from person to person, and grouping similar cases may guide care better than one average picture.

Using scores for depression, anxiety and sleep quality, the team found three groups: low symptoms, high reported sleep trouble, and high symptoms overall. Family trauma and violent events were linked to the high-symptom group, and the link held after hormone measures entered the model. Hormone results added little, so the authors treat them as early leads rather than firm tools for sorting patients.
pmc-13397575:
Hu and co-authors build, in 2026, Ex3DSP, a self-improving experimental platform for three-dimensional sand printing used in metal casting. Rather than optimizing from data alone, the system carries a machine learning brain that steers physical experiments toward what it calls can-think capability. It chooses the next casting trial from what previous trials taught it. Its working loop runs experiments, reads results, and redesigns the following round automatically.

As a test, the platform attacked a high-dimensional optimization of casting performance across three objectives at once. Sampling each process parameter at 2.5 percent intervals across its range created a space of 68,921 possible parameter combinations, far too many to test exhaustively by hand. The platform's chosen solutions were then applied to real casting parameter selection. Resulting castings showed up to 385 percent improvement in physicochemical and mechanical performance, including tensile strength, against the starting point reported by the authors.
pmc-13397675:
Nair and colleagues measure, in 2026, the burden of betel quid chewing among tribal adults in Wayanad, Kerala, a culturally embedded habit with addictive and carcinogenic ingredients. Their community-based cross-sectional study interviewed 283 adults aged 18 and over in selected habitations. It administered the 16-item Betel Quid Dependence Scale and examined oral health using the DMFT index of decayed, missing, and filled teeth.

Chewing prevalence was 67.5 percent in the surveyed communities, and among the 191 current users, 56.5 percent showed high dependence on the scale. Separated or widowed participants had nearly four times the odds of high dependence, with an adjusted odds ratio of 3.93 in the multivariable analysis. Dental damage was heavy overall, with a mean DMFT score of 6.43 across participants, and high dependence independently predicted worse scores. The authors urge targeted cessation programs, early screening for oral lesions, and oral health promotion in tribal communities.
pmc-13398575:
Fariza Khozhamkul and colleagues track a deadly tick-borne fever across southern Kazakhstan as the climate shifts. Their 2026 study covers Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever in the Zhambyl, Turkistan and Kyzylorda regions plus Shymkent City, from 2014 to 2023. The disease has been rooted in the south for decades, and its natural range has lately spread.

National records counted 214 cases across the study regions in that decade. Weather data from the Climatic Research Unit let the team regress case counts against temperature and rainfall patterns. Linking outbreaks to climate variables, the authors argue, can warn health services which seasons and districts need tick control and hospital readiness most.
pmc-13400275:
Huan Zhao and a large team report in 2026 that a gene switch called IRF5, known for immune work in macrophages, also helps build bone. Macrophages can turn into osteoclasts, the cells that break bone down. Bone stays healthy when breakdown and new growth stay in balance.

Mice lacking IRF5 only in myeloid cells developed thin, weak bone. Surprisingly, bone breakdown stayed normal while new bone formation fell. Fluid from normal early osteoclasts helped bone-forming cells grow, but fluid from cells without IRF5 did not. Gene scans pointed to changes in matrix, bone growth and Notch signals, revealing a fresh link between immune cells and bone building.
pmc-13400475:
Chia-Chi Hsu and co-authors examine, in 2026, whether young athletes process arithmetic differently, using brain wave recordings during a multiplication checking task. Whether sport training transfers to school skills is debated. The study compared 19 high school cycling athletes with 19 matched peers.

Athletes started with lower math scores, answered less accurately and responded more slowly. Their brains also showed larger P300 waves, a signal tied to attention, over the back of the head. Once baseline math skill was accounted for statistically, those brain differences largely faded. The authors conclude the gap reflects math proficiency more than any general brain disadvantage from sport, and that training benefits may stay within their own domain.
pmc-13400675:
Viviana Soto-Mercado and colleagues test, in 2026, a three-drug mix meant to push leukemia cells into programmed death. Two leukemia types, acute lymphoblastic and chronic myeloid, often resist treatment by dodging that death program. Searching combinations of three or more drugs is complex, so the team built a stepwise dosing method.

Eight candidate drugs were first screened on a leukemia cell line across several death-related readouts. The winning trio combined an antimalarial, artemisinin, an antiparasitic, moxidectin, and a chemotherapy drug, doxorubicin, each at half its individual effective dose. Together they stalled the cell cycle, collapsed cell power stations and switched on death enzymes in two cell lines and in patient cells grown outside the body, while sparing non-leukemic cells.
pmc-13401875:
Majidah AlOtaibi, Deema E Jomar, and Muhammad Ali Ahad evaluated full-thickness corneal transplants done for treatment or structural rescue in advanced eye disease, in a 2026 retrospective study from Saudi Arabia. These therapeutic and tectonic grafts are last resorts, and their survival is far poorer than routine transplants.

At King Khaled Eye Specialist Hospital in Riyadh, records covered all such operations from June 2014 to December 2020. 90 eyes from 90 patients met the criteria with at least two years of follow-up for clear grafts. Microbial keratitis, an infected corneal ulcer, drove most surgery at about 77 percent of cases, followed by autoimmune disease and trauma. Kaplan-Meier graft survival was just under half at one year and fell to about a quarter by three years. A larger donor graft was the sole significant risk factor for failure.
pmc-13402675:
Zhang and co-authors present, in 2026, a control system that lets one reinforcement learning policy steer many different soft robots. It lifts their dynamics into a shared linear embedding space based on Koopman theory. Soft robots reshape themselves like octopus arms, but each new body demands retraining. Encoding dynamics into the common space decouples the policy from any specific morphology, allowing real-time adaptation without starting over.

The team validated the system across 33 robot configurations, built from segments such as honeycomb pieces of 65.5 and 101.5 millimeters and muscle segments up to 229 millimeters in testbeds. Transferring a policy to a new configuration needed 75 times fewer samples than learning from scratch. Performance held under high-speed motion, heavy payloads, and even multiple actuator faults. The system achieved real-world skills the authors describe as previously unattainable in soft robotics, and the framework should generalize beyond robots to complex physical systems.
pmc-13402875:
Khulood K Burashed, Ali J AlHilly, and Yusuf J Hejres surveyed Bahraini adults without medical training on how well they know stroke risks and warning signs. Stroke incidence in Bahrain has nearly doubled in 16 years, and fast recognition saves brain. An online questionnaire spread by convenience and snowball sampling gathered 1564 answers, and the team tested how schooling related to each answer.

Smoking was the best-known risk factor at 91.3 percent, while inflammatory conditions and newborn age sat near the bottom at about 30 percent each. Face numbness was the most recognized symptom at 87.7 percent; coordination trouble and dizziness were missed by most. Education strongly shaped most answers, with one odd twist: headache recognition fell as education rose, hinting at misconceptions among the better schooled. The authors call for public teaching aimed at the least-known signs.
pmc-13403275:
Ahdyie Ahmadi leads a team testing whether electrically triggered epileptic spikes can help locate the seizure onset zone in drug-resistant epilepsy. Surgery cures only when that zone is found and removed, and mapping usually waits for spontaneous seizures. Interictal discharges, the spikes between seizures, are easier to catch but underused for localization. The team analyzed brain recordings from 30 surgical patients who became seizure-free, a built-in proof of correct targeting.

Stimulating cortex at 50 hertz through depth electrodes raised spike rates afterward inside the true onset zone. No significant change appeared outside it. The separation reached an area under the curve of 98 percent for zone tissue. The effect appeared whether the stimulus landed inside or outside the zone, suggesting stimulation wakes the epileptogenic network broadly. The authors offer spike counting after stimulation as a quantitative mapping tool.
pmc-13403575:
Chantal Berna and co-authors followed 172 pregnant people in 2026 to untangle how pain feeds stress symptoms after birth. Strong birth pain can seed later trauma stress, yet many pain traits may play a part. Surveys ran before birth and again one week and one month after.

Expected birth pain and pain's daily drag during pregnancy tied to how strong birth pain felt. Worry-heavy thinking about pain during birth sat between pain level and how the whole birth felt. That overall feeling then tied to early stress signs, which tied to later trauma signs. Easing pain worry before birth may blunt the chain.
pmc-13404175:
Stéphane-Hans Bateyi Mustafa and co-authors reviewed oral cholera vaccines in 2026 as tools that can break chains of spread, not just shield one person. About 1.3 billion people live at risk in regions where cholera keeps returning. The review drew on work from 2000 to February 2026 across six sources.

Two-dose killed vaccines guard about 66 to 81 percent of people at six months. When over half a community is covered, herd effects can cut cases by more than three quarters in some settings. Campaigns started within a week of an outbreak can avert up to 70 percent of cases. Clean water work must still anchor control.
pmc-13404375:
Paula Quijano and colleagues watched energy units inside alpaca eggs in 2026 as the eggs ripened in the lab. Picking good eggs matters for breeding alpacas, whose natural birth rates run low. The team tracked how the tiny power units, mitochondria, sat and clumped before and after ripening.

Centered clusters and grainy clumps of the units went with higher energy activity. Those patterns likely mark eggs whose inner contents have matured well. Such eggs may hold the best odds of growing into embryos. The markers could sharpen egg choice for breeding work and for guarding rare camel family lines in South America.
pmc-13405175:
Jaydeep N Pol and colleagues describe a rare nerve-related tumour in a boy's spermatic cord, with a literature review, in 2026. Paragangliomas grow from hormone-related cells outside the adrenal glands and almost never appear in the spermatic cord. Their vague presentation often leads to confusion with more common groin lumps.

The patient, aged 13, had a slowly growing, painless groin mass. Surgeons removed it, and microscopy showed the classic Zellballen nest pattern with little abnormality and slow division. Staining for synaptophysin and chromogranin A confirmed the diagnosis. Three years on he remains free of disease. The authors stress adding this rare tumour to the list considered for groin masses in children.
pmc-13406675:
Ahmad Kharoufeh and colleagues report a very premature baby whose brain bleeding led to fluid build-up needing a shunt, in a 2026 case. Born at twenty-six weeks, the boy first showed a grade two bleed inside the brain's ventricles, usually a milder injury. Follow-up scans told a worse story.

The ventricles swelled into severe post-haemorrhagic dilatation, and imaging hinted at a blocked fluid pathway without proving it. Such progression from a low-grade bleed is uncommon and hard to manage. The authors stress repeated brain imaging even after apparently mild bleeds in extremely premature infants. Early recognition and prompt neurosurgery offer the best chance of limiting developmental harm.
pmc-13406775:
Xinlei Zou and co-authors review the cleanup of damaged cell power stations in liver injury from restored blood flow, in a 2026 article. Cutting then restoring liver blood supply during surgery or shock floods tissue with oxygen radicals and calcium, wrecking mitochondria. The cleanup process, mitophagy, decides much of what follows.

Well-judged cleanup removes broken mitochondria, limits oxidative stress and calms inflammasome alarms, protecting liver cells. Too little cleanup, or a disordered version, lets damage pile up and inflammation spread. The review follows the pathway from energy failure to cell death signals. Drug strategies that tune mitophagy are assessed as future treatment for this surgical complication.
pmc-13407575:
Ofran Almossawi and co-authors ask, in 2026, whether a child's sex itself influences death risk in English paediatric intensive care. Their population study linked intensive care and hospital records for 48,500 children first admitted between 2010 and 2019, most as babies, and applied causal methods designed to mimic a fair comparison.

During first admissions, 3.81 percent of girls and 3.50 percent of boys died, a reversal of the usual childhood pattern where boys die more often. After doubly robust causal adjustment, the excess mortality for girls stood at 0.31 percentage points, with a confidence range just above zero. The authors argue the assumption that pre-pubertal children respond identically to critical illness and its treatment deserves re-examination, and they frame sex as a causal factor rather than a mere association.
pmc-13409275:
Wajiha Ahmad and colleagues interview cancer doctors in Bahawalpur, Pakistan, in 2026 about financial toxicity, the economic side effect that can quietly wreck treatment. Twelve of thirteen approached oncologists took part in the exploratory study across two tertiary hospitals. Four themes emerged from the conversations: what the oncologist's role should be, how money trouble damages outcomes, what blocks honest discussion, and what might fix it.

Doctors accepted a duty to plan cost-effective treatment and counsel patients, yet time, training, and system gaps made such conversations hard. Their proposed remedies reach beyond the clinic: embed financial counselling in cancer services, widen the national health coverage programme, improve infrastructure, and regulate drug prices. The authors conclude financial toxicity is a systems failure, and they call for studies that include patients and other stakeholders across more regions.
pmc-13411475:
Po-Jen Hsiao and co-authors profile in 2026 immune brake signals and regulatory T cells in lupus patients versus healthy volunteers. Both the brake protein PD-1 and the calming Treg cells keep immunity balanced, and both misbehave in lupus. How their profiles shift between flare and calm was the open question.

Flow cytometry measured many cell features at once in twenty healthy Taiwanese controls and ten lupus patients. Lupus samples varied far more between individuals in brake signal levels and Treg makeup. Paired samples from active and stable phases, plus a few infection and post-surgery cases, added context. Small numbers make every result exploratory, the authors stress, fit for generating hypotheses rather than guiding treatment.
pmc-13413275:
Maryam Hassanesfahani and co-authors review in 2026 which bariatric surgery patients need rescue opioids in the first two days after their operation. Pain control speeds recovery, yet little was known about what drives opioid demand after weight-loss surgery. Charts covered 442 patients operated on between 2021 and 2023 at a community hospital, comparing robotic with laparoscopic approaches across bypass and sleeve procedures.

Robotic cases used more opioids than laparoscopic ones, averaging 13.3 versus 10.1 morphine-equivalent units in the reported data, a gap driven by sleeve patients. A psychiatric history and any prior surgery also raised the odds of higher use, alongside the robotic platform itself. Sex, body mass index, and procedure type showed no such link. The authors suggest pre-surgery mental health review and multi-drug pain plans.
pmc-13415475:
Adam Reeves published this correction in 2026 to fix typesetting damage in his article on mental imagery for Attention, Perception, and Psychophysics. Greek letters alpha, beta, and sigma had been replaced by Roman letters, and subscripts were dropped through the main text. Equations stayed correct, so text and formulas no longer matched.

The notice prints the repaired passages for three spots in the article, covering variance symbols and the signal detection quantities d prime and c. One passage clarifies that two uses of alpha, in competing models, must be kept apart. Another fixes how the Perky effect follows from a ratio of those quantities.
pmc-13418275:
Liu and colleagues report a 2026 study of how to stop fast droplets from splashing and spreading out of control, a problem in inkjet printing and farm spraying. The team changed the inner structure of a common soap-like ingredient. Adding a charged partner ingredient turned its clusters into long, tangled threads called wormlike micelles, forming a network inside each droplet.

On cotton fabric, used as a test surface, treated droplets landed without splashing and stayed in a tight area. The micelle network gripped the cotton fibers' tiny structures and bonded with the cellulose, which held the liquid during the first wetting moments. Untreated droplets, by contrast, splash and soak outward unevenly. Controlling where each droplet ends up, without slowing it down, could sharpen printed patterns and cut the drift and waste that plague crop spraying.
pmc-13418475:
Zaid Al-Hamdan and colleagues survey flu vaccination drivers among health workers in Jordan, in a 2026 cross sectional study. Five hundred twenty three workers across the country's three regions answered questions on behaviour, social, and practical factors. Awareness of flu vaccination was near universal, yet only 48 percent had taken it in the prior three years.

Past vaccination was the strongest predictor of motivation, raising odds more than twentyfold. Belief in benefit, effectiveness, and safety, plus social responsibility and service satisfaction, also mattered greatly. Fewer than a third rated the vaccine very safe or very important. Campaigns should target confidence and misconceptions, the authors conclude.
pmc-13418575:
Costabile and Loveys built an interactive computer simulation that teaches life-science students to read a micropipette dial before they ever touch the real instrument in a teaching laboratory. Reading the dial wrong leads students to deliver wrong volumes, which corrupts experiments and undermines confidence, so the simulation isolates that reading skill for safe practice.

Students at two separate universities completed the simulation and were tested before and afterwards on confidence, unit conversion, and dial-reading accuracy. Both groups improved significantly in self-rated confidence and in reading micropipette scales correctly after the practice session. Student feedback was strongly positive about learning the skill and feeling more capable in the laboratory. The authors present the tool as a low-cost preparation step within blended learning, readying students for hands-on bench work.
pmc-13419075:
Boric and colleagues reviewed in 2026 what drives complications after a common breast reduction method in 643 patients. The method, superomedial pedicle reduction, reshapes very large breasts while keeping the nipple on a bridge of tissue with a strong blood supply. Records covered operations from 2004 to 2024 at one surgeon's hospitals.

About 22 in 100 patients had some complication, with roughly 15 in 100 minor and 7 in 100 major. Every obesity class raised the risk of minor problems and slow healing. Heavier patients also faced more infections, while the amount of tissue removed did not predict most problems. Smoking predicted major problems and repeat operations, and high blood pressure predicted readmission. The authors conclude that patient health factors, not resection size, drive most risk after this surgery.
pmc-13419175:
Jalene and colleagues report a 2026 survey study of recovery after a mass casualty event, a campus shooting, at a minority-serving university in the United States. Four to five months after the event, students, faculty, and staff answered an anonymous survey. They rated depression and anxiety before the event and at survey time, plus belonging and fitness.

Respondents reported clear rises in both depression and anxiety scores from before the event to the survey. The team examined how a sense of belonging on campus, estimated heart and lung fitness, and preferred forms of help related to those changes. The survey also asked which supports people would actually use to cope. Pairing harm with belonging and fitness points planners to factors that may soften trauma.
pmc-13419275:
Ju and colleagues tested a rapid magnetic resonance method that follows creatine and phosphocreatine, two molecules that shuttle energy inside muscle, while volunteers exercised inside a 3 Tesla scanner. Their ultrafast CEST approach, which detects molecules indirectly through water signal changes, aimed to capture second-by-second energy shifts without invasive sampling.

Five healthy volunteers performed calf raises inside the magnet while the team recorded images every 7.6 seconds during exercise and recovery. Phosphocreatine signals dropped by about 77 percent during exercise while creatine signals climbed roughly 469 percent above resting levels. After exercise stopped, phosphocreatine refilled with a recovery time near 73 seconds, closely matching creatine's decay of about 62 seconds on average. The authors say the method could support noninvasive checks of mitochondrial function, the cell's energy-producing machinery.
pmc-13419975:
Trwska A. Amin and colleagues report two patients who carried both beta-thalassemia major and inflammatory bowel disease, a rare and easily missed pairing. The blood disorder causes severe anemia, while bowel inflammation adds belly pain, bleeding, and fatigue that can hide inside the blood picture. Such overlap can delay the bowel diagnosis for years.

One patient's blood work showed hemoglobin down to 50 grams per liter with inflammation markers far above normal in the reported values. Stool checks and further workup separated infection from chronic bowel disease. The authors scan the thin prior literature beside their two cases. Their message is plain: lasting gut symptoms in thalassemia deserve a bowel workup even when anemia seems to explain them.
pmc-13420275:
Wu and colleagues report a 2026 study of kidney damage in diabetes, focused on a small gene-switching RNA and ferroptosis, a cell-death path in which iron drives fat damage in membranes. The team worked with diabetic mice and mouse kidney tube cells grown in high sugar. They traced a chain: the RNA miR-145-5p acts on guard gene NRF2, which controls SLC7A11, a ferroptosis-shield gene.

The small RNA ran high in the kidneys of diabetic mice. Blocking it cut ferroptosis, scarring, and harmful cell change, and improved kidney measures. Blocking NRF2 or adding a drug that forces ferroptosis undid part of that gain, which supports the proposed chain. Lab tests confirmed the RNA binds NRF2 directly and that NRF2 switches on SLC7A11. The chain offers drug targets for a leading cause of kidney failure.
pmc-13421475:
Salem and colleagues tested in 2026 whether treating barley seeds with helpful microbes before sprouting boosts its health effects. The method, called biopriming, inoculates seeds with microbes that enrich the grain as it germinates. The team compared plain germinated barley extract with versions primed by Bacillus subtilis or Aspergillus niger.

The Bacillus-primed barley showed the strongest profile, richer in phenolic acids and B vitamins, notably B2, B9, and B12. Rats on this extract moved more normally and remembered locations better than untreated MSG rats. Brain chemical balance moved back toward normal, and markers of oxidative stress and brain inflammation fell. Survival pathways tied to cell cleanup, called autophagy, were also switched on. The authors identify Bacillus priming as a promising, sustainable way to make barley a stronger functional food.
pmc-13422275:
Liudmyla Krupelnytska leads an eight-author team asking, in a 2026 study, why many Ukrainian women chose to give birth at home in a war zone rather than flee. Russia's full-scale invasion shattered maternity care, and the decisions of those who stayed — framed in the title as bravery — had not been systematically explained.

Online data came from 730 women pregnant or newly delivered during the invasion's first two years. Decision-tree and random-forest models found circumstance dominating: how disrupted daily life felt, and how close the fighting was, predicted relocation best. Personality traits, including the Big Five, did not separate stayers from leavers overall, though extraversion played a minor secondary role. The authors stress situation over disposition.
pmc-13423075:
Matanda and co-authors measure how community talks shift norms around female genital mutilation in this 2026 survey study from Narok County, Kenya, where expectations about marriage keep cutting entrenched. They surveyed 2,658 adults in 2024. The survey set people who had joined mixed-sex community dialogues against those who had not. It also traced the pathways between beliefs and behavior.

People who took part held more progressive positions. Adjusted odds of endorsing pro-cutting beliefs were 0.61 against those who stayed out. Intentions to cut a daughter came in at 0.49 in the same models. Odds of outright opposing the practice reached 2.39 in the adjusted models. Couples-only dialogues showed weaker, less consistent links. Mediation analysis attributed 88 percent of the dialogue effect on opposition to shifts in beliefs and intentions. Intentions were the strongest single bridge. The authors back dialogue-centered elimination strategies.
pmc-13424275:
Salvatore Nesci argues that adolescent depression should be read as an energy crisis in the brain's dopamine system, not simply adult depression arriving early. Adolescence rewires reward circuits while motivation and priorities are being reset, and the nucleus accumbens, the hub that turns dopamine signals into effort and anticipation, sits at the centre of that change.

Loss of pleasure, a core and treatment-resistant feature in young patients, tracks with faulty signalling in this hub. Nesci's proposal ties that failure to mitochondria, the cell's power plants, arguing their performance governs how strongly dopamine neurons can signal. The piece builds an integrative model meant to explain stubborn reward failure and to point treatment research toward bioenergetics.
pmc-13424775:
Naoto Aoyama leads a sixteen-author prospective study of a stubborn step in endoscopic bile drainage: pushing the stent delivery tube through a freshly made tract between stomach and liver ducts. Failure often forces extra dilation, adding time and cost, and the team suspected the angle between guidewire and duct decides success.

Twenty-five patients received a new double-lumen dilator; twenty-five matched historical patients had standard dilation. Delivery succeeded without extra dilation in 92% of the new group against 48% of controls. The wire-to-duct angle just before insertion averaged 153.4 degrees with the new tool against 123.3 degrees conventionally. Wider angles predicted success in adjusted analysis, supporting an angle-first explanation over brute mechanical advantage.
pmc-13424875:
Malmberg, Kawalerowicz, and Andersson explore in 2026 how the sorting of whole life courses across places feeds political polarization in Sweden. A life course here means the chain of positions a person holds over time in school, work, family, and housing.

Tracking such trajectories geographically, the authors show that places come to hold sharply contrasting mixes of life experience. They show that the resulting divides are written into the landscape itself. Segregation between trajectory types grows with age: young adults are far less sorted than older adults, and the move into homeownership is a major driver of the split. Studies that measure sorting with single markers like income or education understate its strength. The concentration of particular life courses in particular places also lines up with the geography of political polarization.
pmc-13425575:
M. S. Anagha and colleagues set out a 2026 systematic review protocol on measurement instruments built for Ayurveda research. Ayurvedic diagnosis uses qualitative concepts that newer questionnaires and clinical tools try to quantify, yet many tools show inconsistent methods and weak validation. The planned review will identify, map, and characterize instruments developed or adapted for Ayurvedic constructs.

Beyond cataloguing tools, the reviewers will document problems met during development and validation and propose directions for stronger instruments. Researchers gain a route toward measures that clinicians and journals can trust for trials of traditional concepts. Good tools of this kind would let staff check the same signs in the same way at each visit and in each new trial. The list will name each tool, who made it, and how well it was checked at the time it first came out for use in wards.
pmc-13427575:
Piyush Baindara and co-authors introduce, in 2026, a new compound that kills the fungus Candida albicans, a common cause of serious infections. They call the compound cardio-green butyl acetate, shortened to CaGA. It was made in the lab and had not been tested as an antifungal before. Resistant Candida strains and slimy biofilm growth make new options badly needed.

CaGA killed free-growing fungus cells and cut down biofilms, the dense films fungi form on surfaces. Tests showed it punched holes in the fungal membrane by latching onto ergosterol, the main fat that stiffens that membrane. Computer models of the membrane backed up the lab picture. Work so far is in dishes and models, yet the distinct attack route makes CaGA worth further study.
pmc-13428075:
Zaizen and colleagues published a 2026 case report on scarring lung disease in a rare illness. Their patient had autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis for 15 years. In that illness, lung air sacs fill with fatty protein the body cannot clear. Over time, his lungs also began to scar, a newer concern in this illness.

Scans before referral showed slow scar growth rather than a return of the filling illness. His breathing capacity slipped over six months of watching, so treatment began. He started nintedanib, a drug that slows lung scarring in other diseases. His breathing capacity then held steady for two years of follow-up. Telling scar growth apart from illness return guided the whole plan.
pmc-13429275:
Murayama and Hoshi trial a knee extension aid for walking training after stroke with one sided weakness. Slow walkers often land on the forefoot because the swinging leg lacks momentum to straighten the knee. That pattern trains the ankle into bad habits. Their 2026 trial assigns thirty inpatients at five Japanese rehab wards to gait training for two weeks. One group uses an ankle foot brace alone. The other adds the knee aid to that brace.

The aid group straightened the knee by four degrees more at the end of the swing phase. The control pattern did not show that shift. A straighter knee at contact favors a heel first landing, which the authors link to calmer muscle overactivity during weight acceptance. The device is simple and worn only in training. Brief mechanical help, the result hints, can retrain a key joint timing without complex robotics.
pmc-13429875:
Alson and colleagues follow pregnancy outcomes after fertility treatment in women with endometriosis or adenomyosis. Their 2026 prospective cohort study enrolled 1,035 women undergoing IVF or ICSI at a university hospital, with diagnoses made by ultrasound using international consensus definitions. Outcomes were known for 607 women who gave birth.

Compared with women without either condition, those affected faced higher risks on several fronts. Preterm birth was more common, as were hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, placenta previa, bleeding before delivery, and pelvic pain. Earlier evidence on these questions had been inconsistent, largely because studies defined the diseases differently. By applying standardised ultrasound criteria within one treated population, the authors give clinicians a firmer basis for planning antenatal care in this group.
pmc-13430175:
Muhammad Sanusi and a large team describe, in a 2026 case report, a dangerous heart rhythm as the first sign of probable cardiac sarcoidosis. The disease inflames organs with clusters of immune cells, and in the heart it can scar the electrical system. Their patient was a 69-year-old man who arrived with palpitations, dizziness, and breathlessness after a therapy session. Monitors caught repeated runs of ventricular tachycardia, a fast rhythm from the heart's lower chambers, topping 200 beats per minute.

A standard drug steadied the rhythm. Scans of his heart arteries showed only minor disease, ruling out the usual cause. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed scar in a pattern typical of sarcoidosis rather than a heart attack. He received an implanted defibrillator to guard against recurrence and went home stable. Biopsy was skipped because heart sampling often misses this patchy disease, a practice guidelines now support.
pmc-13430275:
Sezgin and colleagues validate an informant questionnaire for spotting cognitive decline after stroke. The IQCODE asks a spouse or caregiver how the patient's thinking compares with years before, which suits patients who cannot test well themselves. Their 2026 study gives the brief version by phone to informants of 179 stroke patients. Calls come within a week of a standard clinic test. The team checks reliability, structure, and how well scores sort impaired from unimpaired patients.

The scale proved consistent, and factor analysis found a four part structure that fit the data after three weak items were dropped. The sixteen item version sorted patients with fair accuracy. A trimmed thirteen item version kept the same sensitivity while raising specificity, meaning fewer false alarms. An informant can answer by phone in minutes, so the authors recommend the tool for remote screening after stroke, with full testing to follow a positive screen.
pmc-13430975:
Lv and colleagues trace how chronic smoking harms the adolescent brain in this 2026 mouse study. Smoking is a major dementia risk factor, especially when started young, and the brain's glymphatic system, a waste-clearance network, is suspected to be involved. The team exposed adolescent mice to chronic smoke and measured glymphatic transport with microscopy, alongside heart function, tau protein buildup, and performance in maze and object-recognition tests.

The longer the exposure, the worse glymphatic transport became, and phosphorylated tau accumulated in the hippocampus's dentate gyrus while new synapses and new neurons there dwindled. Cognition declined in step with these changes across the exposure period. The authors link the clearance failure to three cooperating problems. The heart ejected more weakly. Arterial pulsatility, the pulse that drives fluid flow, was reduced. And the aquaporin-4 water channel around blood vessels was lost.
pmc-13433375:
Sutherland and team costed out BEST in CLASS-Elementary. It is a Tier 2 program that trains and coaches elementary teachers to support individual students with problem behavior. They used the ingredients method, which prices every input. Data came from kindergarten through third-grade classrooms in a multisite randomized trial. The trial spanned 136 teacher-student pairs and 63 teachers.

The average cost came to 2,866 dollars per teacher-student pair in a classroom receiving the program. That figure includes teacher recruitment. Adding one more focal student to an already treated classroom cost only 101 dollars at the margin. Even two additions stayed cheap relative to starting fresh. The intervention itself accounted for less than half of total spending across the implementation sites studied. Coaches consumed the largest share, almost half of all costs. The model rests on ongoing one-to-one coaching rather than one-off workshops for teachers.
pmc-13437275:
Kübra Özkaya Toraman and colleagues measured how dental implants distort radiation dose during head and neck cancer treatment.
