Their 2026 lab study set three implant kinds into fake jawbone models: titanium, zirconia, and a custom frame that sits on the bone surface. Sensors at four spots around each implant recorded real dose, which the team compared with the planned dose.

Measured and planned doses differed clearly, with a median gap near eight percent below plan. Dose rose slightly on the cheek side from backscatter, while the tongue and front sides lost dose, falling as much as about fourteen percent short. Zirconia showed the widest mismatch, and planning software predicted hot spots above some implants. The custom surface frame behaved most predictably of the three. The authors stress that the work was done in models, not patients, so larger studies with real outcomes must test whether these gaps change care.
pmc-13437475:
Guido Kobbe and co-authors chart how a drug class became the backbone of care when blood cancers return after a donor stem cell transplant. Relapse of myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia is the top cause of transplant failure. Over twenty years, hypomethylating agents moved from experiment to standard first move. Their 2026 review gathers the findings behind that shift.

Trials named RELAZA showed starting azacytidine at the first molecular whisper of relapse can delay full return of disease. Lasting control usually needs the donor immune system too, so infusions of donor lymphocytes often join the drug. Patients fare best when treatment starts at low disease levels, when relapse is molecular rather than visible, and when more time has passed since transplant. Newer pairings with targeted drugs against FLT3 or IDH changes show early promise. The authors look toward personal, biology-guided plans, with second transplants reserved for chosen cases.
pmc-13437675:
Li Du and colleagues compared the mental health of Chinese teenagers learning online at home against peers back in school during the pandemic. Their 2026 survey covered 5,787 students in grades seven through twelve at fourteen Gansu schools across 2020 and 2021. Standard questionnaires measured mood, distress, and sleep. Scores were set against national norms and sorted by learning mode, sex, and stage.

Students showed more distress than national yardsticks on several fronts, and nearly a quarter carried moderate to severe depressive symptoms. Surprisingly, in-school students reported worse distress and depression than online learners at home. Sleep told a consistent story: teens who felt their sleep poor, took long to fall asleep, or slept fewer hours all fared worse mentally. Because the survey caught one moment, learning mode cannot be said to have caused the gaps. They suggest sleep coaching and calmer school climates as supports worth building either way.
pmc-13437875:
Hao Zhang and co-authors gathered the family of MYB switches helping plants survive cold. MYB proteins are transcription factors, gene controllers switching whole programs on and off as temperatures fall. Their 2026 review curated 106 cold-linked MYBs proven in experiments, drawn from forty-five plant species, and set them inside their family tree.

One large subfamily supplies most known cold switches, while two smaller branches remain unexplored. Related switches in different species sometimes keep the same job, sometimes drift into new ones. The pathways they run span hormone response, the classic cold-response cascade, protective compounds, leaf wax, and even chemical marks on DNA packaging. The authors map what to chase next: the neglected branches, cross-species checks guided by the family tree, and tests under mixed stresses, since fields rarely send cold alone. Breeders hunting hardier crops get a chart of proven levers.
pmc-13438675:
Jerzy Twarowski and colleagues caught meiosis mutating its own DNA across long stretches. Meiosis, the division that makes eggs and sperm, deliberately breaks DNA to shuffle genes, and the single-stranded DNA exposed in repair was suspected of soaking up errors. Their 2026 yeast study planted a human enzyme attacking single-stranded DNA and leaving a readable scar, letting the team map where such DNA appears.

The scars clustered thickly, up to 134 mutations spanning more than twenty-five thousand letters in one tract. Making the clusters required the programmed breaks that start meiotic shuffling. Two repair behaviors explained the long strands: break-induced replication, and extra-long chewing back of broken ends. Gene promoters and transfer RNA genes also collected single strands, adding quiet hot spots. The results recast meiosis as high-risk, high-reward: the machinery creating diversity also writes clusters of fresh mutations, some the seeds of inherited disease.
pmc-13439175:
Nayem Haque, Ronald Cutler, Simone Sidoli, and Robert A Coleman film single gene-copying machines inside living human cells, reporting in 2026 how they pause and restart. RNA polymerase II copies DNA into RNA, yet it often stalls soon after starting, and that stall gates how much gene product gets made. Live-cell single-molecule imaging let the team time how long each machine stayed bound to chromatin, the DNA and protein mix in the nucleus.

Most binding events ended within tens of seconds, with only a small share reaching full productive copying. Cells differed widely in that share. Removing the TFIID part TAF1, a scaffold protein, cut clustering and raised pausing across genes. The work supports a role for TAF1 in releasing paused machines into active copying.
pmc-13439275:
Chang Seok Bang and Eun Jeong Gong weigh two routes for feeding tubes that reach the small bowel, in a 2026 commentary. Some patients cannot be fed into the stomach, due to a still stomach, a blockage, or high risk of food entering the lungs. Parkinson's patients on gel medicine also need steady delivery into the jejunum. Two scope-based routes exist: a tube threaded through a stomach opening, or a tube placed straight through the jejunal wall.

The through-stomach route is simpler to place, yet its thin extension slips or clogs often and sends patients back for repeat scopes. The direct route is harder to perform but holds up far longer once placed. The writers argue that the kinder choice is the one that lasts, sparing frail patients repeated procedures. Skill at the centre should shape which route is offered.
pmc-13440675:
Calderón-Garcidueñas and colleagues document brain-disease proteins in young Mexico City residents exposed to heavy air pollution. Their 2026 forensic autopsy study examined 189 brains, average age 26, mostly from the metropolitan area where fine particle pollution is high, plus ten low-pollution controls. Using targeted staining, they measured Alzheimer-type change, the Parkinson protein alpha-synuclein, and TDP-43, a third disease-linked protein.

Overlaps were common even in children. Among 37 children averaging 13 years, about a quarter showed Alzheimer-type change alone, and most of the rest carried two or three protein pathologies combined. Adults aged 18 to 40 showed similar stacking, with half carrying Alzheimer change plus alpha-synuclein. The authors propose routine measurement of these abnormal proteins in young urban autopsies to size the problem and guide prevention and pollution control.
pmc-13441375:
Perrykkad and colleagues tracked sense of coherence in 680 Australian women. Sense of coherence is a person's feeling that life makes sense and can be handled. The women were tracked four times across pregnancy and the postpartum year. Earlier work tied higher coherence to less pregnancy distress and better births. But how the trait moves through the period around birth was unknown.

A growth mixture model split the women into four paths. A high group held steady at 67 percent of women, and a low group sat at 21 percent. A rising group made up 8 percent, and a falling group 3 percent. An early-pregnancy depression label pointed most to landing in the low and rising paths. Childhood trauma history pointed to the low and falling paths. Trauma survivors were most likely to end the postpartum year with drained coping reserves. The authors urge support around birth to protect those reserves.
pmc-13441775:
Tim Salomonsson and colleagues test a specialised MRI method for predicting a gene switch that governs brain tumour drug response, reporting in 2026. Methylation of the MGMT promoter shapes how high-grade gliomas answer chemotherapy, yet measuring it needs tissue. Chemical exchange saturation transfer imaging reads protein-related signals without a biopsy. Forty-four patients with grade four gliomas or glioblastoma had such scans before surgery, with tumours outlined by hand and by two machine learning segmenters.

Unmethylated tumours showed higher signal peaks in dead tumour core across every outlining method. Machine-drawn outlines added further separations in living tumour rim. Patterns held within the glioblastoma-only group as well. The authors read the consistency across segmenters as encouraging for automated pipelines. Fluid-suppressed versions of the signals are presented as candidate non-invasive markers of methylation status, pending larger validation.
pmc-13442875:
Zahra Ghoreyshi and colleagues build a physics-led model that predicts what a T cell will target in a 2026 paper. T cells read short bits shown on cell surfaces, and guessing their targets from receptor codes alone is error-prone. Their frame joins receptor text with shape data for receptor-target pairs, drawn from past work and from computer builds.

Tests used stem cell transplant samples and a set of HLA-A*02 shown bits from flu, a herpes virus, and a melanoma mark. Forecasts for fresh receptors from donors and patients hit the mark, and gains grew when like receptors were grouped first. Shape-led learning stayed strong even with thin training sets. The authors offer the frame for cell therapy design, shot work, and immune watch in clinic samples.
pmc-13443175:
Nurzhan Abishev and colleagues report surgery for weak-bone spine breaks in two patients in a 2026 paper. Bone loss makes spine screws grip poorly, so firm fixation is a known hard step. Both patients had pathologic breaks that pressed the spinal canal.

Care used cemented hollow screws plus a cage that fuses the spine from the front path. Pain scores fell from 7.3 points before surgery to a mark of 1.2 points right after, and to 0.5 points by two years. A function index fell from 69 percent to 20 percent across the same span. Curve angle eased from 38.0 degrees to a value of 29.0 degrees after surgery. No bone loss ringed the screws at checks. The authors share the tweak as a workable path for frail spines.
pmc-13443675:
Ecem Kara tested how five heavy metals affect seed sprouting and early growth in two onion types, Gence and Karbeyazı, grown in lab dishes. The 2026 study used controlled doses to screen which metals harm young plants most.

Seeds grew on a standard plant medium with copper, cadmium, lead, nickel, or cobalt at four dose levels. Kara tracked sprouting rates, root and shoot length, and plant weight at each dose. Higher doses mostly cut sprouting, root growth, and weight gain. Copper and cadmium pulled sprouting rates down by more than twenty points. Nickel behaved oddly, lifting final sprouting at low doses while weakening early vigour. Gence kept higher final sprouting, while Karbeyazı held on to root traits better, so final sprouting alone misses much of the harm.
pmc-13444075:
Samuel Benedict and colleagues show mycobacteria firing a wall-cutting toxin at rival kin in a 2026 study. These germs were thought to shun toxin duels, since their thick waxy walls look like full armor. Their type VII secretion system, a needle-like exporter, ships an enzyme that cleaves the arabinogalactan layer of rival walls.

Structure and chemistry work maps how the cutter grips and snips its target layer. A shield protein family guards the shooter from its own toxin. Genes for like toxins dot the wider mycobacterial order, which hints at widespread duels. The authors reframe these germs as active rivals, not lone dwellers. Wall layers once read as pure defense now double as the duel's weak point.
pmc-13445775:
Khonakdar and colleagues scoped the evidence on AI for checking suspected acute coronary syndrome before hospital arrival. In the field, care teams carry limited tests and doubt runs high. Using scoping review rules, they searched four databases to May 2026. They mapped diagnosis, prediction, and triage uses.

19 studies covering 319,709 patients met the bar for the final evidence map. Electrocardiogram-based deep learning and multimodal models performed best. Discrimination values ran from about 0.81 at the low end to 0.99 at the high end, with sensitivity of 73 to 94 percent and specificity spanning 56 to 99 percent across studies. Risk prediction models were more variable, ranging roughly from 0.71 at the bottom to 0.95 at the top for discrimination. New uses covered flagging cardiogenic shock and the need for revascularization. The authors call for future multi-site checks before routine rollout.
pmc-13447275:
Jaiteg Singh and fellow editors introduce a 2026 collection on machine learning for cognitive ageing and behaviour change. Ageing affects memory, attention and self-control unevenly across people, and dementia now burdens families and health systems worldwide. Standard tests and clinic visits often miss that variety, while learning algorithms can sift imaging, body signals and digital records at scale.

Contributions gathered here span early warning signs of mild impairment, personalised support and risk prediction in older groups. One line of work uses skin features around the eye as a non-invasive marker of biological ageing, analysed with learning models. Other papers tackle behaviour patterns and health outcomes from mixed data sources. The editors stress that models must stay interpretable, fair and valid beyond their training data to earn clinical trust.
pmc-13447575:
Rui-Feng Zhang and colleagues study antibody-making plasma cells inside bowel cancer in 2026 work on immunotherapy response. Checkpoint drugs free the immune system to attack cancer, yet many bowel cancer patients never respond. Most research focuses on T cells, while B-lineage plasma cells inside tumours have gained attention as possible helpers or blockers depending on their state.

One plasma cell group, marked by a specific antibody type, gathered in tumours of patients who responded to checkpoint treatment. Those cells ran programmes for showing tumour material to other immune cells and for a central inflammatory switch. Activity of that switch in B cells boosted T cell killing power and restrained tumour growth in the authors' tests. The subset is offered as both a response marker and a lever for improving therapy.
pmc-13448275:
Gecici and colleagues at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center studied which clinical and genetic features predict survival after surgery for cancer spread to the brain. Their 2026 conference report covers 228 patients whose tumors were removed, most often cancers that began in the lung, breast, urinary tract, gut, or skin. Survival after such surgery varies widely, and genetic predictors remain poorly understood.

Gecici profiled tumor genes in about three fifths of the patients and ranked predictors using forest models and survival analysis. TP53 gene changes were most common, followed by KRAS changes and losses near CDKN2A and CDKN2B. Patients in good physical condition before surgery lived far longer than frail patients, with median survival more than three times as long. Extra KRAS copies and poor condition predicted worse survival, while systemic drug treatment after surgery strongly predicted longer life, supporting combined genetic and clinical risk scoring.
pmc-13448475:
Zhang and colleagues built in 2026 a nano-delivery system to rescue immune therapy for tumors choked by lactate, the acid waste that builds up in cancer tissue and suppresses immunity. Response rates to PD-L1 blocking drugs sit low, at one to three in ten patients. Their micelles, carrier spheres made with hyaluronic acid, haul a lactate-eating enzyme plus copper-doped carbon dots into tumors displaying the CD44 docking protein.

Zhang shows the cargo releases in the acidic tumor setting. The enzyme clears lactate and produces peroxide that feeds copper-driven reactions, triggering cuproptosis, a copper-linked form of cell death. In dishes, the system matured dendritic cells and flipped suppressive macrophages toward an attacking type. In mice, adding the carriers to laser treatment and the immune drug shrank treated and distant tumors while staying safe. The authors link lactate level to copper-death sensitivity as a treatment lever.
pmc-13448675:
Daniele Canarutto and colleagues studied in 2026 how children respond to busulfan, a drug used to prepare the marrow for stem cell gene therapy. Dosing must hit a narrow target: too little risks failure, while too much brings acute harm. The group reviewed 54 young patients whose drug levels were closely tracked.

Dose changes matched exposure changes in a straight line only up to about 1.16-fold increases, and a curved model fit larger escalations better. High peak exposure in a single dose, rather than the total, tracked with longer mouth sores and more days of tube feeding. Starting at 80 milligrams per square meter gave lower peaks and fewer corrections than 120, with no loss in graft success.
pmc-13448775:
Zhang and colleagues test a new body-shape measure in people with type 2 diabetes in this 2026 cohort study from Fuzhou, China. Body mass index misses where fat sits, so the team studied the waist-to-BMI ratio, which rises when the waist is large relative to overall mass. They examined 4,157 adults cross-sectionally and followed 440 of them for a median of about 34 months, tracking bone loss, muscle loss, and fractures.

A higher ratio was independently tied to every outcome. These were thinner bones, less muscle, and the combination of both. Sarcopenic obesity and fractures followed the same pattern. Links for muscle loss were notably strong in both sexes. Follow-up data showed the ratio also predicted who would newly develop these conditions. A blood antibody scan in 30 selected patients found differing immune reactivity tied to muscle structure, hinting at underlying biology.
pmc-13448875:
Viveca Ritsinger and colleagues describe in 2026 what actually happens to Swedish patients who resemble the volunteers of the SELECT trial, which tested semaglutide for heart protection in obesity without diabetes. From registries covering about 40 percent of Sweden's population between 2013 and 2023, they identified 9,652 adults with obesity and established cardiovascular disease but no diabetes. Their average age was 68.4 years and average body mass index 33.1.

Across a mean follow-up of 5.4 years, 21.7 percent suffered a major cardiovascular event. That rate exceeded the matched general population's risk by more than twofold. Applying the treatment effect seen in SELECT suggested 35 such patients would need semaglutide treatment to prevent one major event. The authors note this real-world group was older, included more women, and had more prior strokes than the trial's volunteers.
pmc-13449075:
David Vadsholt and colleagues run in 2026 a nationwide Danish case-control study on whether steroid medicines raise the odds of type 2 diabetes in a dose-dependent way. Registry data from 2013 to 2021 supplied 149,113 people newly diagnosed with diabetes and 447,339 matched controls. Exposure meant prescriptions in the years before diagnosis, split into systemic pills and skin preparations, and converted to daily prednisolone-equivalent doses.

Odds climbed steadily with dose for oral steroids: an adjusted odds ratio of 1.25 for doses below 2.5 milligrams a day, 1.49 in the middle band, and 3.02 once doses reached 7.5 milligrams or more. Skin steroids showed the same staircase pattern, from 1.21 at the low end up to 1.51 at the highest doses tested. Nasal, rectal, eye, and ear preparations showed no progressive link after adjustment. The authors advise prescribers to count cumulative steroid exposure, even from creams, when weighing diabetes risk.
pmc-13449375:
Versino and colleagues assembled a multicenter European study in 2026 of acquired pure red cell aplasia, a rare marrow failure in which red cell precursors vanish while other blood lines persist. The acquired form may be unexplained or tied to infections, autoimmune disease, tumors, or a related marrow disorder, and no dedicated trials guide care. The team pooled cases to describe how the disease presents, what it travels with, and how treatments fare.

Diagnosis varied widely across patients, and gene data helped unmask hard cases, including forms linked to myelodysplastic syndrome, a pre-leukemic marrow condition. Starting cyclosporine A, a T-cell calming drug, early improved outcomes, and mTOR blockers, another immune-modulating class, proved valuable as second-line treatment. Deaths from infection remained a real cost of the immune suppression involved. The authors call for sharper diagnostic use of molecular data and prompt first-line treatment in this rare condition.
pmc-13450575:
Taha Rasul and co-authors report a 2026 case where a drug aimed at immune signaling eased a hard mix of two hardening skin diseases. The overlap of morphea and lichen sclerosus outside the genital area is rare and can spread widely. Their patient, a woman aged 67, had sore, tight plaques across her trunk, sides, and upper thighs.

Biopsies confirmed the overlap, which covered over a quarter of her skin and limited her movement. Creams, light therapy, and several whole-body drugs had failed or were not tolerated. The new drug, upadacitinib, blocks a Janus kinase path, and her skin improved markedly once she started it, a result the team offers as a lead for others stuck without options.
pmc-13451875:
Fahimi and colleagues gathered in 2026 a vast set of measures of the carbon-to-ATP ratio in living cells. ATP is the main energy currency of cells, and the ratio helps estimate living biomass in oceans and soils.  The team compiled about 400 measures from more than 80 studies across bacteria, single-celled eukaryotes, animals, plants, and tissues.

The true ratio varied by five orders of magnitude, from tiny values to values a hundred thousand times larger. Their model traced the spread to how fast cells make ATP, how fast they use it, and how much cell carbon is active. The old value of 250 still sat near the median for bacteria and single-celled marine eukaryotes.  The authors urge field studies to treat the ratio as a trait that shifts with context, not a fixed constant.
pmc-13452375:
Qingshan Wu and co-authors release in 2026 the genome and trait data for a fresh phage that infects a crop-wilting germ. The host germ, Ralstonia, wilts many food plants, and phages are a green line of defense. The phage was fished from soil near Guiyang, China, and grown on a lab strain of the germ in plate tests.

Its genome runs a little over 42,000 letters, rich in two of the four letter kinds, with 53 gene calls, of which 18 got job guesses. Modules cover packing, shell build, host bursting, and copying. Tree reads set it closest to a known Ralstonia phage, with about four fifths of its letters matching. The set backs phage work against wilt.
pmc-13452975:
Stephanie Wemm, Rachel Hart, Gretchen Hermes, Zachary Harvanek, and Rajita Sinha ask whether the drug prazosin cuts drinking by first cutting craving. Their 2026 study sits inside a 12 week trial of prazosin against placebo for alcohol use disorder, with 52 people on the drug and 45 on placebo. Daily phone surveys tracked each person's craving and drinking, adding up to 4,289 daily reports.

Prazosin lowered daily craving, while placebo did not show the same drop. On days after craving fell, those on prazosin drank less the next day, a link that did not hold for the placebo group. The craving path explained about two thirds of the drug group's drop in drinking, against about a quarter for placebo. The authors read the result as proof that craving relief is the engine of the drug's effect.
pmc-13453475:
Contreras, Priesemann, and many co-authors published a 2026 paper on the shared rules behind pandemics. Each outbreak differs, since germs and societies keep changing together. Yet some basic patterns of spread and control hold across outbreaks. The team drew members from health, math, physics, and social science fields.

The paper sets out ten core mechanisms that shape how pandemics unfold. These cover spread routes, human behavior, and how societies react under stress. The authors say these rules can guide choices before hard data arrive. Early action built on sound patterns beats waiting for perfect numbers. The work aims to help officials prepare for the next crisis with clearer thinking. The list is meant as shared ground for both science advice and policy planning work.
pmc-13453575:
Xinping Yang and ten co-authors warn that cleaner vehicle rules cut total exhaust gases while raising the share of the most toxic kinds. The gases, volatile organic compounds, feed city ozone and haze and can harm health directly. Their 2026 study sorts these gases species by species across standard and hybrid cars under tightening rules.

Tougher rules cut total gases from standard cars by 75 percent. Yet the share of reactive oxygenated gases climbed from 20 to 35 percent of the mix. One modern hybrid let out nearly twice that toxic group per kilometre as its standard twin, blamed on frequent engine restarts that chill the exhaust cleaner. Its health risk scores ran far higher despite better fuel economy. The authors urge rules that cap the worst species, not just total mass.
pmc-13454375:
Olsen and colleagues investigate a possible new seasonal allergen in northern Norway in this 2026 prospective study. Birch rust is a fungus that infects birch trees and releases huge numbers of spores each autumn, when few other airborne allergens circulate there. The team followed 160 allergy patients and 94 controls through the spore season from August to October and again out of season, tracking symptoms, nasal airflow, and lung function.

During spore season, patients reported significantly worse symptoms than controls. They also showed measurably reduced nasal airflow. The difference was about twelve liters per minute on the peak flow test. Symptoms rose across the season, and worsening was tied to living near birch forests. Ralph Shirley lined up a gallery of occultists and mystics from many periods, sketching lives, claims, and followings. Astrologers, alchemists, and seers pass in review. Shirley writes as a curious observer of the borderlands of belief rather than as a disciple of any one figure.

Each sketch treats its subject as a window on what an age believed possible: hidden forces, secret knowledge, second sight. Some figures are famous, others nearly forgotten, and the tone stays entertaining rather than credulous. Readers get a compact tour of occult reputations across history, useful as a starting map before deeper studies of any single tradition.
tob-13329-15475:
Books four to seven, in volume two of Ganguli's Mahabharata, carry the Pandavas from hiding back to open war. A year in disguise at a foreign court ends in revelation and alliance. Krishna's peace mission to the Kauravas fails against pride and envy.

Then Kurukshetra's eighteen days begin in earnest. The Bhagavad Gita stands at the center, Krishna's teaching to a warrior who cannot bear to fight his kin. Armies clash, vows are kept at terrible price, and heroes fall daily. Ganguli's prose rises to the scale of the fighting. The epic's blazing middle is all here.
tob-14475:
C. W. Leadbeater mapped the astral plane in his 1895 Theosophical manual, describing the realm of emotion and desire said to lie just beyond the physical world. Scenery, inhabitants, and phenomena receive systematic treatment. The traveler in sleep, the recently dead, and various non-human beings all have assigned places in his geography.

Leadbeater wrote as a clairvoyant investigator reporting a country, complete with its dangers and its uses for students. Concise and orderly, the manual became the Theosophical movement's standard guidebook to the unseen, shaping how occultists pictured the afterlife and dreams for decades. Readers can judge his calm, cataloging tone against the strangeness of the territory claimed.
tob-4075:
Michal Sedziwój, the Polish alchemist known as Michael Sendivogius, published A New Light of Alchymie in 1604, drawn, by its title, from the fountain of nature and manual experience. His treatise gives nature its own confession: all metals grow in the earth from a central life force, and the adept can learn its ways by study and experiment.

Sendivogius writes alchemy at its most philosophical, arguing about air, seed, and the hidden food of life in terms later chemists would echo in new vocabularies. Isaac Newton annotated Sendivogius closely, one sign of his reach. Among alchemical texts, few influenced the coming chemistry as directly as this Polish courtier's dialogues.
tob-4146-15475:
Exile ends in volume two of Ganguli's Mahabharata, which covers books four through seven of the Sanskrit epic. The Pandavas come out of hiding, demand their share of the kingdom, and send Krishna as a peace envoy to the Kaurava court. The mission fails, and both sides gather huge armies.

Then the eighteen-day war of Kurukshetra begins. At its heart stands the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's counsel to the warrior Arjuna, who shrinks from killing kin. Battle follows counsel: duels, slaughters, and falls of famous heroes crowd the pages. Ganguli keeps the vast cast and carnage clear, and the tragedy lands with full weight.
tob-9052-15475:
Volume two of Ganguli's Mahabharata brings the Pandavas out of exile to claim their rights. Krishna himself carries their peace terms to the Kaurava court, speaks with courtesy, and is refused with contempt. Both sides then muster armies drawn from half the kings of India.

On the field of Kurukshetra the slaughter begins. The Bhagavad Gita sounds at the battle's heart, as Krishna steadies Arjuna for the fight. Days of duels and massed charges follow, with famous warriors falling in turn. Ganguli's Victorian prose keeps the huge action clear. The peace has failed; the epic's terrible center has begun.
treaty-of-orleans-1275:
The Treaty of Orléans of 1275 joins England and France in this record. The pact belongs to the reign of Edward I of England. Medieval kings settle their cross-Channel claims in formal, sworn terms.

Homage is rendered, disputes are compromised, and peace is sworn. Two great crowns of Christendom compose their quarrel for a season. The forms are solemn: seals, oaths, and kinship ties bind the deal. Thirteenth-century statecraft shows its formal face in the treaty's clauses. Short truces like this one paved the road to longer wars between the crowns. The record's sparse detail leaves the pact's exact terms to the clauses themselves.
un-ga-res-52-175:
Guatemala's peace moved into its next phase under Resolution 52/175, passed by the General Assembly in 1998. The UN Verification Mission in Guatemala had its mandate stretched to 31 March 1998 by a vote of March 1997. A July 1997 text had urged all sides to push ahead with the second phase of the peace plan, which ran to the end of that year.

The text weighs the mission's seventh report on human rights. It also weighs a report on the strides made by Central American lands in peace, freedom, and growth. The Secretary-General's counsel on the mission's work is before the Assembly: how to shape it so it can meet the needs of the peace check in full.
un-ga-res-a-69-75: Young diplomats learn the trade of disarmament through a UN training plan backed in Resolution A/69/75, from the Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The programme of fellowships on disarmament dates to the first special session on the subject. The text notes that the plan still builds grasp of why disarmament counts, and of the worries states bring to the table. A large corps of trained officials, from many lands, has passed through it.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly resolution 52/175 was adopted on 18 December 1997. It keeps the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala, known as MINUGUA, working through the third full year after the country's peace accords were signed. The short resolution reviews how the long civil war settlement is holding up, including reports by the Secretary-General and Guatemala's own peace commission.

The Assembly renews the mission for 1 April to 31 December 1998. It asks the Secretary-General to keep reporting. It asks him to recommend how the mission should continue after that. It thanks Guatemala's government, its former insurgent movement, and donor countries for backing the process. The renewal mattered because a standing United Nations presence was the main outside guarantee that the 1996 peace accords would actually be carried out.

Adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, resolution 69/75 of the General Assembly reviews the United Nations disarmament fellowship, training and advisory services, then in their thirty-sixth year. It thanks China, Germany, Japan, Kazakhstan and Switzerland for hosting study visits in 2013 and 2014. It asks the Secretary-General to keep running the programme each year within existing resources. The programme trains officials from member states in arms control and disarmament.
un-sc-res-1375: The official series of Council decisions runs through Resolution 1375, catalogued here for 2001. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1475:
A detailed Cyprus settlement plan failed at The Hague in March 2003. The Secretary-General and his adviser had worked on it since 1999. On 14 April 2003 the Security Council praised that extraordinary effort. The plan of 26 February 2003 was balanced with care, the Council said. It gave the text its full support as a rare chance for a deal. The plan aimed to bridge decades of division on the island.

The Council regretted how the talks had ended. It blamed the negative approach of the Turkish Cypriot leader. His stance at The Hague blocked a vote on the plan. Both communities were meant to decide in referenda. A year later a revised plan did reach a vote, and the sides split.
un-sc-res-1575: Under its sequence number 1575, a formal Security Council decision is preserved in official-record form. English Wikisource supplied the transcription held here. The text's two-part shape does the work: recitals justify, operative clauses command or request. For anyone tracing what the Council required at a given moment, that primary wording is the evidence.
un-sc-res-1675:
Western Sahara's mission was renewed in the spring of 2006. On 28 April 2006 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 31 October 2006. The Secretary-General had reported on the territory days earlier. The Council restated its promise to help the parties find a settlement. That settlement must be just, lasting, and accepted by both sides. It must also let the territory's people choose their future.

The military agreements behind the ceasefire had to be respected in full. Member states were asked to fund family visits for divided Sahrawi families. Such visits were the main trust-building step on offer. The Secretary-General owed a report before the term ended. His zero-tolerance rules on abuse also applied to the mission.
un-sc-res-1775: Resolution 1775, adopted in 2007, is preserved in this collection as a Security Council decision in record form. Its record notes a December 31 adoption, the Council working to the year's last day. The text itself follows the standard pattern, and the entry keeps it whole through the Wikisource transcription of the official record.
un-sc-res-1875:
UNDOF's mandate ran through another renewal in June 2009. On 23 June 2009 the Security Council extended the Golan force until 31 December 2009. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission that month. The conduct clause took its now-standard place in the text. UNDOF had to enforce the zero-tolerance policy on abuse. Its personnel had to meet the United Nations code of conduct.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 at once. A report was due at the end of the term. It would cover events in the area and steps toward 338. The force's observers kept their posts along the separation line. The renewal passed without debate, as most UNDOF texts do.
un-sc-res-275:
Portuguese attacks on Guinea's villages drew the Council's anger in 1969. Guinea had sent three letters detailing the raids. Forces based in Portuguese Guinea-Bissau had caused heavy damage. On 22 December 1969 the Council deplored the loss of life and the harm done. It said such incidents endanger world peace. No state, it added, may act against the Charter's principles.

Portugal had to stop violating Guinea's sovereignty and borders at once. Its authorities had to free a captured Guinean civilian plane and its pilots. They also had to release a seized motor barge, the Patrice Lumumba, with its passengers. Both seizures dated from 1968 and 1969. Six members abstained, but the text passed.
un-sc-res-675:
Central America's observer group won six more months in November 1990. On 5 November 1990 the Security Council extended ONUCA until 7 May 1991. The Secretary-General's October report received approval. The group watched the region's peace agreements from its 1989 mandate. Nicaragua's civil war had ended in elections that year. Demobilization of fighters was the mission's core task.

The Council noted the need to watch spending with care. Demands on peacekeeping funds were growing fast in 1990. The extension kept observers in place across five countries. Their reports helped confirm that the peace accords held. ONUCA was among the first missions of the post-Cold War wave.
un-sc-res-75: Who pays for the helpers of UN field teams? Security Council Resolution 75, passed on 27 September 1949, takes up that small but real cost. A 1948 Assembly vote had left it to the Council to rule if a team member needs a deputy at his side. Where that need is found, the UN may pay back the travel and daily costs of such deputies, for time past as well. The text lists the teams whose members had each needed such help, from the Good Offices team in Indonesia on.
un-sc-res-975:
Haiti's security handover from the multinational force to the United Nations was set in motion on 30 January 1995. The United States-led force had declared a secure and stable environment in place. The former military leaders had left, and the elected president had returned. Haiti's own letter of 27 January supported the transfer.

The Council found the conditions of resolution 940 (1994) for ending the multinational force were met. It authorized the Secretary-General to prepare for the United Nations Mission in Haiti, UNMIH, to take over the force's functions. He would work with the force commander on the steps needed. States that had served in the multinational force won the Council's thanks, as did the Organization of American States and its civilian mission. UNMIH's mandate was extended to 31 July 1995, at up to 6,000 troops and 900 civilian police.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Burundi's peace process, and a transitional government taking shape, win the Council's backing on 29 October 2001. The Arusha Peace and Reconciliation Agreement of August 2000 remained, in the Council's view, the best basis for ending the conflict. A summit in Pretoria had just agreed the new government's framework and membership.

Armed groups, the FDD and the FNL, were called on to stop attacks on civilians, end the fighting, and join the talks. The Council strongly backed an interim multinational security presence, requested by Burundi's government and led by South Africa, to protect returning exiles and train an all-Burundian protection force. Donors were urged to fund relief, the return of refugees, and rebuilding.

A grand plan to heal Cyprus died at The Hague in March 2003. The UN chief had built the plan since 1999. He had honed it twice, in December 2002 and in February 2003. Votes in both halves of the isle were to seal it. The Turkish Cypriot chief balked at the last meet, on 10 and 11 March. Resolution 1475 passed with no dissent on 14 April 2003.

The Council voiced its deep regret. A chance to vote on a shared land had been lost. Greek and Turkish Cypriots alike had been denied their say. Faith in the chief's plan stayed firm. It was named the sole base for fresh talks. His good offices stood open. All sides were urged back to the table to forge a full deal on its lines.

Bosnia and Herzegovina's peacekeeping changes hands in this text of 22 November 2004. The NATO-led SFOR was ending its mission, and a European Union force was set to succeed it in December. Full support is restated for the High Representative and for carrying out the 1995 peace agreement.

Acting under Chapter VII, states working through the European Union are authorized to run the stabilization force for a further planned period. Those states may take all necessary measures to carry out the peace agreement's military terms and to defend the force. The parties are told to respect the force's safety and freedom of movement, and reporting to the Council will continue.

Spring 2006 found Western Sahara's file in its long groove. The truce held. The vote on the land's fate did not move. The chief's report of 19 April set out the stall. A long clause on staff codes fills much of the text. Resolution 1675 passed on 28 April 2006.

MINURSO, the UN team, won six months more, to 31 October 2006. The truce pacts had to be kept in full. States were asked to fund goodwill steps. The chief ask was trips for kin split by the long fight. Fresh word on the land was due near the term's end. The staff code clause had teeth in this text. Plans to bar, spot, and meet abuse were spelled out. Troop states had to drill their men on the rules before they shipped out.

Trinidad and Tobago entered the United Nations through Resolution 175, adopted unanimously on 12 September 1962. The Council had examined the application of the twin-island Caribbean state, which had become independent from Britain at the end of August that year. Its application was among the first acts of the new government.

The resolution simply recommends that the General Assembly admit Trinidad and Tobago to membership. The brevity is normal for admission cases, where the real decision happened in consultations before the vote. Still, the text marks a clear milestone: a small oil-producing island nation in the southern Caribbean taking its place in the General Assembly for the first time.

A prosecutor's appointment is extended for a final period on 14 September 2007. Carla Del Ponte's term as Prosecutor of the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal was expiring that day, and the Secretary-General had asked for the extension to ensure a smooth handover to her successor. The Council set aside the usual term rule in the tribunal's Statute and extended her appointment from 15 September to 31 December 2007.

The Golan watch came up for its mid-2009 turn. The chief's report of 8 June found the line calm. UNDOF had held its posts since 1974. Its term was days from its end. Resolution 1875 passed on 23 June 2009.

The force gained six months, to 31 December 2009. The Council called on both sides to act on the 1973 text at once. A full clause goes to staff rules. The force must keep faith with the UN's zero-tolerance line. Troop states must drill, probe, and punish as the code asks. A report on events and on steps toward the old text was due at the close. These late renewals read like twins, yet each kept a real force in place through a tense age.

Guinea's complaint against Portugal sits at the heart of Resolution 275, adopted on 22 December 1969 by nine votes to none with six abstentions. Portuguese forces based in the neighboring territory of Guinea-Bissau had shelled Guinean villages, causing deaths and heavy damage. The Council said attacks of this kind put international peace at risk.

Beyond deploring the shelling, the Council ordered Portugal to stop violating Guinea's sovereignty at once. It also demanded the return of a captured Guinean civilian plane, held since March 1968, and of a seized motor barge named Patrice Lumumba, together with everyone taken aboard both. Portugal was warned that repeat attacks would force the Council to weigh stronger steps.

Papua New Guinea is the subject of Resolution 375. The Council passed it by a full vote on 22 September 1975. The Pacific land had won its freedom from Australia six days before, on 16 September. It joined the north and south halves of one big island under a single state.

The Council asks the General Assembly to admit Papua New Guinea as a member. The Assembly then did so. The short text marks the start of a singular state. Its people speak more tongues than any other land on earth. Building one nation from so many groups was a hard task from day one.

Central America's wars were winding down in 1990. A small UN team, known as ONUCA, watched the peace deals hold. Its task was set by a 1989 text. The Secretary-General sent a fresh report on 26 October 1990. Resolution 675 passed on 5 November 1990.

The members backed the report in full. They stretched the team's mandate by six months, to 7 May 1991. They also sent a note of caution. Peacekeeping costs were rising fast across the world. Spending on this mission had to be watched with care. The Secretary-General owed the Council full news of events. A last report was due before the new term ran out.

A small question of costs for the Council's own fact-finding missions was settled on 27 September 1949. Under a General Assembly decision of 1948, the Council could judge whether a member state's representative on such a commission needed an alternate. If the need existed, the Secretary-General could repay travel and living costs. Resolution 75 applies that rule to two real cases.

The Council noted that on two of its commissions, the representatives had each needed an alternate. One was the Committee of Good Offices, by then renamed the United Nations Commission for Indonesia. The other was the United Nations Commission for India and Pakistan. That finding cleared the way for the costs in both cases to be repaid. The text is a minor piece of early United Nations housekeeping, but it shows how even the new body's fact-finding work depended on small rulings about money and staffing.

Haiti's security passes from a US-led coalition to the United Nations in Resolution 975, adopted on 30 January 1995 by fourteen votes to none with China abstaining. The multinational force sent in during 1994 had restored the elected president and reported that a secure and stable environment now existed. Its commander recommended a smooth handover to the UN mission, UNMIH, which the Council had created on paper in 1993.

The Council set the transfer in motion, deciding that UNMIH would deploy with up to six thousand troops and take over from the coalition by the end of March 1995. Haiti's file, crowded with sanctions and authorizations since 1993, now became a peacekeeping operation.
zola-abbe-mouret-1875:
Vizetelly's opening essay places Abbe Mouret's Transgression with care in the saga. Issued fourth, it stands ninth in Zola's final plan for the set. It grows out of The Conquest of Plassans and its wrecked Mouret home.

Serge Mouret, seen as a child there, now serves as priest of Les Artaud. That near-pagan hamlet sits in bare, burning country in Provence. Illness strands him in the wild walled garden of Le Paradou. There he loves the free Albine, and nature wars with the Church in him. Lush and sad, the tale holds one of the finest love stories in the cycle.
